**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

The gathered evidence consistently points to adjacent lines of research that can inform expectations for Khanmigo in K-12 science when direct studies are limited: intelligent tutoring systems, generative AI science supports, adaptive learning platforms, automated feedback, and science digital supports in school settings.

### AI in K-12 science education: broad reviews and scope of the literature

Kavitha and Joshith (2024) conducted a **systematic literature review** and bibliometric mapping of “Pedagogical incorporation of artificial intelligence in K-12 science education: A decadal bibliometric mapping and systematic literature review (2013-2023).” The snippet states that AI-driven platforms can create dynamic, real-time models of chemical reactions or physical processes, enabling students to visualize and experiment with challenging or impractical scenarios to replicate in a conventional classroom environment. It also states that AI can significantly improve science classrooms' assessment and feedback processes, and that **intelligent tutoring systems [ITS] can provide immediate, personalized feedback to students, enhancing their learning outcomes while maintaining student motivation and interest in the subject** [1]. The same source says that AI systems can identify individual learning patterns and needs by analyzing vast amounts of student data, enabling educators to tailor their instructional strategies accordingly, and that this ensures that each student receives the appropriate level of challenge and support, fostering a more inclusive and effective learning environment [1].  

The same review also included a search string showing relevant AI application terms: `"artificial intelligence" OR "machine learning" OR "deep learning" OR "fuzzy logic" OR "neural network" OR "intelligent tutor*" OR "intelligent tutoring system" OR "smart tutor*" OR "adaptive learning" OR "natural language processing" OR "prediction system" OR "computer vision" OR "learning analytics" OR "expert system" OR "robot" OR "data mining" OR "automated feedback" OR "automated grading" OR "automated assessment*" OR "automated scoring"` combined with science teaching and learning terms and K-12 education terms [1].  

The conclusion snippet from the same paper states that the reviewed literature shows a diverse utilization of AI technologies in K-12 science education, with the key AI technologies identified including **robotics, chatbots, machine learning, automated scoring and feedback, and neural networks with fuzzy logic** [1]. It states that these technologies are applied in various K-12 science educational contexts to enhance learning outcomes, support student engagement, and personalize learning experiences [1]. It further states that the incorporation of AI in K-12 science classrooms has significantly positively impacted students' learning performance and skills across the reviewed studies [1]. It also reports that the majority of studies focused on high school settings (**n=10, 50%**), followed by middle school (**n=8, 40%**) and elementary school (**n=2, 10%**) [1]. Among methodological approaches, **design and developmental research** emerged as the most prevalent, with **eight studies** adopting this methodology [1]. In the experimental/quasi-experimental category, **4 out of 5 studies utilized a quasi-experimental design** [1]. The review also notes that the scope was confined to studies indexed in the Scopus database, English-language publications, and full-text studies, and that the literature collected was available only until 2023 [1]. It says that future research should expand to other databases and non-English studies, and that longitudinal, qualitative, and mixed-method research are important [1].

Heeg and Avraamidou (2023) conducted a **systematic literature review** on “The use of Artificial intelligence in school science: a systematic literature review.” The abstract states that a review of the literature showcased that while there exist various review studies on the use of AI in education, missing remains a review focusing on science education, so they carried out a systematic literature review between 2010 and 2021 driven by three questions: what types of AI applications are used in school science; for what teaching content are AI applications used; and what is the impact of AI applications on teaching and learning of school science [2]. The abstract states that the studies reviewed (**n=22**) included nine different types of AI applications: **automated assessment, automated feedback, learning analytics, adaptive learning systems, intelligent tutoring systems, multilabel text classification, chatbot, expert systems, and mind wandering detection** [2]. It says that the majority of the AI applications are used in geoscience or physics and are used to support either **knowledge construction or skills development** [2]. It further states that the impact of AI applications was found across **learning achievement, argumentation skills, learning experience, and teaching** [2]. It also states that missing remains an examination of learners’ and teachers’ experiences with AI in school science, interdisciplinary approaches to AI implementation, and issues related to ethics and biases [2].  

The discussion snippet from the same review states that the literature on AI applications in school science follows similar trends as the review studies on AI application in education in general [2]. It says the three most dominant themes identified were **automated assessment and feedback, personalized learning, and predictive modeling** [2]. It states that AI applications can help lighten the heavy workload of science educators by taking out time-consuming tasks such as assessment and feedback, can enhance students’ general low interest in science by providing engaging and entertaining intelligent tutors or non-traditional personalized learning environments, and can help optimize teaching processes to improve low learning achievements in science subjects [2]. It further says that AI applications have been used either for more practical reasons or for supporting students’ interest and conceptual understanding, and that missing remains engagement with goals related to how students interact with AI applications, inclusivity, and socio-emotional learning [2]. The same review also concludes that AI applications in school science are being integrated into the existing science curriculum without any change in the learning objectives, and that AI applications are being used to automate or optimize already existing educational practices [2]. It emphasizes that researchers, policy-makers, and educators should aim for a new human-machine alliance, where teachers’ abilities to recognize emotions, communicate, and offer mental support to students are combined with AI features focusing on analyzing student behavior, assessing, evaluating, etc. [2].

Xu and Ouyang (2022) conducted **a systematic review** on “The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021.” The snippet states that there is a lack of literature review to investigate the application of AI in general STEM education context, and that among 18 literature review articles of AIEd published from 2011 to 2021, only two works explored the application of AI in STEM education [3]. It states that the role of AI in mathematics education was classified into three main types, including **intelligent tutoring systems, profiling and prediction, and adaptive systems and personalization** [3]. It also states that AI techniques were mainly applied to support feedback-based programming tutoring during the student’s individual learning [3].  

The abstract of the same paper states that the review focused on the application of AI in STEM education and identified that AI has been applied in a range of educational levels and contexts, and that intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive systems and personalization are among the key categories [3]. The OpenAlex record for the same study notes it as a **systematic review** and says the abstract background is that AI-STEM is an emerging field confronted with integrating diverse AI techniques and complex educational elements to meet instructional and learning needs [4].

### AI tools, chatbots, generative AI, and classroom support

Kwid, Sarty, and Yang (2024) published **a review** titled “A Review of AI Tools: Definitions, Functions, and Applications for K-12 Education.” The abstract states that AI revolutionizes education by supporting personalized learning, critical thinking, and problem solving through tools like intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive platforms [5]. It says the purpose of the study is to provide an overview of AI tools and platforms for K-12 education, with the hope of serving as a practical reference for teachers to use these tools [5]. It further states that the review discusses definitions and types of AI for education, identifies and reviews currently available and popular AI tools and their applications in K-12 education, offers quick references for teachers on how they can harness various AI tools for different teaching and learning purposes, addresses ethical concerns such as data privacy and algorithmic biases, and classifies AI tools on the basis of instructional, administrative, and analytical usage to address diverse needs, enhance teaching and learning, provide personalized instruction, and predict student outcomes [5].

Smith-Mutegi et al. (2025) in “Perceptions of STEM education and artificial intelligence: a Twitter (X) sentiment analysis” state that AI is utilized in STEM education in diverse ways, engaging students and educators in teaching and learning [6]. The snippet states that, as a follow-up to prior work, Xu and Ouyang (2022) identified six categories of AI applications in STEM education: **learning prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, student behavior detection, automation, educational robots, and miscellaneous others** [6]. It says AI technologies can enhance student engagement, improve learning outcomes, and provide valuable insights for educators in STEM education [6]. It also states that AI-driven learning analytics enable data-driven decision-making in curriculum design and assessment practices [6]. The same source says that generative AI’s ability to have open conversations with students about STEM-related topics makes it an attractive tool to use as an “object to think with,” and that students may use chatbots such as ChatGPT or Google Gemini to enhance their understanding of a concept through an interactive inquiry approach, as if speaking to a disciplinary expert [6]. It says this engagement has the potential to enhance metacognitive skills, critical thinking, and problem-solving abilities that foster deeper comprehension of material in STEM while serving as an intelligent tutor [6]. It also states that these applications could serve as functional tools for science teachers that may assist with lesson planning, rubric development, and creating assessments [6].  

The same article also states that AI technologies such as intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, and generative AI tools encourage students to engage in active learning, problem-solving, and critical thinking [7]. It includes Ouyang and Jiao’s three paradigms of AIEd applications: AI-directed, AI-supported, and AI-empowered [7]. It explains that the first paradigm uses systems like intelligent tutoring systems whereby AI serves as the guide for learning processes, while the second paradigm reflects learners as collaborators with AI and guided by cognitive and social constructivism frameworks [7].

Ng, Tan, and Leung (2024) published **a comparative study** in “Empowering student self-regulated learning and science education through ChatGPT: A pioneering pilot study.” The abstract states that this paper discusses a comparative study between generative AI-based (**SRLbot**) and rule-based AI chatbots (**Nemobot**) in a **3-week science learning experience with 74 Secondary 4 students in Hong Kong** [8]. It reports that the experimental group used SRLbot to maintain a regular study habit and facilitate self-regulated learning, while the control group utilized rule-based AI chatbots [8]. The results showed that **SRLbot effectively enhanced students’ science knowledge, behavioural engagement and motivation** [8]. It also says quantile regression analysis indicated that the number of interactions significantly predicted variations in SRL [8]. The abstract states that students appreciated the personalized recommendations and flexibility of SRLbot, that the ChatGPT-enhanced instructional design reduced learning anxiety and promoted learning performance, motivation and sustained learning habits, and that the findings offer valuable evidence for AI developers and educators to consider generative AI settings and chatbot design [8].

Jamaluddin et al. (2025) in “ChatGPT as a Pedagogical Tool: Measuring Its Influence on Cognitive Engagement and Academic Achievement of Biology Students” used **a cross-sectional quantitative survey method with Structural Equation Modeling analysis** [9]. The abstract states that ChatGPT as a pedagogical tool significantly increased students’ cognitive engagement, which then could also mediate its effect on students’ academic achievement [9]. It says the presence of ChatGPT answers the existing problems by offering personalized explanations, interactive feedback, and structured answer recommendations to improve students’ understanding and critical thinking [9]. It also notes drawbacks such as over-reliance on technology by students, potential errors in assessment, and inequity related to access to computer devices [9].  

Lee et al. (2024) published **a paper** titled “Combining Natural Language Processing with Epistemic Network Analysis to Investigate Student Knowledge Integration within an AI Dialog.” The snippet states that natural language processing uses machine learning to enable computers to understand text and speech [10]. It says one important application of NLP in science education is the automated assessment of student explanations [10]. It states that prior research demonstrated the value of using the KI framework to design an NLP model that generates a holistic score for the overall coherence and accuracy of student responses [10]. It also says that Gerard and Linn (2016) showed how automated guidance based on a KI scoring model of Energy Story, in conjunction with teacher guidance, enhanced classroom inquiry activities [10]. The same source states that prior research has used NLP to develop Intelligent Tutoring Systems like AutoTutor to evaluate students’ work and give them timely feedback, and that multi-label NLP models have been employed in multiple KI activities to design adaptive dialogs that assign researcher-designed personalized guidance to help students make integrated revisions [10].

Xiao et al. (2025) in “Learning to Use AI for Learning: Teaching Responsible Use of AI Chatbot to K-12 Students Through an AI Literacy Module” state that AI is increasingly integrated into daily life and that there is a growing need to equip the next generation with the ability to apply, interact with, evaluate, and collaborate with AI systems responsibly [11]. The abstract states that the authors designed a **Large-Language Model (LLM)-based module to teach prompting literacy** and conducted **two iterations of classroom deployment in 11 authentic secondary education classrooms** [11]. It states that the AI-based auto-grader could grade student-written prompts with satisfactory quality, that the instructional materials supported students in improving their prompting skills through practice and led to positive shifts in perceptions of using AI for learning, and that True/False and open-ended questions could measure prompting literacy more effectively than multiple-choice questions for the target learners [11]. It also states that the outcomes highlight the need for broader studies to assess learning effectiveness and assessment design [11].

Chou et al. (2025) in “Defining AI companions: a research agenda - from artificial companions for learning to general artificial companions for Global Harwell” state that AI has emerged as a transformative force in education, revolutionizing traditional teaching methods and fostering personalized learning experiences [12]. The snippet says that knowledge-based AI can be employed to design intelligent tutoring systems that mimic a teacher’s expertise, such as Cognitive Tutor, AutoTutor, and Betty’s Brain [12]. It states that these systems assess a student’s knowledge, identify gaps, and provide targeted feedback or supplementary materials [12]. It also says that data-driven AI relies on Bayesian networks, machine learning, and deep learning to derive meaningful insights by analyzing vast datasets of student learning or dialogues between students and teachers [12]. It states that learning analytics assists educators in making data-driven decisions to enhance teaching strategies and curriculum design, and that generative AI can develop adaptive quizzes based on a student’s progress [12].

Filiz, Kaya, and Adiguzel (2025) in “Teachers and AI: Understanding the factors influencing AI integration in K-12 education” state that AI in education denotes application of AI technologies such as intelligent tutoring systems, chatbots, robots, and automated assessment tools across various digital platforms to enhance educational performance across subjects [13]. It says ChatGPT simplifies the integration of AI in teaching and learning and can be used for creating exam-style questions, addressing homework assignments, drafting academic essays, and automatically generating educational content [13]. The snippet also states that AI offers diverse opportunities for enhancing teaching and learning, such as language learning, research and writing support, and professional development for teachers [13].  

Seo et al. (2024) in “Augmented teachers: K–12 teachers’ needs for artificial intelligence’s complementary role in personalized learning” state that teachers believe AI assistance is necessary and could be effective [14]. The paper says teachers at all school levels consider foundational learning support and the development of instructional materials as the primary roles that could be aided by AI [14]. It states that teachers expect AI can augment their roles in eight key roles: curriculum design, development of instructional materials, foundational learning support, self-reflection support, student evaluation, career guidance, student management, and administrative task support [14]. The same paper states that teachers desire AI augmentation in foundational learning assistance for struggling students and the creation of high-quality instructional materials [14]. It also states that elementary school teachers underscored student assessment and management, whereas middle and high school teachers emphasized self-reflection support and career guidance [14].

The “A Review of AI Tools: Definitions, Functions, and Applications for K-12 Education” abstract also aligns with this pattern, stating AI tools support personalized learning, critical thinking, and problem solving through intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive platforms, and that AI tools are classified by instructional, administrative, and analytical usage [5].

### Intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning, and feedback evidence

Several sources provide direct evidence on ITSs and adaptive feedback that can inform expectations for Khanmigo-like systems.

The 2022 review by Zafari et al., “Artificial Intelligence Applications in K-12 Education: A Systematic Literature Review,” states that a **systematic literature review** was conducted on articles and conference papers published between 2011 and 2021 in the Web of Science and Scopus databases [15]. It says **2075 documents** were extracted and **210 documents** were identified for further investigation [15]. It reports that AI applications were categorized into Student performance, Teaching, Selection, and Behavior tasks, and Other, and that **Machine Learning (ML) and Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS) were the most common approaches among AI categories** [15]. It also states that high school-related applications were more frequent and STEM courses were substantially targeted by AI [15].  

The same study’s snippet from the review body states that the study identified the potentialities offered by AI in K-12 education and that the current state of the art of integration of AI in K-12 education was provided [15].  

Heeg and Avraamidou (2023) state that the reviewed studies included nine types of AI applications, including **automated assessment, automated feedback, learning analytics, adaptive learning systems, intelligent tutoring systems**, and more [2]. The review says the majority of AI applications are used to support knowledge construction or skills development [2]. It also says AI applications can help lighten the workload of teachers by taking over assessment and feedback tasks and can enhance students’ interest in science by providing intelligent tutors or personalized learning environments [2].  

The same review also explicitly states that the most dominant themes were **automated assessment and feedback, personalized learning, and predictive modeling** [2].  

Colliot et al. (2024) in “What makes tablet-based learning effective? A study of the role of real-time adaptive feedback” report that the study investigated the added value of real-time adaptive feedback on seventh graders’ performances in tablet-based geometry learning [16]. The abstract states that **A total of 85 French students** drew three geometric shapes, either on paper or on a tablet, and then performed a transfer task on paper [16]. It reports that students in the tablet with feedback group performed significantly better than the other two groups on learning, as well as on transfer [16]. It states that the study was the first to combine media comparison and added-value approaches to test the effects on students’ geometry performances of using a new educational app in a naturalistic classroom environment, and that the data indicate that artificial intelligence is a promising way of providing learners with real-time adaptive feedback in order to improve their performances [16]. The abstract also says tablet use increased children’s interest but not their learning outcomes, while feedback improved children’s performance in a training task and later transfer task [16].

The same paper’s body snippet states that feedback can be characterized by content, functions, mode of presentation, and source, and that feedback generated by an artificial intelligence system that analyses students’ performances over time and provides support during learning can be regarded as adaptive scaffolding [17]. It also says that without technology, feedback has to be provided by either teachers or peers, which prevents learners from receiving real-time corrective feedback at each step of their performance [17]. It states that there is little research investigating the effects of intelligent tutoring systems in the area of geometry and a dearth of research on adaptive feedback on learning [17].  

Guo et al. (2013), “Intelligent diagnostic feedback for online multiple-choice questions,” states that intelligent tutoring systems attempt to simulate a teacher, who can guide the student’s study based on the student’s level of knowledge by giving intelligent instructional feedback [18]. It also states that the intense interaction and feedback achieved by intelligent tutoring systems can significantly improve student learning gains, and that meaningful, constructive and adaptive feedback is the essential feature of ITSs [18].  

Liao et al. (2024), “Can human-machine feedback in a smart learning environment enhance learners’ learning performance? A meta-analysis,” states that literature for the meta-analysis was conducted by searching Web of Science, EBSCO, PsycINFO, and Science Direct using keywords such as `"intelligent tutoring systems," "intelligent interactive education," "intelligent learning environment," "online feedback teaching," "intelligent learning companion," and "virtual teacher"` [19]. It states that **726 articles** were identified, with **additional 6 articles** found through backtracking, and after screening, **35 articles were included in the meta-analysis** [19]. It also states that the inclusion criteria required only experimental and quasi-experimental studies, and that the sample size meets the basic requirements of meta-analysis when not less than 30 [19].  

Morris, Perry, and Wardle (2021), “Formative assessment and feedback for learning in higher education: A systematic review,” states that systematic reviews and meta-analyses, mostly conducted with compulsory school-age children, report relatively high average effect sizes (**d ≈ 0.4-0.8**), albeit with large variation [20]. It also states that corrective feedback is more useful than praise, punishment or rewards for improving students’ ability to learn new skills and complete tasks effectively [20]. It says feedback with more information is more beneficial, and comments are more helpful than sharing grades or marks [20]. It adds that feedback directed by agents other than the student, i.e. a teacher or computer program, is more effective [20].  

Belland et al. (2017), “Synthesizing Results From Empirical Research on Computer-Based Scaffolding in STEM Education,” states that a pilot meta-analysis of computer-based scaffolding indicated that computer-based scaffolding led to an average effect of **ḡ = 0.53** [21]. It also states that a meta-analysis of intelligent tutoring systems indicated that step-based intelligent tutoring systems led to an average effect of **ES = 0.76 versus control** and that substep-based intelligent tutoring systems led to an average effect of **ES = 0.40** [21]. It further states that other meta-analyses found varied average effects for ITSs, including **ḡ = 0.41** among students of various levels, **ḡ = 0.09** among K-12 students engaged in mathematics learning, and **ḡ = 0.37** among college students [21].  

Xu et al. (2019), “The Effectiveness of Intelligent Tutoring Systems on K-12 Students’ Reading Comprehension: A Meta-Analysis,” states in the ERIC abstract that **Nineteen studies from 13 publications incorporating approximately 10 000 students** were included in the final analysis [22]. It states that ITSs are a computer-based learning environment that provides customizable and immediate feedback to the learner [22].  

Ma et al. (2014), “Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Learning Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis,” is listed in ERIC as a meta-analysis of ITSs across diverse subject areas such as algebra, medicine, law, and reading [23]. The ERIC abstract says ITSs are computer programs that model learners’ psychological states to provide individualized instruction [23].  

The arXiv result “Do intelligent tutoring systems benefit K-12 students? A meta-analysis and evaluation of heterogeneity of treatment effects in the U.S” states that it is a **meta-analysis** and that it included **18 studies with 77 effect sizes across 11 ITS** [24]. It says overall there was a significant positive effect, but the snippet provided did not include the exact effect size [24].

The ERIC result “Enhancing Students' Learning Outcomes in Mathematics through Intelligent Tutoring Systems Based on Real-Time Feedback” states it is a **randomized controlled trial** involving **120 students** from the Mathematics Program for Gifted Students [25]. It says the study examined the effectiveness of an intelligent tutoring system driven by real-time feedback in enhancing students' mathematical learning outcomes [25].  

The ERIC result “Implementation of an Automated Grading System with an Adaptive Learning Component to Affect Student Feedback and Response Time” states that the research focuses on the development and implementation of an adaptive learning and grading system with a goal to increase the effectiveness and quality of feedback to students [26].  

The ERIC result “Automated Detection of Essay Revising Patterns: Applications for Intelligent Feedback in a Writing Tutor” states that the Writing Pal is an intelligent tutoring system designed to support writing proficiency and strategy acquisition for adolescent writers [27]. It says a fundamental aspect of the instructional model is automated formative feedback that provides concrete information and strategies oriented toward student improvement [27].  

The ERIC result “Developing Pedagogically-Guided Algorithms for Intelligent Writing Feedback” states that various computer tools have been developed to support educators’ assessment of student writing, including automated essay scoring and automated writing evaluation systems [28]. It says research demonstrates that these systems exhibit relatively high scoring accuracy but uncertain instructional efficacy, and that students’ writing proficiency does not necessarily improve as a result of interacting with the software [28].  

The arXiv result “A Chain-of-Thought Prompting Approach with LLMs for Evaluating Students’ Formative Assessment Responses in Science” states that it explores the use of LLMs to score and explain short-answer assessments in K-12 science [29]. It says existing methods can score more structured math and computer science assessments, but often do not provide explanations for the scores [29]. It states the study focuses on employing GPT-4 for automated assessment in middle school Earth Science, combining few-shot and active learning [29]. The snippet text visible in the result does not provide the quantitative results in the excerpt shown.  

The arXiv result “3DG: A Framework for Using Generative AI for Handling Sparse Learner Performance Data From Intelligent Tutoring Systems” states that learning performance data collected from ITSs often suffers from sparsity, impacting the accuracy of learner modeling and knowledge assessments [30]. It introduces the 3DG framework to address this [30].  

The arXiv result “Bringing Generative AI to Adaptive Learning in Education” states that generative AI technologies such as large language models and diffusion models have boosted the development of AI applications in various domains including education, and that adaptive learning has proven its efficacy in enhancing students’ learning efficiency [31].  

The arXiv result “Generative AI and Its Impact on Personalized Intelligent Tutoring Systems” states that generative AI is revolutionizing educational technology by enabling highly personalized and adaptive learning environments within intelligent tutoring systems [32].  

### AI in science education, classroom supports, and digital environments

Heeg and Avraamidou (2023) state that AI applications in school science are used in geoscience or physics most often and are used to support either knowledge construction or skills development [2]. They also state that AI applications are being integrated into the existing science curriculum without any change in the learning objectives, which is both fragmented and limited [2].  

Kavitha and Joshith (2024) state that the reviewed literature highlights hands-on learning through robotics, blended strategies, inquiry-based learning, project-based learning, cooperative learning, and feedback-based learning strategies [1]. It says robotics has applications in hands-on learning, cooperative learning, inquiry-based learning, and project-based learning [1]. It specifically states that **seven studies** highlight the effectiveness of robotics in improving scientific literacy, motivation, and inquiry skills among students [1]. It also says that studies such as Mayub et al. (2023) and Omari et al. (2023) suggest robotics can efficiently engage students in active learning and enhance understanding of scientific concepts [1].  

The same review states that the AGILEST approach by Zahid Iqbal and Campbell (2023) uses machine learning agents and real-time touchless hand interaction to facilitate active learning through learning by doing experiences [1]. It says blended pedagogical strategies include educational chatbot systems aimed at improving students’ performance in biology, intelligent virtual reality for experimental chemistry education, and chatbots in a 5th-grade science course [1]. It also states that inquiry-based learning was highlighted by a study by Pedaste and Altin (2020), and that Cooper (2023) explored science education with ChatGPT, emphasizing the role of generative artificial intelligence in fostering inquiry-based, student-centered learning experiences [1].  

The same review says that project-based learning and cooperative learning were exemplified by Fuhrmann (2021), who integrated computational thinking and robotics in middle school science inquiry, and D’Amico et al. (2020), who developed experiential learning systems with educational robotics to promote collaborative problem-solving skills [1]. It says feedback-based learning strategies, including automated feedback on students’ scientific argumentation, underscore the importance of timely and constructive feedback in enhancing learning outcomes [1]. It further states that hands-on learning and learning-by-doing approaches, especially robotics and machine learning, can significantly enhance student engagement and scientific literacy by providing experiential learning opportunities that align with real-world applications [1].  

The paper “The use of Artificial intelligence in school science: a systematic literature review” also states that AI applications are used to support science education in existing curricula, and that the majority of the applications are used in geoscience or physics [2].  

The ERIC result “AI Adaptivity in a Mixed-Reality System Improves Learning” states that adaptivity in advanced learning technologies offers the possibility to adapt to different student backgrounds, and introduces AI adaptivity in the context of a new genre of Intelligent Science Stations [33].  

The arXiv result “Intelligent science exhibits: Transforming hands-on exhibits into mixed-reality learning experiences” states that a controlled random-assignment experiment tested scaffolding that not only prompts with questions but also gives automated feedback on students’ decisions during scientific inquiry with physical phenomenon [34]. It says the project introduces a novel AI technology, an “Intelligent Science Exhibit,” that provides a means to scale these techniques to more children [34]. It says the exhibit uses intelligent camera sensing to track children’s interactions in physical and virtual spaces and provides interactive personalized feedback through the help of an engaging character [34]. It also says the exhibit adapts to different needs of children, provides personalized support, and helps achieve equity goals [34].  

The arXiv result “Personalized Multimodal Feedback Using Multiple External Representations: Strategy Profiles and Learning in High School Physics” states that it is a **16-24 week observational study** in high school physics with **N=661** [35]. It says the platform provided personalized and multimodal feedback [35].  

The OpenAlex result “A Multimedia Adaptive Tutoring System for Mathematics that Addresses Cognition, Metacognition and Affect” is listed as **full text extracted** and is an adaptive tutoring system paper [36].  

The ERIC result “Data-Driven Decision-Making: Utilising AI-Powered Learning Analytics to Make Informed Primary Educators’ Decisions” states that AI in primary education can enhance teaching and learning processes, with a focus on AI-powered learning analytics [37].  

The ERIC result “The SIETTE Automatic Assessment Environment” states that Siette supports different assessment methods including classical test theory, item response theory, and computer adaptive testing and integrates them with multidimensional student models used by intelligent educational systems [38].  

The arXiv result “The Landscape of AI in Science Education: What is Changing and How to Respond” states that AI-supported scoring of open-ended written explanations and arguments or drawn models delivers rubric-aligned scores and formative feedback at scale [39]. It also states that adaptive learning platforms tailor instruction to individual students’ cognitive and emotional profiles, that intelligent tutoring systems such as AutoTutor and EER-Tutor replicate aspects of one-on-one instruction by offering real-time, customized feedback based on student inputs, and that generative AI further enables automatic creation of instructional materials such as lesson plans and assessments [39].  

The arXiv result “A review of clustering models in educational data science towards fairness-aware learning” states that machine learning is increasingly supporting the education system and educational data science domain, from decision support to educational activities and learning analytics [40]. It says the results can be biased because algorithms may generate results based on students’ protected attributes, and that fairness is essential [40].

### Teacher readiness, attitudes, ethics, and implementation constraints

Alshorman (2024), “THE READINESS TO USE AI IN TEACHING SCIENCE: SCIENCE TEACHERS’ PERSPECTIVE,” states that AI can offer personalized learning experiences and adaptive assessments, enhancing student engagement and outcomes [41]. It says that by automating tasks such as grading and lesson planning, AI allows educators to focus more on personalized teaching and student engagement [41]. It also says the effective integration of AI in science classrooms heavily depends on teachers’ readiness and acceptance, and that teachers need to be well-equipped with the necessary knowledge and skills for AI utilisation [41]. The same paper states that AI can assist in developing lesson plans, evaluating student performance, and providing customised learning materials, which can reduce the workload of teachers and enhance the learning experience for students [41]. It also notes that AI models can support teachers in creating educational activities and overcoming implementation challenges [41].  

Seo et al. (2024) state that the design of human-AI complementarity needs to adapt to the school level and that teachers across all levels recognized the value of AI technology for creating instructional materials that align with students’ learning needs [14]. The paper also states that AI systems should harness the respective strengths of human teachers and AI to achieve enhanced educational outcomes [14].  

Kavitha and Joshith (2024) state that limitations in the AI-in-science review included the Scopus-only scope, English-language-only publications, full-text-only inclusion, and a cutoff at 2023 [1]. They also say that future research should address ethical implications and challenges of AI integration in educational settings to ensure responsible and equitable use [1].  

Heeg and Avraamidou (2023) state that ethical considerations should not only be taken into account during the implementation of AI tools but also during the development and implementation to ensure safe and fair AI applications for school science [2]. They also say that missing remains understanding of how teachers and AI tools might work in synergy to support science engagement and learning [2].  

Bond et al. (2024), “A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour,” provides search-string evidence that AI review literature includes `"intelligent tutor*"`, `"adaptive learning system*"`, `"adaptive educational system*"`, `"chat bot*"`, `"machine learning"`, `"natural language processing"`, `"automated tutor"`, `"personal tutor*"`, and `"intelligent agent*"` among others [42]. The snippet shows that their search string included education sectors such as K-12, primary school, middle school, high school, and elementary school, though the paper itself is about higher education review synthesis [42].

The arXiv result “A systematic review of AI-driven intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) in K-12 education” and the related ERIC record state that the review aims to identify the effects of ITSs on K-12 students’ learning and performance and which experimental designs are currently used [43]. The Tavily source snippet says overall effects of ITSs on learning and performance in K-12 education are generally positive but are mitigated when implementation conditions vary [44]. The search result also indicates that this review is by **A Létourneau et al.** and is a **systematic review** [43].  

The arXiv/open result “A systematic review of intelligent and robot tutoring systems” says the study highlights the complementary strengths of ITS and RTS, proposes integrated hybrid solutions to maximize educational benefits, and identifies three distinct categories: computer-based ITS, robot-based RTS, and multimodal systems integrating various interaction modes [45].

### Source-by-source preservation of key statements and statistics

Below are the key findings preserved from the raw search results, rewritten only for clarity and organization while keeping the underlying content intact:

- AI-driven platforms can create dynamic, real-time models of chemical reactions or physical processes [1].
- AI can significantly improve science classrooms’ assessment and feedback processes [1].
- ITS can provide immediate, personalized feedback to students [1].
- AI systems can identify individual learning patterns and needs by analyzing vast amounts of student data [1].
- The key AI technologies identified in K-12 science include robotics, chatbots, machine learning, automated scoring and feedback, and neural networks with fuzzy logic [1].
- Seven studies highlight the effectiveness of robotics in improving scientific literacy, motivation, and inquiry skills among students [1].
- The majority of studies in Kavitha and Joshith focused on high school settings (**n=10, 50%**), followed by middle school (**n=8, 40%**) and elementary school (**n=2, 10%**) [1].
- Design and developmental research was the most prevalent methodology, with eight studies [1].
- In the experimental/quasi-experimental category, 4 out of 5 studies utilized a quasi-experimental design [1].
- Heeg and Avraamidou’s review included **n=22** studies and nine AI application types [2].
- Heeg and Avraamidou identified the three most dominant themes as automated assessment and feedback, personalized learning, and predictive modeling [2].
- AI applications are used to automate or optimize already existing educational practices, and AI applications in school science are being integrated into existing curricula without changing learning objectives [2].
- The study by Ng et al. used a **3-week science learning experience with 74 Secondary 4 students in Hong Kong** [8].
- The Jamaluddin et al. study used a cross-sectional quantitative survey method with Structural Equation Modeling analysis [9].
- The Smith-Mutegi et al. article states that AI technologies can enhance student engagement, improve learning outcomes, and provide valuable insights for educators [6].
- The Zafari et al. review found that Machine Learning and Intelligent Tutoring System were the most common approaches among AI categories [15].
- The Xu and Ouyang review included 18 literature review articles of AIEd and identified only two works exploring AI in STEM education among those review articles [3].
- The Liao et al. meta-analysis identified **726 articles**, plus **additional 6 articles** by backtracking, and **35 articles were included in the meta-analysis** [19].
- Morris et al. state that systematic reviews and meta-analyses mostly conducted with compulsory school-age children report relatively high average effect sizes (**d ≈ 0.4-0.8**) [20].
- Belland et al. report meta-analytic effects of **ḡ = 0.53**, **ES = 0.76**, **ES = 0.40**, **ḡ = 0.41**, **ḡ = 0.09**, and **ḡ = 0.37** in scaffolding and ITS research [21].
- Xu et al. (ERIC) state that **Nineteen studies from 13 publications incorporating approximately 10 000 students** were included in their K-12 reading comprehension ITS meta-analysis [22].
- The arXiv ITS meta-analysis included **18 studies with 77 effect sizes across 11 ITS** [24].
- The ERIC real-time feedback ITS RCT involved **120 students** [25].
- The Colliot et al. tablet-feedback study involved **85 French students** and found that the tablet with feedback group performed significantly better than the other two groups on learning and transfer [16].
- The AR and other digital support sources are not central to the question, but they show related school science digital supports and interactive learning environments [62].

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

No directly evaluative, K-12 science-outcome study of Khanmigo was located in the database results. The raw search thread repeatedly indicates that Semantic Scholar, ERIC, and Elsevier/Scopus returned no results for the targeted thread [database result]. The openai_web_search explicitly states: “I couldn't locate a specific unpublished evaluation PDF detailing the science outcomes of Khanmigo's district pilot” [database result].

The most directly relevant Khanmigo evidence found is descriptive, not evaluative, and does not report K-12 science outcome effects.

1. In the paper **“The role of GPT in promoting inclusive higher education for people with various learning disabilities: a review”**, the snippet states: “Khan Academy, a non-profit educational organization, is implementing a pilot initiative to provide Khanmigo AI to over 8,000 K-12 teachers and students. According to the project description provided by Khan Academy, Khanmigo is built around the underpinned version of the LLM of OpenAI's GPT-4, which has been trained using educational materials sourced from Khan Academy. To enhance the personalized and helpful response tone of Khanmigo, as well as to mitigate the speedy provision of responses to students, additional parameters have been included in the product (Khan Academy, 2023).” This is a review article, not an outcome evaluation of Khanmigo in K-12 science [1].

2. In the paper **“Utilization of GPT-4 to Improve Education Quality Through Personalized Learning for Generation Z in Indonesia”**, the snippet states: “Khanmigo is an artificial intelligence (AI)-based guide developed by Khan Academy, a non-profit educational organization. Khanmigo aims to replicate the one-on-one tutoring experience by providing customized support, encouraging critical thinking, and suggesting relevant resources. Khanmigo can also help teachers with lesson planning and providing feedback to students. Khanmigo is still in the experimental stage and can only be accessed by a limited number of users who meet certain requirements. Khanmigo can be used to help students as a virtual tutor and as a debate partner. Teachers can also access it to generate lesson plans and help with other administrative tasks. Part of the purpose of the pilot launch is to determine what the demand is for the tutor and how educators and students are using it.” This is descriptive and does not report science learning outcomes for K-12 students [2].

3. In the paper **“Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning”**, the snippet states: “For example, when students present Khanmigo with a problem on fractions, it guides them through the underlying concepts of denominators and numerators, encouraging them to apply these concepts to solve the problem through a series of guiding questions. Khanmigo functions as a facilitator, aligning with the principles of inquiry-based learning [16], a human-centred learning theory that emphasises the importance of active learning through inquiry. This theory encourages students to ask questions, explore, and engage deeply with the learning material to develop deep knowledge. This iterative methodology reflects Vygotsky's emphasis on the importance of the learning journey over the destination by fostering deep conceptual comprehension and retention [12,16]. By engaging learners in a dialogic process, GenAI-driven systems such as Khanmigo aim to enhance learners' critical thinking and problem-solving skills. Despite the promising design of systems like Khanmigo and students' positive attitudes towards using such technologies for personalised learning support [17], it is important to acknowledge the current limitations in empirical evidence regarding their short-and long-term impacts on learning outcomes [18]. Emerging evidence indicates that the impact on learning engagement, agency, and performance can paint a complicated and mixed picture (e.g., lack of learning gains after removing GenAI supports) [19,20]. Therefore, further research is needed to substantiate GenAI's long-term benefits to human learning. This includes conducting longitudinal and randomised controlled studies that compare the effectiveness of GenAI tutoring with conventional rule-based tutoring systems over several academic terms and across different subjects to contextualise its impacts within various educational settings.” This explicitly notes limitations in empirical evidence and calls for longitudinal and randomized controlled studies [3].

4. In the paper **“An Evaluation of Khanmigo, a Generative AI Tool, as a Computer-Assisted Language Learning App”**, the snippet states that “Even though the developers do not claim that Khanmigo is designed for language learning, its capability as a language learning tool would still merit further exploration based on research-based grounds. ... Khanmigo, which is powered by ChatGPT's most sophisticated Large Language Model (LLM), GPT-4, via an Application Programming Interface (API), claims its superiority when compared to other AI tools because its content is developed by teachers. ... Despite the technical sophistication in developing Khanmigo using GPT-4 model, the app needs to be evaluated like other previous language learning technologies for its appropriateness for certain contexts and groups of language learners. ... This paper, therefore, provides an overview of Khanmigo's capabilities as a language learning tool using Chapelle's (2001) Evaluation Framework for CALL task appropriateness.” This is an evaluation in language-learning context, not K-12 science outcomes [4].

There is also a direct mention in the paper **“Exploring the Applications of Generative AI in High School STEM Education”**. The snippet states: “Khanmigo was the initial candidate for this study as it was developed specifically through an educational point-of-view and was geared towards leading students towards the answers rather than providing them outright, and thus would be more beneficial to students learning. Due to a lack of funding, Khanmigo could not be utilized in this study; however, a future study focusing on the difference between it and a general purpose GAI could show the benefits of having an educational GAI in the classroom and thus encourage more educators to implement such technologies into the classroom due to its inbuilt filters against academic dishonesty, which is still a major concern with the aforementioned general purpose GAI models such as Bing AI (GPT-4 based) which was used in this study. I will be using an experimental method, giving students pre-and post-tests along with surveys to determine the impact of various learning aides on their performance and understanding of a given topic.” This indicates Khanmigo was not used due to lack of funding and therefore provides no Khanmigo outcome data [5].

- “Khanmigo encompasses several different activities for learners to choose from.They vary based on the subject or topic offered or the nature of the task itself.The main categories of activities are referred to as follows: Tutor Me, Refresh, Write, Debate, Chat, Play.The Tutor Me format, as illustrated in Figure 1, is primarily designed to help learners with problem solving in math, science, or the humanities.Learners have to enter their questions, and Khanmigo will break the problem into its components and provide a series of steps to get the answer.It also offers more practice problems as needed.” [5]
- “The Refresh format, as illustrated in Figure 2, allows learners to test their understanding of what they learned by taking a quiz.Khanmigo asks learners to enter their topic of interest and their grade level.Several questions will be posed, but one at a time.Feedback will be provided for learners' input, and more questions will be generated based on learners' previously demonstrated understanding of the subject.” [6]
- “The Write format, as shown in Figure 3, deals with exposition writing.In this format, learners get feedback on their essays, or they are able to craft stories by brainstorming with Khanmigo.Besides general essay writing, this format specializes in brainstorming and providing feedback on users' admission essays. The Debate format is specifically designed with young learners in mind, especially those in elementary, middle, and high school.Learners can brainstorm on different topics they provide or choose a topic from the selection provided by Khanmigo.The Chat format allows learners to choose a literary character or historical figure and have a simulated conversation with them.There are 29 fictional (e.g., Helen of Troy, Winnie the Pooh, Zeus) and 68 historical characters (e.g., Nikolas Tesla, Mahatma Gandhi, Plato, Napoleon Bonaparte) to choose from.The Play format offers learners the opportunity to play a variety of games involving the creation of new words or exploration of existing ones.The Extra section allows learners to converse with Khanmigo on various topics that spark their curiosity.They can navigate college admissions, discuss their personal interests, or seek academic or career-related advice.While each activity has a specialized focus, the Tutor Me, Write, and Extra are more suited for learning and writing through multiple discussions or text construction with Khanmigo; therefore, these will be explored further in the study.” [7]
- “This app is also intended to serve as an autonomous learning tool and was not developed for language learning per se.It is not known which languages can be learned using the app.However, it immediately gets on task when asked if it can teach French, as depicted in Figure 4.Even though the app has the capability of speech-to-text and text-to-speech recognition, it is not available for learning French at the current time.It is more suitable for developing writing and reading skills.Despite this, learners can still ask questions about the pronunciation of words, and it will be spelled out, as illustrated in Figure 5.” [8]
- “Khanmigo's interface is easy to navigate and intuitive.The activities are all aligned on the left navigation pane, and the space in the center enables users to interact with the app depending on the activities they choose.Teachers and learners can both use the app based on the preferences specified.However, this evaluation will be presented from a learner's perspective.The app is available on multiple platforms, iOS and Android, and can be accessed via mobile devices.Chapelle's (2001) Framework delineates six criteria for assessing the task appropriateness of CALL Tools: Language Learning Potential, Learner Fit, Meaning Focus, Authenticity, Positive Impact, and Practicality.” [9]
- “Additionally, Chapelle's (2001) framework also considers other important factors, such as learners' individual differences, and integrates pedagogical perspectives that may be overlooked in other SLA theories (e.g., Intercultural Competence).However, the point is that if the evaluator specifies the pedagogical goals, the framework allows for the inclusion of such pedagogical perspectives (Chapelle, 2017).Moreover, using this framework, makes it possible to do the evaluation on multiple levels: a judgmental level (i.e., to analyze if the software allows enough interactional opportunities), and the empirical level (i.e., by gathering data if the learner had enough opportunities to interact with the software).” [10]
- “When it comes to practicality, several facets merit attention.First is the concern about access to the hardware or software.Khanmigo is not an open-source app and comes with a paid subscription ($4 monthly as of May 2024).Consequently, not all learners and educators can afford to pay a monthly fee.Secondly, although Khanmigo is designed to be an autonomous learning tool, practicality also means that knowledgeable personnel need to be around to help with learning.This may not always be feasible.However, Khanmigo has a feature that allows educators to log in and review students' progress if the students are assigned to a specific class.The toggle mode on the app allows users to switch between two modes: learners or students and teacher.This still makes an option worth considering.As far as the usability of the software, it is considerably intuitive, and learners and educators can access the app with minimal difficulty.Concerning the portability of the app, it can be accessed from mobile platforms, Android and iOS devices.It can be installed on any device.So, when it comes to practicality, the evidence from Khanmigo partially supports this criterion.” [11]
- “This criterion refers to the degree to which the tasks can provide learners with opportunities to hone their metacognitive strategies, or "techniques used to help students understand the way they learn and do this more effectively" (Hornby & Greaves, 2022, p.2), and gain pragmatic competence, which is "the knowledge of form-function-context mappingswhich forms to use for what communicative functions in what social contexts" (Taguchi, 2019, p. 13).Khanmigo provides scaffolding for learners to complete a task.This, in a way, helps learners to develop their metacognitive skills, as it gives time for learners to reflect and add content.However, the method is tacit and is not explicitly taught to learners when they use the app.As for pragmatic competence, Khanmigo is not necessarily able to improve learners' skills in pragmatics, unless learners ask questions related to pragmatics.So, the evidence from Khanmigo does not support the positive impact criterion.” [12]
- “Khanmigo provides ample opportunities for learners to engage in communicative tasks that focus on meaning.All task types encourage learners to pick up a topic of interest and communicate without explicit focus on forms or grammatical corrections.The feedback provided by Khanmigo mostly focuses on verifying the meaning and the context.Learners can also ask specific questions to get feedback on their form.” [13]
- “Khanmigo can be seen as an asset as it can generate texts that are more authentic in nature.Learners can choose a subject that they may need to practice.It could be humanities or even science subjects.Learners, while learning a language, can focus on specific purposes that meet their current needs.Moreover, Khanmigo claims to model a Socratic approach to teaching in that it does not provide students with answers, but guides their learning by asking thought-provoking, open-ended questions, which then lead them to learn more.This pedagogical approach may resonate with many classroom teachers and speaks to the authenticity of the method.” [14]
