**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

The gathered evidence includes systematic reviews, meta-analyses, randomized controlled experiments, quasi-experimental studies, observational/report-type studies, and conceptual/review papers on intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning, scaffolding, formative feedback, and digital science supports for K-12 and adjacent STEM contexts.

A number of sources explicitly state that Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) or closely related adaptive systems can improve learning outcomes through personalized feedback, guidance, and adaptation to student performance. One snippet stated: “There is evidence that they can be effective, particularly for the teaching of mathematics and science” and described adaptive learning systems as using algorithms to tailor content and pace to students’ needs [1]. Another snippet stated: “AI can also serve as an intelligent tutor, providing real-time feedback, guidance, and support to students in STEM disciplines. Intelligent tutoring systems can analyze student responses, identify misconceptions, and offer targeted interventions to address learning gaps” [2]. The same source continued that “These AI-driven tools enhance student engagement, improve problem-solving abilities, and promote active learning experiences” [2]. It further stated that “Research studies have shown the effectiveness of intelligent tutoring systems and virtual laboratories in STEM education” and specifically mentioned a study using an intelligent tutoring system for computer programming that found students who received personalized feedback and guidance performed significantly better than those in traditional instruction [2]. It also mentioned virtual laboratories powered by AI with improved problem-solving abilities and conceptual understanding in chemistry [2].

A systematic review of AI-driven ITS in K-12 education reported that the use of artificial intelligence in education has grown exponentially in the last decade, particularly intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs). It stated that the review aimed to identify the effects of ITSs on K-12 students’ learning and performance and which experimental designs were used [3]. The abstract reported that “The 28 studies analyzed in this systematic review included a total of 4597 students (N = 4597) and used quasi-experimental designs with varying intervention durations” [3]. It stated: “Overall, our findings suggest that the effects of ITSs on learning and performance in K-12 education are generally positive but are found to be mitigated when compared to non-intelligent tutoring systems” [3]. It also noted that “additional research with longer interventions and increased sample sizes with greater diversity is warranted” [3]. In the discussion snippet, the authors stated that “middle school students frequently demonstrate more pronounced learning gains than their high school counterparts” and that “effects reported by analyzed studies are somewhat mitigated, and are hard to generalize due to the great variations in experimental designs” [4]. They also wrote that “Further research is needed to evaluate the effects of ITSs on learning and performance in primary and secondary (K-12) education” and that future research should assess ITSs with longer interventions, larger and more diverse sample sizes including younger students, and better experimental control [4].

The open-access snippet from the arXiv paper on AI tutors in Ghana described ITSs and adaptive learning systems more generally, stating that high-dosage tutoring is effective but scalability is limited, and that “Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) which aim to adapt the learning experience to individual student needs, customizing the content and pace, thus emulating one-on-one tutoring” have been implemented in “K-12 classrooms and universities” and that “there is evidence that they can be effective, particularly for the teaching of mathematics and science” [5]. This same snippet emphasized that adaptive learning systems use algorithms to tailor content and pace and hold promise for resource-constrained education systems [5].

Several sources focused on science education specifically. One paper on K-12 science education stated that AI-driven platforms can create dynamic, real-time models of chemical reactions or physical processes, and that “Intelligent tutoring systems [ITS] can provide immediate, personalized feedback to students, enhancing their learning outcomes while maintaining student motivation and interest in the subject” [6]. It further stated that AI systems can identify individual learning patterns and needs to tailor instructional strategies and foster a more inclusive and effective learning environment [6]. Another source on K-12 science education said: “Intelligent tutoring systems [ITS] can provide immediate, personalized feedback to students, enhancing their learning outcomes while maintaining student motivation and interest in the subject” and “AI-driven tools enhance student engagement, improve problem-solving abilities, and promote active learning experiences” [7]. The same source noted that AI systems can identify learning patterns and needs, enabling educators to tailor instructional strategies [7].

A pedagogical review focused on K-12 science education stated that “AI-driven platforms can create dynamic, real-time models of chemical reactions or physical processes, enabling students to visualize and experiment with challenging or impractical scenarios to replicate in a conventional classroom environment” and that “Intelligent tutoring systems [ITS] can provide immediate, personalized feedback to students, enhancing their learning outcomes while maintaining student motivation and interest in the subject” [6]. It also stated that AI can improve science classrooms’ assessment and feedback processes [6].

A mixed-reality science learning paper reported a randomized controlled experiment comparing an Intelligent Science Station with task-loop adaptivity versus a random-task version without adaptivity [8]. The abstract stated that the results show “adaptivity using Bayesian Knowledge Tracing in the context of a mixed-reality system leads to better learning of scientific principles, without sacrificing enjoyment” [8]. It concluded that these results demonstrate benefits of adaptivity in a mixed-reality setting to improve children’s science learning [8]. In a related snippet, children were randomly assigned to Randomized and Adaptive conditions; in the Adaptive condition, Adaptive Task Selection based on Bayesian Knowledge Tracing was used, with average intervention times approximately 9.61 min and 9.76 min and no significant difference between time on task in different conditions [9]. The same paper reported that after interacting with the system, students were given a matched paper post-test [9]. A related follow-up discussion stated that adaptivity using Bayesian Knowledge Tracing in the Intelligent Science Station led to better learning of scientific principles compared to random task selection, without sacrificing enjoyment; it also said that log analysis showed students in the adaptive condition were getting more opportunities to work on concepts they were having a hard time learning, and that the mastery-based algorithm effectively adjusted the inquiry experience to adapt to content and student differences producing better learning outcomes [10].

Another Intelligent Science Exhibit paper stated that the technology uses effective learning mechanisms of intelligent tutoring systems such as contrasting cases, predict-observe-explain, inquiry-based learning, guided-discovery, and menu-based self-explanation [11]. It described the physical setup as including an earthquake table, physical towers, a display screen, a depth camera and specialized AI technology to track what kids are doing and provide feedback accordingly [11]. It asked whether adding more guidance and scaffolding structure to an exhibit enhances visitor learning and noted a competing hypothesis that learning may be more effective when guidance and scaffolding are provided in structured inquiry activities [11]. The paper also said that guidance may interrupt flow and decrease engagement [11]. The enrichment summary for this paper said that evidence was found that the Intelligent Science Exhibit produces substantially better learning for both scientific and engineering outcomes, equivalent levels of self-reported enjoyment, and higher levels of engagement as measured by the length of time voluntarily spent at the exhibit [12].

A web-based inquiry-learning system paper reported that a large study by Geier et al. (2008) with “over 1,800 middle-school students in the experimental condition versus more than 17,000 students in the control” showed that students who were given scaffolded tools for performing inquiry learning exercises in earth, physical and life science did significantly better on standardized exams than students who did not use the tools [13]. The same source stated that there is evidence that supporting and guiding students in inquiry learning is beneficial, but questions remain about how much support is the right amount and how assistance should vary according to prior knowledge [13]. It also stated that the authors were testing whether high assistance helps low prior knowledge learners and low assistance is better for high prior knowledge learners [13].

A paper on scaffolding and feedback in open-ended learning environments stated that scaffolds are “tools, strategies, and guides used to support understanding beyond one’s immediate grasp,” that scaffolds and feedback can improve critical thinking and learning outcomes, and that properly designed scaffolds can help foster self-regulation and engagement and reduce frustration [14]. It also stated that students may exploit scaffolding features and that feedback that frequently interrupts workflow or focuses on summative evaluation can negatively affect learning [14]. Another paper on adaptive scaffolds in Betty’s Brain, a learning-by-teaching OELE for middle school science, described a classroom study with 98 middle schoolers and said that adaptive scaffolding produced mixed results, with some scaffolds being more useful than others, and that findings suggest how adaptive scaffolding in OELEs can be further improved to narrow the gap between High and Low performers [15]. That paper also stated that contextualized conversational feedback from virtual agents led to better overall performance by students [15].

A study on adaptive scientific reasoning instruction in children reported an experimental design with macro-adaptive, micro-adaptive, and non-adaptive control conditions [16]. The abstract stated that there were comparable improvements in all three instructional conditions, with macro-adaptive n = 58, micro-adaptive n = 46, and non-adaptive control n = 49 [16]. It stated that learning gains for the groups were similar and that children’s overall task performance during the lessons improved [16]. The authors suggested that more specific information on children’s performance and more frequent and precise adaptations might lead to better learning outcomes [16]. This study was labeled as not explicitly an RCT in the snippet, and design details were described as an adaptive instruction study rather than a randomized controlled trial [16].

A scientific competency diagnostics paper reported that “The evaluation of the consistency of situations, content scope, questions, and scoring in diagnosing the three dimensions of scientific competency revealed that all three dimensions Explanation of Scientific Phenomena (ES), Interpretation of Data and Use of Evidence (IE), and Evaluation and Design of Scientific Inquiry (ED) demonstrated a high level of coherence” [17]. It said this validates the initial hypothesis that implementing an intelligent coaching module with automated feedback can enhance students’ scientific competency [17]. It also stated that “The adaptive feature of ‘Seis Tutor’ improves its consistency by tailoring feedback and learning paths to cater to the unique requirements of individual students” and that Assistment and other real-time reporting technologies enhance the dependability of evaluating student achievement by providing immediate and continuous feedback [17]. A second snippet from the same paper described the study as using a diagnostic system for scientific competency combined with a personalized intelligent tutoring module through machine learning and said it was intended to enhance the learning progression of seventh grade students [18]. It also reported that the decision tree algorithm was used to analyze secondary data from 847 students [19]. The excerpt said the paper employed a decision tree algorithm in Python to create a predictive model that could diagnose individual scientific competency levels [19].

A STEM higher education review stated that “AI can also serve as an intelligent tutor, providing real-time feedback, guidance, and support to students in STEM disciplines” and that intelligent tutoring systems can analyze student responses, identify misconceptions, and offer targeted interventions [20]. It also stated that “The AI tutor can adapt its teaching strategies to address individual learning needs” and that “These AI-driven tools enhance student engagement, improve problem-solving abilities, and promote active learning experiences” [20]. It further said that research studies have shown effectiveness of ITSs and virtual laboratories in STEM education [20]. A separate section of that review stated that personalized and adaptive learning is a crucial aspect of AI in STEM higher education, with systems adapting the pace, depth, and focus of instruction to optimize learning outcomes [21]. It said: “Research studies have shown the effectiveness of AI-powered personalized learning in STEM education. Beghetto et al. (2019) conducted a study where an AI-based intelligent tutoring system was used to teach algebra to middle school students. The results demonstrated significant improvements in student performance and engagement compared to traditional classroom instruction. Similarly, Van Lehn (2011) found that adaptive learning environments enhanced student learning outcomes in STEM subjects by providing personalized feedback and support” [21].

A review on AIED for helping students apply knowledge stated that intelligent systems are able to provide personalised support for problem solving in a variety of domains “(e.g., chemistry, physics, programming, and mathematics)” [22]. It further stated that ITSs designed for understanding concepts in STEM were “just as effective as one-to-one human tutoring” [22]. Another review with an exploratory orientation stated that adaptive learning content is key and that ITS research has asserted that intelligent systems can provide personalised support for problem solving in domains including chemistry, physics, programming, and mathematics [23]. It also stated: “Van Lehn [78] concluded that ITS systems particularly used for understanding concepts in STEM were just as effective as one-to-one human tutoring” [23]. A separate historical survey of ITSs described the field as beginning in the late 1960s, with computer-assisted instruction evolving into intelligent tutoring systems, and stated that “ITSs have successfully been used in all educational and training markets, including homes, schools, universities, businesses, and governments” [24]. It also noted that one of the goals of ITSs is to better understand student behaviors through interaction with students [24]. The same survey said that a CAI generally lacks the ability to monitor the learner’s solution steps and provide instant help, which ITSs are intended to address [24].

Another source stated: “An intelligent tutoring system is a computer-based learning system that uses AI to provide immediate and customized instruction or feedback to learners, usually without requiring intervention from a human teacher” [25]. It listed the four basic components as the domain model, student model, tutoring model, and user interface model [25]. It said intelligent tutoring systems promote interaction, can engage in turn-by-turn conversations, can give relevant feedback to motivate learners individually, and can host multimedia learning including text, multimedia, simulations, and games [25]. It also stated that AutoTutor, Atlas and Why2 are examples of intelligent tutoring projects based on conversational dialogue and that the upgraded ElectronixTutor incorporated multiple intelligent learning platforms, aiming to provide students with an integrated STEM learning environment [25].

A paper on online pedagogical tutorial tactics optimization described ITSs as one of the most effective educational interventions and said tutored students often perform significantly better than students in group instructional methods [26]. It stated that an ITS aims to provide immediate and customized instruction or feedback to learners and consists of four basic components based on a general consensus amongst researchers: the expert knowledge module, the student model module, the tutoring module, and the user interface module [26]. It also said numerous intelligent tutoring systems have been developed and applied to real world, especially in high schools and universities [26].

A review on teachers’ perceptions of AI in education stated that “the use of learning analytics within elementary and secondary level schools is a relatively underresearched area” and that learning analytics and related tools have evolved from early CAI into more adaptive and personalised learning solutions [27]. It said that some tools can be seen as “smarter systems offering intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) and adaptive environments and providing different, more personal paths with different materials and tasks based on the data collected from each student” [27]. This source used learning analytics as an adjacent mechanism for adaptive digital support rather than an outcome study [27].

A systematic review and meta-analysis of twenty-first century adaptive teaching and individualized learning stated that AI e-learning and computer-assisted instruction research includes many forms of tutoring and adaptive systems and cited older meta-analyses showing individualized instruction in science education more effective than traditional lectures [28]. It reported that the highly cited meta-analysis of active learning in science, engineering, and mathematics found a moderate effect size (d = 0.47) based on 158 studies [28]. It also reported that Ma, Adesope, Nesbit, and Liu (2014) meta-analyzed studies of ITS in a variety of subject matters, from reading and math to law and medical education [28]. The same source stated that teacher coaching had a minor effect on achievement (d = 0.08) [28]. It described a broad literature on CBI and ITS, including moderator variables such as outcome type, student academic level, and discipline [28].

A source on AI in education stated: “Adaptive learning systems use data analytics and machine learning algorithms to assess individual students’ strengths and weaknesses in real time” and that these systems generate tailored learning pathways by adapting instructional content to each student’s pace and preferences [29]. It also stated that intelligent tutoring systems provide personalised advice, promote self-directed learning, and reinforce concepts through interactive exercises [29]. The source further said AI algorithms can provide insights into learning patterns, instructional efficacy, and curriculum design by evaluating massive amounts of educational data [29].

A source on personalized and adaptive learning described intelligent tutoring systems as some of the earliest adaptive learning technologies and stated that they offer personalized and interactive learning experiences that help students engage in learning more effectively than traditionally based instructional methods [30]. It also said they enable personalization of learning and evaluation of performance in real time and enhance students’ engagement and individual learning experiences by providing immediate and adjusted feedback based on each student’s learning progression and actions [30]. The same source said adaptive learning systems go one step further to supply scaffolding [30].

A source on mixed-reality and intelligent science exhibits stated that a novel AI technology called an “Intelligent Science Exhibit” provides personalized feedback through intelligent camera sensing and that the exhibit adapts to different needs of children, provides personalized support, and helps achieve equity goals [11]. Another related source on intelligent science exhibits said the system uses effective learning mechanisms of ITS and asked whether adding more guidance and scaffolding structure to an exhibit enhances visitor learning [11].

A source on a web-based system to support inquiry learning stated that “Systems of this kind that have demonstrated learning benefits include BGUILE, the Co-Lab collaborative learning system, a chemistry virtual laboratory, WISE, and Metafora” [13]. It also said there is evidence supporting and guiding students in inquiry learning is beneficial, but the right amount of support remains an open question [13].

A source on preschool scaffolding and evidence-based reasoning reported an experimental training study with pre-post design [31]. It said adaptive prompts with modeling “will advance reasoning in preschoolers” and found that preschoolers supported by adaptive prompts including modeling gained significantly in correct evaluations of irrelevant events compared to the control group and a group receiving adaptive prompts only [31]. It also stated that the mere use of adaptive prompts led to mixed results [31]. The same source situates scaffolding in early science education and emphasizes the role of instructional support [32].

A source on dynamic media and digital media infusion in STEM education stated that documented benefits of digital media incorporation range from content comprehension and retention to emergent literacies and impact on overall school culture [33]. It also stated that initiatives within science education, technology, engineering, and design education, and mathematics education that build or implement digital tools for educational consumption highlight engagement and heightened learner outcomes [33]. This source is broad and not specific to ITS but is related to digital science support mechanisms [33].

The search results also included several adjacent but less directly relevant studies on literacy, mathematics, and general AI/adaptive learning. These include:
- A computer-adaptive curriculum study in kindergarten and first grade that found experimental group students benefited from significantly higher gains, percent gains, or end of year scores than control group students [34].
- A randomized controlled trial of tutor- and computer-delivered inferential comprehension interventions for middle school students with reading difficulties, noting the feasibility and comparative issues of computer-assisted intervention [35].
- A study of a computer-based reading program in grade 5 that discussed adaptive technology for reading assessment and instruction [36].
- A study on early math and science CAI stating that CAI can improve mathematical performance and that the Waterford Early Math and Science Program was expected to improve math scores [37].
- A study comparing computer-based simulations to traditional hands-on methods for middle school science that found no significant difference on science achievement between the traditional hands-on method and the computer-based simulation method [38].
- A cluster randomized controlled trial of personalized learning games in early math that stated the more games students played, the greater the learning gains they experienced [39].
- Studies and reviews on blended learning, learning analytics, educational robotics, CAI in literacy and math, and other general adaptive learning tools that are related but not science-specific [27][28][34][36][37][39].

Some papers were review or conceptual pieces rather than outcome studies. For example, “Power to the Teachers: An Exploratory Review on Artificial Intelligence in Education” synthesized evidence from the literature and stated that ITSs are used to help students understand basic scientific concepts through problem-based situations, and that VanLehn concluded ITSs in STEM are just as effective as one-to-one human tutoring [23]. The paper also stated that adaptive learning content is key for students to gradually acquire knowledge and that AIED systems may support students through examples, experiments, and scenarios designed to encounter their needs, interests, and knowledge [23]. Another review, “Intelligent Tutoring Systems: A Comprehensive Historical Survey with Recent Developments,” explained the historical development of ITSs and their components, and described their ability to provide immediate and customized instruction or feedback [24]. Another conceptual paper, “Evaluation of domain ontology requirements in e-tutor framework,” defined ITS and emphasized individualized instruction and immediate feedback [25]. Another conceptual paper, “Implications of Artificial Intelligence for Teaching and Learning,” described intelligent tutoring systems as autonomous and human-like and detailed the four components [25].

Some sources include explicit sample sizes and effect sizes. The systematic review of AI-driven ITS in K-12 education reported 28 studies and 4597 students and used quasi-experimental designs [3]. The adaptive scientific reasoning instruction study reported macro-adaptive n = 58, micro-adaptive n = 46, and non-adaptive control n = 49 [16]. The mixed-reality science station study described a randomized controlled experiment but did not report sample size in the snippet [8]. The diagnostic system for scientific competency study reported secondary data from 847 students [19]. The web-based inquiry-learning study reported over 1,800 middle-school students in the experimental condition and more than 17,000 students in the control [13]. The intelligent science exhibit studies did not provide exact sample sizes in the snippets, but one said that the exhibit produces substantially better learning and higher engagement [12]. The adaptive learning meta-analysis snippet reported a moderate effect size d = 0.47 for active learning in science, engineering, and mathematics based on 158 studies [28]. Another snippet reported the effect size of intelligent tutoring systems as 0.76 and human tutors as 0.79 [32]. Another meta-analytic review stated that “the effect size of intelligent tutoring systems was 0.76, while the effect size of human tutors was 0.79” [32]. Another review on teacher training stated that VanLehn found the effect size of intelligent tutoring systems was 0.76 and the effect size of human tutors was 0.79, and that Kulik and Fletcher (2017) on 50 controlled evaluations found ITSs typically raise student performance well beyond the level of conventional classes and even beyond other forms of computer tutoring or human tutors [32].

The gathered evidence also includes statements about mechanisms. Repeated mechanisms across sources include:
- immediate feedback [2][3][6][7][17][18][20][23][25][26][29]
- personalized and adaptive instruction or learning paths [1][2][3][5][6][7][17][20][21][23][25][29][30]
- diagnosis of misconceptions / student model updates [2][6][17][20][25][26]
- scaffolding, hints, and worked examples [11][13][14][15][23][24][25][30][31]
- adaptive task selection, mastery learning, and Bayesian Knowledge Tracing [8][9][10]
- learning analytics and real-time data usage for instructional adaptation [17][27][29]
- support for inquiry learning and problem solving in science/STEM [11][13][14][15][20][22][23][24][25][31][33]
- motivation and enjoyment effects [3][8][11][12][20][29][30][31]
- teacher dashboards, teacher support, and teacher-facing analytics [27][33]

The sources together show that for K-12 science learning outcomes, the strongest directly relevant evidence in the gathered material comes from:
- the systematic review of AI-driven ITS in K-12 education, which found generally positive effects but mitigated compared to non-intelligent tutoring systems and used quasi-experimental designs with 4597 students [3];
- the randomized controlled experiment on AI adaptivity in a mixed-reality science learning system, which found better learning of scientific principles without sacrificing enjoyment [8][10];
- the intelligent science exhibit / intelligent science station studies showing better learning and engagement outcomes [11][12];
- the web-based inquiry learning system study showing significantly better standardized exam performance with scaffolded tools [13];
- the preschool scaffolding study showing adaptive prompts with modeling improved some reasoning outcomes while prompts alone had mixed results [31];
- the scientific competency diagnostic and personalized ITS study using 847 students and arguing automated feedback and adaptive assessment improve scientific competency and evaluation consistency [17][19];
- the K-12 science education review stating ITS can provide immediate personalized feedback and enhance learning outcomes while maintaining motivation and interest [6].

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

- Direct evidence for Khanmigo in K-12 science learning outcomes and implementation artifacts appears limited in the retrieved academic database results. The most direct relevant statement found was: “Khan Academy, a non-profit educational organization, is implementing a pilot initiative to provide Khanmigo AI to over 8,000 K-12 teachers and students. According to the project description provided by Khan Academy, Khanmigo is built around the underpinned version of the LLM of OpenAI's GPT-4, which has been trained using educational materials sourced from Khan Academy. To enhance the personalized and helpful response tone of Khanmigo, as well as to mitigate the speedy provision of responses to students, additional parameters have been included in the product (Khan Academy, 2023).” This came from a review paper snippet and is the clearest direct implementation artifact statement located in the search thread [1].

- Another directly relevant implementation statement was: “Khanmigo is an artificial intelligence (AI)-based guide developed by Khan Academy, a non-profit educational organization. Khanmigo aims to replicate the one-on-one tutoring experience by providing customized support, encouraging critical thinking, and suggesting relevant resources. Khanmigo can also help teachers with lesson planning and providing feedback to students. Khanmigo is still in the experimental stage and can only be accessed by a limited number of users who meet certain requirements. Khanmigo can be used to help students as a virtual tutor and as a debate partner. Teachers can also access it to generate lesson plans and help with other administrative tasks. Part of the purpose of the pilot launch is to determine what the demand is for the tutor and how educators and students are using it.” This is a strong implementation-artifact statement, but it is from a non-primary source paper discussing GPT-4 / Khanmigo [2].

- The most direct academic evidence specifically naming Khanmigo and the classroom was from the OpenAlex / arXiv item titled “Would You Want an AI Tutor?” Understanding Stakeholder Perceptions of LLM-based Systems in the Classroom. The snippet stated: “We highlighted how the introduction of LLMbased tools, such as Khanmigo, in the classroom has followed a top-down decision-making process, where partnerships between private companies and governmental institutions or school districts often make decisions on behalf of direct stakeholders, such as teachers and students, or indirect stakeholders, such as parents and school staff.” This is directly relevant to implementation context, but it is not K-12 science-specific and is stakeholder/perception-focused rather than outcome-focused [3].

- The openai_web_search returned non-peer-reviewed but directly implementation-related artifacts from Khan Academy support pages: “In January 2026, Khan Academy introduced six reports within the Khanmigo Classroom Pilot to assist teachers in monitoring student progress:
  1. Activity Report: Offers interactive and customizable metrics, including learning time, skill comprehension, and mastery levels.
  2. Skills Report: Displays students’ mastery levels across various skills.
  3. Assignments Report: Provides scores and completion data for individual assignments.
  4. Khanmigo Usage Report: Details the number of Khanmigo interactions, flagged chats, message counts per conversation, and activity usage.”
  These were described as tools that aim to empower teachers with data-driven insights to tailor instruction effectively [4].

- The openai_web_search also returned a second support-page style description of Khanmigo implementation artifacts: “Khanmigo Usage Report” and “Khanmigo Activity Report” for administrators, and a classroom pilot report set including “Activity Report,” “Skills Report,” “Assignments Report,” “Khanmigo Usage Report,” “Khanmigo Activity Report,” and “Assignment Completion Report.” The message also stated that Khan Academy has developed “a framework for responsible AI in education” emphasizing “transparency and user privacy.” These are implementation artifacts, but not direct learning outcome studies [5].

However, several resources provide insights into the integration and usage of Khanmigo within educational settings.” It then listed the administrator reports and classroom pilot reports noted above and concluded: “While these resources offer valuable insights into Khanmigo's implementation and usage, a specific, publicly available report focusing solely on its application in K-12 science education is not currently accessible.” This is a direct statement about the evidence gap [6].

- The search thread also surfaced a non-Khanmigo but directly Khan Academy / K-12 related result from ERIC: “Leveraging ‘Khanmigo’ Generative AI-Powered Tool for Personalized Tutoring to Learn Scientific Concepts” (EJ1487444), described as a mixed-methods study of generative AI-powered intelligent tutoring systems in undergraduate physics education comparing Khanmigo and Google search. This is not K-12, but it is the closest explicit Khanmigo learning-outcome study retrieved in the database searches [7].

- Another directly Khanmigo-relevant OpenAlex snippet in the search thread was from a 2023/2025 AI-in-education paper stating: “Khanmigo is an artificial intelligence (AI)-based guide developed by Khan Academy, a non-profit educational organization. Khanmigo is still in the experimental stage and can only be accessed by a limited number of users who meet certain requirements. Khanmigo can be used to help students as a virtual tutor and as a debate partner. Teachers can also access it to generate lesson plans and help with other administrative tasks. ## Executive Summary

The central finding is straightforward: no direct empirical evidence was located in the provided source pool showing that Khanmigo improves K-12 science learning outcomes. Specifically, the pool contains no Khanmigo-specific randomized controlled trial, quasi-experimental study, observational study, or implementation study measuring K-12 science achievement, conceptual understanding, scientific reasoning, science vocabulary, inquiry skills, retention, engagement, or assignment performance. The core question therefore remains unresolved for the focal intervention itself. The most defensible conclusion is narrower: expectations about Khanmigo in K-12 science must currently be inferred from adjacent evidence on intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), AI-enabled personalized learning, generative-AI science supports, and LLM-based tutoring prototypes rather than from intervention-specific evaluation. That adjacent evidence is cautiously promising for some structured AI tutoring approaches, but it is heterogeneous by domain, age group, comparator, and tool architecture, and it should not be treated as proof of Khanmigo’s effectiveness in K-12 science [1]; [3]; [4]; [14]; [22]; [18].

The strongest experimental evidence in the pool comes from adjacent, not Khanmigo-specific, studies. In BEETLE II, an undergraduate science tutoring experiment, a natural-language tutoring curriculum in electricity and electronics produced a large learning gain versus no-training control, d=1.72, with n=114 analyzed; however, the study could not show that dynamically generated NLP feedback outperformed a non-NLP version of the same curriculum, indicating that the benefit may have come from the structured curriculum and simulation environment rather than the language-generation component alone [19]. In a small RCT on personalized science text rewriting for middle-school-age learners, students exposed to GPT-4-personalized science paragraphs were more likely to select the personalized version, g=0.715, n=23; this supports feasibility and preference for science personalization but does not establish science learning gains on curriculum assessments [33]. In a high-school physics RCT, Physics-STAR outperformed generic GPT-4o tutoring and teacher-led review on physics understanding, with n=12, and also shortened completion time on information-based questions, but the source pool does not report an exact effect size, so the result is suggestive rather than conclusive [34]. Outside science, a K-12 RCT found that AI-driven ITS interface changes increased engagement by up to 25.13% in one A/B test (n=2,877) and up to 12.57% in another (n=19,164), showing that design features can materially alter uptake even when core tutoring functions are unchanged [20]. A 2025 elementary RCT in mathematics found that an adaptive ITS improved learning, with the adaptive condition outperforming a predefined sequence at η²=0.034, n=265, and choice features improved emotional experience at η²=0.044 [38]. Meta-analytic and systematic review evidence broadly indicates that ITS and AI-enabled personalized STEM supports often produce positive learning effects, but the brief summaries in the source pool do not report pooled effect sizes for the main K-12 ITS and science reviews, so exact quantitative synthesis for the target question cannot be extracted here [1]; [4]; [3].

Quasi-experimental and observationally oriented adjacent evidence both supports and complicates the experimental picture. Reviews of AI in STEM education, AI-supported personalized learning, tutoring systems, and K-12 generative AI consistently report benefits such as personalization, timely feedback, and support for practice, but they also emphasize uneven evidence quality, strong contextual dependence, and implementation risks including ethics, teacher roles, and overgeneralization from narrow prototypes [14]; [6]; [9]; [35]; [22]. The closest domain-specific synthesis, a 2025 systematic review of generative AI in science education, indicates growing interest in middle- and secondary-school science applications but also implies that rigorous outcome evidence remains limited and recent [3]. A QED on AI-assisted writing feedback in secondary education and a QED on generative-AI-supported programming education show that AI can improve some performance outcomes in non-science domains under classroom conditions, but these are indirect analogues and cannot establish science effects for Khanmigo [25]; [42]. An adult RCT on GPT-based reading supports further complicates expectations by showing differential effects: lower-performing readers benefited from summaries, d=0.45, n=71, while higher-performing readers performed worse, d=0.83, n=124, suggesting that AI support can help some learners while undermining performance for others depending on task and baseline skill [46].

Across the tiered questions, Tier 1 is only partially answered: Khanmigo can be situated within the literature as an LLM-based conversational tutoring or learning-support tool, but the source pool does not provide a science-specific scholarly definition or stable usage model for Khanmigo itself in K-12 settings [18]; [22]; [9]. Tier 2 is partially answered: baseline comparators in adjacent studies typically include standard instruction, teacher-led review, no-training controls, generic GPT tutoring, predefined tutoring sequences, and other non-personalized digital conditions [19]; [34]; [38]; [43]. Tier 3 is partially answered by analogue evidence: outcomes appear most plausible when AI supports are structured, curriculum-linked, adaptive, and teacher-mediated rather than open-ended, and when they provide targeted scaffolding, personalized questioning, and immediate feedback [14]; [43]; [32]; [47]. Tier 4, the priority question on direct comparative impact of Khanmigo on K-12 science outcomes, is unresolved: no direct evidence was found, subgroup variation is unknown, and risks such as inaccurate science explanations, overreliance, and inequitable access are not empirically established for Khanmigo in the target population within this pool [22]; [18]; [4].

Overall confidence is low for any claim that Khanmigo itself improves K-12 science learning outcomes, because the intervention-specific evidence base is absent. Confidence is moderate that some AI tutoring approaches can improve learning or engagement under constrained conditions, especially when the system is highly structured and aligned to a narrow task, but that inference is extrapolative rather than product-specific [19]; [38]; [32]; [1]. The single most important caveat is architectural and contextual mismatch: classic ITS evidence often comes from tightly bounded domains with explicit knowledge models and controlled feedback, whereas Khanmigo is a generative, conversational tool whose effects in open-ended K-12 science use may differ substantially from those of traditional ITS or small research prototypes [1]; [18]; [35].

## Defining the Intervention and the Scope of Available Evidence

The provided source pool does not contain a direct evaluative study of Khanmigo in K-12 science. As a result, Khanmigo can only be positioned indirectly within the broader literature on LLMs in education, generative AI in K-12, AI-enabled personalized learning, and tutoring systems. These reviews generally frame LLM-based educational tools as conversational systems that can provide explanations, hints, feedback, personalization, and tutoring-like dialogue, but they also note that the literature is still emergent and often descriptive rather than evaluative [18]; [22]; [4]; [35]; [9]. That framing is compatible with describing Khanmigo as an AI-assisted tutoring or chat-based instructional support tool, but the pool does not establish a science-specific operational definition for Khanmigo itself.

The most relevant outcome domains for the brief—science achievement, conceptual understanding, scientific reasoning, science vocabulary, inquiry skills, retention, engagement, and assignment performance—are also not measured directly for Khanmigo in this pool. Instead, adjacent science and AI tutoring studies operationalize nearby constructs in varied ways: post-test learning in electricity/electronics [19], preference for personalized science text [33], physics understanding and task completion time [34], learning-related performance and skip rates in an ITS [43], and engagement metrics such as conversion and revenue proxies in a large-scale educational platform A/B test [20]. Reviews of AI in STEM and science education further indicate that outcomes in this literature are commonly fragmented across achievement, engagement, self-regulation, and usability rather than consistently aligned to science standards or inquiry constructs [14]; [3]; [35].

Population coverage is similarly uneven. The source pool includes elementary, middle, and high school populations in broad reviews of ITS, STEM AI, K-12 generative AI, and tutoring systems [1]; [14]; [22]; [9]. Yet the most science-specific experimental analogues are not evenly distributed across K-12: one study concerns middle-school-age science text personalization [33], another involves high-school physics [34], and the strongest science-tutoring RCT is in undergraduate electricity/electronics rather than K-12 [19]. There is no direct Khanmigo evidence for elementary science learners, multilingual science learners, students with disabilities, or under-resourced schools in the pool. Reviews on multilingual learners, teacher roles, and AI literacy identify these populations and implementation issues as important, but they do not provide Khanmigo-science outcome estimates [12]; [17]; [37].

## What Counts as the Counterfactual?

Because no Khanmigo-science evaluation is present, the comparator question must be answered through adjacent studies. In the strongest science tutoring RCT, BEETLE II compared two tutoring conditions with a no-training control; this gives a clean counterfactual for the value of a structured tutoring curriculum, but not for Khanmigo specifically [19]. In the high-school physics study, the LLM-powered tutoring system was compared against both generic GPT-4o tutoring and traditional teacher-led review, which is directly relevant to the brief’s likely comparators, though the sample was only n=12 and exact effect sizes are not reported in the source pool [34]. In the middle-school science text personalization experiment, the comparison was between experimental and control text conditions rather than between tutoring systems or instruction types [33].

Outside science, adjacent tutoring studies suggest what counterfactuals are common in AI-learning research. The elementary math RCT compared adaptive sequencing and learner-choice conditions against predefined tutoring sequences, showing that AI adaptivity is often evaluated against a digital-but-less-adaptive baseline rather than against teacher-only instruction [38]. The question-personalization study compared expected-variant personalized questions, non-expected variants, and control conditions over two months with more than 400 students, again using within-system alternatives as the counterfactual rather than a fully non-digital condition [43]. The personalized XAI study compared an ITS with explanations versus the same ITS without explanations, yielding d=.12 on learning and ηp²=.28 on trust-related outcomes, which is informative about feature-level mechanisms but not about whether any ITS is better than standard classroom instruction [47].

The review literature reinforces this point. Systematic reviews of ITS, AI-enabled personalized STEM education, and tutoring systems describe a field in which counterfactuals vary widely: no-treatment, business-as-usual instruction, alternate digital tools, different versions of the same AI system, or teacher-mediated support [1]; [4]; [9]. That heterogeneity matters because it limits transportability to Khanmigo. A finding that one adaptive feature improves learning over a weaker digital baseline does not show that a conversational LLM tutor will outperform well-implemented teacher-led science instruction. Reviews of differentiated instruction, gamification, and science game-based learning likewise indicate that implementation and comparator choice strongly shape observed effects, making direct extrapolation from “AI versus control” summaries risky [15]; [21]; [28].

## Direct Evidence on Khanmigo and Why the Core Question Remains Unresolved

No direct empirical study in the source pool evaluates Khanmigo in K-12 science. There is no RCT, QED, observational analysis, usage-log study, or classroom implementation report measuring science outcomes for K-12 Khanmigo users. This means the core priority question—whether Khanmigo improves K-12 science learning outcomes relative to standard instruction, teacher-led instruction without Khanmigo, conventional homework support, non-AI tutoring, or other digital tools—cannot be answered from the current evidence base.

This absence is more than a missing RCT. The pool also lacks weaker but still informative designs for the focal intervention: no quasi-experimental science classroom study, no district implementation study with pre/post science measures, no subgroup analysis by grade band or language status, and no longitudinal retention study for Khanmigo. Reviews of generative AI in K-12 and science education document fast-growing interest in these tools, but they also suggest that rigorous school-based evidence remains limited and uneven [22]; [3]. Broader surveys of LLMs in education similarly highlight the field’s rapid expansion but warn that many claims are ahead of robust classroom evidence [18]; [4].

The practical implication is that any statement about Khanmigo’s likely science impact must be framed as extrapolation. Reviews of AI-supported personalized learning, AI-enabled personalized teaching, and AI in education describe plausible mechanisms—personalized explanations, immediate feedback, scalable practice, adaptive questioning—but they do not establish that a particular commercial conversational tutor produces gains in K-12 science [35]; [4]; [36]; [27]. The report therefore treats adjacent evidence as boundary-setting rather than confirmatory.

## Closest Science-Specific Experimental Analogues

### BEETLE II: Structured Science Tutoring With Dialogue and Simulation

Dzikovska et al. studied BEETLE II, an intelligent tutoring curriculum for basic electricity and electronics that combined simulation with reflective dialogue (Design: Randomized Controlled Trial, n=114 analyzed) [19]. The intervention produced substantial pre- to post-test gains compared with a no-training control, d=1.72 [19]. This is the strongest science-tutoring causal result in the pool. However, the population was undergraduate, not K-12, and the domain was tightly bounded. Crucially, the study could not demonstrate that dynamically generated NLP feedback was superior to non-NLP feedback between the two treatment versions (n=73 analyzed across the two active conditions) [19]. For Khanmigo, that distinction is central: the evidence supports a structured science tutoring environment, but not a conclusion that free-form language generation itself is the active ingredient.

### Personalized Science Text for Middle-School-Age Learners

The science-personalization study tested whether GPT-4 could personalize science texts for diverse middle-school-age learners (Design: Randomized Controlled Trial, n=23) [33]. Students in the experimental group were more likely to select the GPT-4 rewritten science paragraph aligned with their profile, with g=0.715 [33]. This is one of the few K-12 science-adjacent experiments involving an LLM. Yet the reported outcome is selection or preference for personalized text, not science mastery, reasoning, vocabulary acquisition, or inquiry performance. The study therefore supports feasibility of personalization, not effectiveness on the brief’s target outcomes.

### LLM-Powered Tutoring in High-School Physics

The Physics-STAR study examined an LLM-powered tutoring system in physics education (Design: Randomized Controlled Trial, n=12) [34]. The source pool reports that Physics-STAR outperformed both generic GPT-4o tutoring and traditional teacher-led review on physics understanding, especially for information-based problems, and that it shortened completion time on informational items, with mean post-test completion time M=257s for Physics-STAR versus longer times in comparison groups [34]. The study also reports improvements in deep learning, reflective learning, and critical thinking, though exact effect sizes are not provided in the source pool [34]. This is the closest analogue to Khanmigo in secondary science, but the evidence is highly preliminary because the sample is extremely small and the missing exact effect statistics constrain interpretation.

### Science-Linked but Not Science-Outcome Evidence

The SRSD Plus trial for first- and second-grade students used close reading of science texts to support informative writing (Design: Randomized Controlled Trial, n=93; posttest n=90) (Ray, 2023). The intervention produced large effects on writing quality, d=1.02, and planning/discourse knowledge, d=1.40, but the authors did not assess science content mastery directly; the nearest science-related outcome was expository text quality, d=0.48 (Ray, 2023). This study is relevant only as an example of science-text-mediated learning tasks, not as evidence that AI tutoring improves science learning.

Taken together, the science-specific experimental evidence is promising in narrow contexts but insufficient for strong inference about Khanmigo. The strongest positive result is non-K-12 and may owe more to structured tutoring design than to generative dialogue alone [19]. The closest K-12 LLM studies are either too small, focused on preference rather than learning, or lack exact reported effect sizes [33]; [34].

## Broader K-12 ITS and AI-Personalization Evidence Relevant to Expected Effects

The most relevant broad synthesis is the K-12 ITS meta-analysis for U.S. students (Design: Meta-Analysis / Systematic Review) [1]. Its summary states that it evaluates whether intelligent tutoring systems benefit K-12 students and examines heterogeneity of treatment effects by population, study quality, intervention, and context [1]. Because the source pool does not provide the pooled effect size, the review can support only the general claim that the field has sufficient studies for meta-analytic assessment, not a specific estimate for likely impact. Even so, its focus on heterogeneity is important for the Khanmigo question because it implies that average effects may conceal strong variation by implementation, learner group, and comparator [1].

The 2025 meta-analysis of AI-enabled personalized STEM education in schools similarly addresses the overall impact of AI-supported personalized learning and the conditions under which effects vary [4]. Again, the source pool does not report the pooled effect size, so no exact average can be stated. The review is still useful for showing that the evidence base spans school STEM settings rather than only higher education [4]. Complementary reviews of AI-based personalised learning, AI-enabled personalised teaching, and personalized learning through AI underscore recurring themes: personalization, adaptation, feedback, and learner modeling are treated as promising mechanisms, but study quality and implementation detail are often weak or inconsistent [35]; [36]; [6].

More descriptive reviews reach similar conclusions with less direct evidential weight. Reviews of AI in STEM education, AI in education broadly, tutoring systems, and intelligent tutoring systems toward sustainable education all describe a long-standing literature in which AI systems can support practice, feedback, and differentiated learning pathways, but they also emphasize ethical issues, data needs, design complexity, and uneven pedagogical integration [14]; [27]; [9]; [24]. These reviews support the interpretation that Khanmigo belongs to a family of tools with plausible educational affordances, but they do not resolve whether those affordances translate into science learning gains in K-12 classrooms.

A narrower subgroup review examines ITS effectiveness for multilingual learners in secondary education [12]. Although the source pool does not provide quantitative results, the review is relevant because science learning often depends heavily on language comprehension, academic vocabulary, and disciplinary explanation. Its inclusion signals that language background may moderate AI tutoring effectiveness, but the lack of Khanmigo-specific science evidence means no subgroup claim can be made for the focal tool [12].

## Experimental Evidence on Mechanisms That May Matter for Khanmigo

### Adaptivity and Sequencing

The 2025 elementary mathematics study tested whether an AI-driven ITS with adaptive sequencing and learner choice improves learning and motivation (Design: Randomized Controlled Trial, n=265) [38]. In this four-arm trial, the ITS improved math learning from pre- to post-test, and the adaptive ZPDES condition outperformed the predefined sequence with η²=0.034 [38]. Choice improved emotional valence, η²=0.044, and showed a motivation trend, η²=0.013 [38]. Although the domain is mathematics rather than science, the result is highly relevant to mechanism: structured adaptivity and limited learner agency can matter, and the magnitude appears modest rather than transformative. For Khanmigo, this implies that any benefit may depend less on mere conversational access and more on how the tool sequences challenge and choices.

A later adaptive-scaffolding study tested worked-example selection based on cognitive engagement and mastery estimates (Design: Randomized Controlled Trial, N=113 enrolled; completers Control 36, BKT 35, DRL 42) [32]. Both adaptive policies significantly improved posttest outcomes with A=.58 and confidence intervals reported for each adaptive condition, and they improved efficiency measures such as time and steps with A=.58 for BKT time and A=.56 for DRL time/steps compared with control [32]. This study is undergraduate and not science-specific in the source summary, but it supports a mechanism that matters for Khanmigo-like systems: adaptivity grounded in engagement or mastery estimates may improve both learning and efficiency more reliably than unconstrained conversation.

### Personalization of Questions and Explanations

The question-personalization study examined whether adapting question phrasing to student proficiency in an ITS improves outcomes (Design: Randomized Controlled Trial; over 400 students, expected n=190, non-expected n=139, control n=141) [43]. Over a two-month A/B test, personalized question phrasing improved learning-related performance and lowered skip rates relative to comparison conditions [43]. Exact effect sizes are not reported in the source pool, but the study indicates that relatively small linguistic changes in prompts can influence both learning and engagement. This is directly relevant to Khanmigo because an LLM tutor’s prompt framing, not only its content, may shape student persistence and understanding.

The personalized XAI study compared an ITS with explanations versus without explanations for learning the AC-3 algorithm (Design: Randomized Controlled Trial, n=41) [47]. Learning differences were small, d=.12, but explanation functionality improved trust, perceived usefulness, and intention to use, ηp²=.28 [47]. This suggests that explainability features may matter more for acceptance and help-seeking than for immediate achievement. For science settings, that implies a possible tradeoff: students may like and trust a system that explains itself, but such trust does not automatically translate into larger learning gains.

### Interface and Engagement Design

The AI-driven interface design study tested whether interface expressiveness and explainability improve engagement in an ITS (Design: Randomized Controlled Trial, n=2,877 in one A/B test and n=19,164 in another) [20]. Adding a radar chart increased conversion from 5.25% to 6.26% and produced up to a 25.13% increase; a second test showed up to a 12.57% increase with a more informative design [20]. These are not learning outcomes, but they matter because Khanmigo’s likely effectiveness in homework or blended learning depends partly on whether students actually use it. The study suggests that feature and interface design can strongly affect uptake independently of the tutoring algorithm.

### Retrieval and Grounding

The KG-RAG study compared knowledge-graph-enhanced retrieval-augmented generation with standard RAG (Design: Randomized Controlled Trial, n=76) [31]. First-year university students using KG-RAG scored higher on a post-interaction assessment, M=6.37 (SD=1.92) versus M=4.71, with d=0.86 [31]. This is not K-12 science, but it is highly relevant to Khanmigo’s likely boundary conditions because grounded retrieval and preservation of conceptual relationships can mitigate one known weakness of free-form LLM tutoring: concept drift or factual inaccuracy. The result supports a hypothesis that science tutoring may work better when the model is constrained by structured knowledge sources.

## Evidence on Risks, Heterogeneity, and Why Open-Ended AI Support May Not Help Everyone

The adult reading-comprehension RCT provides one of the clearest demonstrations of heterogeneous AI effects (Design: Randomized Controlled Trial) [46]. For lower-performing participants, the GPT-based summary tool improved quiz accuracy from 44.9% (SD 15.8) in control to 55.4% (SD 18.7), d=0.45, n=71 [46]. For higher-performing participants, the same tool worsened comprehension from 82.5% (SD 10.5) in control to 66.5% (SD 18.4), d=0.83, n=124 [46]. The SAT/ACT-based subgroup split showed no significant effect for lower performers [46]. Although this is not a K-12 science study, it is directly relevant to Khanmigo expectations: AI supports can produce opposite effects across learner groups, perhaps by reducing desirable struggle or encouraging overreliance among stronger students.

The programming-feedback RCT likewise suggests that AI assistance can help on supported tasks without generalizing cleanly to unsupported tasks (Design: Randomized Controlled Trial, n=93 active submitters) [39]. Students performed better on the 38 tasks where GPT hints were available, but on eight harder tasks where hints were unavailable, the control group initially outperformed the experimental group during the first six attempts [39]. There was no significant time advantage when GPT hints were available across 1,784 successful submissions [39]. This pattern raises a caution relevant to science homework help: students may perform better when assisted, yet transfer or independence may not improve in parallel.

Reviews of generative AI in K-12, LLMs in education, and large language models in learning environments repeatedly point to risks around accuracy, authenticity, assessment, and overreliance [22]; [18]; [29]; [41]. The science-specific risk is especially important because inaccurate explanations can reinforce misconceptions rather than correct them. However, the source pool does not provide a Khanmigo-specific empirical estimate of hallucination or error rates in K-12 science. This gap should materially lower confidence in claims about safe autonomous use.

Teacher-facing reviews add a second layer of caution. The systematic review on AI for teachers finds that teacher roles, data use, and classroom integration are central and often under-specified [17]. Reviews of AI applications in higher education note that educators are often marginal in the research design, even though their mediation shapes pedagogy and ethics [23]; [44]. For Khanmigo in science, this implies that teacher facilitation is likely not optional implementation detail but a core moderator.

## What Baseline Science Support Looks Like Without Khanmigo

The brief asks how science learning is typically supported without Khanmigo. The source pool does not contain a direct synthesis of ordinary K-12 science instruction, but comparator conditions in relevant studies provide some evidence. Teacher-led review appears explicitly in the high-school physics tutoring experiment [34]. No-training control appears in BEETLE II [19]. Business-as-usual writing workshop appears in the science-text-linked SRSD study (Ray, 2023). Predefined or non-adaptive tutoring sequences appear in the elementary ITS trial [38]. These counterfactuals suggest that, in adjacent literature, AI tutoring is often benchmarked against standard teacher instruction, no additional support, or less adaptive digital practice rather than against full-featured human tutoring.

Broader instructional reviews help contextualize the non-AI baseline. The differentiated-instruction review suggests that tailoring instruction in secondary education is complex and variably operationalized, which matters because AI tools are often marketed as scalable differentiation engines [15]. The concept-mapping review emphasizes that science learning often benefits from tools that help students integrate complex ideas and represent relationships explicitly [16]. The review of value-added digital game-based learning in K-12 science highlights that design mechanisms, not merely digital delivery, influence science engagement and learning [28]. The gamification review similarly warns that motivational affordances should not be assumed to produce robust learning gains on their own [21]. These literatures imply that Khanmigo should be compared not only to “no AI” but also to established structured supports such as concept mapping, guided inquiry, differentiated tasks, and carefully designed science games.

## How the Intervention Is Implemented in Practice: What the Evidence Can and Cannot Say

There is no direct empirical implementation study of Khanmigo in K-12 science in the source pool. Therefore, the report cannot state how science teachers actually deploy Khanmigo for prompts, misconceptions, labs, homework, or formative assessment. No source here reports dosage, assignment design, frequency of use, prompt libraries, or teacher monitoring protocols for Khanmigo science use. This is a major Tier 3 gap.

Adjacent evidence nevertheless suggests several implementation features likely to matter. First, structure matters. BEETLE II paired dialogue with a simulator and a fixed science curriculum rather than relying on unconstrained chat [19]. Physics-STAR appears to have used a prompting structure designed to deepen reasoning on information-rich physics tasks rather than generic open prompting [34]. KG-RAG improved outcomes relative to standard RAG by grounding responses in a knowledge graph, indicating that stronger content constraints can improve instructional quality [31]. Across reviews of tutoring systems and AI-supported personalized learning, effective systems are generally described as tightly integrated with tasks, models of learner knowledge, and pedagogical decisions rather than as free-form assistants [9]; [35]; [6].

Second, teacher mediation likely matters. The review on AI for teachers emphasizes that benefits and challenges depend on how teachers interpret data, supervise use, and incorporate AI into pedagogy [17]. The K-12 generative AI review and LLM survey both suggest that classroom use of generative systems raises issues of monitoring, age-appropriate scaffolding, and curricular alignment [22]; [18]. Science is a domain where explanation accuracy, evidence use, and misconception repair are central, so teacher oversight may be particularly important. Yet no direct Khanmigo-science study in the pool tests teacher-mediated versus student-alone use.

Third, language and task design likely moderate outcomes. Personalized question wording improved learning-related performance and reduced skipping in an ITS [43]. Interface design changed engagement materially [20]. Explanation features changed trust more than learning [47]. Reviews focused on multilingual learners and AI literacy indicate that language load, disciplinary vocabulary, and digital competence can influence whether AI assistance helps or confuses learners [12]; [37]. For science, that points toward careful prompt engineering, bounded tasks, and explicit teacher framing rather than generic chatbot access.

## How Effects Vary Across Populations, Designs, and Conditions

The effect-size picture is uneven because direct Khanmigo evidence is absent and many reviews do not report pooled estimates in the source pool. Still, several patterns emerge.

By design, the largest science-learning effect in the pool comes from a tightly structured RCT in undergraduate electricity and electronics, d=1.72 against a no-training control [19]. More feature-level or personalization-level studies show smaller or more qualified effects: d=.12 for learning with explanations in an ITS [47], η²=0.034 for adaptive versus predefined sequencing in an elementary math ITS [38], and g=0.715 for selecting personalized science text rather than demonstrating learning gains [33]. This suggests a likely pattern: large effects may be more plausible when the intervention is a full curriculum or tutoring environment compared with weak controls, while incremental feature changes within a system tend to produce smaller gains.

By population, the limited evidence suggests heterogeneity rather than uniform benefit. Elementary learners benefited from adaptive ITS sequencing in mathematics [38]. Middle-school-age learners preferred personalized science texts [33]. High-school students in a tiny physics study appeared to benefit from a specialized tutoring structure [34]. Adults showed sharply divergent comprehension effects from GPT summaries depending on prior performance [46]. The reviews of multilingual learners and K-12 generative AI further imply that learner characteristics and context likely condition outcomes, but exact subgroup effects are not available for Khanmigo or for most science applications [12]; [22].

By implementation condition, studies suggest that adaptivity, grounding, and constrained support outperform looser alternatives. KG-RAG beat standard RAG at d=0.86 [31]. Adaptive worked-example selection beat control with A=.58 [32]. Personalized question phrasing improved performance and engagement relative to less aligned conditions [43]. Physics-STAR outperformed generic GPT-4o tutoring and teacher review in a small high-school sample [34]. These findings collectively indicate that specialized pedagogical and technical design may matter more than the mere presence of AI.

By outcome type, the evidence is stronger for engagement and proximal task performance than for durable science learning. Large-scale A/B tests show sizable engagement gains from interface design [20]. Trust and intention-to-use benefits from explanations are clearer than achievement gains [47]. Supported-task performance can improve without clear transfer once support is removed [39]. The source pool provides almost no delayed post-test or retention data for science-relevant K-12 AI tutoring. Retention therefore remains unresolved.

## What the Reviews Say About Science Education Specifically

The 2025 systematic review of generative AI applications in science education is the most directly relevant synthesis to the brief [3]. According to the source summary, it focuses on how GAI affects student learning outcomes in science education, particularly in middle school. Its existence indicates that science-specific GenAI evidence is emerging, but the pool summary does not report pooled effect sizes, sample totals, or strong causal conclusions [3]. This limits its use to contextualization: the field is active enough to review, but not yet mature enough in the provided summary to support definitive quantitative claims about expected effect.

The broader STEM AI review similarly treats AI-STEM as a complex educational system rather than a set of isolated tools [14]. That framing is helpful because it cautions against reducing science learning to chatbot interaction alone; outcomes likely depend on curriculum, teacher practice, task design, and assessment alignment. Reviews of tutoring systems, virtual tutoring with GPT-3, and AI-supported personalized learning also suggest that tutoring efficacy is shaped by affordances such as feedback timing, domain modeling, dialogue quality, and pedagogical orchestration [9]; [7]; [35]. For science, where conceptual dependencies and misconceptions are central, these conditions may be especially consequential.

The review of value-added digital game-based learning in K-12 science offers a parallel lesson from another digital-support literature: what matters is not just the technology category but the value-added mechanism [28]. That logic likely transfers to AI tutoring. A Khanmigo implementation that provides generic answers may differ fundamentally from one that prompts prediction, explanation, evidence use, and reflection. The current source pool, however, does not document which of these mechanisms Khanmigo actually deploys in school science.

## Synthesis and Implications

The evidence does not justify a claim that Khanmigo has been shown to improve K-12 science learning outcomes. No direct study in the provided pool evaluates the focal intervention on the focal population and outcomes. The honest answer to the main brief is therefore that the intervention-specific evidence base is absent.

The adjacent evidence supports a more limited conclusion. AI tutoring can improve learning or engagement under some conditions, especially when the system is structured, domain-constrained, adaptive, and paired with strong pedagogical design [19]; [38]; [32]; [31]. Science-specific analogues suggest potential in personalized reading materials and specialized physics tutoring, but those studies are small or measure indirect outcomes [33]; [34]. Reviews of K-12 ITS, AI-enabled STEM personalization, and science GenAI describe a promising but heterogeneous field in which effects likely vary by comparator, domain, and implementation [1]; [4]; [3].

For schools and practitioners, the strongest practical implication is to avoid assuming that conversational AI alone will raise science achievement. If Khanmigo is used, the adjacent evidence suggests it should be embedded in structured, curriculum-aligned science tasks; bounded to prompting, explanation, and misconception-checking rather than answer substitution; and monitored closely by teachers [17]; [43]; [47]; [31]. Use cases that resemble the stronger analogue studies—guided problem solving, grounded content retrieval, scaffolded reasoning, personalized wording, and explicit instructional sequences—are more defensible than open-ended unsupervised homework help [19]; [34]; [32].

A second implication is assessment discipline. Because some AI tools improve engagement more readily than learning, and because effects may differ by prior achievement, schools should evaluate science use with direct outcome measures rather than usage enthusiasm alone [20]; [46]. Useful local metrics would include curriculum-aligned science quizzes, explanation quality, misconception correction, transfer to unsupported tasks, and subgroup analyses for multilingual learners and lower- versus higher-performing students. Without such measurement, positive adoption signals could mask neutral or even negative academic effects.

### Limitations and Research Gaps

The evidence base is limited first by intervention specificity: there is no direct Khanmigo study on K-12 science outcomes in the source pool. This leaves the primary question unanswered and forces reliance on indirect analogues. The report therefore cannot estimate Khanmigo’s effect size, identify the most responsive science topics, or determine whether benefits differ across elementary, middle, and high school science.

A second limitation is evidence-type mismatch. Much of the adjacent literature is composed of broad systematic reviews whose source-pool summaries do not report pooled effect sizes, or of studies in mathematics, writing, programming, and higher education rather than K-12 science [4]; [35]; [9]; [44]. These sources are useful for mechanisms and implementation hypotheses, but they do not directly establish science learning effects for Khanmigo.

A third limitation is study quality and scale within the most relevant analogue evidence. The high-school physics RCT has n=12 [34]. The middle-school science personalization study has n=23 and measures preference rather than achievement [33]. The strongest science tutoring RCT is undergraduate rather than K-12 [19]. Several reviews explicitly note heterogeneity, ethical concerns, and the need for better-designed studies [1]; [22]; [18].

Key research gaps are clear. First, direct Khanmigo evaluations are needed in K-12 science classrooms, homework contexts, and tutoring/blended-learning settings, using science outcomes aligned to conceptual understanding, scientific reasoning, vocabulary, inquiry, retention, and assignment quality. Second, studies should compare Khanmigo against meaningful counterfactuals: teacher-led review, standard digital homework support, non-AI tutoring, and other AI systems. Third, implementation moderators need direct study, including teacher mediation, dosage, curriculum alignment, prompt restrictions, and whether the system is grounded in vetted science content. Fourth, subgroup analyses are essential for grade band, multilingual learners, students with disabilities, prior achievement, and school resource context. Fifth, risk studies are needed on inaccurate science explanations, misconception reinforcement, overreliance, and transfer after support removal. Until such evidence exists, claims about Khanmigo in K-12 science should remain explicitly provisional and extrapolative rather than evidentially established [17]; [12]; [22]; [18].
