paper_profiles.title: AI-Powered Tools for Enhancing Writing Skills of English Language Learners: A Systematic Literature Review
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science (IJRISS)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the growing use of artificial intelligence tools to support English writing among English as a Second Language (ESL) and English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners. The review asks two main questions: which AI tools have been used to enhance writing skills, and how these tools improve different dimensions of writing. The authors argue that rapid AI development, especially since 2023, has outpaced earlier reviews and created a need for an updated synthesis.

Using PRISMA 2020 procedures, the authors systematically reviewed 31 studies published between 2021 and 2025 from ERIC and Web of Science. The included studies covered a range of methodologies and focused mainly on AI-powered writing tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, QuillBot, Gemini, and other automated writing evaluation or feedback systems. The synthesis examined outcomes across grammar and mechanics, vocabulary and style, feedback and revision, and narrative writing.

The reviewed evidence largely concerns student populations in ESL/EFL contexts, with a strong skew toward tertiary education and limited representation from primary and secondary settings. The paper notes that the included studies span varied sample sizes and designs, including mixed-methods, quasi-experimental, experimental, qualitative, and case studies. The review is not confined to one country; it synthesizes studies from multiple contexts, though a single study-country for the review itself is not specified beyond the authors’ institutional affiliation in Malaysia.

The main conclusion is that AI tools generally function as effective writing supports, especially for feedback and revision, grammar accuracy, and vocabulary development. ChatGPT was the most frequently studied tool, followed by Grammarly, QuillBot, and Gemini. The authors conclude that AI tools can improve ESL/EFL learners’ writing quality, but they also caution that AI should supplement rather than replace teachers, and that more longitudinal and non-tertiary research is needed to determine whether gains persist after the tools are removed.

paper_profiles.title: A qualitative systematic review on AI empowered self-regulated learning in higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how artificial intelligence applications are being used to support self-regulated learning (SRL) in higher education, and what benefits, drawbacks, theories, and implementation patterns appear in the empirical literature. The review is motivated by growing use of AI in higher education alongside a recognized need to connect these tools to established learning theory, especially SRL frameworks.

Using a qualitative systematic review guided by PRISMA, the authors identified 14 empirical studies on AI-supported SRL in higher education. The reviewed interventions included chatbots, explainable AI dashboards and evaluation systems, automated writing evaluation tools, serious games with intelligent tutoring features, and an AI-enriched e-textbook. Across studies, these tools were used to support different SRL phases such as goal setting, progress monitoring, help-seeking, feedback, and self-evaluation.

The evidence base covered university students in higher education contexts, with most studies involving STEM or language-learning tasks and a smaller number addressing non-academic areas such as communication skills and exam anxiety. The studies were geographically diverse, including work from China, Sweden, the United States, Germany, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Ukraine, Australia, Spain, Finland, and New Zealand. Because this is a review, no single implementation setting or duration applies consistently across all included studies.

The main conclusion is that AI shows promise for supporting SRL, especially in the performance phase through real-time guidance, monitoring, feedback, and help-seeking support. However, support is often partial rather than holistic across all SRL phases, and outcomes are mixed depending on tool design, learner characteristics, and the balance between human-centered and AI-centered regulation. The review also highlights concerns about usability, feedback accuracy, inconsistent gains in self-efficacy, and the need for stronger theory-building and more rigorous empirical research on AI-supported SRL.

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging Process-Action Epistemic Network Analysis to Illuminate Student Self-Regulated Learning with a Socratic Chatbot
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines how student interactions with a generative AI Socratic chatbot can be analyzed through a self-regulated learning (SRL) lens. The authors aimed to answer two questions: how chatbot conversations can be processed using an SRL framework, and how interaction patterns differ across student ability and learning-gain groups. The work is positioned as a learning analytics study focused on understanding, rather than definitively proving, how chatbot-supported learning relates to SRL behaviors.

The intervention was an in-house Socratic chatbot for an introductory undergraduate statistics course. Unlike answer-giving chatbots, it was prompt-engineered to respond with scaffolded questions that encourage students to reason through concepts independently. Students completed a pre-test, participated in a three-week pilot course using asynchronous blended learning with required chatbot interaction and online videos, and then completed a post-test. Chat logs were coded using a process-action SRL framework and analyzed with epistemic network analysis and ordered network analysis.

The study involved 34 undergraduate students in a three-week pilot class at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. The first week was onsite and the following two weeks were online, all conducted asynchronously, with no human tutor involved. Students interacted with the chatbot at their own pace while learning introductory statistics content.

The authors report significant pre-post score improvement overall, but the main findings concern behavioral differences in chatbot use. Higher-ability students showed more goal-setting, review, organization, and reflective/evaluative behaviors, whereas lower-ability students focused more on information searching. Students with higher learning gains were more likely to ask fundamental conceptual questions and seek examples, while medium-gain students were more likely to paste in problem statements and focus on complex problem solving. The paper concludes that learning analytics from chatbot interactions can reveal meaningful SRL patterns and can inform more adaptive chatbot prompting and scaffolding, though results should be interpreted cautiously given the pilot design and limited sample.

finding.finding_summary: In a sample of 34 undergraduates, post-course statistics test scores were significantly higher than pre-course scores following the 3-week course that included chatbot use. The mean gain was approximately 27.21 points (SD=21.18), with p<0.001 and a large within-sample effect size of about d≈1.28.
finding.measure: pre-course versus post-course statistics test score

finding.finding_summary: Interaction analyses indicated that higher-scoring students more often engaged in reflective and evaluative self-regulated learning activities, whereas lower-scoring students more often focused on searching for answers. No effect size was reported for these group differences.
finding.measure: SRL interaction patterns in chatbot conversations, including reflective/evaluative activities versus answer-searching behaviors

finding.finding_summary: Ordered epistemic network analysis suggested that learning-gain groups differed in their chatbot interaction patterns, with higher gains associated with more concept-questioning and example-seeking behaviors. No numeric effect size was reported.
finding.measure: association between chatbot interaction behaviors and learning gains, especially concept-questioning and example-seeking behaviors

paper_profiles.title: Differential effects of GPT-based tools on comprehension of standardized passages
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examined whether GPT-based educational tools improve or hinder reading comprehension, and whether effects differ by students’ baseline ability. The authors note that AI tools are already widely used in education, but empirical evidence on their learning effects is limited. They focused on standardized reading comprehension as a foundational academic skill and tested whether AI support benefits lower-performing learners while potentially undermining higher-performing learners.

The intervention consisted of four GPT-4-based tools: an AI-generated summary, an AI-generated outline, a Q&A tutor chatbot, and a Socratic discussion chatbot. In a pre-registered randomized within-subject cross-over online experiment, participants completed five ACT-style reading comprehension conditions in a single session: four AI-tool conditions and one no-AI control. Passage order and condition order were randomized, and comprehension was measured using standardized 10-item ACT-derived quizzes.

The population was 195 college-aged adults (ages 18–22) in the United States recruited through Prolific after exclusions from an initial 228 participants. The study took place online through a custom web portal and used standardized ACT reading passages. Participants were split into lower- and higher-performing groups primarily based on control-passage performance, with SAT/ACT scores used as a secondary validation split.

The main conclusion was that GPT-based tools had strongly differential effects by baseline performance. Across the control-based split, all four AI tools improved comprehension for lower-performing participants but reduced comprehension for higher-performing participants. The Socratic chatbot showed the largest gains for lower performers, while the summary tool produced the largest declines for higher performers. The authors conclude that AI tools may help struggling learners but that universal implementation could unintentionally harm stronger readers, so deployment should be targeted and tested cautiously.

finding.finding_summary: Using a subgroup split based on control-passage performance, the summary tool improved quiz accuracy for lower-performing participants: 55.4% (SD 18.7) with summary versus 44.9% (SD 15.8) in control, t(70)=3.8, p<0.001, d=0.45. The paper notes this positive pattern for lower performers was not robust across alternative subgroup definitions.
finding.measure: ACT-derived reading comprehension quiz accuracy

finding.finding_summary: Using the control-passage subgroup split, the summary tool worsened reading comprehension for higher-performing participants: 66.5% (SD 18.4) with summary versus 82.5% (SD 10.5) in control, t(123)=9.2, p<0.001, d=0.83.
finding.measure: ACT-derived reading comprehension quiz accuracy

finding.finding_summary: Using the SAT/ACT-based subgroup split, the summary tool did not significantly affect quiz performance for lower SAT/ACT performers: 61.5% (SD 18.3) with summary versus 66.2% (SD 22.9) in control.
finding.measure: ACT-derived reading comprehension quiz accuracy

paper_profiles.title: A Review of Virtual Tutoring Systems and Student Performance Analysis Using GPT-3
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how virtual tutoring systems, particularly those involving GPT-3 and related AI approaches, may support student performance and feedback in education. The review is guided by three questions: the advantages and disadvantages of virtual tutoring compared with face-to-face instruction, the effectiveness of GPT-3 for improving tutoring experiences and learning outcomes, and future directions for AI-driven tutoring and student performance analysis.

The intervention studied is not a single implemented program but the body of literature on virtual tutoring, online tutoring, AI in educational technology, and GPT-3 integration in education. The authors conducted a systematic review using keyword-based searches across databases including IEEE, Science Direct, Springer, Wiley, Google Scholar, PubMed, and SCOPUS for publications from 2017 to 2024. They report that 130 studies were excluded and six articles were retained for data extraction, with PRISMA adapted to structure the review.

The population covered across the included literature is mixed, spanning both K-12 and higher education students, including vulnerable children as well as university learners. The context is primarily online and virtual learning environments rather than face-to-face classrooms. The review also discusses implications for educators, especially around feedback, adaptive learning, automated assessment, and the use of student data to personalize instruction.

The main conclusions are that GPT-3 and AI-enabled virtual tutoring show promise for personalizing learning, increasing engagement, providing immediate feedback, and potentially improving student outcomes. At the same time, the authors emphasize important limitations and implementation concerns, including bias, privacy, cultural relevance, accessibility, and the need for human oversight. They conclude that GPT-3 should be used as an assistive tool alongside educators and call for more longitudinal, ethical, and context-sensitive research on scalable deployment.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that GPT-3 has potential to personalise learning experiences, provide real-time assistance, and generate personalised feedback, with existing studies described as suggesting benefits for student performance. The paper does not provide pooled effect sizes or direct quantitative estimates.
finding.measure: Student learning outcomes and performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that GPT-3-powered virtual tutors can create more dynamic and interactive educational experiences and may enhance student engagement. This claim is presented as a narrative synthesis without pooled quantitative evidence.
finding.measure: Student engagement in learning

finding.finding_summary: The review notes that GPT-3 can support automated grading and timely feedback, and that its language-processing capabilities enable prompt, individualised assistance in virtual learning environments. No quantitative efficiency metrics are reported.
finding.measure: Automated feedback and grading efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence Interventions in Mathematics Education: A Systematic Literature Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a systematic literature review of empirical studies published from 2020 to 2024 on artificial intelligence interventions in mathematics education. The review asks two main questions: what kinds of AI-based interventions are being used in mathematics classrooms, and what impact these interventions have on student outcomes such as academic performance, engagement, and personalization. The authors position the review as addressing a gap in prior work by focusing specifically on classroom-based mathematics applications rather than broader STEM or theoretical AI-in-education discussions.

The interventions reviewed include intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), adaptive learning platforms, AI-powered educational applications such as Photomath and ChatGPT, and a smaller number of other tools such as AI-supported virtual reality and AI engines for task personalization. Across the 14 included empirical studies, the review synthesizes findings on outcomes including mathematics achievement, problem-solving, engagement, and some teaching-related outcomes. The review follows PRISMA procedures, searched multiple databases, and included both quantitative and qualitative studies.

The reviewed studies span elementary through postsecondary education and were conducted across multiple countries, including the United States, Slovakia, Philippines, Israel, Spain, Nigeria, Argentina, Taiwan, South Korea, Sweden, and Jordan. Most studies focused on students, though some examined teachers or preservice teachers. The instructional context emphasized classroom-integrated AI tools in mathematics domains such as fractions, arithmetic, algebra, and pre-calculus, with intervention durations ranging from very short sessions to a full school year.

The review concludes that AI tools in mathematics education are generally promising, especially ITS and adaptive platforms used over sustained periods and aligned with instructional goals. Larger effects were associated with longer-duration interventions and with tools providing personalized instruction and real-time feedback; for example, Photomath and some adaptive systems showed moderate to large effects. At the same time, the authors stress that impact depends heavily on context, duration, and teacher involvement, and that shorter interventions or poorly integrated tools tend to show smaller or more limited gains. They also highlight ethical issues such as privacy, fairness, transparency, and the continuing importance of teachers in mediating AI use.

finding.finding_summary: In the reviewed randomized controlled trial, ALEKS showed no statistically significant effect on end-of-course algebra exam scores compared with the comparison condition.
finding.measure: End-of-course algebra exam scores

finding.finding_summary: In Shin (2022), integration of ITS tools including ALEKS was associated with moderate improvement in prospective teachers’ technological pedagogical content knowledge when the systems were positioned as instructional partners.
finding.measure: TPACK scores

finding.finding_summary: Most students benefited from ASSISTments, with 65-71% mastering key skills after initial ITS practice, but some subgroups showed wheel-spinning and needed additional support.
finding.measure: Skill mastery after initial practice

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Models (GPT) for automating feedback on programming assignments
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 31st International Conference on Computers in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language model-generated feedback can improve students’ work on programming assignments in an automated assessment environment. The authors focus on a core challenge in computer science education: providing personalized, constructive feedback on code is difficult because students can make many different kinds of syntax and logic errors, and there are multiple valid ways to solve a task. The study asks whether GPT-generated hints can improve performance, change how students use platform feedback, affect time to solve problems, and influence student affect.

The intervention was the integration of OpenAI’s GPT-3.5 via API into the RunCode platform to automatically generate personalized hints after incorrect programming submissions. Students in the experimental condition received GPT-generated explanations and debugging guidance for 38 of 46 object-oriented programming tasks, while the control group received only the platform’s standard feedback based on compiler and unit test results. For 8 more difficult transfer tasks, GPT hints were withheld from the experimental group to test downstream effects after prior exposure to GPT support.

The population consisted of second-semester computer science undergraduates at Warsaw University of Life Sciences in Poland taking a required object-oriented programming course in C#. A total of 132 consenting students were randomly assigned to control and experimental groups, though 93 submitted at least one solution during the 9-week study window. The intervention took place in an online automated coding environment already familiar to students, and platform use was voluntary and did not count toward course grades.

Students generally rated GPT hints as useful. Compared with controls, students with GPT access used the platform’s regular feedback less often yet showed better cumulative success rates on tasks where GPT hints were available. On later tasks without GPT hints, the experimental group solved assignments faster but was initially less likely to solve them correctly, suggesting some short-term over-reliance on GPT feedback before adapting. GPT hint availability did not significantly affect reported affective states. Overall, the findings suggest that LLM-generated feedback can support programming performance, while also raising implementation questions about dependency and generalizability.

finding.finding_summary: Students in the experimental group performed better on the 38 tasks where GPT hints were available, with a higher percentage of successful submissions across cumulative attempts than the control group. A linear mixed-effects model found a significant main effect of group, t(13)=5.38, p<0.001, while the group-by-attempt interaction was not significant, t(13)=-0.172, p=0.866.
finding.measure: percentage of successful programming submissions across cumulative attempts on tasks with GPT hints enabled

finding.finding_summary: On the 8 harder tasks where GPT hints were no longer available, the control group outperformed the experimental group during the first six attempts, but correctness rates were comparable from the seventh attempt onward. The linear mixed-effects model showed a significant group-by-attempt interaction, t(13)=7.13, p<0.001, indicating different performance trajectories between groups.
finding.measure: percentage of successful programming submissions across cumulative attempts on later tasks without GPT hints

finding.finding_summary: When GPT hints were available, group assignment was not a significant predictor of time needed to solve tasks. Rank-based regression showed no significant difference between conditions, t(89)=-0.24, p=0.811.
finding.measure: time needed to successfully solve assignments when GPT hints were available

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of ChatGPT as a Brainstorming Tool on Gifted Students’ Persuasive Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examined whether using ChatGPT 3.5 as a prewriting brainstorming tool could improve the persuasive writing of gifted university students. The authors were motivated by concerns that gifted students, despite strong writing ability, may struggle with idea generation because of perfectionism and pressure to meet high expectations. They also sought to understand whether any writing gains would persist over time and how students perceived ChatGPT as a brainstorming support.

The intervention involved explicit instruction in using ChatGPT 3.5 for brainstorming only, not for drafting, editing, or translation. Students practiced asking ChatGPT questions to generate arguments, supporting evidence, counterarguments, and ways to present ideas. During intervention sessions, students read a prompt, brainstormed with ChatGPT for 20 minutes, then the internet was turned off and notes were collected before they independently wrote persuasive essays. The study used an integrated single-subject design with multiple probes across multiple baselines, and also included a focus group on social validity.

Participants were five gifted senior students majoring in Arabic at Kuwait University, all female and native Arabic speakers; four were typically developing and one was twice exceptional (gifted with high-functioning autism and depression). The study took place in a quiet, unoccupied classroom at Kuwait University during the 2023–2024 academic year. Group A completed three baseline probes, four intervention points, and one maintenance session; Group B completed five baseline probes, four intervention points, and one maintenance session. Maintenance occurred 3 weeks after intervention.

Results showed clear improvements in persuasive essay quality for all five participants from baseline to intervention, with mean score increases ranging from 30.7% to 68.1%. Gains were especially strong in persuasive-writing components such as argument quality, supporting evidence, opposing viewpoints, and voice/tone, while more general writing mechanics changed little. Four participants improved slightly further at maintenance, and one maintained intervention-level performance. Focus group responses suggested students viewed ChatGPT as efficient, idea-rich, and useful for discussing sensitive topics, while also recognizing limits such as outdated information, repetition, and possible cultural bias. Overall, the study concludes that ChatGPT 3.5 can function as a useful complementary brainstorming tool for gifted students’ persuasive writing, but should be used alongside other sources rather than relied on exclusively.

finding.finding_summary: Across all five participants, mean persuasive essay quality scores increased from baseline to intervention after ChatGPT was introduced as a brainstorming tool. Reported mean score changes were Hajar 29 to 40 (+37.9%), Maryam 26 to 34 (+30.7%), Tahany 24 to 38 (+58.3%), Asma' 23 to 36 (+56.5%), and Retaj 22 to 37 (+68.1%); the percentage of non-overlapping data (PND) was 100% for all five participants, which the authors interpret as documenting effectiveness.
finding.measure: Overall quality score on persuasive essays using an adapted Persuasive Essay Rubric (0-48 scale)

finding.finding_summary: Maintenance data collected 3 weeks after intervention showed continued improvement for four participants and stable maintenance for one participant. Mean maintenance scores were Hajar 41 (+2.5% from intervention), Maryam 35 (+2.9%), Tahany 39 (+2.6%), Asma' 36 (0%; unchanged from intervention), and Retaj 39 (+5.4%).
finding.measure: Maintenance-phase overall quality score on persuasive essays using an adapted Persuasive Essay Rubric (0-48 scale)

finding.finding_summary: Across all five participants, mean persuasive essay quality scores increased from baseline to intervention after ChatGPT was introduced as a brainstorming tool. Reported mean score changes were Hajar 29 to 40 (+37.9%), Maryam 26 to 34 (+30.7%), Tahany 24 to 38 (+58.3%), Asma' 23 to 36 (+56.5%), and Retaj 22 to 37 (+68.1%); the percentage of non-overlapping data (PND) was 100% for all five participants, which the authors interpret as documenting effectiveness.
finding.measure: Overall quality score on persuasive essays using an adapted Persuasive Essay Rubric (0-48 scale)

paper_profiles.title: A meta-analysis of AI-enabled personalized STEM education in schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for quantitative evidence on the effectiveness of AI-enabled personalized STEM education in K-12 schools. Prior reviews had largely been qualitative or focused on narrower technologies, leaving unclear the overall impact of AI-supported personalized learning and the conditions under which it works best. The study therefore asks how effective AI-enabled personalized STEM education is in schools and which moderator variables explain differences in outcomes.

The authors conducted a meta-analysis following PRISMA procedures, synthesizing 99 effect sizes from 32 randomized controlled trial studies published between 2012 and 2024. The review focused on AI-enabled personalized learning interventions in school STEM subjects and coded moderators including school level, AI application type, personalized learning model, outcome type, subject area, and whether generative AI was used. The included AI applications spanned intelligent tutoring systems, personalized educational games, AR/VR, and other AI-supported tools.

The population was K-12 students across multiple school levels, including kindergarten, elementary, junior high, and senior high school, in school-based STEM learning contexts worldwide. Because this is a meta-analysis, the paper aggregates evidence across many settings rather than reporting a single intervention site or country. The focus is explicitly on student learning outcomes in school STEM education.

The main conclusion is that AI-enabled personalized STEM education produces a statistically significant small-to-medium positive effect overall compared with non-AI approaches (reported overall g = 0.455). The strongest effects were found for junior and senior high school students, AR/VR-based tools, and more learner-centered models that combine AI with classroom or collaborative pedagogies. Effects also varied by subject, with comprehensive courses showing the largest gains. By contrast, observed outcome type and generative-AI versus non-generative-AI status did not significantly moderate effects. The authors argue for evidence-based, pedagogically aligned integration of AI in K-12 STEM education.

paper_profiles.title: The role of AI assisted writing feedback in developing secondary students writing skills
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether AI-assisted writing feedback improves the writing performance of secondary-level English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students more than traditional teacher feedback alone. The authors focus on a common instructional problem in EFL writing classrooms: teachers often have limited time to provide detailed, individualized feedback, while students need frequent revision opportunities to improve grammar, vocabulary, coherence, and overall writing quality. The study also examines students’ perceptions of using an AI writing assistant as a feedback tool.

The intervention compared two feedback conditions over an 8-week period. The experimental group used Grammarly to receive immediate AI-generated feedback on drafts, including grammar, spelling, punctuation, word choice, style, sentence clarity, and coherence; after revision, the teacher also provided brief higher-order feedback. The control group followed a traditional process in which the teacher provided delayed written feedback on drafts. Both groups completed pre-test and post-test timed persuasive essays and followed the same writing curriculum with the same instructor. Writing was scored analytically across content, organization, language use, and mechanics by two independent EFL raters, and the experimental group also completed a post-study perception questionnaire.

Participants were 60 Turkish public high school students aged 15–17 enrolled in an EFL program, divided into an experimental group and a control group of 30 each. The study took place in a secondary school setting in Türkiye during regular class time, with use of the school computer lab for the AI tool. Students had little prior experience with AI-based writing tools, and parental consent was obtained because participants were minors.

The main conclusion is that AI-assisted feedback significantly improved students’ writing more than teacher-only feedback. The experimental group showed larger gains in total writing scores, especially in language use and organization, while both groups improved over time. Students also reported positive perceptions of the AI tool, including improved confidence and satisfaction with the feedback. The authors conclude that AI writing tools can effectively supplement secondary EFL writing instruction, particularly when combined with teacher guidance rather than used as a replacement for human feedback.

paper_profiles.title: How AI feedback supports lesson planning in vocational teacher education: a longitudinal intervention study using an analytical AI platform
paper_profiles.venue: Empirical Research in Vocational Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether an analytical AI feedback system can improve lesson planning in vocational teacher education. The authors focus on a practical problem in higher education: detailed, individualized feedback on complex lesson plans is valuable for student teachers but difficult for university instructors to provide consistently and at scale. The study asks whether AI-based feedback can support or outperform human feedback on key didactic planning dimensions, and whether using such a system also influences students’ motivation, AI literacy, attitudes toward AI, digital competence, and technology self-efficacy.

The intervention centers on EDDA, an analytical AI platform that analyzes uploaded lesson plans and teaching materials using a BERT-based model trained on coded lesson plans and textbook tasks. EDDA does not generate open-ended responses like a large language model; instead, it classifies lesson plans into predefined didactic categories and returns expert-level text and visual feedback tied to established criteria. In the study, the experimental group used EDDA throughout a semester and could also consult the university instructor to discuss the AI feedback, while the control group received human feedback only. Both groups completed the same lesson-planning tasks and theoretical coursework.

The population consisted of 103 master’s students in business education in Germany, working in small groups to design 90-minute vocational lessons. The intervention spanned a semester, with students iteratively incorporating six focal dimensions or principles into the same lesson plan: sustainability, process orientation, problem orientation, action orientation, individualization, and digitalization. Outcomes included coded analyses of lesson plans as well as repeated self-report surveys on AI literacy and related meta-dimensions.

The main conclusion is that analytical AI feedback can effectively supplement traditional instructor feedback and, on some lesson-planning dimensions, match or exceed human-only feedback. The experimental group showed advantages on selected planning aspects, including some sustainability-related dimensions, social competences for sustainable development, reflexivity, and several planning features highlighted in the abstract such as action orientation, relatedness, technology use, lesson structure, and learner engagement. However, simply using the AI platform did not automatically improve AI literacy, attitudes toward AI, or motivation. The authors therefore argue that analytical AI tools are promising for feedback in teacher education, but should be embedded in a broader, human-centered instructional framework rather than treated as a standalone solution.

paper_profiles.title: Current practices and future direction of artificial intelligence in mathematics education: A systematic review
paper_profiles.venue: International Electronic Journal of Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for a practical and up-to-date synthesis of how artificial intelligence is being used in mathematics education. The authors argue that prior reviews often focused on broad AI categories or research-stage systems, but gave less attention to specific, market-ready tools that educators could actually implement. The review therefore asks four main questions: how AI in mathematics education studies are distributed across educational levels, what AI tools are used and how they can be categorized, which commercialized tools are available online and what they do, and what emerging trends and future directions appear in the literature.

The study uses a systematic literature review approach. The authors searched Web of Science and Scopus for English-language journal articles published between 2019 and 2024, focused on AI in mathematics education. After screening and deduplication, 32 studies were included. The review categorizes AI tools into adaptive learning systems/intelligent tutoring systems, chatbots, augmented reality, virtual reality, learning analytics, serious games, and AI mathematics problem solvers. It also identifies named tools such as Khan Academy, Squirrel AI, ChatGPT, Bard, GeoGebra, GeoGebra AR, Photomath, Vuforia, and NeoTrieVR, and distinguishes between generative AI tools and pedagogical AI tools.

The population represented across the reviewed studies spans primary/elementary, middle/high school, university, and adult learners, with the largest share of studies at the middle/high school level, followed by university/adult and then primary levels. Because this is a review, the context is not one single intervention site but a synthesis of studies conducted across multiple countries, with especially strong representation from China, the United States, and Spain. The paper is situated in mathematics education broadly and examines both classroom-oriented and digital learning applications of AI.

The main conclusions are that AI in mathematics education is expanding rapidly and serves multiple instructional purposes, especially personalization, adaptive feedback, interactive visualization, and problem support. Chatbots were the most common category in recent studies, while AR/VR showed strong promise for engagement and conceptual understanding, especially for geometry and spatial learning. The authors conclude that commercialized pedagogical AI tools currently dominate the field, but generative AI tools are increasingly important. They also emphasize the need for more longitudinal research, stronger understanding of long-term effects and equity implications, and more work on how AI can complement rather than replace teachers.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that adaptive learning systems and intelligent tutoring systems are among the AI approaches associated with enhanced mathematics learning and achievement in the literature reviewed. The paper references their personalized learning and adaptive feedback functions but does not provide pooled effect sizes.
finding.measure: mathematics achievement/learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that adaptive learning systems and intelligent tutoring systems are among the AI approaches associated with enhanced mathematics learning and achievement in the literature reviewed. The paper references their personalized learning and adaptive feedback functions but does not provide pooled effect sizes.
finding.measure: mathematics achievement/learning outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Advancing Education through Tutoring Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how tutoring systems have evolved from early computer-assisted instruction to modern AI-driven Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) and Robot Tutoring Systems (RTS), and what that evolution means for learning, engagement, and ethics in education. The authors ask three main questions: which technological breakthroughs enabled personalized tutoring, how current systems use real-time adaptation to improve engagement and academic performance, and what ethical challenges have emerged alongside these technologies. The review is motivated by persistent global learning gaps and interest in AI-based tools that can personalize instruction at scale.

The study uses a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review of 86 representative studies selected from an initial pool of 340 records spanning 1972 to 2024. The authors analyze tutoring systems through a four-part framework covering artificial intelligence, system behavior, engagement, and affordances. They also conduct a latent class analysis that groups systems into three categories: computer-based ITS, robot-based verbal tutoring systems, and multimodal tutoring systems that combine verbal, visual, and physical interaction. Across the reviewed studies, key AI techniques include Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, natural language processing, and large language models.

The population context is broad rather than tied to a single sample, because this is a review of prior studies across educational settings. The included literature spans multiple learner groups, with examples and discussion prominently involving younger learners, middle school mathematics students, secondary physics learners, and some higher-education contexts. The review focuses primarily on students as end users of tutoring systems in educational environments, rather than on teachers or administrators as the main participants.

The main conclusions are that tutoring systems show strong promise for improving learning outcomes, personalization, and student engagement, but different forms have different strengths. Computer-based ITS are more scalable and cognitively adaptive, while robot-based systems are stronger for social and emotional engagement. The authors argue that hybrid systems integrating both approaches may offer the greatest educational benefit. They also conclude that important challenges remain, especially around scalability, data privacy, bias, transparency, and the still-limited cognitive adaptability of robotic systems.

paper_profiles.title: Generative artificial intelligence-supported programming education: Effects on learning performance, self-efficacy and processes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), specifically ChatGPT, improves programming education outcomes and how it shapes students’ learning processes. The authors focus on four questions: whether GenAI improves programming output quality and knowledge transfer, whether it affects programming self-efficacy, how it changes students’ programming behaviours, and how different behaviour patterns under GenAI relate to academic performance. The study responds to mixed prior findings suggesting that GenAI may improve immediate task performance but may not always support deeper learning.

The intervention was a quasi-experiment in which one group of students used a ChatGPT-based platform (ChatGPT-Next-Web using GPT-3.5-turbo) for self-directed programming learning, while a control group used other Internet resources instead of GenAI. Both groups completed the same Turtle-library programming learning tasks in a standardized computer lab setting. Measures included ratings of programming products across multiple dimensions, pre/post programming self-efficacy surveys, and fine-grained behavioural trace data captured through scripts and analysed with frequency analysis, process mining, and clustering.

Participants were 55 undergraduate Physics Education students at a public university in China. All had prior foundational Python experience but were new to the Python Turtle library. The experimental activity itself lasted 120 minutes, followed by a 40-minute post-test task completed without external resources. The study took place in university computer labs with uniform hardware, and the authors also provided the experimental group with a GenAI user guide to support interaction with the tool.

The main conclusions are that GenAI support improved short-term programming performance and increased self-efficacy, especially in self-regulation and complex programming tasks, but did not improve longer-term knowledge transfer when students later had to work without external resources. Behavioural analyses showed that GenAI-supported learners relied more on information retrieval and copying, whereas control students engaged more in independent coding and code revision. Within the GenAI group, higher-performing students used the tool more critically and interactively, showing greater epistemic agency, while lower-performing students were more likely to copy outputs directly. The authors argue that GenAI can be beneficial for programming education, but only when instructional design discourages over-reliance and supports active cognitive engagement.

paper_profiles.title: Harnessing Generative AI (GenAI) for Automated Feedback in Higher Education: A Systematic Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the emerging use of generative AI for automated feedback in higher education. The authors note that higher education instructors face growing pressure to provide timely, personalized, and scalable feedback, especially in online and large-enrollment courses. Prior reviews had examined automated feedback or generative AI separately, but had not focused specifically on GenAI-based feedback in higher education or on how these systems are implemented in authentic instructional settings. The review therefore asks three questions: what contexts GenAI feedback systems are used in, what their main characteristics are, and what possibilities they create for higher education.

The authors conducted a systematic review following PRISMA-style procedures and Arksey and O'Malley's framework. They searched peer-reviewed English-language journal articles published from 2019 to 2023 in Academic Search Premier and Education Source, screened 1,976 non-duplicate records, and ultimately included 10 empirical studies from Q1 or Q2 journals. The reviewed studies examined GenAI-based feedback tools such as ChatGPT, chatbots, digital tutors, and specialized writing/assessment systems. These tools were used for automated feedback in contexts including language learning, academic writing, creative thinking, and STEM courses. Across the reviewed studies, GenAI systems served purposes such as personalized learning, collaborative problem-solving, self-regulated learning, and motivation/engagement.

The population and context are higher education settings, including undergraduate and some graduate-level contexts, with both students and educators implicated in implementation. The review synthesizes studies conducted in varied instructional environments, with frequent relevance to online learning and large-scale courses. It also emphasizes instructor roles in implementation, including guiding students' use of GenAI, providing higher-level or final feedback, engineering prompts, and facilitating deeper learning beyond what automated systems can provide.

The main conclusions are that GenAI automated feedback systems show strong promise for improving educational efficiency and support in higher education. The reviewed evidence suggests these systems can reduce instructor workload, provide timely and personalized feedback, improve communication, support cognitive and emotional needs, and expand access to feedback in lower-pressure environments. At the same time, the review highlights unresolved issues such as ethical concerns, accuracy, overreliance, and the need to better define instructors' roles in AI-supported feedback ecosystems. The authors conclude that GenAI should be integrated in ways that augment rather than replace human instruction, and they call for more research as the field develops.

paper_profiles.title: Impact of AI-Blended Learning and AI-Personalized Learning on Undergraduate Biology Students' Attitude and Performance in Climate Change Education
paper_profiles.venue: Anchor University Journal of Science and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-enhanced instructional approaches improve undergraduate biology students’ attitudes toward climate change and their academic performance in climate change education better than traditional classroom teaching. The study is motivated by the concern that conventional instruction may not sufficiently engage students or address diverse learning needs when teaching complex environmental topics.

The intervention compared three instructional conditions: AI-Blended Learning, AI-Personalized Learning, and Traditional Classroom Instruction. In the AI-Blended Learning condition, students used ChatGPT-3.5 alongside face-to-face teaching. In the AI-Personalized Learning condition, students relied on ChatGPT-3.5 as the primary instructional support in a fully AI-driven personalized environment. The comparison group received conventional face-to-face instruction without the AI intervention. Outcomes were measured using a Climate Change Attitude Assessment (CCAA) and a Climate Change Achievement Test (CCAT), with pretest and posttest scores analyzed using ANCOVA.

The study involved 70 300-level undergraduate biology students at Federal University Gusau in Nigeria. Students were drawn from existing classes and assigned into three groups: AI-Blended Learning (20), AI-Personalized Learning (20), and Traditional Classroom Instruction (30). The intervention lasted four weeks and covered climate change topics such as causes, impacts, mitigation strategies, and policy actions.

The main finding is that AI-Blended Learning produced substantially stronger gains in both attitude and performance than either AI-Personalized Learning or Traditional Classroom Instruction. Post hoc analyses showed that the blended approach significantly outperformed both alternatives, while AI-Personalized Learning did not significantly differ from traditional instruction on the reported comparisons. The paper concludes that integrating ChatGPT-3.5 with teacher-led classroom instruction is more effective than relying on AI alone, and recommends that higher education lecturers adopt AI-blended approaches to improve engagement and learning outcomes in environmental education.

paper_profiles.title: Studying the effect of AI Code Generators on Supporting Novice Learners in Introductory Programming
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI code generators such as OpenAI Codex help or hinder novice learners who are first learning introductory text-based programming. The authors focus on a key educational concern: although AI-generated code may improve immediate task performance, it could also create over-reliance and weaken learners’ ability to understand, modify, or retain programming knowledge. The study addresses whether novices can effectively use AI code generation, how it changes task performance, and whether prior access to such tools affects later independent coding and retention.

To study this, the researchers built a web-based Python learning environment called Coding Steps. Learners completed a three-week, 10-session remote program consisting of a Scratch-based introduction and pre-test, seven Python training sessions, and two evaluation sessions (an immediate post-test and a one-week retention test). During training, one group had access to an AI code generator powered by OpenAI Codex, while a comparison group did not. Participants worked through 45 code-authoring tasks, each followed by a code-modification task, plus multiple-choice questions on core introductory Python topics such as variables, conditionals, loops, and arrays. The system logged code edits, documentation use, errors, submissions, and AI prompt/code-generation behavior.

The population consisted of 69 novice learners aged 10-17 recruited through coding camps in two major North American cities. All reported no prior text-based programming experience, though many had experience with block-based programming environments such as Scratch. Participants were assigned to conditions using a matched-groups design based on Scratch pre-test scores to balance prior programming knowledge. The study was conducted remotely via Google Meet, with instructors available to provide support and personalized feedback during training.

The main findings were that access to Codex substantially improved performance on training-phase code-authoring tasks: learners completed more tasks, achieved higher correctness, made fewer errors, and finished faster. Importantly, prior use of the AI tool did not reduce performance on subsequent manual code-modification tasks, and learners in the Codex group performed similarly to the baseline group on the immediate post-test without access to the tool. On the one-week retention test, the Codex group showed slightly better performance, though differences were not statistically significant overall. The authors conclude that AI code generators can support novice programming learning without clear evidence of harming short-term retention, and that learners with stronger prior programming competency may benefit the most.

paper_profiles.title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-generated feedback on student writing can be used effectively in higher education language learning, and whether students prefer it to feedback from human tutors. The authors focus on the emerging use of generative AI, specifically ChatGPT/GPT-4, as an automated writing evaluation tool for English as a new language (ENL) learners. The study addresses two core questions: whether AI feedback produces stronger writing gains than human feedback, and whether students prefer AI-generated or tutor-generated feedback.

The paper reports two longitudinal studies conducted over six weeks. In Study 1, the intervention compared GPT-4-generated writing feedback with feedback from human tutors in a repeated-measures quasi-experimental design. ENL students completed weekly 300-word academic writing tasks, received either AI or human feedback, revised their work, and were assessed through pre- and post-writing tests scored with an analytic rubric. In Study 2, a separate group of students received both AI-generated and human tutor feedback on weekly assignments, then completed weekly surveys with Likert-scale and open-ended items about satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and overall preference.

The population consisted of 91 ENL university students enrolled in an academic reading and writing course at a small liberal arts university in the Asia-Pacific region. Study 1 included 48 students, and Study 2 included 43 different students. Human tutors were trained English language tutors from the university’s ENL Tutor Program, while GPT-4 feedback was generated using an iteratively developed prompt designed by experienced language educators. The intervention occurred in the context of regular course writing assignments during a shortened Spring 2023 semester.

The main conclusion is that AI-generated feedback did not produce significantly different writing gains compared with human tutor feedback. Students in both conditions improved similarly over the six-week period. Preference data showed an almost even split between AI and human feedback. Students who preferred human tutors valued face-to-face interaction, engagement, and the ability to ask immediate follow-up questions, while those preferring AI valued clarity, specificity, consistency, and detailed academic language suggestions. The authors conclude that AI-generated feedback can likely be incorporated into ENL writing instruction without harming learning outcomes, and they recommend a blended approach that combines the efficiency and specificity of AI with the interpersonal benefits of human tutoring.

paper_profiles.title: Examining Faculty and Student Perceptions of Generative AI in University Courses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students and faculty perceive generative AI tools such as ChatGPT in higher education, with particular attention to perceived ease of use, ethical concerns, intentions to use, and views about impacts on learning. The study addresses a gap in empirical evidence about how attitudes toward generative AI differ across university roles and across student subgroups defined by gender and STEM versus non-STEM disciplines.

The study used an anonymous online survey grounded in a modified UTAUT framework and supplemented with items about perceived effects on learning competencies and ethics. The survey measured constructs such as performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, hedonic motivation, habit, personal innovativeness, and behavioral intention, along with views about academic integrity, policy needs, and the frequency of generative AI use. The approach was descriptive and comparative rather than experimental.

Participants were 982 students and 76 faculty members at a single large land-grant public university in the southeastern United States during the Fall 2023 semester. The student sample included both undergraduate and other university students, and analyses compared students with faculty as well as four student subgroups: STEM male, STEM female, non-STEM male, and non-STEM female. Data were collected between December 2023 and January 2024 through voluntary online survey distribution.

The authors conclude that students and faculty were broadly similar in their attitudes toward generative AI, though students reported higher ease of use, hedonic motivation, and personal innovativeness, while faculty reported more habitual use. Both groups used generative AI at similarly low rates overall and shared concerns about negative effects on learning competencies and academic dishonesty, while also supporting the development of institutional policies. Within the student sample, male STEM students tended to express the most positive attitudes and non-STEM female students the least positive, suggesting that gender and disciplinary context shape how generative AI is received in higher education.

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Students’ Multimodal Representations of Ideas About Epistemic Reading of Scientific Texts in Generative AI Tools
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how students represent their ideas about reading scientific texts generated by generative AI tools, a process the authors call GenAI-science epistemic reading. The problem addressed is that students need to draw on both their understanding of science and their understanding of GenAI in order to critically interpret AI-generated scientific information, yet existing measures in this area are often limited to Likert-scale surveys. The study asks what students’ multimodal representations of these ideas look like in terms of presentational, organisational, and orientational meanings.

The study uses a qualitative collective case study approach and develops a multimodal instrument in which students draw and write short explanations about (1) how ChatGPT/Poe generates scientific texts and (2) how they themselves read scientific texts in these tools. The authors analyze 44 students’ drawings and written responses using Lemke’s framework of presentational, organisational, and orientational meaning, and from these data they construct an analytical framework with categories such as epistemic trust, epistemic knowledge, organisational form, and representations of the nature of science and GenAI. Although the responses were collected before an explicit-reflective instructional activity that was part of a larger project, this paper focuses on the pre-instruction representations rather than testing intervention effects.

Participants were 44 Grade 8 and Grade 9 students in Hong Kong participating in extracurricular lessons. The instructional context involved a bilingual teacher who had prior online training workshops on implementing the teaching approach. Students completed the multimodal task in two classrooms before instruction, and the broader project centered on improving students’ understanding of epistemic reading of scientific texts from sources including GenAI and online media.

The main conclusion is that a multimodal approach is useful for characterising students’ ideas about GenAI-science epistemic reading in ways that standard survey instruments may miss. Students expressed a range of epistemic trust positions, including trust, critical thinking, confusion, and non-evaluation, and used different semiotic modes to express these ideas. The paper’s core contribution is an analytical framework teachers and researchers can use to diagnose and discuss students’ epistemic understanding of AI-generated scientific texts. The authors argue that such multimodal representations can serve as a richer diagnostic and instructional tool for future intervention studies on GenAI in science education.

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence (AI) has been studied and applied in higher education, with particular attention to who is doing the research, how AI is conceptualised, what ethical issues are discussed, and what kinds of AI applications are being reported. The authors conducted a systematic review of peer-reviewed English- and Spanish-language journal articles published from 2007 to November 2018 and synthesised 146 included studies.

The review covers a wide range of AI-related approaches, including profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalisation, and intelligent tutoring systems. These applications are discussed in terms of both academic support services and institutional/administrative services, such as dropout prediction, automated grading, feedback, personalised learning, and tutoring support. Most studies were quantitative, many used machine learning methods, and the majority focused on undergraduate learners in higher education contexts.

The authors conclude that AI research in higher education is growing but is dominated by computer science and STEM perspectives, with relatively little involvement from educators. They also find very limited critical reflection on ethical risks such as privacy and cost, and note a weak connection to pedagogical theory. The paper argues for more educationally grounded and ethically informed research on AI in higher education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review, but the paper is descriptive rather than a meta-analysis and does not provide pooled effect estimates. The review synthesizes heterogeneous studies with mixed designs, so credibility for causal claims is limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests promising but mostly indirect or study-specific benefits of AI interventions, with no pooled effect sizes and limited evidence on student learning outcomes. The likely impact on general K-12 science learning is therefore unclear and modest at best.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of machine-learning-based student profiling and prediction for admissions, dropout/retention, engagement, and academic achievement in higher education.

Systematic review of classical intelligent tutoring systems that teach course content, diagnose student knowledge gaps, provide automated feedback, curate learning materials, and sometimes support collaboration.
Systematic review of AI systems that automatically grade work and generate feedback on essays, problem solving, and student responses.
Systematic review of adaptive and personalized learning systems that recommend content, adjust learning pathways, and monitor/guide students using learner models.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed higher-education studies, AI systems were repeatedly described as improving efficiency in admissions, dropout prediction, grading, feedback, and student support. The review reports that machine-learning classifiers often outperformed logistic regression in prediction tasks, and that automated grading systems achieved very high agreement with human raters (e.g. 94.6%–98.2% in one AES study), suggesting time- and labor-saving potential rather than student-learning gains per se.
finding.measure: Prediction/classification accuracy; human-machine grading agreement; workflow efficiency claims in administrative and assessment tasks
finding.study_size: n=146 studies in review; individual primary-study sample sizes vary

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes generally positive but uneven evidence that ITS and adaptive systems can support course content learning across subjects such as computer science, mathematics, physics, medicine, and language learning. However, the authors note that most studies were short-term pilots, that novelty effects were rarely addressed, and that at least one ITS study reported negative results when the support was too basic for advanced learners.
finding.measure: Pre/post performance, task success, learning gains, and preliminary pilot outcomes reported in the primary studies
finding.study_size: n=146 studies in review; ITS subset n=29, adaptive systems subset n=27

finding.finding_summary: For automated essay scoring and related feedback systems, the review reports high scoring agreement with human raters in some studies and suggests that automated feedback can encourage revisions and reduce grading burdens. At the same time, the authors highlight persistent concerns about feedback quality and appropriateness for beginning language learners, indicating that literacy benefits are promising but not uniform.
finding.measure: Essay scoring agreement; revision behavior; qualitative judgments about feedback usefulness
finding.study_size: n=146 studies in review; automated grading subset n=13, feedback subset includes multiple writing studies

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed AI systems targeted engagement, motivation, and self-regulation, especially through learner modeling and early-warning systems that identify at-risk or low-engagement students. The review cites studies using VLE click data and behavioral traces to flag students for intervention, and some systems were explicitly designed to support self-regulatory processes during learning.
finding.measure: Engagement indicators, behavioral logs, motivation/self-regulation proxies
finding.study_size: n=146 studies in review; individual studies vary widely

paper_profiles.title: Domain-Specific Inhibitory Control Training to Improve Children’s Learning of Counterintuitive Concepts in Mathematics and Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether children’s inhibitory control (IC) is related to learning counterintuitive concepts in mathematics and science, and whether IC can be improved through a domain-specific classroom intervention. The authors argue that misconceptions and misleading perceptual cues interfere with children’s understanding of science and mathematics, and that training children to “stop and think” may help them inhibit intuitive but incorrect responses.

The study had two parts. First, the authors conducted cross-sectional analyses with 627 primary school children in Years 3 and 5 in London schools, examining associations among IC, counterintuitive reasoning, and standardized mathematics and science achievement. Second, they evaluated a computer-based intervention called Stop & Think, delivered either as a teacher-led whole-class activity or a pupil-led individual activity during mathematics and science lessons over 10 weeks. The software embedded IC prompts, scaffolded practice, and virtual peer explanations within curriculum-based math and science content.

Results showed that children frequently selected misconception-based answers on the counterintuitive reasoning task, and that better IC was associated with better counterintuitive reasoning and higher academic achievement. The intervention produced evidence of near transfer for Year 3 children on counterintuitive reasoning in both delivery modes, and teacher-led Stop & Think also improved Year 3 science achievement. Effects were weaker or absent for Year 5 and no transfer was found to the Stroop-like IC measure. The authors conclude that domain-specific IC training embedded in curriculum content may support science and mathematics learning, but the evidence is preliminary and effects vary by age and delivery mode.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental classroom study with baseline/post measures, but conditions were not fully randomized and some outcome data were missing by condition. It is stronger than purely correlational work, yet has notable internal-validity limitations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention shows small-to-moderate gains on near-transfer counterintuitive reasoning in Year 3 and a modest science-achievement effect (ηp²=.077), but results are inconsistent across age groups and delivery modes. Overall impact appears promising but limited and context-specific.

interventions.use_case: Classroom-based computerised practice called Stop & Think that embeds inhibitory-control prompts within mathematics and science curriculum content, delivered either teacher-led on an interactive whiteboard or pupil-led on individual computers.

finding.finding_summary: Children showed strong baseline misconceptions in mathematics, with Year 3 making significantly more misconception than other errors (t(350)=20.76, p<.001, d=1.11) and Year 5 also showing this pattern (t(242)=2.38, p=.018, d=0.15). The intervention improved mathematics achievement only weakly/inconsistently: Year 3 showed no significant effect for mathematics achievement, while Year 5 pupil-led Stop & Think showed a small effect that did not survive Bonferroni correction (F(1,124)=4.85, p=.029, ηp²=.038).
finding.measure: Counterintuitive reasoning test (mathematics items); Progress Test in Mathematics 7/9
finding.study_size: n=594 baseline reasoning; n=283 achievement; intervention subsamples varied

finding.finding_summary: Children also showed strong baseline misconceptions in science, with Year 3 making more misconception than other errors (t(350)=12.89, p<.001, d=0.69) and Year 5 showing the same pattern (t(242)=11.02, p<.001, d=0.71). Stop & Think produced a significant gain in Year 3 teacher-led science achievement relative to teaching as usual (F(1,64)=5.37, p<.05, ηp²=.077), but there was no significant science-achievement effect for Year 5 pupil-led delivery.
finding.measure: Counterintuitive reasoning test (science items); Progress Test in Science 8/9
finding.study_size: n=594 baseline reasoning; n=129 achievement; intervention subsamples varied

finding.finding_summary: The intervention targeted inhibitory control as a domain-specific support for counterintuitive reasoning, but it did not improve the separate Stroop-like inhibitory-control measure overall. At baseline, inhibitory control was associated with better counterintuitive reasoning and achievement, and the intervention improved near-transfer counterintuitive reasoning in Year 3 (STT ηp²=.067; STP ηp²=.041), suggesting gains in applied reasoning/self-regulation rather than the generic IC task.
finding.measure: Stroop-like inhibitory-control task; counterintuitive reasoning test
finding.study_size: n=451 baseline IC; intervention subsamples varied
finding.effect_size: baseline r up to .33; intervention ηp²=.067/.041; no overall IC effect

paper_profiles.title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the question of how to build a clearer theory of formative assessment and how to situate formative feedback within broader theories of pedagogy and learning. The authors argue that formative assessment had previously been described through lists of practices, but that a stronger conceptual basis was needed to explain how those practices fit together and how they support learning.

The paper develops a framework that defines formative assessment as the elicitation, interpretation, and use of evidence about student achievement by teachers, learners, or peers to make better-founded instructional decisions. It organizes formative assessment into five strategies: clarifying learning intentions and success criteria, engineering classroom discussions and tasks that elicit evidence, providing feedback that moves learning forward, activating students as resources for one another, and activating students as owners of their own learning. The authors connect this framework to self-regulated learning, classroom discourse, cognitive acceleration, and dynamic assessment, and discuss how feedback decisions depend on interpreting learner responses and matching them to instructional goals.

The context is broad classroom teaching rather than a single empirical study: the paper draws on prior literature from school settings, including examples from science and mathematics classrooms, to show how formative practices operate in everyday instruction. The main conclusion is that formative assessment should be understood as contingent interaction that regulates learning, and that stronger theoretical models can help teachers implement feedback more effectively and avoid superficial adoption of isolated techniques.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/review paper on formative assessment, not an empirical evaluation of a technology or AI intervention. It is peer-reviewed academic work, but it does not present a study design with primary outcome data for the requested taxonomy.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct intervention impact is measured in this paper, so there is no empirical effect to classify. The paper is influential conceptually for formative assessment, but it does not provide outcome evidence for K-12 science learning or any technology-based support.

paper_profiles.title: Yes, they can: Developing transcription skills and oral language in tandem with SRSD instruction on close reading of science text to write informative essays at grades 1 and 2
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a long-standing debate in early writing instruction: whether primary-grade students should first master transcription and oral language skills before learning to compose, or whether these skills can be taught alongside writing strategies and the writing process. It also asks whether first- and second-grade students can be taught close reading of science text and then use that reading to plan and write informative essays.

The intervention, called SRSD Plus, combined Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD) for close reading and writing with explicit instruction in handwriting, spelling, vocabulary, and sentence proficiency. The program used science anchor texts aligned to NGSS, was delivered by teachers in small groups, and included practice-based professional development and ongoing implementation support. Students were randomly assigned within class to SRSD Plus or a business-as-usual writers workshop comparison.

Participants were 93 first- and second-grade children in one high-poverty school in the southeastern United States. The study found that students receiving SRSD Plus outperformed the comparison group on writing quality, planning, use of source text, structural elements, and several language and transcription outcomes. Effects on productivity measures were especially strong in Grade 2. The authors conclude that integrating skills instruction with strategy-based writing and close reading is feasible and beneficial in the primary grades, especially for science-related informative writing.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled trial with blinded assessment, nested multilevel modeling, pretest adjustment, and fidelity checks, making it a strong causal design. The study is peer-reviewed and directly evaluates an instructional intervention in a relevant K-12 population.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced large improvements in several literacy outcomes, including writing quality (ES=1.02) and planning (ES=1.40), with additional benefits in words written and transition use. Because the sample is a high-poverty K-12 population and the effects are substantial, the practical impact is high.

finding.finding_summary: In this randomized controlled trial (n=93; posttest n=90), students receiving SRSD Plus outperformed business-as-usual writers workshop on multiple writing outcomes. Effects were large for writing quality (ES=1.02), planning (ES=1.40), and use of transition words was especially strong in Grade 2 (ES=2.46; Grade 1 ES=1.33), with additional positive effects for structural elements (ES=0.29), use of source text (ES=0.48), and number of words written (Grade 2 ES=1.39; Grade 1 ES=0.82).
finding.measure: Source-based informative writing tasks scored for planning, writing quality, structural elements, number of words written, transition words, and use of source text

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved oral language-related writing skills, including vocabulary and sentence proficiency. The paper reports moderate to large effect sizes for these outcomes, although exact values are not provided in the text excerpt.
finding.measure: Researcher-developed vocabulary recognition and sentence proficiency tasks

finding.finding_summary: Students in SRSD Plus showed gains in discourse knowledge about writing, including understanding of planning, rereading, audience awareness, and elements of informative writing. These gains suggest improved writing-related metacognitive awareness and self-regulatory knowledge, though the excerpt does not report an exact effect size.
finding.measure: Open-ended discourse knowledge questions about writing processes, audience, and informational essay structure

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved planning and discourse knowledge, both of which reflect metacognitive and self-regulatory dimensions of writing performance. Students in SRSD Plus created stronger planning sheets than BAU peers (ES=1.40), indicating better strategy use and task planning for expository writing.
finding.measure: Planning rubric and discourse knowledge measures

finding.finding_summary: Although the intervention was delivered through science texts aligned to NGSS, the study did not assess science content mastery directly. The closest substantive scientific outcome was expository text comprehension using science-related source texts, where students in SRSD Plus used source text more effectively in writing (ES=0.48), but this is better understood as literacy-based science learning support than direct science reasoning.
finding.measure: Use of source text on science-related informative writing tasks

paper_profiles.title: Confronting the Challenges of Participatory Culture: Media Education for the 21st Century
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report addresses how young people can be prepared to participate effectively in contemporary participatory media culture. The central question is not whether children and teens use digital media—they clearly do—but whether they have the skills, critical understanding, and ethical frameworks needed to participate fully, especially given inequalities in access and differences in the quality of their media experiences. The authors frame this as a shift from a narrow focus on technology access to a broader concern with cultural competencies, social skills, and media literacy.

The paper is not an empirical intervention study; rather, it synthesizes examples and prior research to argue for a systemic approach to media education. It discusses participatory culture, affinity spaces, peer-to-peer learning, and the role of new media literacies such as play, performance, simulation, appropriation, multitasking, collective intelligence, judgment, transmedia navigation, networking, and negotiation. The context is primarily U.S. youth culture, schools, after-school programs, informal learning communities, and home media environments, with examples drawn from teens’ online creative practices, gaming, and fan communities.

The report concludes that schools alone are not enough to close the participation gap or teach transparency and ethics; parents, after-school programs, and educators all have roles to play.
