It argues that youth already gain valuable skills through participatory media, but these experiences are unevenly distributed and often opaque. The authors therefore call for intentional media education that helps young people critically interpret media systems, evaluate information credibility, and develop norms for responsible participation in networked culture.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a MacArthur Foundation report/book chapter rather than an empirical study, and it presents theory, synthesis, and illustrative examples without a clear experimental or correlational evaluation design. No peer-reviewed effect estimates are reported.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The report is influential for educational theory and policy discourse, but it does not demonstrate measurable intervention impact on student outcomes. Its practical implications are substantial, yet the evidence base here is primarily conceptual and descriptive.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual/report-style synthesis arguing for systemic media education in schools, after-school programs, and families rather than an intervention evaluation. It identifies three institutional problems—participation gap, transparency problem, and ethics challenge—and claims that schools have been slow to respond, but it does not report effect sizes or experimental outcome data (n not reported).
finding.measure: Policy and educational framework arguments about media literacy, participation gap, and institutional response

finding.finding_summary: The report argues that participatory culture supports durable skills such as collaboration, networking, judgment, multitasking, and negotiation, drawing on illustrative cases and prior scholarship rather than direct causal estimates. It cites examples like peer-to-peer fan community feedback and game-based collaboration, but reports no effect sizes or sample sizes for skill gains (n not reported).
finding.measure: Theoretical/qualitative evidence about collaboration, networking, judgment, multitasking, and negotiation in participatory media environments

finding.finding_summary: The report suggests participatory media experiences can increase self-confidence, social connection, motivation, and a sense that one’s contributions matter. This claim is supported by descriptive evidence about teens as media creators and by affinity-space examples, but it does not provide quantified outcomes or a study sample for causal estimation (n not reported).
finding.measure: Self-confidence, sense of belonging, motivation to participate in communities

paper_profiles.title: Early Alert of Academically At-Risk Students: An Open Source Analytics Initiative
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the Open Academic Analytics Initiative (OAAI), a multi-year effort to build and evaluate an open-source early alert system for higher education. The core problem addressed is how to identify academically at-risk students early enough to improve course success and retention, especially in institutions serving underserved populations. The authors frame the work as an applied learning analytics initiative rather than a study of a specific commercial product.

The intervention approach combines predictive modeling with targeted supports. Student demographic, aptitude, course, and learning management system data from Sakai were used to train classifiers that flagged students likely to earn below a C. Four machine-learning methods were compared: logistic regression, SVM/SMO, decision trees, and Naïve Bayes. When students were identified as at risk, they were placed into an Online Academic Support Environment (OASE) that offered open educational resources, academic support staff facilitation, and peer mentoring, along with instructor email notifications and other outreach strategies.

The study population consisted of undergraduate students at Marist College and partner higher-education institutions in the United States, including community colleges and HBCUs. The paper reports on model development, portability across institutions, and the implementation of intervention strategies, with emphasis on course completion, retention, and academic performance indicators. The authors conclude that the OAAI successfully produced an open-source early alert prototype and that predictive models and interventions can be deployed across multiple institutions, though the paper is primarily a system-and-model report rather than a rigorous causal impact study on learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical/technical case study, but it is primarily descriptive and correlational rather than a rigorous causal evaluation of student learning outcomes. The paper reports model development and deployment, with limited direct outcome evidence and no randomized comparison for the main educational claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows meaningful institutional implementation of an early-warning analytics system, but it does not demonstrate measurable gains in K-12 science achievement or other student learning outcomes. Any impact is therefore indirect and unclear for the user’s target question.

interventions.use_case: open-source early alert system that uses LMS logs, demographics, aptitude data, and gradebook data to predict which higher-education students are academically at risk and trigger interventions

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily evaluates predictive modeling for identifying at-risk students rather than direct learning gains. It reports that models were trained/tested on 9,938 training samples and 5,212 test samples, with performance assessed via accuracy, recall, precision, and false-positive rate, but no science learning outcomes are reported.
finding.measure: classification performance for academic risk detection (accuracy, recall, precision, false-positive rate)

finding.finding_summary: The system is intended to improve institutional efficiency by automating early identification of academically at-risk students and supporting targeted intervention delivery. The paper describes successful deployment of open-source predictive models across partner institutions, but does not provide a numeric effect size for efficiency gains.
finding.measure: deployment and predictive model performance for early alert workflow

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that the Open Academic Analytics Initiative successfully developed and deployed an open-source early alert prototype, released predictive models under open license, and explored portability across institutions. This indicates implementation and scalability impact at the institutional level, but the paper does not report a direct causal effect on student learning achievement.
finding.measure: prototype deployment, model portability across institutions, and intervention implementation outcomes
finding.study_size: 4 partner institutions plus Marist College development dataset

paper_profiles.title: MOOCs and Open Education: Implications for Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This white paper examines the rapid emergence of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) and places them within the broader movement toward open education in higher education. The report asks how MOOCs should be understood, what motivates institutions and providers to adopt them, what challenges they face, and whether they may act as disruptive innovations in the higher education market.

The paper does not study a single instructional intervention or report original learning-outcome data. Instead, it synthesizes a literature review drawing on scholarly blogs, press releases, and openly available reports and research papers. It discusses major MOOC initiatives such as edX, Coursera, Udacity, Udemy, P2PU, and Khan Academy, focusing on their business models, access policies, assessment practices, and pedagogical models (especially the distinction between cMOOCs and xMOOCs).

The intended audience is higher-education decision makers, particularly administrators and policy stakeholders in the UK context. The main conclusion is that MOOCs may expand access, support experimentation, and contribute to new business and teaching models, but significant concerns remain about sustainability, quality, pedagogy, completion rates, and credit recognition. The paper argues that MOOCs should be understood as part of a wider shift toward openness in higher education rather than as a standalone solution.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a grey-literature white paper on MOOCs and open education, not an empirical study. It synthesizes commentary and reports from other sources but does not present a primary research design, comparison groups, or original outcome data.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct K-12 or science-learning intervention is evaluated, and the paper reports no measurable educational effects. Its relevance is purely conceptual and policy-oriented rather than evidence of impact.

paper_profiles.title: Health Professions Education: Accelerating Innovation Through Technology
paper_profiles.venue: Blue Ridge Academic Health Group Report 17
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This Blue Ridge Academic Health Group report addresses how academic health centers and health professional schools can respond to two converging forces: the need for major reform in health professions education and the rapid expansion of online learning, open educational resources, and learning platforms. The report asks how technology can help institutions move toward a more flexible, competency-based, cost-conscious, and learner-centered educational model.

Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the paper surveys emerging practices and institutional initiatives in medical and health professions education, including flipped classrooms, learning management systems, open courseware, MOOCs, virtual patients, simulations, and e-portfolios. It highlights examples from the University of Michigan, Stanford, New York University, Johns Hopkins, and others to illustrate how technology is being used to support continuous learning, competency tracking, interactive learning, and broader access to educational content.

The report focuses primarily on undergraduate and professional health education in the United States. Its main conclusion is that technology offers meaningful opportunities to improve flexibility, reach, and efficiency, but that the evidence base was still limited in 2012–2013. The authors therefore argue for careful implementation, institutional capacity-building, and a stronger research agenda to evaluate whether these approaches truly improve learning outcomes and competency development.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a 2013 policy/report article describing online learning trends and citing Khan Academy as an example; it does not present a primary empirical study of Khanmigo or any K-12 science learning intervention. There is no rigorous experimental or quasi-experimental methodology in the paper itself.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct outcome data are reported for K-12 science achievement, conceptual understanding, reasoning, vocabulary, inquiry skills, retention, engagement, or assignment performance. The paper only offers conceptual discussion and illustrative examples, so no measurable impact can be attributed.

interventions.use_case: Khan Academy-style mastery-based platform that tracks student progress, recommends new topics after mastery, and provides problem sets for K-12 math and science learners

paper_profiles.title: Promoting Science, Technology, and Engineering Self-Efficacy and Knowledge for All With an Autism Inclusion Maker Program
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an inclusive maker program, IDEAS (Inventing, Designing, and Engineering for All Students), can improve STEM-related outcomes for middle school students in autism-inclusion settings. The authors ask whether participation in the program increases students’ STEM self-efficacy, career interest, and understanding/engagement with the engineering design process (EDP), and whether effects differ for autistic students versus their general education peers.

IDEAS was adapted from a museum-based maker curriculum and delivered as an afterschool or lunchtime club in three public middle schools in New York City. The intervention was designed collaboratively by maker educators, autism inclusion specialists, engineers, researchers, and school staff, and included supports such as checklists, visual templates, and explicit prompts. Students in grades 6–8 participated voluntarily; treatment students joined the maker club while comparison students did not. The study combined hierarchical linear modeling of pre/post survey and EDP assessment data with observations and interviews.

The quantitative findings showed positive effects for the maker group overall on technology and engineering self-efficacy, technology and engineering interest, vicarious experience, science appreciation, and EDP understanding. However, the program’s effects on technology/engineering interest and science appreciation were stronger for neurotypical students than for autistic students. Qualitative findings suggested that the program supported repeated use of the EDP, enabled students to complete personally meaningful projects, and gave autistic students opportunities to demonstrate capability and socialize around shared interests. The paper concludes that interest-driven, well-supported maker programming can benefit diverse middle school learners in inclusive settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods quasi-experimental study with a comparison group, baseline adjustment, and hierarchical linear modeling. It is not randomized and includes some concerns about self-selection into the maker program, so it does not meet blue-tier criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports medium-to-large positive effects on a priority population, including g=0.82 for self-efficacy and g=0.56 for engineering design process understanding. Even though the intervention is not Khanmigo and is not a science-achievement test, the observed impacts are substantively meaningful on relevant STEM learning and engagement outcomes.

interventions.use_case: inclusive interest-driven maker program for middle school students with autism inclusion, centered on engineering design activities such as paper circuits, 3D design/fabrication, and iterative prototyping

finding.finding_summary: The maker program improved students' understanding of the engineering design process (EDP) relative to the business-as-usual comparison group. The adjusted Hedges' g was 0.56, based on n=109 total participants (54 makers, 55 non-makers), with the EDP assessment measured via brief audio-recorded interviews coded on a 3-point scale.
finding.measure: Engineering Design Process (EDP) assessment; audio-recorded interview responses scored on a 3-point rubric

finding.finding_summary: The intervention produced positive gains in technology and engineering self-efficacy compared with the comparison group, with Hedges' g=0.82. The study also found improvement in vicarious experience (g=0.60) and science appreciation (g=0.20), indicating increased confidence and interest in STEM-related engagement among makers (n=109).
finding.measure: STEM self-efficacy survey constructs: technology and engineering self-efficacy, vicarious experience of science, and science appreciation

finding.finding_summary: The qualitative findings suggest improved collaboration, persistence, and problem solving during maker activities, but these were not measured with a standardized durable-skills instrument. Students repeatedly iterated on designs, used peers as resources, and persisted through failures; however, these outcomes are descriptive rather than rigorously estimated effects.
finding.measure: Observations and teacher/student interviews focused on collaboration, iteration, persistence, and problem solving

paper_profiles.title: Mobartech, an informal education project for bringing people closer to cultural heritage
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the MOBARTECH project, an informal education and cultural heritage initiative aimed at engaging the public in the study, conservation, and interpretation of heritage assets. The author frames the work as a response to the need for more participatory, learner-centered approaches to heritage education, especially in contexts where cultural sites are poorly understood by local residents and visitors.

The intervention was developed around the UNESCO World Heritage site of Mantua and Sabbioneta in Italy. The project combined questionnaires, interviews with key informants, observations, archival research, and collaborative work with secondary school students to design a guided-discovery kit for visitors. The kit incorporated hands-on and digitally supported activities such as observation, drawing, writing, maps, photographs, and downloadable videos.

Participants included local and tourist respondents, community members, and groups of middle and high school students, some of whom were on educational work placements or field trips. The paper reports that involving students in the kit-development process encouraged critical thinking about local heritage and helped them identify meaningful information for communication to others. The main conclusion is that direct participation, co-construction of knowledge, and active engagement can strengthen cultural awareness and heritage appreciation; however, the paper does not provide rigorous comparative evidence of learning gains or any science-achievement outcomes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/descriptive conference paper with no rigorous experimental or quasi-experimental evaluation of an AI or educational technology intervention. It does not provide a controlled design, outcome statistics, or causal evidence relevant to K-12 science learning.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No measurable impact on science achievement, reasoning, vocabulary, inquiry skills, retention, engagement, or assignment performance is reported. The paper is about cultural heritage informal education, so it shows no direct evidence of impact for Khanmigo or K-12 science learning.

finding.finding_summary: This is an informal education/cultural heritage project, not a Khanmigo or other AI-tutoring study. The paper describes a participatory community project that aimed to increase public engagement with heritage and strengthen links between local communities, schools, and the UNESCO site; however, it reports no quantitative learning gains or causal comparison against standard instruction. Evidence is descriptive and process-oriented, centered on pilot testing and iterative refinement of a guided discovery kit rather than measured achievement outcomes.
finding.measure: Questionnaires, interviews, observations, pilot testing of a guided discovery kit, and qualitative documentation of project phases

paper_profiles.title: Human-centered Strategic Planning at a Rural Rwandan Medical School: A Case Study for Navigating Institutional Challenges and Strengthening Community and National Population Health in Low and Middle Income Countries
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses strategic planning challenges faced by a new rural medical school in Rwanda and explores how a human-centered design (HCD) approach can be used to guide institutional development. The question is not about student learning outcomes, but about how to structure educational, infrastructural, and financial planning so that a medical school can better meet local healthcare and training needs.

The authors describe an HCD process built around empathetic needs finding, challenge definition, ideation, prototyping, and iterative testing. They conducted semi-structured interviews with a wide range of stakeholders, including patients, physicians, nurses, students, educators, community leaders, planners, and international partners, and used those inputs to build a 15-year phased development model for the University of Gitwe Faculty of Medicine and Allied Health Sciences.

The context is a rural medical school in Gitwe, Rwanda, the first rural medical school in the country, opened in 2013. The paper concludes that HCD can provide a useful framework for aligning institutional planning with community and national health priorities in low- and middle-income settings. It is a planning and case-study paper rather than an evaluation of an educational intervention, and it does not report evidence relevant to Khanmigo or K-12 science learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is not about Khanmigo or K-12 science learning. It is a conference abstract on human-centered design of a pediatric medical device and contains no clear educational intervention study, no comparator, and no learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no evidence of impact on educational outcomes, science achievement, or any K-12 learning measure. The text is unrelated to the requested intervention and topic.

paper_profiles.title: Data-Driven Education in University Physics: A Comprehensive Analysis of Learning Analytics Dashboards and AI Tutoring
paper_profiles.venue: Main Issues of Pedagogy and Psychology (MIOPAP)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines the role of data-driven educational technologies in undergraduate physics, focusing on learning analytics (LA) dashboards and AI tutoring systems. It asks how these tools are being used, what evidence exists for their educational effects, and what social, pedagogical, and ethical conditions shape their impact. The paper frames its analysis using technology acceptance and sociological theories, especially TAM, ANT, and Bourdieu, to interpret adoption, use, and equity implications.

Rather than evaluating a single intervention experimentally, the paper synthesizes international case examples and prior literature on LA dashboards and AI tutors. For dashboards, it discusses instructor-facing and student-facing systems used in physics and engineering contexts, including remote labs and eBook-linked dashboards. For AI tutoring, it reviews cognitive tutors, dialogue-based systems, and generative AI/RAG tutors such as NotebookLM, with a brief mention of Khanmigo as part of the broader AI tutoring landscape. The context is primarily undergraduate physics education, with additional discussion of Armenia’s higher education setting and broader STEM applications.

The main conclusion is that both LA dashboards and AI tutors can support engagement, feedback, and personalization, but their educational effects are highly context-dependent. The paper argues that dashboards show more consistent benefits for engagement and task completion than for direct achievement gains, while AI tutors appear more promising for conceptual understanding and problem-solving, though rigorous evidence remains uneven. It concludes that successful use depends on pedagogical integration, readiness of faculty and students, institutional support, and attention to equity, privacy, and reliability concerns.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative, theory-heavy review/synthesis with no direct empirical evaluation of Khanmigo and no rigorous original outcome study reported in the paper text. The paper aggregates prior studies and surveys, but the evidence for the retrieved topic is indirect and not methodologically strong enough for a higher tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially modest benefits for engagement, task completion, and some physics learning outcomes in related AI/tutoring systems, but it does not provide direct evidence on Khanmigo or K-12 science achievement. Any impact claim for the target intervention remains unclear and indirect.

interventions.use_case: machine-learning early warning models for introductory calculus-based physics to identify students at risk of D/F/withdrawal using GPA, ACT, homework, clicker, and exam data
BookRoll/LAViEW-integrated data-driven learning platform supporting eBook-based physics learning with analytics-informed feedback and pedagogy adaptation
classical physics tutoring systems such as Andes and other adaptive tutor architectures providing stepwise problem-solving support, hints, and modeled feedback
RAG-grounded generative AI physics tutoring with Socratic dialogue and question-answer support using uploaded course materials

finding.finding_summary: The article synthesizes evidence that AI tutoring systems can improve conceptual understanding and problem-solving in physics, but it does not present a new controlled study on Khanmigo. For AI tutors generally, the paper cites prior work showing positive effects on conceptual understanding and problem-solving, while also noting concerns about over-reliance; no effect sizes or sample sizes are reported for Khanmigo specifically.
finding.measure: conceptual understanding and problem-solving performance in physics

finding.finding_summary: For learning analytics dashboards in physics, the paper reports inconsistent direct effects on academic achievement but positive results on targeted quiz performance in specific implementations. Examples summarized include improved quiz scores in the GITAM study and higher task completion in the Edinburgh remote-lab dashboard, but the article also notes a systematic review finding no strong overall evidence that dashboards improve achievement.
finding.measure: quiz scores, task completion, academic achievement indicators

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that dashboards and AI tutors can improve engagement, self-regulation, and motivation when well integrated into pedagogy. It cites cases where student-facing dashboards supported reflection and self-monitoring, and notes positive student ratings of usefulness, but no standardized effect size is reported.
finding.measure: engagement, self-regulation, usefulness ratings

finding.finding_summary: The synthesis suggests AI tutors and dashboards may support self-regulation, reflection, and problem-solving processes, which the article treats as durable skills. This is based on mixed evidence from international case studies and prior literature rather than a direct Khanmigo study, and no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: self-regulation, reflection, problem-solving process measures

paper_profiles.title: Through the looking glass: a synthesis of systematic reviews and meta-analyses on pedagogy paradigms facilitated by large language models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a gap in the literature on large language models (LLMs) in education by synthesizing existing systematic reviews and meta-analyses, with a particular focus on how LLMs align with established pedagogy paradigms. Rather than evaluating a single LLM application directly, the authors examine the broader research landscape to identify trends, gaps, and future directions in educational LLM research.

The synthesis follows PRISMA guidelines and uses AMSTAR to assess review quality. The authors searched major academic databases and ultimately included 50 review studies published in journals. Their coding framework examined publication trends, geographic distribution, review types, research-question types, pedagogy paradigms, learning outcomes, and implementation challenges.

The paper reports that constructivism and cognitivism are the most frequently addressed paradigms, while connectivism and behaviorism are less common and social constructivism and humanism are rare. Across the reviewed literature, cognitive outcomes are the most frequently discussed and are generally positive, but the paper also highlights a notable risk of over-reliance that may undermine critical thinking. Affective and behavioral outcomes are also mostly positive, though less frequently studied. The authors conclude that research on LLMs in education has so far emphasized descriptive and interpretive questions over rigorous causal or economic evaluations, and they call for more primary research, especially longitudinal and context-rich studies.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a secondary synthesis of reviews and meta-analyses, not a primary empirical study of Khanmigo or K-12 science learning. It uses PRISMA/AMSTAR methods, but it does not provide direct experimental or quasi-experimental evidence on the target intervention-outcome pair.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct Khanmigo-specific or K-12 science-specific effect size is reported, and the paper only offers indirect, high-level synthesis of LLM literature. For the requested outcome domain, the evidence here does not demonstrate measurable impact relative to standard instruction or comparators.

interventions.use_case: Umbrella review/synthesis of systematic reviews and meta-analyses on LLMs in education, including chatbots, ChatGPT-style tutors, and AI assistants used for pedagogical support, scaffolding, feedback, and dialogue-based learning.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is a synthesis of 50 reviews and meta-analyses, not a primary study of student science outcomes, so it does not report direct effect sizes for K-12 science achievement or conceptual understanding from Khanmigo specifically. Across the reviewed literature, the authors conclude that LLMs are most often associated with cognitive learning gains (40 positive instances vs 9 negative), but they do not provide a science-specific, K-12, or Khanmigo-specific estimate.
finding.measure: Reported learning outcomes across reviewed studies/reviews; no direct K-12 science achievement measure for Khanmigo

finding.finding_summary: Within the reviewed literature, affective outcomes such as motivation and engagement were commonly reported as improved by LLM-based tools, with 18 positive instances and 3 negative instances across 21 affective outcomes. The paper does not provide a Khanmigo-specific effect size or a K-12 science engagement estimate; the evidence is synthesized from prior reviews and remains indirect for the user’s target question.
finding.measure: Motivation and engagement outcomes reported in prior reviews/meta-analyses

finding.finding_summary: The synthesis reports that cognitive outcomes are the dominant focus and are often positive, but it also highlights a meaningful negative pattern: over-reliance on LLMs may impair critical thinking capacities. Across the reviewed literature, cognitive outcomes were reported 44 times, with 40 positive and 9 negative instances; however, no study-level effect size for Khanmigo or K-12 science reasoning was reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, higher-order thinking, problem-solving, and related cognitive outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes that behavioral/efficiency outcomes were the least explored but were consistently positive when reported, with 14 positive instances and 1 negative instance across 15 behavioral outcomes. These findings are about productivity and task completion in the broader LLM-in-education literature, not direct evidence that Khanmigo improves K-12 science assignment performance relative to standard instruction.
finding.measure: Productivity, efficiency, and task completion outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Unpacking Graduate Students’ Learning Experience with Generative AI Teaching Assistant in A Quantitative Methodology Course
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how graduate students interacted with a generative AI teaching assistant in an advanced quantitative methods course, with a focus on their question patterns, perceptions, and learning experiences. The study was motivated by the growing use of generative AI in education and a gap in understanding not just whether students use these tools, but how they use them and what kinds of cognitive engagement the interactions reflect.

The intervention was a GPT-4-powered course-specific AI assistant built from course materials, textbooks, previous Q&A records, and other structured course knowledge. Over a 10-week course at an elite university in China, 20 graduate students used the assistant; their dialogues were logged, coded using Bloom’s taxonomy and the CLEAR framework, and supplemented with surveys and 10 semi-structured interviews. The study compared usage patterns across students with stronger versus weaker mathematical foundations and also asked students to evaluate the AI assistant relative to teachers, human TAs, textbooks, and course recordings.

The main findings were that students used the AI more heavily at the beginning of the course and less in the middle weeks, that most questions were low- to mid-level cognitive questions (knowledge, comprehension, application), and that higher-order questioning was relatively rare. Students with weaker mathematical foundations used the assistant more frequently and tended to ask more follow-up questions, while stronger students wrote more logical and explicit prompts. Students reported that the AI was convenient, available, and helpful, but they also expressed concerns about accuracy, fragmented explanations, and limited support for complex tasks. The authors conclude that generative AI can support learning, especially for students with weaker prior knowledge, but that students need better AI literacy and more targeted guidance to use it for deeper learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods case study with 20 graduate students, but it is not a controlled trial and does not measure rigorous learning outcomes against a comparator. The evidence is primarily descriptive and qualitative, with t-tests and regression used for interaction patterns rather than causal impact on achievement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potential benefits for engagement, comfort, and immediate support, but it provides no direct evidence of improved achievement or other substantive learning gains. Any impact is therefore modest and unclear, especially for the requested K-12 science-learning question.

interventions.use_case: GPT-4-powered course-specific AI teaching assistant for an advanced quantitative research methods course, answering student questions, explaining concepts, translating materials, and supporting assignment-related Stata and methodology queries

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not measure science achievement or any K-12 learning outcome; it is an observational study of graduate students’ interaction patterns with a GenAI teaching assistant in a quantitative methods course. The closest academic outcome is assignment/course support, where students reported the assistant helped with homework and Stata tasks, but no pre-post or comparator-based achievement data were reported (n=20; 1,418 dialogue rounds, 1,357 course-related).
finding.measure: Student dialogue patterns, interview reports of assignment help, and perceived usefulness for course work

finding.finding_summary: Students consistently reported reduced social pressure, greater comfort asking questions, and a judgement-free environment when using the AI assistant. However, these are self-reported perceptions rather than measured learning gains, and no comparison group or effect size for engagement/motivation was provided (n=20).
finding.measure: Survey ratings and semi-structured interview themes on comfort, reliance, and perceived support

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined the cognitive level and structure of student questions using Bloom’s taxonomy and the CLEAR framework. Most questions were lower-order (knowledge 29%, comprehension 36%, application 27%), with very few higher-order questions (analysis 5%, evaluation 2%, creation 1%), suggesting limited evidence of deep reasoning use; follow-up questions were more adaptive/reflective, but this was still based on interaction coding rather than achievement outcomes (1,174 coded questions).
finding.measure: Bloom’s taxonomy category of student questions; CLEAR framework ratings (concise, logical, explicit, adaptive, reflective)
finding.std_deviation: CLEAR dimension SDs reported in Table 2 and 3, not a single outcome SD

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived the AI assistant as faster and more convenient than human support, and they used it more frequently than teachers or teaching assistants (paired t-tests: usage frequency vs teachers t=3.86, p<.001; vs TAs t=3.71, p<.001; helpfulness vs TAs t=2.38, p=.014). The study also found 1,418 dialogue rounds over 10 weeks, indicating substantial use, but no direct productivity or time-saved metric was reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported frequency, reliance, helpfulness, and interview reports of convenience/timeliness

paper_profiles.title: Perceptions of High School Graduates and Educators Regarding a Mathematics Intervention for College and Career Readiness
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This dissertation examines a local mathematics achievement problem at Midwest High School in Iowa, where more than 68% of 11th-grade students from 2017 through 2024 did not meet the ACT college- and career-readiness benchmark in mathematics despite the school’s use of the Kendall Hunt Illustrative Mathematics (KHIM) curriculum. The study asks why the curriculum did not appear to improve outcomes and what changes graduates and educators believed would better support student success.

The study used a basic qualitative design with semistructured interviews. Participants included eight high school graduates and four non-administrative educators from Midwest High School. The author analyzed interview transcripts using in vivo coding to identify themes in participants’ perceptions of learning and teaching with KHIM. Participants generally viewed the curriculum as supporting procedural skill, fluency, peer collaboration, and conceptual integrity, but they also reported insufficient support, guidance, practice, timely feedback, and instructional presence.

The project component proposes integrating lower-cost generative AI tools into mathematics instruction to provide personalized practice, real-world applications, timely feedback, and more instructional presence. The dissertation positions this as a means to improve college- and career-readiness at Midwest High School. It is not an empirical study of Khanmigo or any AI system, and it does not report achievement effects from an intervention trial.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative dissertation focused on perceptions and a proposed AI-enabled project, not a rigorous intervention study. It provides contextual evidence and implementation rationale, but no causal evaluation of Khanmigo or any AI tool on student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No empirical effect on science learning outcomes is reported, and the paper is not about Khanmigo or science instruction. The text only suggests potential future benefits of generative AI in mathematics, without measurable impact data.

interventions.use_case: The dissertation proposes integrating lower-cost generative AI tools into mathematics instruction to provide personalized practice, real-world application opportunities, timely feedback, and increased instructional presence.

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Three Pivotal Concepts in K-12 Science State Standards and Maps of Conceptual Growth to Research in Physics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how K-12 science standards align with core physics concepts that are foundational for later learning yet notoriously difficult for students to master. The authors analyze U.S. national and four state science standards, together with concept maps from Project 2061 and the research literature on learning difficulties, to identify physics ideas that are both prominent in standards and especially important for instruction.

The paper focuses on three conceptual areas: Newton’s laws (especially force and motion), conservation of energy, and geometrical optics. Rather than testing a new technological or classroom intervention, it synthesizes existing research and describes instructional approaches that have shown some success, such as prediction-based demonstrations, interactive lecture demonstrations, and guided explorations. The intended context is K-12 science education in the United States, spanning elementary through high school, though the paper also discusses evidence from introductory college physics research to explain student misconceptions.

The main conclusion is that these three areas are pivotal conceptual building blocks, appear across multiple state standards, and are deeply resistant to conventional instruction. The authors argue that K-12 science teaching should emphasize deeper inquiry into a smaller number of foundational ideas and use research-based strategies to help students overcome persistent misconceptions. The paper does not report direct empirical evidence about Khanmigo or any AI tool, and it does not evaluate science achievement outcomes relative to a comparison group.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a conceptual review/standards analysis rather than an empirical evaluation of Khanmigo or any educational technology intervention. It presents no original study design, comparison condition, or causal estimate tied to K-12 science learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct measured impact of any intervention in this paper, and it does not evaluate Khanmigo or other technology on student science outcomes. The paper is useful as background on physics learning difficulties, but it provides no outcome evidence for the requested topic.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual/theoretical review of K-12 physics standards and student difficulties, not a direct intervention study, so it does not report a causal effect on science achievement. It argues that Newton’s laws and conservation of energy are foundational scientific reasoning targets and summarizes prior studies showing persistent misconceptions and some instructional approaches that can improve understanding, but without a single new evaluative estimate from this paper.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of standards; synthesis of prior physics education research on misconceptions and instructional strategies

paper_profiles.title: Accessible Computer Science for K-12 Students with Hearing Impairments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of accessible computer science instruction for Deaf and Hard of Hearing (D/HH) K-12 students, especially those whose primary language is American Sign Language (ASL). The authors argue that existing captions, text-based explanations, and generic online materials are often inaccessible or linguistically mismatched for D/HH learners, particularly for technical STEM vocabulary and programming concepts.

The paper proposes a new project to create an accessible block-based coding curriculum and web application for K-12 students with disabilities, with a specific focus on D/HH middle-school learners. The approach includes ASL video explanations of core computer science topics such as algorithms, conditionals, loops, variables, functions, debugging, and object-oriented programming, paired with block-based programming demonstrations and robot-based activities. The design also incorporates accessibility features such as captions, visual feedback, adjustable video speed, and ASL tooltips for programming blocks.

The work is conceptual and developmental rather than an evaluation of learning outcomes. The authors describe planned collaboration with ASL experts, Deaf educators, and Deaf Kids Code, and state that a study with a middle-school deaf population will be conducted in the future to examine impact. As written, the paper does not report empirical evidence that the intervention improves science or computing achievement, reasoning, vocabulary, inquiry skills, retention, engagement, or assignment performance relative to standard instruction or any comparator.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a design/proposal paper describing an ongoing accessibility project and future planned evaluation, not a completed empirical study. It reports no rigorous outcome data, comparison group, or quantitative methodology for student learning gains.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No measured impact is reported for science or computing outcomes, so there is no evidence of positive or negative intervention effect. The paper only hypothesizes potential benefits and states that a study will be conducted later.

interventions.use_case: accessible block-based coding curriculum for K-12 deaf and hard-of-hearing students, with embedded ASL video tutorials, captions, and visual tooltips for programming concepts

paper_profiles.title: The Photometric LSST Astronomical Time-Series Classification Challenge (PLAsTiCC): Selection of a Performance Metric for Classification Probabilities Balancing Diverse Science Goals
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to choose an evaluation metric for a probabilistic multi-class classification challenge in astronomy, specifically the Photometric LSST Astronomical Time-series Classification Challenge (PLAsTiCC). The authors argue that traditional deterministic classification metrics are not suitable because PLAsTiCC requires participants to submit class probabilities rather than single labels, and because the challenge must balance many scientific uses of the results rather than optimize for one target class or one application.

The paper studies candidate metrics using simulated mock classification submissions designed to mimic realistic failure modes such as uncertainty, overconfidence, class confusion, class imbalance effects, tunnel vision on common classes, cruise control behavior, and class subsumption. It compares log-loss and Brier score under different class-weighting schemes, and also benchmarks them against a metric used in a prior supernova classification challenge (SNPhotCC). The paper does not study educational users or learners; its population is astronomy classification systems and mock challenge submissions.

The main conclusion is that a weighted log-loss is the best fit for the current PLAsTiCC challenge because it preserves probabilistic information, handles multi-class outputs, and is sensitive to problematic systematic errors while allowing class weighting to reflect diverse science goals. The authors also note that the log-loss is generally more sensitive than the Brier score, especially for distinguishing high-performing classifiers and penalizing subsuming behavior. The paper is methodological and theoretical rather than an empirical intervention study, so it provides no evidence about K-12 science learning or Khanmigo.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a methods/theory paper about selecting a performance metric for an astronomy classification challenge, not an empirical study of an educational intervention. It contains no K-12 instructional sample, no learner outcomes, and no causal or correlational evidence relevant to Khanmigo or science learning.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational impact is measured or reported. The paper does not evaluate science achievement, conceptual understanding, engagement, or assignment performance in any learner population.

paper_profiles.title: Critical Science Plan for the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents the Critical Science Plan (CSP) for the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST), a large solar observatory designed to advance fundamental solar physics. The article does not report an educational intervention or study of student learning; instead, it outlines the scientific questions DKIST is intended to address and the unique observational capabilities that will enable those investigations.

The paper describes DKIST’s instrumentation, wavelength coverage, spatial and temporal resolution, and spectropolarimetric capabilities, then maps these capabilities onto major solar research themes such as magnetoconvection and dynamo processes, acoustic-gravity wave excitation, magnetoconvective modulation of solar luminosity, active-region evolution, and sunspot fine structure. It also discusses flares, coronal mass ejections, precursors, magnetic-field changes during eruptions, energy deposition, and flare ribbons.

The context is solar physics rather than schooling: the intended users are solar scientists and instrument scientists working with DKIST and related observatories. The main conclusion is that DKIST’s advanced observations will enable new measurements of small-scale magnetic structure, dynamics, and energy release processes on the Sun, thereby improving theories and models of solar activity and its broader astrophysical implications. No K-12 science learning outcomes, Khanmigo use, or classroom-based comparator study are reported.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a critical science plan and conceptual roadmap for the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope, not an empirical evaluation of an educational intervention. It contains no K-12 science learning study, no comparator, and no measured student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct evidence here of impact on science learning, engagement, assignment performance, or any other K-12 educational outcome. The paper is outside the requested Khanmigo education evidence scope and provides no applicable effect estimate.

paper_profiles.title: Simulating Surveys for ELT-MOSAIC: Status of the MOSAIC Science Case after Phase A
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents the consolidated science case for the MOSAIC multi-object spectrograph concept on the European Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). Rather than evaluating an educational intervention, it describes the scientific goals, instrument requirements, and survey strategies developed during the MOSAIC Phase A study, using simulations to assess feasibility and optimize design trade-offs.

The approach centers on end-to-end scientific simulations with the WEBSIM-COMPASS tool to estimate observing times, signal-to-noise requirements, and survey speed for proposed MOSAIC programmes. The paper outlines four high-priority extragalactic survey themes: mass assembly and evolution of dwarf galaxies, inventory of matter, first-light galaxies and reionisation, and extragalactic stellar populations. It also discusses observational modes such as high-definition IFUs, visible IFUs, and high-multiplex near-IR and visible modes.

The relevant population/context here is astronomical targets such as distant galaxies, intergalactic gas, circumgalactic gas, and resolved stellar populations in nearby galaxies, observed with future ELT instrumentation. The main conclusion is that MOSAIC’s Phase A design can support a broad and transformational extragalactic science programme, though some science cases are limited by wavelength coverage and performance constraints. The paper argues that multiplex, throughput, and spectral resolution are key determinants of survey efficiency and that MOSAIC will be competitive with other future facilities for many of the highlighted programmes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a conceptual/survey-design proceedings article about the MOSAIC astronomical instrument and its simulated science cases, not an educational intervention study. It contains no K-12 education methodology, no student-level empirical comparison, and no direct evidence relevant to Khanmigo or science learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no observed educational impact because the paper does not evaluate any instructional technology in schools or measure student learning outcomes. The content is unrelated to K-12 science learning and provides no evidence of effect.

paper_profiles.title: Navigating the State of Cognitive Flow: Context-Aware AI Interventions for Effective Reasoning Support
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how AI-augmented reasoning systems can provide support without disrupting a user’s cognitive engagement. The authors argue that existing reasoning assistants often use static, one-size-fits-all interventions that may interrupt thinking, reduce focus, and weaken decision-making quality. To address this, the paper introduces the idea of "cognitive flow," extending flow theory to AI-supported reasoning contexts.

The proposed approach is a context-aware cognitive augmentation framework that adapts interventions based on three factors: type, timing, and scale. Rather than evaluating a deployed system with participants, the paper draws on prior literature and behavioral cues such as gaze behavior, typing hesitation, interaction speed, gesture patterns, and other multimodal signals to argue that AI can infer when a user is overloaded, stuck, or under-challenged, and then provide minimally intrusive support. The setting discussed is general AI-augmented reasoning, not a specific classroom or educational deployment.

The main conclusion is a design argument: AI interventions should be personalized and dynamically adapted to sustain or restore flow, thereby supporting deeper reasoning, engagement, and agency. The paper does not report an empirical study, participant outcomes, or evidence of improved learning or achievement; instead it calls for future mixed-method evaluations of context-aware augmentation strategies.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual position paper proposing a framework for context-aware cognitive flow interventions. It reports no empirical study, no evaluation design, and no measured student outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper provides no direct evidence of impact on K-12 learning, science outcomes, engagement, or assignment performance. It is a call for future research rather than an intervention study.

paper_profiles.title: The Operationalization of “Fields” as WoS Subject Categories (WCs) in Evaluative Bibliometrics: The cases of “Library and Information Science” and “Science & Technology Studies”
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether Web of Science Subject Categories (WCs) are suitable for normalizing citation impact in bibliometric evaluation. The authors argue that although WCs are widely treated as a best-practice field classification, they were originally created for information retrieval rather than evaluative research and may therefore blur disciplinary boundaries when used to compare citation performance across fields.

To make this case, the paper presents two empirical illustrations: library and information science (LIS), which is represented by a single WC, and science and technology studies (STS), which is spread across multiple WCs with little common overlap. Using journal-journal citation maps and category assignments from Journal Citation Reports, the authors show that the WC-based grouping can mix journals that do not meaningfully belong together and split journals that are closely related in practice. This is especially problematic for interdisciplinary areas.

The population is not human participants but journal sets in LIS and STS. The context is bibliometric evaluation and research assessment, not education. The authors conclude that WC-based normalization may be acceptable for broad statistical purposes but is too imprecise for detailed evaluative use, particularly at the institutional or individual level. They suggest alternative approaches such as discipline-specific classifications, paper-level indexing systems, or algorithmically generated field structures, while also cautioning that each alternative has its own limitations.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a bibliometrics/methods article about Web of Science subject categories and citation normalization, not an empirical study of an educational technology intervention. It provides no K-12 or student-learning methodology relevant to Khanmigo or science learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no evidence here of any educational impact, let alone effects on science achievement, conceptual understanding, reasoning, vocabulary, inquiry skills, retention, engagement, or assignment performance. The paper is unrelated to the requested intervention and outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: MatScIE: An automated tool for the generation of databases of methods and parameters used in the computational materials science literature
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of extracting structured information from unstructured computational materials science articles. The authors note that the field is producing a rapidly growing body of papers, but details such as materials, methods, codes, parameters, and structures remain difficult to reuse because they are embedded in PDF text and require manual extraction. The goal is to build an automated information-extraction system that can support downstream database creation and literature analysis.

The proposed intervention is MatScIE (Material Science Information Extractor), a sequence-labeling and sentence-classification pipeline built on annotated materials-science PDFs. The system combines word2vec, character-level embeddings, and ELMo embeddings in a BiLSTM-CRF model for named-entity extraction over five categories: material, method, code, parameter, and structure. The authors also train a BERT-based sentence classifier to identify result-bearing sentences in abstracts for summary-level extraction. They further introduce a relabeling/mimicking strategy and post-processing rules to improve extraction accuracy.

The dataset consists of 214 materials science articles mined from arXiv (cond-mat.mtrl-sci) and annotated by experts; a separate set of 90 abstracts was annotated for sentence classification. The work is entirely in the computational materials science domain, not K-12 education, and does not study learners, teachers, or classroom implementation. The paper reports strong extraction performance for some entity types and shows that the mimicking model performs best overall, while also providing a web interface and larger-scale bibliometric-style analysis over 10,000 papers.

Overall, the paper concludes that automated extraction can substantially improve access to materials-science literature and enable database building, tracking of methods and codes over time, and quicker retrieval of relevant experimental parameters. It does not evaluate educational outcomes or any Khanmigo-related intervention.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is not a study of Khanmigo or any educational intervention in K-12 science learning. It is a computational materials science NLP systems paper, so it provides no direct empirical evidence relevant to the requested education outcome domain.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no evidence here of impact on student science achievement, conceptual understanding, reasoning, vocabulary, inquiry skills, retention, engagement, or assignment performance. The paper evaluates information extraction performance on materials-science documents, not learning outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: The Art of Planetary Science: Art as a Tool for Scientific Inquiry and Public Discourse around Space Exploration
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes The Art of Planetary Science (TAPS), an annual art exhibition and related workshop series designed to use science- and data-driven art to increase public engagement with planetary science and space exploration. The author argues that art can help people connect emotionally and intellectually with science, support interdisciplinary inquiry, and create a public forum for discussion about humanity’s relationship with space.

The main intervention is the Making Space workshop, a multi-day program for artists, educators, scientists, engineers, and related adults. Participants completed science-art activities, small-group discussions, and collaborative art-making prompts focused on planetary science concepts and the use of art for scientific inquiry. The paper also describes the broader TAPS exhibitions, which have run since 2013 at the University of Arizona and include artworks from scientists, artists, and the public. Workshop participants were surveyed about changes in interest, accessibility, identity, and willingness to engage in science discourse.

The evidence reported is descriptive and based largely on self-report and informal observation rather than objective learning measures. The author concludes that the exhibitions and workshops appeared to increase participants’ interest in learning about space and science, make science feel more accessible, and encourage future engagement with science-related art and discourse. The paper presents art as a promising tool for science engagement, but it does not provide rigorous causal evidence of learning gains or comparisons against standard instruction.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive/theoretical article with anecdotal and informal survey evidence, not a controlled empirical study. It does not evaluate Khanmigo or any AI tutoring intervention, and it lacks rigorous methodology, comparison groups, or validated outcome measures.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects are positive but small, subjective, and limited to workshop participants in an informal outreach context. There is no evidence of direct K-12 science achievement impact or comparable rigorous outcomes, so the overall impact is unclear and modest at best.

finding.finding_summary: This paper reports informal and survey-based evidence that the art-and-science exhibition/workshop increased participants’ interest in learning about space/science (83% of workshop survey responses) and made space/science feel more accessible (79%). A second workshop found 88% of respondents reported increased interest in participating in space exploration discourse through art; however, these are self-reported perceptions from small workshop samples (n=25 and n=29, with 24 total survey responses), not achievement outcomes.
finding.measure: Post-workshop self-report survey items on interest, accessibility, and willingness to engage in space/science discourse
finding.study_size: n=25 and n=29 workshops; n=24 survey responses

finding.finding_summary: Respondents described shifts in perspective, broader self-identity as artists/scientists, and intent to pursue more science-driven art, suggesting gains in identity, reflection, and interdisciplinary inquiry. The paper also notes that about half of participants created their own artworks after the workshop, indicating some persistence of engagement, but no controlled comparison or standardized durable-skill measure was used.
finding.measure: Open-ended survey responses on identity, perspective, and future intent; follow-up participation/creation of artwork

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines the opportunities and risks of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for human learning. Rather than testing a specific intervention empirically, it synthesizes insights from learning sciences, educational technology, and human-computer interaction to ask how GenAI may transform learning support, learning resources, feedback, and assessment.

The paper discusses GenAI systems such as large language models and multimodal generators, with Khan Academy’s Khanmigo used as one representative example of AI-supported tutoring. The discussion is not limited to one learner group or school context; instead, it spans human learning broadly, with particular attention to implications for schooling and the future of education.

The main argument is that GenAI can scale personalized support, diversify learning materials, provide timely feedback, and enable more authentic assessment, but these benefits depend on human-centered design, educator involvement, and rigorous evidence. The paper also stresses major risks: hallucinations and inaccurate outputs, privacy and equity concerns, overreliance and reduced learner agency, assessment disruption, and increased workload and techno-stress for educators. It concludes that AI literacy, evidence-based decision-making, and methodological rigor are essential for responsible integration of GenAI into education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/theoretical article, not an empirical study, and it does not report original data, design, or causal identification. It synthesizes prior literature and uses examples such as Khanmigo to motivate hypotheses and concerns.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potentially important implications for K-12 AI tutoring practice and policy, but it provides no direct effect estimates for student learning. Its impact is therefore informative and field-shaping rather than evidence of measured educational benefit.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual discussion of Khanmigo as a GPT-4-powered tutoring chatbot for K-12 learning support, especially guiding learners through math problems via step-by-step questions, constructive feedback, and inquiry-based scaffolding rather than giving direct answers.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI/LLM tutors like Khanmigo may support critical thinking and problem-solving by prompting students with guiding questions and step-by-step reasoning, but it also cautions that overreliance can weaken agency, self-regulation, creativity, and deeper learning. No original empirical effect estimate is reported; the discussion cites emerging evidence that removing GenAI support can reduce performance, suggesting a performance illusion rather than durable skill development.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, agency, self-regulation, creativity (conceptual/theoretical discussion; no direct measure in this paper)

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests GenAI may improve engagement and motivation through personalized support and timely interaction, but it also warns that dependence on AI can reduce learner agency and foster overreliance. These claims are presented as a synthesis of prior studies rather than a new empirical test, so no effect size or sample size is reported here.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, agency (conceptual/theoretical discussion; no direct measure in this paper)

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that GenAI can scale personalized learning support and reduce educator burden by handling repetitive explanation and feedback tasks. It also notes a potential downside: implementation may increase teacher workload and techno-stress if professional support is insufficient. No original empirical estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, feedback efficiency, scalability of support (conceptual/theoretical discussion; no direct measure in this paper)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues GenAI could democratize access to high-quality tutoring and learning resources, but also stresses risks of unequal access, English-language dominance, privacy concerns, and broader ethical/governance challenges. This is a perspective synthesis with no direct evaluation, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Access, equity, privacy, transparency, governance (conceptual/theoretical discussion; no direct measure in this paper)

paper_profiles.title: A comprehensive review of large language models: issues and solutions in learning environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the growing use of large language models (LLMs) in education and the need for a structured understanding of their capabilities, benefits, and risks. The authors review the history, training, and working mechanisms of LLMs, then examine how these systems are being used across educational settings, with attention to both opportunities and concerns such as privacy, bias, overreliance, and pedagogical limitations. The paper is motivated by the rapid adoption of tools such as ChatGPT and educational deployments such as Khan Academy’s Khanmigo, although it is not an evaluation of a single classroom intervention.

The approach is a systematic literature review combined with a proposed theoretical framework for integrating LLMs into education. The framework emphasizes three pillars: personalized learning models, ethical and pedagogical balance, and learning adaptability across contexts such as K-12, higher education, and online learning. The review synthesizes prior studies on uses including automated content creation, personalized feedback, intelligent tutoring, language support, and administrative assistance.

The paper concludes that LLMs have substantial potential to support teaching and learning by improving personalization, accessibility, feedback, and efficiency. At the same time, it warns that current educational use is constrained by accuracy issues, bias, data privacy concerns, overreliance on AI, and the need for human oversight. The authors argue that successful adoption depends on teacher-AI collaboration, bias mitigation, data protection, and responsible, energy-efficient deployment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative/systematic review and conceptual framework paper, not an empirical evaluation with a controlled design. Although it is peer-reviewed and methodologically described, it does not provide primary causal evidence for student learning outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper identifies potentially important education-sector implications for LLM adoption, but it does not report measurable effect sizes or direct impact estimates. Its impact is therefore plausible and broad, but still unclear empirically.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of large language models in education, including ChatGPT-style conversational tutors, AI course assistants, and chatbot-supported personalized learning, feedback, and task support across K-12, higher education, and digital learning settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating content creation, answering routine questions, grading support, and other administrative tasks. It does not report an original effect size; the claim is synthesis-based and illustrated with examples such as ChatGPT and Khanmigo-like implementations for personalized feedback and classroom support.
finding.measure: Teacher workload reduction / automation of instructional and administrative tasks

finding.finding_summary: The review states that LLMs may support personalization, guidance, and knowledge access, but also warns that overreliance can undermine critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving. No original quantitative estimate is reported; the conclusion is qualitative and cautionary, based on the reviewed literature.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving concerns/benefits discussed in reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that LLMs may broaden access through translation, remote support, and personalized learning, but it also emphasizes risks around privacy, bias, academic integrity, and unequal access. This is a narrative review rather than an empirical comparison, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Access, inclusivity, privacy, bias, and academic integrity implications

paper_profiles.title: The Potential Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Equity and Inclusion in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This OECD working paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) may affect equity and inclusion in education, with a focus on school education. Rather than evaluating a single tool or intervention experimentally, it synthesises policy guidance, conceptual frameworks, and illustrative examples to clarify the opportunities and risks associated with AI use in educational systems. The central question is how AI can support more equitable and inclusive education while avoiding the exacerbation of existing inequalities.

The paper organises AI in education into three categories: learner-centred tools, teacher-led tools, and other institutional tools. It discusses how learner-centred systems such as intelligent tutoring systems, AI-enabled simulations, chatbots, and tools for students with special education needs may support adaptive learning, content enrichment, information access, and inclusion. It also addresses teacher-led tools for assessment, classroom management, curation of materials, and professional learning, as well as institutional tools for admissions, student-risk identification, and data-based decision making.

The analysis is grounded in desk-based research and draws on examples from OECD and other countries, but it is not an empirical evaluation of a specific intervention. The main conclusions are that AI may improve tailoring, access, efficiency, and support for diverse learners and educators, but only if issues such as unequal access, techno-ableism, bias, privacy, accountability, commercial influence, and teacher preparation are addressed. The paper argues that many claimed benefits remain hypotheses rather than well-established evidence and calls for more robust research, stronger policy guidance, and continuing professional learning in AI.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a grey-literature OECD working paper that is primarily a policy and conceptual review, not an empirical evaluation of a specific intervention. It does not present a clear study design, counterfactual, or original causal estimate for Khanmigo or the other tools discussed.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful equity and inclusion implications, but it provides no direct outcome estimates for students or teachers. As a descriptive synthesis, the impact on learning or implementation remains unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Khan Academy's Khanmigo is described as AI one-on-one tutoring for students, mimicking a writing coach by giving prompts and suggestions to move students forward as they write, debate, and collaborate. The paper frames it as a learner-centred conversational AI/tutoring tool rather than reporting an evaluation study.

AI-enabled simulations including chatbots, virtual reality, augmented reality, and game-based learning are discussed as immersive learning tools that can enrich content and support culturally responsive and accessible instruction, especially in science, history, and special education contexts.

Institutional AI tools are discussed for identifying students at risk of early leaving from education and training, using data-based decision making to support institutional equity and inclusion goals.

AI tools are discussed as supporting assessment and providing prompts/suggestions to move student work forward, which includes feedback-like functions within teacher-led and learner-centred applications.

paper_profiles.title: New Era of Artificial Intelligence in Education: Towards a Sustainable Multifaceted Revolution
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the emerging literature on artificial intelligence in education, with a focus on its applications, benefits, and challenges. The authors frame the discussion around major AI-enabled functions such as personalized learning, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment automation, and teacher–student collaboration, arguing that these are the main pathways through which AI may reshape schooling and higher education.

The paper does not study a single intervention or collect original participant data. Instead, it conducts a scoping review of studies published between 2019 and mid-2023, drawing on Scopus and Google Scholar and ultimately including 44 eligible sources. The review is centered on higher education overall, though the discussion also references schools and K-12-related implications in a general way.

Across the reviewed literature, the authors conclude that AI can improve learning outcomes, increase time and cost efficiency, and expand access to quality education through scalable personalization and feedback. At the same time, they emphasize risks including data privacy and security, bias and discrimination, academic integrity concerns, technical failures, and the potential erosion of teacher–student interaction. Their overall position is supportive but cautious: AI should be integrated into education with safeguards and human oversight.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a scoping review / narrative synthesis rather than an empirical evaluation, and it explicitly notes that quality appraisal was not performed. It does not test an intervention or estimate causal effects, so it provides low-methodological evidence for the specific K-12 Khanmigo use-case.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues that AI may improve learning, efficiency, and access, but it reports no original effect sizes or direct K-12 outcomes. Its impact is therefore suggestive and broad rather than demonstrated, with no clear quantified effect for practice.

interventions.use_case: scoping review discussion of ChatGPT-style generative AI as an educational chatbot/tutor that can answer student questions, support dialogue, and provide tutoring-like assistance in higher education and classroom settings
review of AI-driven tutoring systems that model student knowledge, provide adaptive instruction, generate personalized feedback, and support one-on-one tutoring-like interactions
review of AI systems for automated assessment, grading, and immediate feedback on student work including quizzes, essays, problem-solving responses, and spoken answers
review of personalized learning platforms that adapt pacing, content, and recommendations to student data and performance patterns
review mentions learning analytics, knowledge tracing, and student performance prediction to identify students needing support and inform teacher decisions
review includes AI-supported instructional tools, smart content, and technology-driven instruction that deliver educational content with limited dialogue

paper_profiles.title: Personalized learning through AI: Pedagogical approaches and critical insights
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence-supported personalized learning is being studied in education, with particular attention to pedagogical approaches, implementation challenges, and the roles AI plays in tailoring instruction. The authors frame the problem as a gap in the literature: AI in education is expanding quickly, but pedagogical issues, real classroom implementation, and constraints such as privacy, access, and teacher preparation are not always analyzed in depth.

To address this, the study conducts a systematic literature review of 30 journal articles identified through Scopus and Web of Science using PRISMA-guided screening.
