The review synthesizes research from 2010–2024 on AI-supported personalized learning systems, including chatbots, machine learning, NLP, intelligent tutoring systems, and generative AI such as ChatGPT. The review is not limited to one subject area; it includes general education, language education, science education, STEM, mathematics, medical education, and professional development, with many studies involving university students and some involving high school students, teachers, and teacher candidates.

The paper concludes that AI is most often used for automated feedback, adaptive content delivery, personalized learning paths, and interactive support. Across the reviewed studies, the most common pedagogical mechanisms are dynamic content adaptation, real-time feedback, learner-centered and task-based activities, and guided autonomy. The authors also identify major limitations and risks: technical constraints, data privacy concerns, implementation complexity, weak integration with teaching practice, accuracy and reliability problems, plagiarism risks, overreliance on technology, unequal access, and the need for substantial teacher training. Overall, the study argues that effective AI-enabled personalized learning requires a balanced strategy that integrates technology, pedagogy, and ethics.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review using PRISMA and qualitative content analysis, but it is not a primary causal evaluation and does not provide pooled quantitative estimates. The evidence base is synthesized from heterogeneous studies with mostly mixed-methods, qualitative, and theoretical designs.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper indicates likely benefits for personalized learning, engagement, and instructional efficiency, but it reports no robust effect sizes from a controlled study of learner outcomes. Impact is therefore suggestive and important for practice, yet still unclear in magnitude.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of generative AI tutors and chatbots in AI-supported personalized learning, including ChatGPT-like tools used for interactive dialogue, real-time feedback, individualized guidance, and adaptive support in education.
AI-enabled personalized learning systems that adapt content, pacing, and learning pathways based on learner profiles, prior knowledge, preferences, and performance data.
Classical AI tutoring systems and multi-agent/adaptive tutoring approaches discussed as examples of personalized learning environments that monitor progress and tailor instruction.
AI systems that generate automated assessment, formative feedback, and immediate responses on student work or task performance as part of personalized learning.
Language-learning and writing-support tools, including ChatGPT-supported language practice, vocabulary/writing assistance, and other AI tools used in language education.

finding.finding_summary: The review found that AI-supported personalized learning is expanding but faces substantial implementation barriers at the institutional level, especially teacher preparation, curriculum integration, privacy, and equity. Across the reviewed literature (30 studies), the most frequent challenge category was pedagogical and implementation issues (f=33), followed by access/equity (f=18) and technical challenges (f=16), indicating that system-level adoption remains constrained by organizational readiness and governance concerns.
finding.measure: Frequency and thematic coding of implementation challenges across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests AI tools can improve instructional efficiency by automating feedback, assessment, and content adaptation, and by supporting lesson planning and data analysis for teachers. However, these gains are tempered by workload from integration, validation, and training demands, so the net efficiency effect is beneficial but not uniformly achieved across settings.
finding.measure: Thematic synthesis of reported roles such as automated response systems, assessment generation, lesson planning support, and teacher preparation demands

finding.finding_summary: The literature synthesis reports consistent positive links between AI-supported personalized learning and engagement, motivation, and learner support. The review notes that AI-driven personalization, real-time feedback, and individualized guidance are associated with higher motivation and engagement, but no pooled effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, and learner support themes reported across the reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies potential support for critical thinking, self-directed learning, and collaboration, but also explicitly flags risks of reduced critical thinking, overreliance on technology, and diminished social interaction. Because findings are qualitative and based on thematic synthesis rather than outcome measurement, the direction is mixed rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Thematic coding of reported pedagogical benefits and risks related to critical thinking, autonomy, collaboration, and social interaction

finding.finding_summary: Across the review, AI-supported personalized learning was framed as improving subject learning through adaptive content delivery, personalized pathways, and real-time support, with the strongest concentration of studies in general education, language education, and STEM-related contexts. One included study is cited as suggesting AI-driven personalized learning systems can improve student performance by 30%, but the review itself does not provide a pooled estimate or sufficient details for meta-analytic interpretation.
finding.measure: Reported performance improvement themes across subject domains; cited individual-study performance claims

paper_profiles.title: A Framework for Approaching AI Education in Educator Preparation Programs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the gap between rapidly advancing AI technologies and the preparation of future educators to use and teach about AI in PreK-12 settings. The authors argue that educator preparation programs (EPPs) have not yet systematically incorporated AI education, even though teachers are increasingly expected to integrate AI-powered instructional tools and help students develop AI literacy.

Rather than reporting an empirical study, the paper presents a framework developed through collaboration among ISTE AI Explorations for EPPs Faculty Fellows. The framework includes seven strategies: building foundational AI understanding, cultivating skills with AI instructional tools, using the Five Big Ideas in AI, creating exploratory and experiential learning opportunities, infusing AI literacy across the curriculum, integrating critical examinations of equity/ethics/culture, and embedding these approaches throughout teacher preparation. The paper discusses generative AI, intelligent tutoring systems, pedagogical agents and chatbots such as Khanmigo, social robots, and XR tools as examples of AI technologies relevant to teacher education.

The intended population is EPP faculty, preservice teachers, and teacher candidates in the United States, with the broader goal of improving how future teachers in PreK-12 classrooms learn with and about AI. The main conclusion is that AI literacy should not be treated as an add-on; it should be systematically infused across teacher preparation programs, with explicit attention to equity, ethics, bias, access, and the evolving capabilities and limitations of AI tools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/framework paper rather than an empirical evaluation. It does not report a study design, comparison group, or outcome data, so there is no assessable causal or correlational evidence base here.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has potentially important institutional implications for teacher preparation and AI literacy, but it does not demonstrate measured impact. Its influence is therefore best characterized as theoretical and programmatic rather than evidence of observed outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Framework and professional-learning guidance for integrating AI education across educator preparation programs, including AI literacy, AI tools, and critical examination of AI in teacher preparation; not an intervention study of a single product.

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Models for Education: A Survey
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper surveys the emerging use of large language models (LLMs) in education, focusing on how they can support teaching, learning, feedback, and educational system development. The authors frame LLMs as a major step in the evolution of AI in education, arguing that they may improve personalized instruction, immediate feedback, adaptive tutoring, and resource generation while also changing teacher roles and educational workflows.

The review synthesizes LLM-related educational applications across several contexts, including intelligent tutoring, homework support, assessment and feedback, interdisciplinary learning, teacher professional development, and online education platforms. It also highlights examples such as Khanmigo, ChatGPT-based educational tools, and Chinese education-oriented LLM products, but these are discussed as illustrative cases rather than as primary study participants. The paper does not report a specific population sample, intervention duration, or empirical evaluation; instead it organizes the field by technologies, integration pathways, and application scenarios.

The main conclusions are that LLMs have strong potential to make education more personalized, interactive, accessible, and efficient, especially through guided questioning, one-to-one support, and content generation. At the same time, the authors emphasize important risks and challenges, including hallucinations/inaccurate answers, high development and deployment costs, privacy and security concerns, the need for prompt optimization, and the importance of human judgment and teacher involvement. Overall, the paper is a conceptual and state-of-the-field review rather than an outcome study of any one classroom implementation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative/systematic survey with no original experimental design, no primary data collection, and no causal identification. It is useful for mapping the field, but it does not meet empirical credibility criteria for impact estimation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for tutoring, feedback, and teacher support, but provides no measured K-12 learning effect sizes. Because the evidence is conceptual and not outcome-tested, the likely practical impact is unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Survey of large language model applications in education, including ChatGPT/Khanmigo-style conversational tutoring, guided questioning, real-time problem-solving, and teacher/student support across subjects.

finding.finding_summary: This is a survey paper rather than an outcome study, but it argues that LLMs can improve teaching quality and support interdisciplinary knowledge coverage across subjects. The paper cites examples such as Khanmigo, ERNIE Bot, Spark Desk, and MathGPT as enabling guided learning, personalized support, and instant feedback, but it reports no original effect sizes or study sample for K-12 science instruction.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of reported LLM capabilities and use cases in education

finding.finding_summary: The review claims LLMs can promote critical thinking and problem-solving by asking questions, simulating teacher dialogue, and guiding students toward self-learning rather than directly supplying answers. These benefits are described conceptually for science and mathematics contexts, but the paper provides no empirical estimate or controlled evaluation.
finding.measure: Narrative claims about critical thinking, problem-solving, and self-directed learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues LLMs can improve teacher effectiveness by helping with lesson preparation, outlining, and faster access to teaching resources, thereby reducing workload and supporting classroom instruction. However, these are descriptive claims in a survey; no implementation study or workload metric is reported.
finding.measure: Narrative description of teacher preparation and instructional support efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The survey presents both potential benefits and risks for institutional adoption of LLMEdu, including support for sustainable development, expanded access, and personalized education, alongside concerns about hallucination, privacy/security, cost, and digital divide. No quantitative institutional outcome is measured, so this is a conceptual mixed assessment rather than an effect estimate.
finding.measure: Narrative discussion of implementation benefits and challenges

paper_profiles.title: Student-teachers’ pedagogical beliefs: learner-centred or teacher-centred when using ICT in the science classroom?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory case study examines whether four PGCE student-teachers’ stated pedagogical beliefs aligned with their actual classroom practice when they used ICT for teaching science. The paper is motivated by the common theory-practice gap in teacher education: student-teachers may espouse constructivist, learner-centred views while enacting more teacher-centred, instructivist lessons.

The study investigated how four South African PGCE students used ICT and what influenced those uses. Data sources included a teacher belief system (TBS) tool, drawing prompts followed by interviews, an open-ended questionnaire, lesson plans, assessment feedback forms, short emailed summaries of ICT use, and interviews with the Science Method lecturer and mentor teacher. The participants were Science/Mathematics student-teachers completing school-based learning at a rural school in the Eastern Cape, South Africa. They had grown up in under-resourced township schools with little or no ICT access.

Findings suggest a mismatch between espoused beliefs and classroom enactment. Although the participants described constructivist and learner-centred beliefs, their ICT use was mostly teacher-centred: PowerPoint, YouTube videos, simulations, and software were used primarily to present content, demonstrate experiments, explain procedures, and manage the lesson flow. Some learner-centred elements appeared, such as group work, question-and-answer exchanges, discussion, and opportunities for reflection, but these were limited. The paper concludes that these student-teachers need stronger support, modelling, and opportunities to design and enact learner-centred ICT lessons; it also highlights how prior schooling, tertiary experiences, and lecturer modelling shaped their practice.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative exploratory case study with four student-teachers, triangulated with mentor/lecturer feedback. It provides rich practice-level evidence but does not estimate causal effects or generalizable outcome impacts.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests modest practical benefits in classroom efficiency and engagement, but it reports no measured learning gains and emphasizes that implementation remained mostly teacher-centred. The impact on student outcomes is therefore unclear and limited.

interventions.use_case: Student-teachers used ICT for science instruction via PowerPoint slides, pre-downloaded YouTube videos, simulations, and computer-assisted learning software (e.g. CAMI maths/science, Khan maths/science) to present content, demonstrate experiments, and support explanations when lab equipment was unavailable.

Science and mathematics simulations were used to illustrate concepts such as electricity circuits and velocity, allowing learners to observe processes that could not easily be done as live practicals.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not test learning gains, but it provides qualitative evidence that ICT use in science lessons supported conceptual explanation, demonstration of experiments, and access to otherwise unavailable practical experiences. At the same time, the enactment was largely teacher-centred, limiting opportunities for learner discovery and scientific inquiry even when videos, simulations, or group work were used.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of lesson plans, interviews, drawings, assessor feedback, and teacher reflections on science lesson practice

finding.finding_summary: The student-teachers reported and were observed to use some questioning, discussion, and group work, which could support collaboration and engagement, but these elements were limited and inconsistent. Overall, ICT lessons were still described by supervisors as largely instructivist, with only small movement toward learner-centred participation.
finding.measure: Observations and reflective accounts of questioning, discussion, and group work during ICT-supported science lessons

finding.finding_summary: Participants believed ICT could make lessons more engaging and less intimidating for learners, and one participant explicitly described a 'humanizing pedagogy' intended to reduce fear and invite questions. However, the overall classroom enactment still showed teacher control and limited learner voice, so the socio-emotional benefits were partial rather than consistent.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of learner engagement, comfort, and willingness to ask questions in ICT-supported lessons

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that PowerPoint, videos, and pre-downloaded materials saved lesson time and reduced the need to redraw diagrams or conduct unavailable experiments. These tools were used as substitutes for scarce resources and to streamline presentation, suggesting improved instructional efficiency rather than measured learning gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of teaching time saved and substitution for scarce apparatus/resources

paper_profiles.title: Studying In-service Teacher Professional Development on Purposeful Integration of Engineering into K-12 STEM Teaching (Research to Practice)
paper_profiles.venue: American Society for Engineering Education Conference Proceedings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how two graduate-level professional development courses supported in-service K-12 teachers’ integration of engineering into STEM teaching. The authors focus on a recurring problem in STEM education: although teachers see value in engineering, many feel underprepared or anxious about implementing engineering practices and design-based instruction in their own classrooms. The study is framed around teacher self-efficacy and social justice-oriented STEM teaching.

The intervention consisted of two courses, Enhancing Mathematics with STEM and Engineering in the K-12 Classroom, embedded in a grant-funded STEM teacher leadership program. The courses included readings, short lectures, guest speakers from engineering and STEM fields, hands-on engineering activities, vertically aligned collaboration across grade bands, lesson planning, microteaching, peer feedback, and reflection. Teachers also worked on 5E lesson plans and engineering unit plans, with the engineering course emphasizing engineering design activities connected to community needs, societal impacts, and equity.

The participants were 18 in-service teachers from elementary, middle, and high school science, math, and computer science contexts in urban or suburban high-need districts in the United States. Data came from autobiographies, reflections, focus groups, lesson plans, microteaching, questionnaires, and instructor field notes. The authors conclude that the courses increased teachers’ self-efficacy for teaching engineering, that active learning and structured collaboration were important supports, and that explicitly linking engineering to social justice and societal problems helped teachers see engineering as relevant and meaningful. The paper also suggests that hands-on practice, feedback, and reflection were key mechanisms for teacher growth.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative case study of a professional development program with thematic analysis of reflections, focus groups, lesson plans, and observations. It provides credible descriptive evidence, but it is not experimental and reports no causal effect sizes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The program appears to have had meaningful benefits for a small group of in-service teachers, especially on self-efficacy and planning capacity, but the paper does not report quantitative impacts on student learning or system-level outcomes. The observed impact is promising but modest and localized.

finding.finding_summary: Across 18 in-service K-12 teachers, the study found increased self-efficacy and confidence for teaching STEM and engineering after two graduate STEM pedagogy courses. Early on, most participants reported low confidence with engineering integration, but by the end of the second course all participants reported strong self-efficacy; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections, focus groups, microteaching lesson plans, instructor observations/field notes, and autobiography/reflection assignments focused on STEM/engineering teaching self-efficacy

finding.finding_summary: The courses appeared to improve teachers’ pedagogical planning, collaboration, and ability to design integrated STEM lessons using engineering design and 5E microteaching. Teachers reported that vertical PLC-style collaboration, hands-on activities, peer feedback, and reflection helped them develop practical skills for lesson design and implementation; no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Integrated STEM lesson plans, engineering unit plans, microteaching performance, peer feedback, and participant reflections/focus groups

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that the professional development increased teachers’ confidence to advocate for STEM/engineering integration with colleagues and administrators and to frame engineering as a social-justice-oriented school practice. Findings are qualitative and program-level, showing likely influence on teacher agency and potential school implementation rather than measured institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Participant reflections and focus groups describing advocacy, STEM teacher identity, and perceptions of school-based implementation

paper_profiles.title: A systematic review of AI, VR, and LLM applications in special education: Opportunities, challenges, and future directions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence (AI), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), and large language models (LLMs) have been used in special education, what opportunities they create, and what challenges and future directions remain. It is positioned as a systematic review of 139 studies and uses deductive thematic analysis to synthesize recurring themes across the literature.

Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the paper reviews a broad set of technologies and use cases for students with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), including personalized learning, communication support, accessibility tools, social-skills interventions, and immersive learning environments. The authors also examine teacher attitudes, SEN methodologies and practices, and syndrome-specific applications across conditions such as autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disabilities, hearing and visual impairments, motor disabilities, speech impairments, learning disabilities, and emotional/psychological disorders.

The review concludes that VR and AI/LLM-based systems have substantial potential to support inclusion through personalized learning, scaffolding, multimodal feedback, communication support, and adaptive environments. However, it emphasizes major barriers and risks, including accessibility gaps, lack of implementation frameworks, limited teacher preparedness, bias, safety/privacy concerns, possible misinformation or hallucination-like errors from LLMs, cyber-security issues, cost barriers for VR, and overreliance on technology. The paper argues for clearer guidelines, policy support, and professional development to enable safe and equitable adoption in special education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review using deductive thematic analysis, but it synthesizes heterogeneous prior studies rather than testing a single intervention with causal identification. Evidence credibility is limited by the absence of a meta-analysis or primary effect estimation, so it fits a qualitative/review-level tier.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially meaningful benefits of AI/VR/LLMs in special education, especially for engagement, personalization, and teacher support, but provides no pooled effect sizes or direct outcome estimates. The likely impact is plausible but unclear in magnitude based on the evidence presented.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of LLMs used in special education as conversational assistants, personalized learning supports, and teacher-support tools, including examples such as Khanmigo, ChatGPT-like virtual assistants, and LLM-based virtual environments for SEND students.
LLM-enabled robotic or virtual-human supports used for therapy, conversational practice, and personalized interaction with autistic learners and other SEND students.
VR/AR game-based learning, immersive simulations, virtual labs, and storytelling environments for skill practice, engagement, and social learning in special education.
Personalized learning systems and individualized pathways that adapt content and pace to learners with disabilities, including special education support platforms and teacher-facing planning tools.

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes prior studies suggesting that AI, VR, and LLM tools can improve engagement, motivation, social interaction, and emotional support for SEND learners. It highlights potential benefits such as reduced isolation, structured and predictable environments, and more emotionally safe interactions, but these are qualitative claims drawn from the reviewed literature rather than a single pooled effect.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, social interaction, emotional support, and self-regulation as reported across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, VR/LLM applications are described as supporting critical thinking, creativity, cognition, communication, and self-regulated learning. The paper emphasizes scaffolding, multimodal feedback, and personalized pathways as plausible mechanisms, but it does not report a quantitative overall effect size.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, cognition, communication, self-regulated learning, creativity

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that LLMs can support teachers through grading, student progress tracking, lesson planning, and personalized feedback generation, potentially reducing workload. At the same time, it flags risks of oversimplified feedback and the need for human oversight, so the net effect is promising but not empirically quantified.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, lesson planning support, grading/progress-tracking assistance

finding.finding_summary: The review finds substantial implementation barriers and policy concerns: accessibility gaps, privacy and security risks, cost constraints, uneven infrastructure, limited access to paid systems, and the absence of clear frameworks for special education use. It argues that governance, inclusive policy, and professional development are necessary for effective adoption, but these conclusions are syntheses of prior literature rather than effect estimates.
finding.measure: Accessibility barriers, policy readiness, governance, implementation feasibility

paper_profiles.title: AI in Education: Rationale, Principles, and Instructional Implications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the broader question of how generative AI should be understood and used in schooling, with an emphasis on its instructional implications, benefits, risks, and the pedagogical conditions under which it may or may not support learning. Rather than testing a specific intervention experimentally, the article develops a theoretical and conceptual argument about AI in education, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, and discusses how they differ from search engines because they generate probabilistic outputs that can be inaccurate or hallucinated.

The paper positions AI as a potential support for personalized learning, explanation, scaffolding, and productivity, while warning that it can also become a shortcut that reduces cognitive effort and undermines deep learning, memory formation, perseverance, and critical thinking. It draws on cognitive theory, ecological theory, distributed cognition, and ideas such as desirable difficulties, learning management, and Socratic questioning to explain how AI might be used in ways that supplement rather than replace student effort. The article also discusses educational platforms and chatbots, including Khanmigo, as examples of tools that can guide students through hints and questions rather than direct answers.

The population discussed is broad and largely conceptual, covering school learners across primary, secondary, and preparatory settings, as well as teachers and school leaders who must decide when and how AI should be used. The context is general schooling, with some references to higher education and vocational education for comparison, but the paper does not report a specific empirical sample or intervention site. The main conclusion is that AI use in education must be guided by pedagogical rationale, student maturity, and subject matter; teachers should use professional judgment to ensure AI supports long-term learning, not superficial task completion. The paper also highlights risks such as hallucinations, political or normative bias in outputs, overreliance, reduced effort, and unequal access, and stresses that evidence on real learning effects remains thin.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/principles article with no original empirical study, no comparison group, and no quantitative evaluation of Khanmigo or other AI tools. It is useful for framing mechanisms and risks, but it does not meet criteria for empirical credibility.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper’s likely impact is modest and indirect: it shapes how practitioners think about AI use, scaffolding, and risks, but it does not demonstrate measured learning gains or implementation effects. Because the evidence is conceptual rather than empirical, the practical impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual discussion of conversational chatbots such as Khanmigo, ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Bing Chat, and similar LLM-based tools used to guide students with questions, hints, Socratic prompting, and explanatory support in school learning tasks.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLM tutors can support metacognition, critical thinking, and independent inquiry when they are used to prompt reflection, ask Socratic questions, and provide hints rather than direct answers. However, it also emphasizes that easy access to answers can weaken deep processing and reduce students' willingness to think independently, so the likely effect on durable skills depends heavily on implementation.
finding.measure: Theoretical synthesis of plausible mechanisms affecting critical thinking, metacognition, independent thinking, and self-reflection; no direct student outcome measure reported.

finding.finding_summary: The paper theorizes that AI can either support motivation and persistence by scaffolding effort through desirable difficulties or undermine self-discipline by enabling shortcuts and procrastination. It cites prior studies suggesting that direct-answer use of ChatGPT may encourage shortcut-taking and procrastination, but it does not report a new empirical effect size in this article.
finding.measure: Theoretical synthesis and cited prior findings on motivation, effort, self-discipline, and procrastination; no direct outcome measure in this paper.

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that conversational AI can make student work faster and more productive by supplying explanations, examples, and information retrieval support, and it notes that educators may perceive platforms with dashboards as helpful for monitoring progress. At the same time, it warns that speed gains may come at the cost of learning quality, so the operational benefit is not equivalent to educational benefit.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of task speed, productivity, and teacher dashboard/monitoring utility; no new quantitative measure reported.

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that LLMs can help students compose text, generate ideas, and get support for writing tasks, but it also warns that directly generated text may be superficial and can undermine actual writing development and deep learning. No original literacy outcome data are reported; the discussion is grounded in theory and cited examples rather than a controlled study.
finding.measure: Theoretical discussion of writing quality, text production, and learning-by-writing; no direct literacy measure reported.

finding.finding_summary: Across school subjects, the paper proposes that LLM-based tutoring can provide personalized explanations, prompts, and source-finding support in areas such as mathematics, humanities, coding, and social sciences. It also emphasizes that suitability depends on age, subject matter, and the need for prerequisite knowledge, with no new subject-specific effect sizes reported.
finding.measure: Theoretical discussion of subject-learning support and contextual suitability across disciplines; no direct academic achievement measure reported.

paper_profiles.title: MathVC: An LLM-Simulated Multi-Persona Virtual Classroom for Collaborative Mathematical Problem Solving
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of supporting collaborative problem solving (CPS) in mathematics classrooms, especially when real classrooms lack enough peers, time, or teacher bandwidth to sustain productive group work. The authors argue that large language models (LLMs) can be used not just to tutor individually, but to simulate multiple peer classmates who collaboratively reason with a student in a mathematically structured discussion.

To explore this idea, the paper introduces MathVC, a multi-persona virtual classroom in which one student interacts with several LLM-simulated virtual peers. The system uses two main mechanisms: a meta-planning controller that manages the stages of CPS (shared understanding, team organization, planning, execution, and validation), and persona simulation that encodes peer knowledge and common misconceptions using task schemas and error-injected persona schemas. The system also controls next-speaker selection and generates short, student-like dialogue acts and responses.

The authors evaluated MathVC with 14 U.S. middle school students in grades 6–8 using math problems aligned to their grade level. Data came from interaction logs, exit surveys, and semi-structured interviews. Students generally reported that the system felt collaborative and helpful, appreciating the diverse perspectives, immediate scaffolding, and human-like fallibility of the virtual peers. The paper concludes that multi-persona LLM systems can plausibly support collaborative mathematical learning, but also notes that authenticity depends on careful conversational design and that some responses can sound too formal or adult-like for middle school settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small qualitative/HCI evaluation with interviews, logs, and an exit survey rather than a controlled impact study. It provides useful design and usability evidence, but it does not establish causal learning effects or include a comparison condition.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported benefits are promising but modest and based on perceptions rather than measured achievement gains. There are no standardized effect sizes, so the impact on learning outcomes remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: LLM-simulated multi-persona virtual classroom for collaborative mathematical problem solving with middle-school students; virtual peers generate dialogue acts, brief peer-like responses, hints, questions, critiques, and scaffolded feedback during CPS.

A simulated virtual classroom environment that recreates peer collaboration for math problem solving, using multiple AI personas to mimic classmates and orchestrate turn-taking, stages of collaboration, and peer discussion.

finding.finding_summary: In a qualitative evaluation with 14 U.S. middle school students across 40 dialogue sessions, participants reported that MathVC helped them reach shared solutions and understand math problems more effectively. Exit survey ratings were high for working effectively in the environment (M=4.21/5), contributing to the task (M=4.29/5), planning steps (M=4.36/5), and coming to a shared understanding or solution (M=4.43/5).
finding.measure: Exit survey items on shared understanding/solution, task contribution, planning, and ability to work on math problems; interview and interaction logs

finding.finding_summary: Students described increased engagement, motivation, persistence, and confidence when collaborating with the virtual peers. The paper reports that reduced cognitive burden, immediate scaffolding, and diverse peer perspectives supported motivation; survey ratings for constructive interaction were high (M=4.36/5), and interviews repeatedly noted that the system felt encouraging and helped students keep working.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interviews; exit survey ratings of constructive interaction and engagement-related perceptions

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests MathVC supported collaborative problem solving, metacognitive planning, and reasoning through peer critique and error correction. Students reported that the virtual peers helped them ask questions, build on ideas, and plan steps; the system’s stage-based orchestration was designed to elicit shared understanding, planning, execution, and validation, though no standardized learning gains were reported.
finding.measure: Exit survey items on planning and collaboration; interviews about peer interaction and reasoning; dialogue logs

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI use in K-12 education: a systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews empirical studies on generative AI (GenAI) use in K-12 education to understand how these tools have been used in teaching and learning, what outcomes have been reported, and what gaps remain. The review responds to a lack of synthesis focused specifically on K-12 practice, as opposed to higher education or general discussions of ChatGPT and related tools.

Using PRISMA and Kitchenham-guided procedures, the author searched Scopus and Web of Science and supplemented the search with snowballing. Thirty empirical papers met the inclusion criteria. The reviewed studies covered mostly high school and middle school settings, with some elementary and broader K-12 work, and the majority were in STEM subjects. ChatGPT was by far the most common tool, often used alone but sometimes alongside Copilot, DALL-E, Bert, Canva, or custom tools based on GPT-4 and DALL·E.

The review finds that quasi-experimental designs were the most common, but many studies relied on self-reported psychological outcomes such as trust, usability, self-efficacy, engagement, and attitudes rather than objective learning measures. The author concludes that GenAI shows promise for supporting learning, problem solving, self-regulation, and teacher development, but the evidence base is still thin in terms of detailed classroom implementation, objective achievement outcomes, teacher-led real-time use, and underrepresented contexts such as early childhood, special education, rural settings, Africa, and non-English scholarship.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review of 30 empirical K-12 GenAI studies, but it is not itself a causal evaluation of a single intervention. The evidence base it summarizes is dominated by quasi-experimental, descriptive, and self-report studies, which limits causal confidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has moderate synthesis value for the field by mapping how GenAI is being used in K-12 and by flagging implementation risks and gaps, but it does not estimate a direct learning effect. Its practical impact is mainly agenda-setting and descriptive rather than demonstrably outcome-changing.

paper_profiles.title: Position: LLMs Can Be Good Tutors in English Education
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper argues that large language models (LLMs) can function as effective tutors in English education and should be understood not merely as generic text generators, but as tools that can support pedagogy in more structured ways. The paper addresses a broad question: how LLMs can be integrated into English teaching and learning while respecting educational principles, learner needs, and classroom realities.

The authors organize their argument around three roles for LLMs. First, LLMs can serve as data enhancers by creating educational materials, reformulating existing texts, simulating students, and annotating learning data. Second, they can act as task predictors for discriminative, generative, and mixed educational tasks such as automated assessment, knowledge tracing, grammatical error correction, feedback generation, and Socratic dialogue. Third, they can operate as agents that support tutoring through knowledge integration, pedagogical alignment, planning, memory, and tool use.

The paper situates these ideas in English education contexts spanning listening, speaking, reading, and writing, with examples such as comprehension questions, pronunciation feedback, text simplification, and individualized writing support. It concludes that LLMs hold substantial promise for personalized, scalable, and inclusive English instruction, but only if they are paired with guardrails, human oversight, and stronger pedagogical alignment. The paper also emphasizes key risks, including hallucinations, bias, privacy concerns, misalignment with expert teaching practices, and the danger of overreliance on automated systems.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed position paper rather than an empirical evaluation, so it does not present a testable study design, comparison, or causal evidence. It argues for potential roles and discusses challenges, but provides no direct outcome data for K-12 learners.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No measured learning or implementation impact is reported, so there is no evidentiary basis for estimating effect size or practical impact. The paper is conceptual and forward-looking rather than outcome-reporting.

interventions.use_case: Position paper on using LLM tutors in English education, including conversational agents for real-time practice, scaffolding, feedback, and personalized instruction; explicitly references Khanmigo as an example of GPT-4-based educational helper.
LLM-mediated grading and formative feedback for essays, short answers, spoken language, grammatical error correction, and error analysis.
LLM-assisted English writing support such as grammar/syntax/style feedback, revision suggestions, text simplification/paraphrasing, and EFL writing education.
LLM-empowered tutoring systems that model learner history, support adaptive instruction, and deliver personalized tutoring interactions in English education.

paper_profiles.title: TPACK-based Professional Development for the AI Era: Fostering Pre-service Teachers' Acceptance of Generative AI in Mathematics Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks how a TPACK-based professional development (PD) workshop influences pre-service teachers’ acceptance of generative AI for mathematics instruction, and what factors shape their willingness to adopt it. The authors argue that existing technology acceptance models do not fully capture GenAI-specific concerns such as trust, perceived risk, and pedagogical knowledge, so they use an extended UTAUT framework that adds trust, perceived risk, and TPACK.

The intervention was a 90-minute workshop delivered in two teacher education courses at a large public university in the Midwestern United States. Participants were 28 pre-service teachers (25 provided usable survey data; 5 were interviewed), spanning undergraduate and master’s levels. The workshop used a TPACK-based professional learning design: PSTs first experienced a modeled Khan Academy/Khanmigo ratio-solving activity, then discussed pedagogical implications and drawbacks, viewed live demonstrations of several GenAI tools for mathematics teaching, and finally designed their own GenAI-supported instructional materials.

Results from pre/post surveys showed significant gains in perceived usefulness, ease of use, social influence, facilitating conditions, trust, TPACK, and behavioral intention, while perceived risk did not significantly decrease. Qualitative themes suggested that participants saw GenAI as a collaborator for efficiency and creativity, but also worried about inaccurate outputs, student overreliance, privacy, and inconsistent institutional guidance. The study concludes that TPACK-based PD can increase pre-service teachers’ willingness to use GenAI, but effective adoption requires critical, ethically grounded preparation that teaches teachers to evaluate, refine, and সীমित? use AI outputs rather than trust them uncritically.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods pre/post workshop study without a control group or randomized assignment. It provides useful evidence about adoption perceptions and implementation concerns, but causal claims about learning impacts are limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study shows clear attitudinal and intended-use gains, but it does not measure student learning outcomes or actual classroom effectiveness. The impact is therefore modest and primarily on pre-service teacher acceptance rather than direct K-12 achievement.

interventions.use_case: Khanmigo used in a TPACK-based pre-service teacher workshop as a GenAI chatbot for a simulated sixth-grade ratio lesson, providing instant feedback, step-by-step scaffolding, differentiated prompts, and model answers; also compared concept explanation versus direct problem-solving support.

ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini, and Anthropic Claude Sonnet were demonstrated to PSTs for mathematics instruction tasks such as generating hints, simplifying word problems, creating differentiated problems, drafting lesson ideas, and producing representations like graphs.

finding.finding_summary: The workshop produced a significant increase in perceptions that GenAI would improve instructional efficiency and support professional tasks. In qualitative data, PSTs described using GenAI to save time on lesson plans, problem generation, differentiated materials, and emails; the pre/post survey also showed a significant rise in performance expectancy (PE) from M=5.33 to 6.00 (p=0.0003), consistent with efficiency gains.
finding.measure: Performance expectancy survey; interview/workshop reports of time-saving uses
finding.std_deviation: Pre/post SDs reported for PE: 0.93 and 0.73

finding.finding_summary: The PD increased PSTs’ perceptions of facilitating conditions and social influence, suggesting stronger perceived institutional support for GenAI adoption. Facilitating conditions rose from M=4.67 to 5.67 (p=0.0199) and social influence from M=4.57 to 5.05 (p=0.0239), although interviews still emphasized inconsistent departmental messages and lack of clear K-12 policy guidance.
finding.measure: Facilitating conditions and social influence survey constructs; interview themes about institutional guidance and policy
finding.std_deviation: FC pre/post SDs: 1.21 and 1.05; SI pre/post SDs: 1.00 and 0.87

finding.finding_summary: The workshop significantly improved PSTs’ confidence in integrating technology, pedagogy, and mathematics content, indicating gains in applied pedagogical reasoning and AI literacy. TPACK increased from M=5.29 to 5.85 (p=0.0052), and qualitative themes described prompt refinement, critical evaluation of outputs, and deciding when human oversight was needed.
finding.measure: TPACK survey construct; interview/workshop evidence of prompt engineering and critical evaluation

finding.finding_summary: PSTs became more willing to engage with GenAI after the PD, reflecting improved intention and confidence rather than reduced concern. Behavioral intention increased from M=5.13 to 5.67 (p=0.0001), while trust also rose from M=5.09 to 5.40 (p=0.0272); however, perceived risk did not significantly decrease (M=3.96 to 3.73, p=0.0842), indicating a mixed but overall more accepting stance.
finding.measure: Behavioral intention, trust, and perceived risk survey constructs; interview themes on cautious engagement
finding.std_deviation: BI pre/post SDs: 0.90 and 0.80; TR pre/post SDs: 1.13 and 1.09; PR pre/post SDs: 1.37 and 1.40

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was embedded in ratio and problem-solving tasks, and PSTs reported that Khanmigo and related GenAI tools could support math learning through scaffolding, differentiation, and hints. Quantitatively, perceived usefulness/performance expectancy for math instruction improved significantly after the workshop, with PE rising from M=5.33 to 6.00 (p=0.0003), but the study did not measure student math achievement directly.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness/performance expectancy for mathematics instruction; qualitative judgments of ratio/problem-solving scaffolds

paper_profiles.title: A Review of AI-Enabled Personalised Teaching (2021–2025): Progress, Impact, and Future Directions
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of the Kenya National Commission for UNESCO
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the emergence and development of AI-enabled personalized teaching from 2021 to 2025, asking how AI teachers have been implemented, what impact they have had, and what directions future development should take. The review is motivated by broader educational challenges such as teacher shortages, learning inequities, low engagement in asynchronous learning, and the need for scalable one-to-one support.

The paper synthesizes literature identified through a systematic search of five databases and supplements this with the authors’ own prior research on OIAI, an AI-teacher system developed and piloted across multiple regions. The review emphasizes systems that directly teach learners, provide personalized feedback and scaffolding, support learning outside the classroom, and increasingly incorporate human-like interaction features such as voice, avatars, and conversational dialogue. It also discusses teacher-support applications and the shift from narrow chatbot use cases to broader, curriculum-integrated AI teaching.

The paper concludes that AI teachers can improve engagement, completion, satisfaction, and learning outcomes when they are personalized, interactive, and contextually adapted. It argues that AI teaching may be especially valuable where access to qualified teachers is limited, including in Africa and other underserved contexts. At the same time, it identifies important limitations and risks: limited rigorous comparative evidence, weak generalizability across contexts, lack of long-term outcome data, dependence on training data quality, infrastructure and cost barriers, privacy concerns, and the continuing inability of AI to fully replicate human emotional and social support.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative/systematic review, but the paper itself does not present a clearly reproducible primary study design or new causal analysis. It synthesizes prior work and author-led case studies, with limited methodological detail for independent evidence grading.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests potentially large educational and institutional reach, but the paper does not report robust effect sizes for the focal interventions and relies heavily on descriptive or cited findings. The impact appears promising but remains indirect and not yet well quantified for K-12 science instruction specifically.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of AI teachers and conversational tutoring systems that directly teach learners one-to-one, including chatbots, AI instructional agents, and generative AI-enabled personal teachers used for personalized instruction outside the classroom.
Reviews embodied AI teachers and AI-driven robotic teacher systems as examples of human-like instructional agents, including avatar-based and robotic pedagogical agents.
Discusses AI systems that tailor learning paths, pacing, and content delivery to student needs as part of personalized teaching, though not as the main focus.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that AI-enabled teaching can improve learning across diverse non-language subjects and core school curriculum areas, including employability, digital skills, maths, and other curriculum content. Across the reviewed studies, reported benefits included high satisfaction and better learning performance, but the paper does not provide a pooled effect size for academic achievement.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes, course completion, satisfaction with AI-delivered instruction, and reported subject-specific performance across reviewed studies

finding.finding_summary: The review reports improved learner engagement, confidence, perceived usefulness, and satisfaction when students interacted with AI teachers. For example, in one cited programme with n=193 in Kenya, 91.9% recommended the programme and 90.7% reported being very or extremely satisfied, suggesting strong motivational and engagement effects rather than measured causal gains.
finding.measure: Engagement, satisfaction, confidence, recommendation rates, and perceived usefulness surveys
finding.study_size: n=193 (cited Kenya programme); other reviewed studies not_reported

finding.finding_summary: A major theme of the review is that AI teachers support durable skills such as critical thinking, problem solving, time management, self-awareness, leadership, and motivation through personalized one-to-one guidance. The Kenya programme cited in the paper included lessons on goal setting, motivation, time management, procrastination, leadership, and critical thinking, but the review reports descriptive outcomes rather than quantified skill gains.
finding.measure: Reported development/support of critical thinking, problem solving, time management, self-awareness, leadership, and motivation

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI teachers can reduce teacher workload, extend access, and scale instruction beyond what human teachers can provide. It cites examples such as AI systems supporting asynchronous delivery and the ability to upload content for broader reuse, but does not report a formal workload effect size in this paper.
finding.measure: Teacher workload reduction, scalability, completion rates, and implementation feasibility

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames AI-enabled personalized teaching as having potential system-level value for addressing teacher shortages, learning disparities, and access gaps, particularly in Kenya and other low-resource settings. It reports rapid progress from small pilots to broader implementation, but this is a narrative synthesis without causal estimates.
finding.measure: Implementation scale, access expansion, and institutional adoption potential

paper_profiles.title: Intelligent Textbooks
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial surveys the evolution of the intelligent textbooks research area and positions recent work within a five-generation framework: engineered intelligence, integrated intelligence, extracted intelligence, datamined intelligence, and generated intelligence. The paper asks how digital textbooks can be made more adaptive, interactive, and supportive for learners by combining classical AI, knowledge graphs, NLP/ML, learning analytics, and recent generative AI methods.

The article does not report a single empirical intervention with participants. Instead, it reviews representative systems and workshop contributions, including adaptive interfaces, smart content, knowledge extraction from textbooks, interaction mining from learner logs, and LLM-based tools for question answering, explanations, and feedback. It also highlights domain-specific applications such as programming, medicine, and K-12 textbook visions, along with phygital textbook companions that connect paper and digital formats.

The main conclusion is that intelligent textbooks are increasingly powered by large-scale extraction of textbook content and learner interaction data, with generative AI opening new possibilities for explanations, questions, and conversational support. The authors argue that the field has matured but still needs careful calibration with real teacher-learner interaction, stronger pedagogical grounding, and better understanding of how to use these technologies effectively in practice.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an editorial and field overview, not an empirical evaluation of Khanmigo or any other intervention. It cites prior work and examples, but does not present a primary study design, sample, or measured outcomes for the target intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct learning or implementation effects are measured in this paper, so there is no evidentiary basis for estimating impact size. The paper is useful for conceptual framing, but it does not demonstrate outcome impact for K-12 science instruction.

interventions.use_case: Editorial/review discussion of Khan Academy's Khanmigo as a GPT-4-based tutoring chatbot around educational content, described as a generative-AI learner support tool for interactive textbook-style tutoring and question answering.

paper_profiles.title: LLMs in Personalized Education: Adaptive Learning Models
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Information Systems Engineering and Management
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the broad problem that conventional education systems and many earlier adaptive learning platforms do not adequately personalize instruction, feedback, pacing, or support for diverse learners. The author argues that large language models (LLMs) can help close this gap by enabling dynamic, context-aware, and scalable personalized education. The paper is primarily a conceptual discussion of why LLMs matter for education, what capabilities they add compared with rule-based adaptive systems, and what concerns must be managed for responsible deployment.

The approach studied is not an empirical intervention but a framework-level examination of LLM-enabled adaptive learning. The paper reviews potential educational uses of LLMs such as interactive tutoring, real-time feedback, personalized content generation, assessment support, multilingual assistance, and integration with learning management systems. It also discusses Khan Academy’s GPT-4 tutor, Khanmigo, as an example of how an LLM can act as an on-demand educational assistant, though the paper does not report any original implementation data from K-12 classrooms.

The paper’s conclusions are that LLMs could improve engagement, retention, and access to individualized support if they are embedded within pedagogically grounded systems and monitored carefully. At the same time, the paper emphasizes major risks including hallucinated or inaccurate outputs, bias, privacy and security concerns, overreliance on automated guidance, lack of transparency, and the need for teacher support and oversight. Overall, it frames LLM-based adaptive learning as promising but requiring careful governance, educator involvement, and further research before widespread use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual review/framework paper with no original empirical design, no comparison group, and no quantitative outcome analysis. It is peer-reviewed, but it does not meet credibility criteria for causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for potentially meaningful benefits of LLM tutoring, but provides no measured effect sizes or implementation evidence. Impact is therefore unclear and best treated as a conceptual, not demonstrated, contribution.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual discussion of GPT-4/Khanmigo-style conversational tutoring for personalized education, including real-time explanations, interactive Q&A, scaffolding, feedback, and adaptive support within learning management systems.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLM-powered adaptive systems can increase student engagement and support motivation by providing always-available, human-like, personalized assistance. No original effect estimate is reported; the claim is conceptual rather than empirically tested in this article.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, and responsiveness to personalized support

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LLM tutors may foster critical thinking and self-directed learning by rephrasing difficult concepts, answering questions, and offering scaffolded guidance aligned with constructivist and mastery-learning principles. No empirical estimate is provided in the paper.
finding.measure: Critical thinking and learner autonomy/self-directed learning (conceptual)

finding.finding_summary: The article claims LLM systems can reduce teacher burden by generating personalized content, providing feedback, identifying struggling learners, and supporting instructional planning. These efficiency gains are described conceptually, without a reported sample, comparison, or effect size.
finding.measure: Teacher support, instructional planning efficiency, and automated feedback generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents LLMs as potentially democratizing access to personalized education, but also emphasizes risks around privacy, bias, unequal access to infrastructure, and the need for governance and educator oversight. No empirical institutional outcome is measured; this is a conceptual policy-oriented discussion.
finding.measure: Educational equity, privacy, bias, and governance considerations

paper_profiles.title: LLM-Powered Virtual Patient Agents for Interactive Clinical Skills Training with Automated Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of providing scalable, realistic practice for Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCEs) in medical education. The authors argue that traditional OSCE preparation is resource-intensive because it requires human standardized patients, expert examiners, and repeated individualized feedback. They propose a system that uses large language models (LLMs) to create both a virtual patient and a virtual tutor, aiming to support richer, more interactive clinical-skills training.

The intervention is a modular framework with a Unity-based frontend and an LLM-powered backend. The virtual patient can handle multimodal interaction through chat, speech, and predefined action spaces, allowing simulated movements and reactive behaviors in addition to text dialogue. The tutor agent can provide in-scenario hints, post-session summaries, and checklist-based OSCE scoring by analyzing the full interaction history rather than relying on keyword matching. The system is designed to be frontend-independent, so it could work with a virtual simulator or a physical robot.

The paper reports performance benchmarks for speech recognition and LLM response latency, along with a preliminary expert evaluation. Eighteen medical professionals, including physicians, medical assistants, and medical students, tested an upper-limb neurological examination scenario and rated the virtual patient and tutor favorably. Experts found the patient’s chat especially realistic and the tutor’s summaries and scores useful, while also noting room for improvement in more nuanced movement handling, multi-command understanding, and more sophisticated reactive behaviors. Overall, the paper concludes that LLM-driven patient simulation and automated feedback can make OSCE practice more accessible, personalized, and scalable, though current cloud-based models and prompt designs still limit realism and accessibility.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed system paper with a small preliminary expert evaluation and engineering benchmarks, but not a controlled learner-outcome study. Evidence is therefore qualitative/early-stage rather than high-credibility causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful training and workflow efficiency benefits, but the reported outcomes are expert ratings and latency benchmarks rather than demonstrated learner gains. Impact on education is promising but still unclear and modest at this stage.

interventions.use_case: LLM-powered virtual tutor for OSCE clinical skills training that provides on-demand hints, formative guidance, post-session summaries, and checklist-based scoring from the full student-patient interaction
Unity-based virtual patient simulation for OSCE-style clinical skills practice, including text/voice dialogue, patient movements, and reactive clinical behaviors
Framework is explicitly designed to be frontend-independent and compatible with a physical robot patient as an alternative to the virtual patient simulator

finding.finding_summary: In a preliminary expert evaluation with n=18 medical professionals, the virtual patient and virtual tutor were both rated highly for OSCE training utility. The virtual patient averaged 4.38/5 (SD=0.74) and the tutor 4.33/5 (SD=0.71), suggesting the system was perceived as good to very good for clinical skills practice.
finding.measure: 5-point Likert ratings of virtual patient fidelity and virtual tutor usefulness during an upper-limb neurological OSCE scenario

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed and benchmarked for real-time use, with speech-to-text and LLM components selected to keep interaction latency low. Whisper-tiny achieved RTF=0.325 with WER=0.245, and Gemini-1.5-Flash averaged 2.07s (SD=0.27) per response, supporting low-latency interactive training.
finding.measure: Speech recognition real-time factor and word error rate; LLM response latency
finding.study_size: n=3 Whisper models; n=10 runs per LLM
finding.std_deviation: LLM response time SD=0.27s; smaller model benchmark SD not fully reported

paper_profiles.title: Shiksha Copilot: Teacher-AI Collaboration for Curating and Customizing Lesson Plans in Low-Resource Schools
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers in low-resource schools collaborate with an AI-assisted lesson planning system, Shiksha Copilot, to create and adapt curriculum-aligned lesson plans. The core question is not only whether generative AI can produce usable instructional materials, but how teachers actually review, customize, and integrate AI-generated plans into their work in multilingual, resource-constrained settings.

Shiksha Copilot combined LLM-based generation, retrieval-augmented generation over textbook content, human curation, bilingual English-Kannada translation, and optional teacher-facing AI tools such as lesson-specific chat and question generation. The system was developed for government schools in Karnataka, India, and deployed to 1,043 teachers teaching grades 5–10 across Kannada- and English-medium public schools. The study used a mixed-methods design with system logs, surveys, and interviews, plus a curation phase involving 23 subject curators.

The findings show that AI-generated lesson plans were generally reliable in English but required heavy linguistic revision in Kannada. Teachers used the tool both for instruction and for bureaucratic record-keeping, and the system reduced planning time and stress while supporting a shift toward more activity-based pedagogy. At the same time, teachers often adapted content mentally or off-platform, and broader change was constrained by structural issues such as administrative demands, staffing shortages, and language/translation quality problems. The paper concludes that effective teacher-AI collaboration depends on human oversight, contextual adaptation, and community-based curation, especially in low-resource and multilingual settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods field deployment with surveys, interviews, and log analysis, but it is not a randomized or quasi-experimental causal impact study. The evidence is strong for implementation and user-perceived outcomes, but weaker for attributing changes to the intervention alone.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clear operational benefits for a priority population of teachers in low-resource schools, especially reduced planning burden and improved access to materials. However, the impact is mostly modest/qualitative, with no direct student achievement effect sizes and substantial constraints on scalability and language quality.

interventions.use_case: teacher-facing LLM-based lesson planning and curriculum-aligned content generation with human-in-the-loop curation, bilingual English-Kannada support, lesson-specific chat, general education chat, and question-generation tools for K-12 teachers
teacher-supported digital lesson-plan distribution and customization platform for classroom instructional planning in low-resource K-12 schools

finding.finding_summary: Shiksha Copilot reduced bureaucratic workload and lesson-planning burden for teachers in low-resource Karnataka schools. Survey and interview evidence indicate measurable reductions in lesson-planning time and teacher stress, with teachers using the tool to generate and customize lesson plans for both instructional delivery and record-keeping; the paper does not report a single pooled effect size for these outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported lesson-planning time, administrative/record-keeping workload, and teacher stress (Teacher Stress Scale)
finding.study_size: n=406 matched survey responses; n=22 teacher interviews; platform logs from 5,544 teacher-created lesson plans

finding.finding_summary: The system supported broader organizational and institutional workflows by helping teachers satisfy administrative documentation requirements and fit state-mandated lesson-plan formats (e.g., 5E). However, the paper also reports that staffing shortages and administrative demands limited broader pedagogical change, so the institutional impact was meaningful but constrained.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview themes about documentation compliance, workflow integration, and organizational change
finding.study_size: n=43 interviews; n=23 curators; n=1,043 teachers in deployment

finding.finding_summary: The tool improved access to curriculum-aligned lesson plans and shifted some teachers toward activity-based pedagogy, but the paper does not provide student learning outcome measures. Curators reported high reliability in English lesson plans (96.13% of content blocks suitable for classroom use, 4.1% edited), while Kannada translations required extensive revision (94.4% of blocks edited), indicating stronger academic utility in English than in Kannada.
finding.measure: Curator ratings of lesson-plan quality, edit rates by content block, and teacher reports of pedagogical use
finding.study_size: 991 curated lesson plans (965 English, 26 Kannada); 5,544 teacher-created lesson plans

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging “Khanmigo” Generative AI-Powered Tool for Personalized Tutoring to Learn Scientific Concepts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This mixed-methods study examined whether using Khanmigo, a generative AI-powered intelligent tutoring system, improved college students’ learning of a science concept relative to other study supports. The paper asks both whether Khanmigo leads to better learning outcomes and how students experience and describe its tutoring behaviors in practice.

The intervention compared three conditions in a short experimental session: a Khanmigo tutoring condition, a Google search condition, and a paper-only condition that emerged post hoc. Participants were 69 undergraduate students in psychology courses at a regional public university in the United States. All students studied lunar phases using the same five-page handout with text and images; the Khanmigo group could ask the AI tutor questions and interact with it, while the search-engine group could use Google, and the paper-only group relied only on the handout. Learning was measured with pre- and post-tests using the Lunar Phases Concept Inventory, and students also completed structured interviews; Khanmigo chat logs were analyzed qualitatively.

Quantitatively, all groups improved from pretest to posttest, but Khanmigo did not produce significantly better gains than Google search or paper-only instruction. Qualitatively, students reported positive experiences with Khanmigo and valued its step-by-step guidance, simplified explanations, practice problems, comprehension checks, and personalized questioning. The authors conclude that Khanmigo may work well as a supplementary scaffold rather than a replacement for traditional instruction, but that brief exposure, limited task demands, and the strength of the paper materials likely reduced the observable advantage of the AI tutor. They recommend longer, more open-ended use cases to better evaluate GenAI tutoring effects.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed mixed-methods study with an experimental pretest-posttest comparison and qualitative interviews, but it is not a randomized controlled trial with strong causal control throughout (post-hoc third group, convenience sample, short exposure). The evidence is informative but has notable internal and external validity limitations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study found no measurable achievement advantage for Khanmigo over Google search or paper-only instruction (d=-0.16; no significant treatment effect), so academic impact appears modest/unclear. Qualitative benefits were positive, but they do not establish strong learning impact in this context.

interventions.use_case: Khanmigo use as a generative AI tutor for brief science concept tutoring in lunar phases, where students asked factual and conceptual questions and received step-by-step guidance, prompts, practice problems, and comprehension checks.

finding.finding_summary: Students using Khanmigo did not show significantly greater gains on lunar phases understanding than students using Google search, despite both groups improving from pretest to posttest. On the LPCI difference scores, the Khanmigo vs. Google comparison was not significant (t(67)=-0.649, p>.05, d=-0.16), and the post-hoc 3-group ANOVA also found no significant treatment effect or treatment-by-time interaction.
finding.measure: Lunar Phases Concept Inventory (LPCI) pretest-posttest scores / difference scores
finding.study_size: n=69 (Khanmigo n=22; search-engine n=22; paper-only n=25)

finding.finding_summary: Interview data indicated students perceived Khanmigo positively as engaging, confidence-building, and helpful for asking questions, especially because it offered simple, personalized responses and reduced hesitation to seek help. Students rated its effectiveness around 3.5/5 and described it as useful for support and clarification, though these were short exposure sessions rather than long-term usage.
finding.measure: Structured interview ratings and thematic analysis of student perceptions of engagement, confidence, and helpfulness
finding.study_size: n=22 Khanmigo users in the interview set (within total n=69)

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative findings suggest Khanmigo supported active recall, self-questioning, and comprehension monitoring through prompts, practice problems, and Socratic-style questioning. However, students often bypassed the dialogue and sought direct answers, limiting deeper metacognitive engagement; thus the mechanism was promising but only partially realized in this short session.
finding.measure: Interview themes and analysis of chat logs for questioning, active recall, and comprehension checks
finding.study_size: n=22 Khanmigo users (chat logs and interviews)

paper_profiles.title: An Interview Reflection on BIntelligent Tutoring Goes to School in the Big City^
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an interview-style reflection on the earlier 1997 study "Intelligent Tutoring Goes to School in the Big City," written by the original lead author, Kenneth Koedinger. Rather than reporting a new intervention trial, it revisits the motivation, design choices, outcomes, and longer-term influence of the original classroom evaluation of the Algebra Cognitive Tutor in a full-year high school algebra curriculum.

The intervention discussed was an intelligent tutoring system embedded in a redesigned algebra course for urban high school students in Pittsburgh. The paper emphasizes that the tutor was not used as a stand-alone tool, but as part of a broader curriculum that included revised instructional materials, classroom collaboration, and alternative assessments. The interview highlights how the study addressed the challenge of integrating AI-based tutoring into the social and instructional context of schools, including teacher coordination and technology logistics.

The population in the original study was about 470 high school students across three city schools in the United States, with a high proportion of low-income and low-performing students. The main conclusion of the reflection is that the original quasi-experimental study helped establish the educational potential of intelligent tutoring systems, supported later dissemination of Cognitive Tutor algebra, and helped shape the field’s emphasis on rigorous school-based evaluation, multiple forms of assessment, and attention to implementation context. The paper also notes continuing open questions about supporting open-ended problem solving, improving adoption, and better translating research innovations into products.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an interview/reflection article rather than a primary empirical report. It summarizes a prior quasi-experimental classroom study and discusses later evidence, but the paper itself does not present a new rigorous evaluation design.
