paper_profiles.title: Learning design to support student-AI collaboration: perspectives of leading teachers for AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of guidance on how to design learning when AI is introduced into K-12 classrooms as a collaborative learning agent. Rather than evaluating a specific AI product or student outcome, it explores teachers’ perspectives on what curriculum, interaction supports, learning environments, and developmental pathways are needed for effective student-AI collaboration (SAC).

The study is framed around a student-AI collaboration model grounded in distributed cognition. The authors conducted semi-structured interviews with 10 Korean leading teachers in AI in education, drawn from primary and secondary schools involved in software education, AI pilot schools, or AI-convergence high schools. Participants discussed desired learning goals, content, assessments, student-AI interaction, and institutional/cultural conditions for SAC in school settings.

Teachers generally viewed SAC as a way to build higher-order cognitive capacities, social capacities, and digital capacities while also strengthening subject-matter learning. They emphasized interdisciplinary, authentic, and creative tasks; process-oriented and collaboration-based assessment; instruction in AI principles, data literacy, error analysis, and ethics; and AI systems that provide scaffolding and intuitive, multi-tool interfaces. They also stressed the need for flexible classrooms, strong digital infrastructure, supportive policy, teacher capacity building, collaborative school culture, and a safe-to-fail environment. The paper concludes that student-AI collaboration may evolve from learning about AI to learning from AI and eventually learning together with AI, offering design implications for educational policy, AI design, and instructional practice.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative interview study with 10 purposively sampled teachers, using thematic analysis. It provides rich conceptual evidence but no experimental design, comparison group, or quantified causal estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not measure student impacts directly; it offers implementation guidance and expectations for AI-supported learning in K-12 settings. Its practical relevance is high, but the empirical impact on outcomes is unclear and unquantified.

interventions.use_case: Qualitative study of student-AI collaboration design in K-12 schools, including AI used as a collaborative learning agent, instructional scaffold, and peer/tutor-like partner across classroom tasks.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed student-AI collaboration should build higher-order and durable skills such as critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving, computational thinking, communication, leadership, and collaboration. This was a qualitative interview study with n=10 Korean leading teachers; no effect size was reported because the paper elicited perceptions rather than testing outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on desired student capacities and learning goals

finding.finding_summary: Teachers expected SAC to strengthen subject-matter knowledge by helping students organize, connect, retrieve, and apply knowledge to tangible products and feasible solutions. The study is qualitative (n=10 teachers) and reports perceived instructional value rather than student outcome estimates.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on subject-matter knowledge building

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described authentic science-related and STEM tasks, including prediction modeling and data analysis, as appropriate SAC activities that could support inquiry, evaluation, and application of knowledge. This was a qualitative interview study (n=10) and did not report quantitative achievement effects.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on authentic STEM/science tasks and inquiry processes

finding.finding_summary: Teachers anticipated SAC could support motivation, persistence, confidence, and a willingness to learn from failure, especially through gamified interactions and a safe-to-fail environment. The study is based on interviews with n=10 teachers and provides no effect size; findings are expectation-based rather than measured student outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on motivation, persistence, confidence, and safe-to-fail norms

finding.finding_summary: Teachers argued that AI should automate repetitive teacher tasks and provide process-oriented assessment support, including data collection, analysis, and feedback, which could reduce workload and improve instructional handling of student data. This was a qualitative study of n=10 teachers; no quantitative workload reduction estimate was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on automation of repetitive tasks and assessment support

finding.finding_summary: A major finding was that successful SAC depends on systemic supports such as national AIED policy, teacher professional development, flexible school structures, digital infrastructure, collaborative school culture, and safe-to-fail norms. Evidence is qualitative from interviews with n=10 leading teachers; the paper does not report effect sizes but strongly emphasizes institutional readiness as a prerequisite for implementation.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on policy, governance, school system flexibility, and culture

paper_profiles.title: Challenges and Future Directions of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a position/review article that examines the current status, opportunities, and challenges of big data and artificial intelligence (AI) in education. It does not evaluate a specific intervention; instead, it synthesizes existing trends and argues for future directions in educational research, policy, and industry. The authors frame big data and AI as increasingly important for learning analytics, individualized learning, precision education, assessment, and adaptive support.

The paper discusses applications across educational settings, including intelligent tutoring systems, learning management systems, online learning environments, dashboards, chatbots, and other AI-enabled tools. It emphasizes that these technologies should be guided by theory from cognitive and educational psychology, carefully designed data/algorithm practices, and empirical validation. The authors also highlight ethical issues such as algorithmic bias, privacy, and the risk of overreliance on machine assistance.

Rather than focusing on a single population, the article speaks broadly to learners and teachers across education levels, including K-12, higher education, and lifelong learning contexts. The main conclusion is that big data and AI have substantial potential to improve personalized learning and teaching, but progress depends on interdisciplinary collaboration, better teacher preparation, strong privacy protections, and a balance between human and machine roles in education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed position paper/review rather than an empirical study, and it does not present original methods, comparison groups, or outcome analyses. Its value is conceptual and agenda-setting, not causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has broad relevance for expectations about AI-enabled education, but it reports no original effect sizes or direct K-12 outcomes. Its impact is therefore informative but indirect, offering moderate guidance rather than measurable evidence of benefit.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual review of big data and AI in education, including intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, predictive models, chatbots, and adaptive/precision learning supports in school and higher-education settings.

finding.finding_summary: This position paper argues that big data and AI in education have substantial promise for assessment, individualized learning, and precision education, but that adoption is constrained by theory gaps, privacy concerns, teacher readiness, and uneven industry-academia alignment. No new empirical effect size is reported; the paper synthesizes prior work and calls for cautious, theory-guided implementation.
finding.measure: Policy and implementation challenges; adoption conditions; institutional guidance for AI and learning analytics

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that AI-enabled analytics can improve teacher instruction, course planning, assessment, and administrative decision-making by extracting actionable patterns from large-scale educational data. It cites prior work showing high predictive accuracy for student performance and notes that such systems may reduce routine teacher tasks, but it does not itself report a new empirical effect size.
finding.measure: Teacher dashboards, prediction/analytics utility, and workflow support

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that big data and AI can support individualized learning and precision education across domains, including science inquiry environments and other subject areas, by identifying learner profiles and tailoring support in real time. It references prior science-oriented systems such as Inq-ITS/Inq-Blotter and automated assessment environments, but provides no direct experimental estimate itself.
finding.measure: Personalized learning, assessment, and learning-support potential in subject learning contexts

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual paper addresses the growing need for teachers to develop artificial intelligence (AI) digital competencies as AI-based educational tools become more common in post-pandemic online and blended learning. The authors argue that while AI can support personalized learning, automated feedback, learning analytics, and efficiency in teaching and assessment, many teachers lack the technical, pedagogical, and ethical knowledge needed to use these tools well.

Rather than reporting an empirical intervention, the paper synthesizes existing literature and examples to identify the opportunities and challenges of AI in education and to specify the competencies teachers need. It revisits and adapts two established frameworks: the European DigCompEdu framework and the P21 framework for twenty-first century learning. The paper also references broader AI competency models and a revised TPACK perspective to argue that teacher AI competence should include both technical and non-technical dimensions.

The intended population is educators, especially teachers and school leaders working in AI-enabled educational environments, with examples drawn broadly from online, blended, and higher-education contexts as well as K-12-related AI literacy discussions. The main conclusion is that teacher preparation should move beyond basic technical skills toward a holistic set of AI competencies spanning professional engagement, instructional design, content choices across disciplines, and student learning competencies, including ethics, collaboration, creativity, and responsible AI use.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/framework paper rather than an empirical evaluation study. It synthesizes prior literature and proposes adaptations of competency frameworks, but does not present a clear study design, sample, or causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No direct intervention effects were measured, so there is no estimable impact on student outcomes or institutional outcomes. The paper is useful for framing expectations and competencies, but it does not demonstrate measurable K-12 impact.

paper_profiles.title: The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the growing but fragmented literature on artificial intelligence (AI) in STEM education by systematically reviewing empirical studies published from 2011 to 2021. The authors argue that AI-STEM should be understood as a complex educational system, not just a set of isolated tools, and use general system theory (GST) to examine how AI applications interact with subject, information, medium, and environment elements in STEM learning settings.

The review included 63 empirical, peer-reviewed studies from education and educational research databases. The AI applications were grouped into six categories: learning prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, student behavior detection, automation, educational robots, and other uses such as AI textbooks and group formation. The studies covered multiple STEM content areas, especially technology and science, and mostly involved higher education, but also included elementary, middle, and high school settings.

Across the reviewed studies, AI was typically used to support instructors and students through prediction of performance or dropout risk, personalized tutoring and recommendations, behavior analysis and monitoring, automated assessment, and robotic learning supports. Most studies reported positive effects on learning performance, motivation, attitudes, or higher-order thinking, though some found no significant gains. The review concludes that AI shows promise for improving STEM learning, but effective use depends on careful alignment with educational context, learner level, medium, and instructional strategy.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review, but it synthesizes heterogeneous empirical studies rather than reporting a single well-controlled causal design. The paper is useful for mapping intervention types and summarizing effects, but the underlying evidence is mixed in design quality and outcome measurement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests generally positive but mostly descriptive and heterogeneous evidence for AI in STEM, with many outcomes reported qualitatively rather than via pooled effect sizes. It indicates promising impact for K-12-adjacent STEM supports, but the direct effect magnitude for general K-12 science use remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of AI applications in STEM education that includes learning performance prediction and at-risk student prediction using machine learning, random forest, Bayesian networks, and related models to flag students needing support.

AI-enabled tutoring systems in STEM that deliver instructional content, provide one-to-one guidance, recommend personalized learning paths, and suggest resources based on student profiles and learning histories.

Automated assessment and feedback systems for STEM tasks, including automatic grading of programming, science arguments, and open-ended physics responses, plus immediate syntactic/structural feedback.
Digital game-based learning and simulation-like personalized learning environments used in STEM contexts, including game-based math learning and adaptive or interactive learning activities.
AI-supported educational robots and humanoid robot tutors used to convey science/STEM concepts, support programming/information technology tasks, and act as tutors or learning companions.
Broader AI-supported instructional software and digital learning environments in STEM that deliver content or support learning without the full tutoring/recommendation structure of ITS.

finding.finding_summary: Across 22 studies reporting learning performance outcomes, most found significantly positive effects of AI-supported STEM interventions on achievement; 20 studies reported positive results. Reported examples include a context-aware ubiquitous learning system improving geoscience achievement, and a cluster-randomized digital math game improving kindergarten learning gains, while two studies found no significant differences.
finding.measure: Learning performance / learning achievement / course exam outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Seventeen studies reported affective outcomes such as attitude, interest, motivation, and satisfaction, and the overall pattern was positive toward AI-supported STEM tools. Examples in the review noted improved student satisfaction with adaptive learning systems and increased interest/attention when using AI-enabled robots and personalized learning environments.
finding.measure: Affective perception surveys, satisfaction, attitude, interest, motivation

finding.finding_summary: Seven studies reported gains in higher-order thinking skills such as problem-solving, computational thinking, self-regulated learning, and argumentation. Examples cited include a flowchart-based ITS improving problem-solving in programming, an AI-based AR system improving computational thinking, and adaptive robotic scaffolding increasing self-regulated learning behaviors.
finding.measure: Problem-solving, computational thinking, self-regulated learning, argumentation

finding.finding_summary: Twelve studies used AI-enabled data mining and learning analytics to identify learning patterns and behaviors in STEM, showing that these tools can reveal heterogeneous novice programmer profiles, course-taking trajectories, and behavior clusters. These are not direct achievement effects, but they substantively demonstrate AI’s ability to support metacognitive and behavioral analysis in learning contexts.
finding.measure: Learning behavior patterns, preference profiles, course-taking trajectories, clusters from learning analytics

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that 24 of 63 articles discussed technological effects, with AI methods showing good efficiency and prediction accuracy for grading, prediction, and recommendation tasks. Examples include automated assessment systems outperforming or matching human scoring in some item-level settings, and multiple machine-learning models achieving high prediction accuracy for STEM outcomes.
finding.measure: Algorithm accuracy, grading performance, efficiency of automated assessment/prediction systems

paper_profiles.title: A Review on Artificial Intelligence in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in education and discusses how AI is changing teaching, learning, assessment, and school operations. The authors frame AI as a broad set of technologies that can support personalized instruction, automate routine teacher tasks, improve evaluation, and enable smarter educational environments.

Rather than testing one intervention, the paper synthesizes prior literature on several AI-enabled approaches, including adaptive learning systems, automated scoring and feedback, virtual classrooms, smart campus infrastructure, and intelligent tutoring robots. The review highlights examples such as ALEKS, BYJU’S, Duolingo, automated essay and speech scoring tools, and AI-supported classroom and campus management systems. These examples span school and higher-education contexts, with some emphasis on K-12 and especially adaptive education and tutoring applications.

The main conclusion is that AI has strong potential to improve personalized learning, teacher efficiency, educational equity, and campus management, but its adoption also raises concerns about fairness, ethics, data privacy, teacher readiness, and student self-regulation. The paper argues that successful AI integration in education requires coordinated effort from developers, teachers, students, and institutions, along with attention to contextual differences across countries and schools.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review, not a primary empirical study or meta-analysis conducted with full systematic methods in the paper itself. It synthesizes prior literature and cites individual studies, but the evidence base is heterogeneous and often descriptive, so methodological credibility is limited to review-level summarization.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests broad positive impacts for AI in education, but most claims are qualitative or based on scattered cited studies without pooled effect sizes. The likely impact is modest and context-dependent rather than clearly demonstrated at a medium or large level for K-12 science.

interventions.use_case: review of AI-enabled adaptive learning systems that personalize learning paths, pacing, and content using student data and analytics
review of AI systems for automated scoring, essay correction, homework grading, and test-paper feedback
review of intelligent tutoring robots and educational robots used for instruction, support, and interaction in school settings
review of AI-supported instructional platforms and digital teaching systems used to assist classroom learning and teaching

finding.finding_summary: The review cites a study of ALEKS showing a statistically significant positive impact on middle school students’ end-of-year mathematics scores. It also notes a meta-analysis finding ALEKS was about as effective as traditional classroom teaching overall, with better results when used for shorter periods rather than longer periods; no pooled effect size is reported in the paper text provided.
finding.measure: End-of-year mathematics scores; learning outcomes in ALEKS meta-analysis

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that AI-supported English learning platforms and speech recognition tools improved learners’ English performance and autonomous learning. For example, a college English teaching platform using AI was associated with higher average student scores than non-users, though the paper does not provide the sample size or effect size.
finding.measure: Average English scores; autonomous learning ability; pronunciation correction performance

finding.finding_summary: The review describes speech recognition and semantic analysis tools as supporting one-to-one oral practice and correcting pronunciation in English teaching. It also notes automated spoken-English assessment tools (e.g., SpeechRater) and reports improved oral-practice support, but no study-level effect sizes are given.
finding.measure: Oral practice, pronunciation correction, spoken English assessment

finding.finding_summary: Several cited studies suggest AI tools improved learners’ self-regulation, autonomy, and engagement. For instance, Duolingo was reported to increase autonomous learning behaviors such as self-regulation of study time and strategy adjustment, and the BYJU’S app was described as interactive and comfortable to use; no quantitative effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Autonomous learning/self-regulation; learner perceptions of interactivity and comfort

finding.finding_summary: A major theme of the review is that AI reduces teacher workload by automating routine tasks such as homework marking, test-paper scoring, question generation, attendance, and assessment. The article describes these effects qualitatively as improving efficiency and reducing teacher fatigue, but it does not report a pooled effect size or experimental estimate.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading time, assessment efficiency, attendance processing efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI-based smart campus systems improve administrative efficiency, safety, and resource allocation through face recognition, data monitoring, and automated access control. These claims are presented as descriptive benefits from prior studies rather than as a single evaluated effect, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Campus management efficiency, safety monitoring, resource allocation

paper_profiles.title: A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the growing and fragmented literature on artificial intelligence in higher education by conducting a tertiary review, or review of reviews. The authors ask what kinds of AI evidence syntheses have been published, what they focus on, how they are conducted, how well they report methods, and what gaps remain in the field. The goal is to map the state of AI in higher education research and provide guidance for future primary and secondary studies.

The review synthesises 66 secondary studies published between 2018 and July 2023, drawn from major bibliographic databases and additional searching. Although the paper is about higher education, the reviewed literature spans several contexts such as undergraduate education, health and welfare, STEM, online or blended learning, foreign language learning, pre-service teachers, students with disabilities, and some institutional or administrative uses. The corpus includes systematic reviews, scoping reviews, meta-analyses, mapping reviews, and other evidence syntheses focused on intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive systems and personalisation, assessment and evaluation, and profiling/prediction.

The main conclusions are that AIHEd reviews most often focus on adaptive systems and personalisation, followed by profiling and prediction, while intelligent tutoring systems are less commonly addressed in the recent review literature. The authors find substantial methodological variation, with many reviews omitting details such as inter-rater reliability, full search strings, coding schemes, or quality appraisal. Overall reporting quality is moderate, and the paper calls for stronger ethics, collaboration, methodological rigour, and more contextualised research in future AI in education work.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed tertiary review with a transparent search and coding approach, but it is not a primary causal study and does not estimate intervention effects. Its credibility is strong for mapping literature, but it is only indirectly informative for K-12 efficacy expectations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct effect sizes or classroom outcome estimates; its value is in shaping expectations and identifying where evidence is concentrated or thin. It is useful background for K-12 science AI planning, but impact on learner outcomes is indirect and therefore unclear.

interventions.use_case: Tertiary review of artificial intelligence in higher education evidence syntheses, mapping research on AI applications such as adaptive systems, profiling/prediction, assessment/evaluation, and intelligent tutoring systems rather than evaluating a single classroom intervention.

finding.finding_summary: This meta-systematic review does not estimate learner effects; instead it maps the AI-in-higher-education evidence base and the quality of reviews. It found 66 reviews, with 47.0% focused on general AIEd, 28.8% on profiling/prediction, 27.3% on adaptive systems/personalisation, 4.5% on assessment/evaluation, and 1.5% on ITS; overall review quality averaged 6.57/10, but 45.5% did not conduct quality appraisal and 51.5% did not report using a digital synthesis tool.
finding.measure: Counts and proportions of evidence syntheses by AI topic, review type, publication characteristics, and methodological quality scores

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests AIHEd evidence synthesis can be conducted more efficiently with dedicated review software, but adoption was limited: only 12.1% of reviews reported using evidence synthesis software such as EPPI Reviewer or Covidence, while 51.5% reported no digital synthesis tool. This is a descriptive finding about review-process efficiency rather than a student outcome.
finding.measure: Reported use of evidence synthesis software, spreadsheets, and reference managers during review conduct

paper_profiles.title: AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is being introduced into K-12 education worldwide. The authors conduct a systematic literature review to map the landscape of AI education in schools, identify the main kinds of approaches being used, and highlight gaps in the evidence base. Their central question is how current approaches integrate AI literacy into K-12 education across different countries and settings.

The review is based on a Scopus search that ultimately included 179 documents. The authors classify the literature into two broad categories: learning experiences and theoretical perspectives. Learning experiences include activities aimed at helping students recognize AI in everyday artifacts, understand how AI works, use AI-related tools, and reflect on AI’s broader social and ethical implications. Theoretical perspectives include curriculum design, AI as a school subject, student perspectives, teacher training, support resources, and gender diversity. The review also notes country-level initiatives, especially in the United States, China, Singapore, Germany, and Canada, which are developing curriculum frameworks and implementation models for AI education.

The main conclusion is that K-12 AI literacy is still in an early stage and is often focused on technical or applied skills in limited domains, with very few studies rigorously assessing learning outcomes. The authors argue that AI literacy should be competency-based, interdisciplinary, integrated into existing subjects rather than added as a separate subject, and co-designed with teachers. They also emphasize the need for stronger attention to ethics, social consequences, and teacher preparation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review with transparent search and screening procedures, but it is not an experimental or quasi-experimental evaluation of an intervention. The evidence is therefore useful for mapping the field and identifying gaps, but it does not provide direct causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has important descriptive and agenda-setting relevance for K-12 AI education policy and curriculum design, but it reports no measurable intervention effect sizes. Its impact is mainly indirect: informing expectations and design choices rather than demonstrating student or institutional gains.

finding.finding_summary: This is a systematic literature review of 179 K-12 AI literacy papers, so it does not estimate a causal effect on student learning. It finds strong growth in AI literacy initiatives worldwide, with learning experiences and theoretical/policy proposals emerging, but also notes that most school-based experiences do not rigorously assess learning outcomes and that implementation is uneven across countries.
finding.measure: Systematic review of K-12 AI literacy literature; bibliometric and qualitative coding of 179 documents

paper_profiles.title: 2020 EDUCAUSE Horizon Report: Teaching and Learning Edition
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report is a horizon-scanning and foresight publication about the future of postsecondary teaching and learning, rather than an empirical study of a specific intervention. It asks what macro trends are shaping higher education and what emerging technologies and practices are likely to matter for institutions, instructors, and learners.

The report synthesizes expert-panel judgment and evidence around social, technological, economic, higher education, and political trends, then highlights six emerging technologies/practices: adaptive learning technologies, AI/machine learning education applications, analytics for student success, elevation of instructional design/learning engineering/UX, open educational resources, and XR technologies. It also presents four possible future scenarios for higher education (growth, constraint, collapse, transformation) and short implications essays from multiple international and institutional perspectives.

Because it is a foresight report, the “population” is not a single study sample but the higher-education community broadly, with illustrative references to institutions and examples from the United States and several other countries. The main conclusion is that adaptive learning, AI-enabled supports, analytics, and related digital practices may improve learning and equity, but adoption is constrained by cost, faculty receptiveness, privacy, and implementation complexity. The report emphasizes that technology alone is insufficient and must be embedded in broader instructional redesign and institutional support.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a grey-literature Horizon Report based on expert panel judgment, examples, and secondary evidence rather than a controlled study or systematic synthesis. It is useful for scoping the landscape, but it does not meet experimental or quasi-experimental credibility criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The report suggests potentially meaningful impacts from adaptive learning and predictive analytics, but the evidence presented is largely descriptive and institution-specific, with no pooled effect sizes. Overall impact is plausible but unclear for general K-12 science expectations.

interventions.use_case: adaptive learning technologies used to personalize pacing, content, and feedback in higher education courses and curricula, including adaptive-active course redesigns and scaffolded support
machine learning models that predict student grade performance and identify students at higher academic risk using SIS and admissions data
AI-based chatbot and virtual assistant systems that answer routine student and faculty questions, support recruiting and library services, and extend off-hours support
AI systems used for feedback on student work and related support tasks, described as providing feedback on student work and virtual teaching assistant functions

finding.finding_summary: The report describes encouraging outcomes from adaptive learning implementations in higher education, including improved course success, mastery, and pass rates when adaptive systems are paired with active learning and course redesign. Examples cited include Oregon State University’s college algebra redesign, where pass rates increased from 65% to 77% and withdrawals fell from 11% to 4%, and Arizona State University’s self-paced algebra redesign, where success rates rose from 54% in 2015 to 84% with adaptive instruction plus a stretch semester.
finding.measure: course pass rates, withdrawal rates, course completion with a C or better, student mastery, and student perception surveys
finding.study_size: multiple institutional examples; sample sizes not reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI chatbots and machine learning systems can extend institutional support capacity and improve operational coverage, such as 24/7 student help and automated routing to knowledge bases or helpdesk tickets. The outcomes are described qualitatively rather than with effect sizes, emphasizing efficiency gains in student services and advising workflows.
finding.measure: service availability, helpdesk support coverage, administrative support efficiency

finding.finding_summary: Predictive analytics is presented as enabling earlier identification of students with higher-than-average academic risk, allowing advisors and administrators to plan interventions in advance. The Penn State example uses more than 8.5 million records (2005-2016) to build a grade-prediction model, but the report does not provide a causal estimate of downstream student outcomes.
finding.measure: predictive accuracy for student grade performance and risk identification

finding.finding_summary: Across the report, the institutional impact of AI, adaptive learning, and analytics is framed as potentially transformative but constrained by cost, privacy, equity, and faculty-receptiveness concerns. The report repeatedly notes that benefits depend on implementation quality and accompanying redesign, while also warning about ethical use of student data and algorithmic bias.
finding.measure: institutional adoption, privacy concerns, equity/inclusion considerations, faculty receptiveness

paper_profiles.title: Reflection on whether Chat GPT should be banned by academia from the perspective of education and teaching
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an opinion essay that argues against a blanket academic ban on ChatGPT and instead calls for regulated, responsible integration of generative AI into education. The author frames the discussion around two competing concerns: risks such as cheating, plagiarism, over-reliance, bias, privacy problems, and reduced independent thinking, versus potential benefits such as personalized tutoring, efficient feedback, content generation, and support for teaching and research.

The paper does not report an empirical intervention or study; rather, it synthesizes recent commentary and examples from higher education, K-12 policy responses, and broader AI developments to make a theoretical case. It discusses ChatGPT in relation to education generally, including classroom use, assessment, digital transformation, and the need to rethink curriculum and evaluation in an AI-rich environment.

The main conclusion is that ChatGPT should not be simply banned, because AI is becoming deeply embedded in learning and work. Instead, schools and governments should develop clear rules, protect academic integrity, and redesign teaching and assessment to emphasize critical thinking, creativity, process-based learning, and appropriate human-AI collaboration. The paper also suggests that some restrictions may be understandable in K-12 settings, but the overall direction should be controlled adoption rather than prohibition.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed opinion essay with no original empirical design, no comparison group, and no measured outcomes. The paper is theoretical and argumentative rather than an evaluative study.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear relevance to emerging AI-in-education policy and practice, but it does not report empirical impact estimates. Its influence is mainly conceptual and anticipatory rather than demonstrably measured in student outcomes.

interventions.use_case: General educational use of ChatGPT/ChatGPT Plus as a conversational AI for student tutoring, self-inquiry, personalized support, and assistance with academic writing and learning tasks in school and higher education settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues ChatGPT can support writing-related academic tasks such as paper drafting, abstract generation, and literature review assistance, which may improve writing efficiency and reduce workload. However, it also emphasizes risks of academic dishonesty, over-reliance, and potentially weaker independent writing and thinking skills; no original effect size is reported because this is an opinion paper.
finding.measure: Narrative discussion of writing support, academic integrity, and perceived writing quality/efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The author repeatedly states that ChatGPT may improve critical thinking support, problem-solving access, and learning motivation through personalized tutoring and iterative feedback, but may also diminish independent thinking, judgment, and self-directed learning through over-reliance. No empirical estimate is provided; claims are theoretical and literature-based.
finding.measure: Narrative discussion of critical thinking, judgment, self-direction, and learning motivation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues ChatGPT can reduce teachers' and researchers' workload by generating text, answering questions, and speeding completion of literature reviews and other routine tasks. This is presented as a plausible efficiency gain, but no quantitative evaluation is reported.
finding.measure: Narrative discussion of time savings, productivity, and workflow efficiency

finding.finding_summary: A central claim is that ChatGPT is prompting policy changes, bans, and regulation debates across schools, universities, publishers, and governments, while also being framed as a driver of educational digital transformation. The paper offers no causal estimates; it is an opinion piece synthesizing institutional responses and governance concerns.
finding.measure: Narrative discussion of bans, policy responses, regulation, and educational transformation

paper_profiles.title: A Multimedia Adaptive Tutoring System for Mathematics that Addresses Cognition, Metacognition and Affect
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how an intelligent adaptive tutoring system, Wayang Outpost (later called MathSpring), can support mathematics learning by addressing three dimensions of student experience at once: cognition, metacognition, and affect. The authors argue that conventional tutoring systems often focus mainly on correctness and mastery, while students also need support for motivation, self-regulation, engagement, and emotional states such as boredom or frustration. The paper therefore asks how educational technology can tailor content and feedback not only to what students know, but also to how hard they are trying, how they are regulating their learning, and how they are feeling.

The intervention is a multimedia intelligent tutoring system that provides adaptive problem selection, worked examples, hints, animated affective learning companions, open student models, progress reports, and math fluency training. The system uses an effort-based tutoring algorithm to infer student states from incorrect answers, hint use, and response time, and then adjusts difficulty and feedback accordingly. It also provides teacher-facing dashboards with real-time information about student performance, skill mastery, effort, and engagement. The paper additionally describes a separate math facts retrieval component (MathSuccess) used to build fluency in foundational arithmetic skills.

The studies described were conducted in middle and high school math classrooms in Massachusetts, primarily across urban, suburban, and rural public school settings. Some analyses used randomized or controlled comparisons, including a randomized four-condition study with 250 middle school students for the fluency-training component and a controlled school-year study with 198 seventh- and eighth-grade students for classroom use of Wayang. The outcomes included pre/post tests, standardized test scores, and system logs, rather than solely self-report. Across these studies, the authors report that the system improved short-term learning, longer-term standardized test performance, math fluency, and indicators of engagement and affect, with the strongest gains often appearing when adaptive tutoring was combined with fluency training. The paper concludes that a single tutoring system can meaningfully integrate cognitive, metacognitive, and affective support, although the authors note that further work is needed to refine how these supports are triggered and optimized.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical article with multiple classroom evaluations, including controlled comparisons and reported effect sizes. It is not a single clean RCT across all components, and several findings are aggregated or partially descriptive, so it falls short of blue.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports modest-to-medium gains in mathematics outcomes, including d=0.38 and d=0.77 on MAP algebra/patterns, which indicate meaningful though not universal impact. The strongest evidence is on a priority K-12 population in school settings, but effects vary by study and outcome, so green is the best fit.

interventions.use_case: Wayang Outpost/MathSpring multimedia adaptive mathematics tutoring with problem selection, worked examples, hints, affective companions, metacognitive scaffolds, and teacher dashboards for middle and high school students
adaptive selection of math problems and difficulty pacing within knowledge units based on recent student performance and effort
automatic feedback through hints, progress reports, open student models, and teacher-facing analytics on student mastery, effort, and engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports repeated positive effects of Wayang Outpost on mathematics learning, including higher state standardized test performance and pre-post gains. In a 2012 controlled study with 198 seventh- and eighth-grade students, 7th graders using Wayang showed a near-significant MCAS advantage (Mean 244.82 vs. 239.50; F(1,93)=2.2, p=0.14), and combined data showed significant MAP gains in the patterns-and-algebra section (d=0.38), with 8th graders showing larger gains in algebra/patterns (d=0.77).
finding.measure: MCAS passing categories and scale scores; MAP mathematics subtest gains (patterns/algebra)
finding.study_size: n=198 (2012 controlled study); other aggregated studies across years not fully reported
finding.effect_size: d=0.38; d=0.77; p=0.14 for MCAS mean difference

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues and reports that affect-aware scaffolds improved engagement, effort, and students’ emotional experience during tutoring. Evidence cited includes improved engagement measured by system logs of gaming/use and affect measured via sensors and self-reports; however, most results are described qualitatively rather than as a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: system logs of gaming/engagement, affect sensors, and student self-reports of emotions

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports positive effects on metacognition and self-regulation through open student models, progress pages, and help-seeking supports. Results are mainly presented as design-and-evaluation evidence rather than a single causal estimate, but the interventions are explicitly intended to improve reflection, goal setting, monitoring, and strategic help use.
finding.measure: use of the Student Progress Page, reflection/goal-setting behavior, and help-seeking/self-monitoring indicators

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-facing dashboards and reports are presented as helping instructors quickly identify students’ strengths, weaknesses, and challenging problems in real time. The paper describes this as valuable instructional support, but does not provide a quantified workload reduction estimate.
finding.measure: teacher reports / real-time analytics use

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Multimodal Feedback Using Multiple External Representations: Strategy Profiles and Learning in High School Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether personalized elaborated feedback that uses multiple external representations (MERs) is associated with better learning in high school physics, and whether students differ in how they select and use those representations. The authors frame the work as relevant to adaptive instruction and intelligent tutoring systems, especially as multimodal AI systems become more capable of generating feedback in verbal, graphical, and mathematical forms.

The intervention-like environment was a custom computer-based platform (KI4SCool) that delivered verification feedback after each physics multiple-choice item, with optional elaborated feedback accessible on demand. Elaborated feedback was offered in three formats: textual/verbal, pictorial/graphical, and mathematical, and students could open one, several, or all formats. The study did not randomly assign students; instead, it observed naturally occurring use of the platform over a 16–24 week period. Data came from 661 high school students in Germany across grades 10–11, with pre-/post-tests, platform logs, confidence ratings, and performance measures.

Analyses showed that more frequent use of elaborated feedback was modestly and positively associated with higher post-test scores, even after adjusting for prior knowledge, platform performance, exercises completed, and confidence. The authors also identified stable MER-use profiles, including students who rarely opened elaborated feedback, those who mostly selected verbal feedback, those who used multiple formats simultaneously, and those who selected all three formats frequently. Differences in these profiles were not strongly explained by initial representational competence, and time-resolved sequence analysis did not reveal meaningful temporal strategy differences beyond feedback frequency. Overall, the findings suggest that adaptive systems for science learning may benefit from offering optional elaborated feedback in multiple formats, but the observational design means causal claims cannot be made.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a prospective observational cohort study with clustering, regression adjustment, and strategy clustering, but it is not randomized and cannot support causal claims. The methodology is reasonably transparent and substantive, yet confounding remains a major concern, so the evidence level is correlational rather than experimental.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed associations are small and/or mixed: the main feedback-frequency effect is modest (β≈0.08-0.13), and the strategy comparisons are not robustly significant. The paper suggests useful design implications for adaptive science feedback, but the direct performance impact appears modest and uncertain.

interventions.use_case: computer-based physics practice platform providing immediate verification feedback plus optional elaborated feedback in verbal, graphical, and mathematical formats for high school kinematics exercises
adaptive feedback design for an ITS-like platform that tailors elaboration level and representational format to learner profiles and representational competence

finding.finding_summary: In an observational cohort of high school physics students (Cohort 1 n=351; Cohort 2 n=310), more frequent access to elaborated multimodal feedback was associated with higher post-test physics scores after adjusting for pre-test performance, platform score, exercises solved, and confidence. The standardized association for feedback frequency was small but positive in both cohorts (Cohort 1 β=0.13, 95% CI [0.05, 0.22]; Cohort 2 β=0.08, 95% CI [0.00, 0.16], p=.054), with no significant interaction by prior knowledge or confidence.
finding.measure: Post-test score on high school kinematics/physics assessments

finding.finding_summary: Learners showed distinct feedback-selection strategies, but the time-resolved sequence analysis did not reveal meaningful temporal strategy differences; most behavior reduced to either no feedback or all three representations at once. More frequent feedback use was associated with longer response times (Cohort 1 r=0.43, Cohort 2 r=0.34), suggesting greater deliberation, but feedback use was not correlated with pre-test score, platform score, number of exercises solved, or confidence.
finding.measure: Feedback-selection logs, response time, and cluster-based strategy patterns
finding.study_size: n=661 overall; n=192 for complete-sequence analysis
finding.effect_size: r=0.43; r=0.34; cluster differences not reported as effect size

finding.finding_summary: Strategy-cluster analyses suggested a possible advantage for students who more often used all three representations, but covariate-adjusted mean differences were not robust. In Cohort 1, the feedback-strategy-cluster main effect was near-significant (F(2,309)=2.90, p=.0566) and cluster 3 trended above cluster 2 (adjusted diff=-8.11, SE=3.47, p=.0597); in Cohort 2, the interaction of feedback frequency and strategy approached significance (F(2,264)=2.97, p=.0529) and only cluster 3 showed a positive slope (estimate=33.83, SE=13.02, p=.01).
finding.measure: Adjusted post-test physics score by feedback strategy cluster

paper_profiles.title: A review of clustering models in educational data science towards fairness-aware learning
paper_profiles.venue: Educational Data Science: Essentials, Approaches, and Tendencies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter reviews clustering models used in educational data science (EDS) with a focus on fairness-aware learning. The paper asks why clustering matters in EDS, how fairness can be defined for clustering, how fair clustering has been evaluated, and what additional practical requirements matter beyond fairness. It is motivated by the increasing use of machine learning in educational decision-making and the risk that clustering-based applications may reproduce or amplify bias against protected groups such as gender or race.

The chapter surveys 133 publications from 2017 to June 2022 identified through Google Scholar, DBLP, and Scopus. It summarizes where clustering has been used in education, including analyzing student behavior, performance, grading, recommendation, collaboration, and wellbeing, across classroom, LMS, MOOC, and intelligent tutoring system contexts. It also reviews common clustering methods such as k-means, hierarchical clustering, fuzzy c-means, EM, SOM, spectral clustering, and DBSCAN, along with their computational properties.

A major contribution is the review of fairness notions and fair clustering methods relevant to education, including balance, bounded representation, social fairness, and individual fairness. The chapter highlights that fair clustering is still underexplored in education, but notes that fair center-based, hierarchical, and spectral clustering approaches are promising for educational applications. The authors conclude that clustering can support educational decision-making and personalized support, but fairness constraints, evaluation practices, and domain requirements such as capacity constraints and interpretability must be considered carefully.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review chapter on clustering models and fairness in educational data science, not an empirical evaluation of an intervention. It synthesizes prior literature and provides technical background, but does not report a primary study design, sample, or outcome analysis of its own.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The chapter has indirect relevance for education technology by organizing fair clustering methods that could inform future student grouping, analytics, and support systems. However, it does not measure learner outcomes or demonstrate direct impact in K-12 settings.

paper_profiles.title: Advancing Education through Tutoring Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the broad question of how tutoring systems have evolved and what educational value they offer, with a focus on intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) and robot tutoring systems (RTS). The authors argue that tutoring systems are important because many learners continue to struggle in core academic areas, and adaptive AI-based tools may help close learning gaps by providing personalized instruction, feedback, and engagement.

The study is a systematic literature review following PRISMA. It synthesizes 86 representative studies published from 1972 to 2024, spanning early computer-assisted instruction through modern systems that use Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, large language models, and robotic interaction. The review organizes the literature around four dimensions: artificial intelligence, system behavior, engagement, and affordances, and then uses latent class analysis to identify three classes of tutoring systems: computer-based ITS, verbal robot-based RTS, and multimodal systems.

The paper focuses on educational technologies rather than one specific student sample or school context. Its conclusions are that ITS tend to excel in cognitive adaptability and scalability, while RTS are especially strong in social and emotional engagement. The authors also conclude that generative AI and multimodal systems can enhance adaptability and responsiveness, but significant concerns remain around data privacy, bias, scalability, and the ethical use of AI in education. They suggest that hybrid systems combining software and robotics may offer the strongest future direction.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic literature review using PRISMA with latent class analysis, so it has a clearer methodology than a narrative review. However, it does not present new primary outcome data or a formal meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes, limiting causal and quantitative credibility.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests broad positive effects of tutoring systems on learning and engagement, but the review itself provides no pooled effect sizes and relies on heterogeneous prior studies. Its implications are useful for expectation-setting, yet the direct measurable impact reported here is unclear rather than demonstrably large.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of classical and modern AI-driven tutoring systems that personalize instruction using student models, Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, and adaptive feedback in educational settings.
Review of generative-AI and LLM-enabled tutors/chatbots that provide conversational tutoring, real-time feedback, and adaptive explanations, including ChatGPT-style supports for learning.
Systematic review of robot tutoring systems used as physical, socially interactive tutors that provide verbal encouragement, gestures, and multimodal engagement for students.
Historical review of early computer-assisted instruction systems as predecessors to modern tutoring systems, emphasizing fixed or minimally adaptive software-delivered instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed tutoring-system literature, math-focused ITS and robot tutors were consistently associated with improved learning outcomes and better performance in school settings. The paper cites studies such as an ITS for 6th-grade math and adaptive tutoring systems using Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, but does not report a pooled effect size for the review itself.
finding.measure: Math learning outcomes, academic performance, and achievement in tutoring-system studies
finding.study_size: n=86 studies reviewed overall; individual study sizes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review indicates that LLM-based and adaptive tutoring systems can support science learning and domain understanding by providing context-sensitive explanations, feedback, and conversational support. The paper particularly highlights secondary physics tutoring and other STEM-oriented tutoring examples, but it does not synthesize a quantitative science-specific effect size.
finding.measure: Science/STEM learning outcomes, understanding, and performance in tutoring-system studies
finding.study_size: n=86 studies reviewed overall; individual study sizes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that robot-based tutoring systems improve student motivation, engagement, and emotional/social involvement through gestures, verbal encouragement, and human-like interaction. These benefits are presented as a recurring pattern across the reviewed studies, but the paper does not provide a pooled effect size or confidence interval.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, and social-emotional engagement outcomes
finding.study_size: n=86 studies reviewed overall; individual study sizes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests tutoring systems may support problem-solving and deeper learning through adaptive feedback and conversational interaction, but this is framed more as a theoretical synthesis than as directly measured evidence. Because the review emphasizes engagement and personalized support more than explicit metacognitive or critical-thinking outcomes, the durable-skills evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive.
finding.measure: Problem-solving, deeper learning, and related higher-order learning outcomes as described in reviewed studies
finding.study_size: n=86 studies reviewed overall; individual study sizes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies substantial ethical and implementation issues, including data privacy, transparency, bias, scalability, and equitable access. It argues these concerns require governance frameworks, encryption, audits, and oversight, but this outcome is based on synthesis of prior literature rather than a direct impact estimate.
finding.measure: Ethical concerns, scalability, access, and governance considerations in educational AI deployment
finding.study_size: n=86 studies reviewed overall; individual study sizes not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Discussion Tracker: Supporting Teacher Learning about Students’ Collaborative Argumentation in High School Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge that many K-12 teachers face in teaching collaborative argumentation well. The authors introduce Discussion Tracker (DT), a classroom discussion analytics system that uses natural language processing to automatically code student talk along three dimensions: argument moves, specificity, and collaboration. The system presents these codes through visualizations such as overview charts, annotated transcripts, collaboration maps, and planning tools intended to help teachers reflect on classroom discussion quality and plan instruction.

The study evaluates DT in high school classrooms using both teacher perceptions and NLP model performance. Eighteen high school English Language Arts teachers from four schools led and recorded discussions about literary texts. Researchers manually annotated the discussions to generate gold-standard labels, and teachers later used DT in cognitive interviews and completed usability surveys. The automated classifiers were trained on a prior corpus and tested on the new classroom discussions.

Results suggest that teachers found DT useful and that its analytics supported reflection on student collaboration and argumentation. Teachers rated most features highly, and the automated classifiers achieved moderate to substantial agreement with human annotations. The paper concludes that discussion analytics can help teachers notice strengths and weaknesses in student discourse, while noting future work to improve automation and make the system fully end-to-end.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a small classroom deployment with teacher usability data and model evaluation, but it is not a randomized or quasi-experimental efficacy study. Evidence is largely qualitative/observational for teacher perceptions, with no causal estimate of student learning impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but indirect benefits: teachers liked the tool and the NLP classifiers achieved moderate-to-substantial agreement with human coding. However, there is no demonstrated student achievement effect, so impact on K-12 learning outcomes remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: classroom discussion analytics system for teacher support, using NLP to automatically code collaborative argumentation in high school literature discussions and present visualizations, annotated transcripts, collaboration maps, strengths/weaknesses, and planning tools

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that Discussion Tracker was helpful for learning to facilitate collaborative argumentation in high school classrooms. Across 13 usability items, nine received mean ratings at or above 4.5/5, and the overall item 'Overall, Discussion Tracker is helpful for my teaching of literature discussions' had a mean of 4.72 (n=18 teachers).
finding.measure: Teacher usability/perceived usefulness Likert-scale survey ratings

finding.finding_summary: The system was perceived as improving teachers' ability to quickly interpret discussion features, identify strengths/weaknesses, and set goals, suggesting reduced effort in analyzing classroom talk. Teachers rated the annotated transcript highly (M=4.89) and the system-generated strengths/weaknesses as helpful (M=4.44), indicating support for more efficient reflection and planning.
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings of usefulness for analysis, reflection, and planning

paper_profiles.title: Emotion in Reinforcement Learning Agents and Robots: A Survey
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper surveys computational models of emotion in reinforcement learning (RL) agents and robots. Its central question is how emotion has been represented in AI systems that learn from reward, and how those emotion models relate to RL mechanisms such as motivation, value functions, temporal-difference error, and action selection. The survey is intended to bridge work across machine learning, affective modeling, and human-robot interaction.

The paper is not an empirical study of learners in classrooms; instead, it reviews 52 prior papers and organizes them into a taxonomy of emotion elicitation, emotion type, and emotion function. It distinguishes four main emotion-elicitation routes: homeostasis/extrinsic motivation, appraisal/intrinsic motivation, value/reward-based elicitation, and hard-wired sensory links. It also reviews categorical and dimensional emotion models and shows how emotions can modify reward, state, meta-learning, action selection, or remain epiphenomenal.

The context is AI agents and robots, including learning architectures that may use internal drives, appraisal-like features, or reward-based signals to produce emotion-like states. The authors conclude that emotions in RL are useful for improving learning efficiency, increasing transparency and social signaling, and providing testbeds for emotion theories. They also note that many existing papers are difficult to replicate because the mapping from elicitation method to emotion type is often underspecified.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative survey and taxonomy paper, not an empirical study of educational intervention effects. It does not report a study design, sample, or causal identification strategy relevant to K-12 outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct educational outcome impact; it is foundational background on affective RL and emotion modeling in agents, with no measured effect on learners or schools.

interventions.use_case: Survey of computational emotion models in reinforcement learning agents and robots, focusing on how emotion is elicited, represented, and used within the agent learning loop.

paper_profiles.title: An Integrated Platform for Studying Learning with Intelligent Tutoring Systems: CTAT+TutorShop
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents CTAT+TutorShop, an integrated platform for building, deploying, and studying intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs). The main question is not the effectiveness of a single intervention, but how a research-enabling platform can support the full lifecycle of learning sciences research: identifying learner difficulties from log data, redesigning tutors, and running experimental studies. The paper argues that CTAT+TutorShop, combined with DataShop logging and analytics, is especially useful because it lets researchers author tutors or tutor variants, configure conditions, and collect detailed interaction data in a form suitable for later analysis.

The platform supports both programmer and non-programmer authoring, includes tools for feedback, hints, tests, task selection, and custom student modeling, and has been used across many domains including mathematics, chemistry, algebra, and games. The authors describe five case studies showing how the platform has supported research on learning sciences principles such as worked examples, polite feedback, paper-vs-tutor comparisons, design-loop adaptivity, and gamification. These examples span school and university contexts, with substantial use in K-12 settings and higher education.

The paper concludes that CTAT+TutorShop has enabled a large body of ITS research over more than 20 years, with many studies in real educational settings. The authors estimate roughly 147 studies and more than 800 content-creating accounts over the platform’s lifetime. They emphasize that the platform’s distinctive value lies in combining authoring tools with research and deployment infrastructure, making it easier to create experimental conditions and study how intelligent tutoring systems support learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a platform/methods paper describing CTAT+Tutorshop and summarizing prior studies, not a direct empirical evaluation of a new intervention in this paper. It is peer-reviewed and cites extensive prior work, but the paper itself does not present a clear causal study design or new outcome data to grade as higher-quality evidence here.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially important enabling impact for K-12 ITS research and reports broad adoption, but it does not evaluate student learning gains of CTAT+Tutorshop itself. Its impact is therefore indirect and institutionally meaningful rather than a direct measured effect on learners.

interventions.use_case: research platform and integrated authoring/deployment environment (CTAT+Tutorshop) for building, deploying, and studying rule/model-based intelligent tutors with step-level hints, feedback, and mastery learning

paper_profiles.title: The Scientific Method in the Science of Machine Learning
paper_profiles.venue: ICLR 2019 Debugging Machine Learning Models Workshop
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper argues that contemporary machine learning research often lacks two core elements of the scientific method: explicit hypothesis formulation/testing and careful statistical treatment of uncertainty. The authors motivate the paper by pointing to reproducibility concerns, inconsistent performance across replications, and the tendency for published ML results to emphasize performance claims without adequately quantifying variation or confounding factors.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or a learner population. Instead, it proposes methodological guidance for the ML research community, drawing analogies from experimental high-energy physics. The authors describe how physics uses null and alternative hypotheses, nuisance parameters, likelihood-based estimation, and pre-registration/registered reports to support rigorous inference, and they suggest similar practices for ML experiments.

The context is research practice in machine learning rather than a school or classroom setting. The main conclusion is that ML researchers should move beyond exploratory “it works” demonstrations toward controlled, reproducible experiments with pre-specified hypotheses and explicit statistical/systematic uncertainty accounting. The paper recommends broader adoption of registered reports, negative-result publication, and closer attention to robustness and variability in claims of state-of-the-art performance.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed position paper, not an empirical study. It provides conceptual arguments and recommendations about scientific rigor in machine learning, but it does not test an intervention, compare groups, or report study methods/results relevant to K-12 outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct educational intervention or measured student outcome in the paper, so there is no demonstrated impact on K-12 learners, teachers, or schools. Any relevance to science education is only indirect and theoretical.

paper_profiles.title: On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies contrastive learning from a theoretical perspective, focusing on how the cosine similarities of learned embeddings behave under full-batch and mini-batch training. The authors ask when positive pairs can be perfectly aligned and how negative pairs are separated in the embedding space, using a unified framework that covers several common contrastive objectives such as InfoNCE, SimCLR, DCL, DHEL, and SigLIP-style losses.

The main contribution is a set of theorems showing that, in full-batch settings, optimal embeddings align positive pairs and place negative pairs at cosine similarity -1/(n-1), but some loss formulations can cause excessive separation of negative pairs and misalignment of positives. In mini-batch settings, the paper proves that smaller batch sizes increase the variance of negative-pair similarities even when the expected similarity remains optimal, which helps explain why mini-batch training can underperform full-batch training.

To address this, the paper proposes an auxiliary loss that reduces the variance of negative-pair similarities by pushing them toward the ideal full-batch value. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet with standard self-supervised contrastive models show that adding this loss lowers variance and improves downstream classification performance, especially for smaller batch sizes.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/methods paper about contrastive learning embeddings, not a study of an educational intervention in K-12 settings. It provides no direct educational outcome evidence, no experimental comparison in schools, and no student- or teacher-level intervention evaluation.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no demonstrated K-12 educational impact in the paper. Any relevance to education would be indirect and upstream (better representation learning), so it does not support an impact claim for classroom practice or learner outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: The Frontiers of Nuclear Science: A Long Range Plan
paper_profiles.venue: National Science Advisory Committee (NSAC) Long Range Plan
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This document is a long-range strategic plan for U.S. nuclear science, prepared by the Nuclear Science Advisory Committee in response to a 2006 charge from DOE and NSF. It does not report an empirical study of an educational intervention or AI system; instead, it synthesizes the state of the field and recommends priorities for facilities, theory, and workforce development over the next decade.

The paper argues that recent discoveries in QCD, nuclear structure, neutrino physics, and astrophysics justify continued and expanded investment in major facilities and tools, including the 12 GeV CEBAF Upgrade, FRIB, RHIC II upgrades, and development of a polarized Electron-Ion Collider. It also identifies education as a key component of the field’s future, emphasizing training the next generation of nuclear scientists and outreach to undergraduates and the public, but it does not evaluate a specific instructional program or learner intervention.

The intended context is the U.S. nuclear science enterprise, especially national laboratories, universities, and large user facilities. The document’s main conclusion is that maintaining U.S. leadership requires new capital investments, sustained operations and research support, and stronger training pipelines for students and future researchers. Because the text is a policy and planning report rather than a study, it provides no participant data, no measured educational outcomes, and no implementation details for a classroom or school-based intervention.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a policy/planning long-range report from an advisory committee, not an empirical study. It contains no study design, no comparative intervention evaluation, and no quantitative outcomes attributable to a technology intervention.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The document has no measured K-12 educational impact; it discusses future directions in nuclear science and broad education recommendations only. It does not provide evidence that would inform educational outcome effects for science tutoring or AI supports.

paper_profiles.title: Revealing Networks: Understanding Effective Teacher Practices in AI-Supported Classrooms using Transmodal Ordered Network Analysis
paper_profiles.venue: The 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK '24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether adding classroom context data to student tutor log data improves understanding of learning in AI-supported classrooms, and what teacher practices are associated with better or worse student progress. The authors focus on teacher-student interactions around the use of an AI tutor, especially teacher monitoring, talking to students, and brief visits, to explain differences in students’ learning rates within the system.

The study uses a multimodal case study from a middle school math classroom using the Lynnette AI tutor for linear equation solving. Data came from 85 seventh-grade students across five classes taught by one experienced teacher in a U.S. public school over three class sessions. The researchers combined tutor log data, classroom observation codes, and teacher position-sensor data, then analyzed them with transmodal ordered network analysis (T/ONA) and qualitative text replay of observation notes. Students were grouped by low vs. high learning rates, and also by whether they had been visited by the teacher.

The main finding is that teacher-practice data improved prediction of student learning rates beyond tutor logs alone. Teacher screen alignment and teacher talking were especially informative: low-learning-rate students tended to request hints after these teacher actions, while high-learning-rate students more often produced correct attempts. After teacher visits, low-learning-rate students’ behavior shifted toward more consecutive correct attempts, suggesting visits were associated with more favorable learning patterns. Qualitative notes suggest that low-learning-rate students often received more procedural help before visits, while visits were more likely to include conceptual support and self-explanation prompts. The authors conclude that making teacher practices visible through analytics could inform dashboards and reflection tools for improving AI-supported classroom instruction.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed observational classroom study using multimodal learning analytics and quantitative ethnography, not an RCT. It provides careful triangulation of log data, observation notes, and teacher positioning, but causal claims remain limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The findings are relevant to AI-supported classroom practice and teacher guidance, but they are mainly correlational/interpretive rather than direct evidence of learning gains from an intervention. Effects are described as improved inference and behavior patterns rather than a clear, generalizable achievement impact of at least modest size.

interventions.use_case: Classroom use of the Lynnette AI tutor for 7th-grade linear equation solving, with step-wise feedback, hints, and mastery-style problem solving practice.

finding.finding_summary: In a 3-day classroom study with 85 seventh-grade students, adding out-of-tutor teacher practice codes to the model improved inference of students’ learning-rate group in the AI tutor. The multimodal model had lower AIC than the in-tutor-only model (AIC=150.60 vs 158.30; t=12.76, 95% CI [7.06, 9.63], p<.001), and students with high learning rates showed more consecutive correct attempts (e.g., FIRST CORRECT ATTEMPT → CORRECT ATTEMPT m_high=0.43 vs m_low=0.29).
finding.measure: AI tutor learning rate / first-attempt correctness, ordered network connections among equation-solving behaviors
