The main conclusion is that explainability methods differ in what they reveal: SHAP and LIME help characterize feature importance, but FairML exposes strong bias related to sensitive attributes such as race, nationality, and sex. The authors conclude that feature importance alone is not sufficient to assess fairness and that transparency and bias mitigation are essential for trustworthy AI in education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a chapter-style exposition and methodological demonstration, not a peer-reviewed experimental or quasi-experimental evaluation of an educational intervention. It uses a public dataset and interpretability tools, but does not present a credible design for estimating educational effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not estimate impact on learning, engagement, or institutional outcomes; it mainly argues that bias and transparency concerns exist in AI systems relevant to education. No effect size or practical impact on an educational population is reported.

interventions.use_case: Explainable AI / post-hoc model interpretability and fairness auditing of an XGBoost income-prediction model used as a proxy for how parental income may relate to educational opportunity; methods include LIME, SHAP, permutation importance, decision-tree surrogate modeling, and FairML bias diagnostics.

finding.finding_summary: This is a conceptual/exploratory chapter rather than an intervention study, so it does not report causal effects on student outcomes. Its main empirical claim is that fairness and transparency analyses of an Adult Census income model reveal notable bias: FairML indicates strong dependence on sensitive attributes such as race White, nac United-States, and sex Male, while SHAP and LIME can miss or inconsistently represent these biases. No effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Model interpretability and fairness diagnostics on an Adult Census XGBoost classifier (AUC, feature importance, local explanations, FairML bias audit)

paper_profiles.title: GREX-PLUS Science Book v1
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a science book / mission concept document for GREX-PLUS, a planned cryogenic space telescope for the 2030s. It lays out the scientific rationale, instrument capabilities, and survey plans for studying extra-galactic, galactic, and planetary science targets, rather than reporting an educational intervention or empirical study. The document argues that a 1.2 m telescope with a wide-field 2–8 µm camera and a 10–18 µm high-resolution spectrometer would enable deep, wide imaging and mid-infrared spectroscopy that are difficult or impossible from the ground.

The paper frames two broad science programs: Extra-Galactic Sciences and Galactic and Planetary Sciences. In the extra-galactic program, GREX-PLUS would search for the first galaxies, study galaxy mass assembly, detect high-redshift supernovae and quasars, examine dusty AGNs, and probe reionization-related physics. In the galactic/planetary program, it would measure water snowlines in protoplanetary disks, study interstellar molecules, exoplanet and Solar System atmospheres, icy bodies, star-forming regions, and the Galactic center.

The main conclusions are prospective: GREX-PLUS is presented as a uniquely capable observatory that would substantially surpass existing and planned surveys in wavelength coverage, depth, area, and spectral resolution. The authors argue that its imaging and spectroscopy would produce legacy datasets that could transform astronomy across multiple subfields, including galaxy formation, cosmic reionization, molecular astrophysics, and planetary science.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mission science book / white paper describing planned astronomical observations and motivating scientific cases, not an empirical education study. It does not evaluate an educational intervention with a research design, comparison group, or student-level outcome measurement.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no educational impact estimated here; the document is unrelated to AI tutoring or science education interventions and reports no measured effect on learners, teachers, or institutions.

paper_profiles.title: Pedagogy-driven Evaluation of Generative AI-powered Intelligent Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a core problem in the evaluation of intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs), especially those powered by generative AI and large language models: existing evaluation practices are fragmented, overly reliant on subjective judgments or generic NLP metrics, and fail to capture pedagogical quality. The authors argue that the field lacks unified, reliable, and scalable evaluation frameworks that can measure whether AI tutors truly support learning rather than merely producing fluent responses.

Rather than reporting an empirical intervention study, the paper reviews the state of the art in ITS evaluation across traditional self-report methods, NLG-based automated metrics, and pedagogy-oriented human or model-based assessments. It then proposes three research directions: unifying evaluation frameworks and benchmarks, measuring pedagogical guidance in tutor responses, and measuring active learning through conversation dynamics. The approach is grounded in learning science concepts such as metacognition, constructivism, and inquiry-based learning.

The context is broad and cross-domain, covering prior ITS work in math, language, writing, and science, with examples drawn from educational dialogue datasets and existing AI tutor systems. The paper concludes that progress in GenAI-powered tutoring depends on developing standardized taxonomies, robust benchmarks, and scalable automated metrics aligned with pedagogical principles. It emphasizes that such unification would improve comparability, transparency, and reliability in both research and real-world deployment.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/review-and-proposal paper, not an empirical evaluation study. It does not report a new quantitative design, causal identification strategy, or original outcome evidence, so it does not meet evidence criteria for higher tiers.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No intervention effect is tested or estimated, and no measurable learning impact is reported. The paper proposes evaluation directions and frameworks, so there is no demonstrated impact size to classify beyond red.

interventions.use_case: A review and evaluation framework paper focused on GenAI/LLM-powered intelligent tutoring systems, including dialogue-based AI tutors such as LearnLM and Khanmigo, with emphasis on how to evaluate their pedagogical responses and learning-science alignment.

A broad evaluation-focused analysis of classical and modern ITSs, including rule-based and deep-learning tutors such as AutoTutor, DeepTutor, and Writing Pal, and discussion of their evaluation methods and pedagogical capabilities.

paper_profiles.title: A Review of Generative AI in Computer Science Education: Challenges and Opportunities in Accuracy, Authenticity, and Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the emerging literature on generative AI in computer science education, with a particular focus on three intertwined issues: accuracy, authenticity, and assessment. The authors ask how tools such as ChatGPT and Claude are being used in computing education and what challenges and opportunities they create for teaching, learning, and evaluation.

The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it synthesizes findings from 52 papers published between 2019 and 2024, retrieved from major academic databases. The context is computer science education, especially programming, coding assistance, feedback generation, grading, and student work verification. The review discusses how generative AI can support real-time tutoring, efficiency, creativity, and formative feedback, while also introducing hallucinations, error propagation, bias, and difficulties distinguishing student-authored work from AI-generated work.

Across the reviewed literature, the authors conclude that generative AI should complement rather than replace human judgment in education. They argue for hybrid assessment models, stronger AI literacy, bias mitigation, and clearer ethical guidelines. The paper also identifies gaps in the evidence base, including the lack of longitudinal research on learning outcomes, limited study of bias detection, and insufficient empirical work on scalable hybrid human-AI assessment models.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative literature review and conceptual discussion, not a controlled empirical study or meta-analysis. It synthesizes prior work but does not provide a clear primary methodology or original causal evidence for outcomes.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear relevance to AI tutoring and science/computing education policy, but it reports no direct effect sizes and no original intervention impact. Its practical influence is mainly conceptual and institutional, with modest and uncertain measurable impact.

interventions.use_case: Use of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude as conversational coding assistants in computer science education, including code suggestion, explanation, troubleshooting, and retrieval-augmented tutoring tied to course materials and instructor instructions.
AI-driven grading and feedback for programming assignments and other student work, including real-time feedback on code correctness, efficiency, and formative support during task completion.

Generative AI used for text and code generation in student-authored work, including writing assistance, code generation, and AI-assisted academic writing/authoring where authenticity and plagiarism concerns are discussed.

finding.finding_summary: This is a narrative review of 52 papers rather than an empirical effectiveness study, so it does not report a single pooled effect size. Across the literature, GenAI is described as improving efficiency and supporting coding/problem-solving work, but also introducing hallucinations, error propagation, and biased outputs that can undermine accuracy in computer science learning.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of reported findings on AI-generated code/content accuracy and educational support

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that GenAI can support creative problem-solving and iterative debugging, but may also weaken independent thinking if students rely on AI-generated answers without critical evaluation. No quantitative effect size is reported; the evidence is thematic and emphasizes the need for AI literacy, prompt engineering, and human oversight to preserve critical thinking and metacognition.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of critical thinking, problem-solving, and creativity implications

finding.finding_summary: The review consistently reports that AI-driven grading and feedback can improve efficiency by automating routine assessment tasks and providing timely formative feedback, especially in large classes. However, it also notes that this efficiency comes with limits for complex or creative tasks that still require human review; no quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of grading efficiency and feedback timeliness

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s core contribution is a review of institutional challenges and responses: academic integrity, assessment redesign, AI literacy, bias detection, and hybrid human-AI governance. It argues for policy and assessment reforms rather than reporting a single measurable intervention effect, so no effect size is available.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of policy, governance, and assessment-design implications

paper_profiles.title: A One-Dimensional Energy Balance Model Parameterization for the Formation of CO2 Ice on the Surfaces of Eccentric Extrasolar Planets
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how the formation of carbon dioxide (CO2) ice on cold, eccentric exoplanets affects planetary climate and habitability. The authors note that existing climate models have typically represented ice-albedo feedback using water ice alone, even though CO2 can condense at sufficiently low temperatures and may substantially change planetary reflectivity. The central question is whether adding a CO2 ice-albedo parameterization changes the predicted climate stability of Earth-like planets across different stellar environments and orbital eccentricities.

To answer this, the authors modify a one-dimensional energy balance climate model to include a CO2 ice-albedo parameterization alongside existing treatments of land, ocean, and water ice. They run simulations for Earth-like planets orbiting F-, G-, K-, and M-dwarf stars under warm-start and cold-start conditions, varying orbital eccentricity, stellar flux, and CO2 ice grain size. The model is also validated against approximate Earth and Mars climates and used to estimate transitions into snowball states, deglaciation thresholds, and runaway greenhouse conditions.

The study finds that including CO2 ice generally increases planetary albedo and strengthens climate hysteresis, especially for planets orbiting brighter stars. F-dwarf planets require substantially more instellation to thaw than in water-ice-only simulations, while M-dwarf planets are less affected in the thawing threshold. Eccentricity reduces the tendency to remain fully glaciated because periastron heating promotes deglaciation, and larger CO2 ice grains lower albedo and make thawing easier. Overall, the paper concludes that CO2 ice should be included in climate models of cold and eccentric planets because it materially changes predicted habitability and climate stability.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed scientific modeling paper in astrobiology, not an education study. It does not evaluate any educational technology, intervention, learners, or learning outcomes, so none of the K-12 evidence credibility criteria apply.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct educational impact because it studies planetary climate modeling and CO2 ice-albedo effects on exoplanet habitability, not student learning, instruction, or educational systems.

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education and asks how the field has developed, how AI is conceptualised, what ethical implications are discussed, and what types of applications are being studied. The authors systematically searched three databases and screened publications from 2007 to November 2018, ultimately including 146 peer-reviewed journal articles for synthesis.

The review is not an intervention study of a single AI tool, but a mapping of applications such as profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalisation, and intelligent tutoring systems. The review covers both learner-facing and teacher-facing uses, including automated grading, feedback generation, student modelling, dropout prediction, and systems intended to reduce teacher workload by automating tasks such as administration and feedback. Most studies involved undergraduate settings in higher education; the review also notes some postgraduate-focused work, but the population is overwhelmingly university-based rather than K-12.

The main conclusions are that AI research in higher education is dominated by computer science and quantitative methods, while critical discussion of risks, ethics, privacy, and educational implications is rare. The paper argues that there is a weak connection to pedagogical theory and that educators are underrepresented in the literature. It also highlights that many systems are promising in narrow technical terms, but there is limited evidence on longer-term educational impact, and very little attention to the challenges and risks that matter for real-world adoption.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review, but it synthesizes mostly descriptive and quantitative primary studies rather than conducting a meta-analysis, and the included evidence is often short-term and heterogeneous. The paper itself notes weak critical reflection and limited methodological depth in much of the underlying literature.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests potentially meaningful benefits for efficiency, feedback, and tutoring support, but it reports no pooled effect sizes for the broad literature and flags important concerns about ethics, privacy, and the novelty effect. Overall impact is promising but unclear rather than clearly large or moderate.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of classical intelligent tutoring systems in higher education, including systems that teach course content, diagnose knowledge gaps, provide automated feedback, curate learning materials, and facilitate collaboration.
Machine-learning models for student profiling and prediction, including dropout/retention risk, admission decisions, course selection, engagement, and academic achievement.
Automated grading and feedback systems, including automated essay scoring, concept feedback, and task-specific feedback on student work.
Adaptive and personalized learning systems that recommend content, adapt courses of action, and use learner profiles to guide learning and teaching.

finding.finding_summary: Across the review, AI applications were repeatedly framed as reducing staff burden by automating grading, feedback, admission decisions, and student support. The paper does not report a pooled effect size, but it explicitly argues that these systems can relieve administrative and teaching workload and improve efficiency, especially in large-enrollment settings.
finding.measure: Reported/argued efficiency gains, workload reduction, automation of administrative and instructional tasks

finding.finding_summary: The review finds substantial institutional use of AI for admissions, course scheduling, retention monitoring, and alignment with workforce needs, but also notes very limited critical reflection on ethics, privacy, and governance. Only 2 of 146 articles explicitly discussed risks, suggesting institutional benefits alongside unresolved governance concerns.
finding.measure: Institutional uses of AI; discussion of ethical/privacy challenges

finding.finding_summary: The review describes several systems targeting engagement, motivation, and self-regulation, including predictive systems that identify low-engaged students and ITS that support self-regulated learning. However, the paper is a systematic review and does not provide a pooled effect size; the evidence is described as generally promising but mostly short-term and preliminary.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, self-regulation indicators
finding.study_size: n=146 studies reviewed; individual studies vary

finding.finding_summary: Some reviewed tools were used to support collaboration, problem solving, and metacognitive processes, such as collaborative writing and peer-dialogue agents. The review characterizes these findings as generally positive or satisfactory, but it reports no quantitative synthesis or pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Collaboration, problem solving, metacognitive/self-regulatory support
finding.study_size: n=146 studies reviewed; individual studies vary

finding.finding_summary: Automated essay scoring and writing-feedback tools were generally associated with encouraging revision and scalable grading, though the review notes concerns about feedback quality and genre suitability. The paper reports high agreement in some studies, such as 94.6%–98.2% agreement between LightSIDE and human raters, but it does not provide a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Essay scoring agreement, writing revision, feedback quality
finding.study_size: n=146 studies reviewed; individual studies vary

finding.finding_summary: A subset of ITS studies targeted mathematics and statistics instruction, and the review reports mostly positive or satisfactory preliminary results. However, the paper provides no pooled estimate for math outcomes and emphasizes that most studies were short-term pilots rather than longitudinal evaluations.
finding.measure: Math/statistics learning performance in ITS studies
finding.study_size: n=146 studies reviewed; individual studies vary

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines the promises and risks of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for human learning. It asks how tools such as large language models and diffusion models might reshape learning support, learning resources, feedback, and assessment, while also surfacing concerns about hallucinations, privacy, equality, beneficence, and the disruption of traditional assessment. The paper is especially relevant to AI tutoring systems such as Khanmigo-like tools because it discusses personalized tutoring, feedback, and assessment at scale, but it does so at a conceptual rather than empirical level.

The authors synthesize ideas from learning sciences, educational technology, and human-computer interaction to argue that GenAI can act as a scalable, adaptive learning companion, generate diverse instructional materials, provide timely feedback, and enable more authentic assessments. They highlight that systems like Khanmigo may support inquiry-based learning by guiding students through problems rather than giving direct answers, but they also warn that empirical evidence on learning outcomes remains limited and mixed.

The paper focuses on broad educational contexts, including K-12, higher education, and lifelong learning, rather than a specific study sample. It concludes that GenAI should be integrated with human-centered learning theory, strong AI literacy, evidence-based decision-making, and rigorous evaluation methods. The authors emphasize the need to prevent overreliance, account for hallucinations and bias, and ensure that educators remain central in design and implementation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/theory article rather than an empirical study. It synthesizes prior literature and examples but does not present original methods, sample, or causal identification relevant to a K-12 intervention estimate.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear relevance for K-12 GenAI tutoring policy and design, especially around hallucinations, overreliance, workload, and equity. However, because it is non-empirical and reports no direct effect sizes, its impact is best characterized as illustrative and concept-setting rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Perspective on generative AI chatbots and LLM-based tutors for human learning, including Khanmigo-like tutoring with step-by-step guidance, personalized support, and conversational questioning in K-12 and other learning contexts.
Generative AI systems that produce formative feedback on student writing, programming, dashboards, and other learning artifacts, including text, audio, and video feedback.
AI systems that personalize learning support, pacing, and content delivery based on learner data, including tutoring-system integrations and adaptive learning support at scale.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI/LLM tutoring may support critical thinking and problem-solving through guided questioning, but also warns that overreliance may weaken learner agency, metacognition, and creativity. It cites emerging evidence of a performance paradox: students may perform better with AI assistance, yet perform worse once that support is removed, suggesting fragile rather than durable skill development (specific effect sizes not reported in the perspective).
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, learner agency, metacognition, creativity, and performance after AI support removal

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes potential benefits for engagement and motivation when GenAI is used for tutoring and feedback, but also highlights risks of reduced agency and fluency bias. It emphasizes that evidence so far is mixed, with some studies reporting positive experiences and others showing reduced engagement or dependence on the tool; no pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Learner engagement, motivation, positive emotions, and perceived agency

finding.finding_summary: A central claim is that GenAI can reduce educator workload by scaling personalized support and automating feedback, curriculum/resource generation, and parts of assessment. The paper does not report a new effect size because it is a perspective, but it repeatedly frames the intervention as improving efficiency by making support and feedback faster and less labor-intensive for teachers.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, time required to provide feedback, and efficiency of content/resource generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that GenAI could democratize access to high-quality support, but also may widen inequities through the digital divide, language bias, privacy risks, and opaque model behavior. It cites a review finding that 92% of GenAI tools in learning are transparent only to AI experts, underscoring substantial governance and equity concerns rather than a single measurable effect size.
finding.measure: Transparency, equity/accessibility, privacy, and governance implications for educational systems

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emergence of ChatGPT and asks what its capabilities and limitations imply for higher education, especially for assessment, learning, and teaching. The authors are concerned with whether ChatGPT-like systems threaten traditional assignments such as essays, while also exploring how they might support learning and instructional practice. Rather than reporting a controlled experiment, the paper combines a literature review with hands-on experimentation using ChatGPT to illustrate strengths and weaknesses.

The intervention or approach studied is ChatGPT itself, framed within the broader landscape of AI in Education (AIEd). The authors situate ChatGPT alongside student-facing, teacher-facing, and system-facing AI applications, and compare it conceptually with earlier AI writing tools such as Grammarly and Wordtune, automated essay scoring, and automated feedback systems. They test the chatbot with prompts involving explanation of statistics, a short essay task, and writing in Chinese, in order to probe its performance in conceptual explanation, writing quality, citation handling, and multilingual output.

The population and context are higher education users and institutions, with the discussion focused on university-level teaching, learning, and assessment. The article does not study a specific sampled cohort in a formal empirical design, but its claims are oriented to students, teachers, and institutional leaders in universities. The main conclusion is that ChatGPT is useful for basic explanations and some drafting tasks, but is unreliable for higher-order reasoning, accurate citation, and some languages; therefore, educators should not simply ban it but instead adapt assessment and teaching practices to account for AI text generation, overreliance risks, and the need for more innovative assessment design.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is primarily a narrative/opinion article with a desktop literature review and a few informal prompt experiments, not a controlled empirical study. It is useful for hypothesis generation and mapping concerns, but it does not meet design standards for causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially substantial impacts on assessment integrity, writing practices, and teacher workload, but these are not quantified and the evidence is largely illustrative. The likely effect on K-12 science tutoring is indirect and unclear, so the practical impact remains modest/uncertain.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT as a general-purpose conversational AI for answering questions, generating explanations, drafting essays, and supporting learning/teaching in higher education; the paper also tests its behavior on academic prompts and assessment-like tasks.

ChatGPT used as a writing assistant for drafting essays, rewriting text to avoid plagiarism detection, and generating Chinese composition text; the paper discusses Grammarly and Wordtune as related AI writing tools in the same ecosystem.

The paper discusses AI-powered assessment and feedback systems such as automated essay scoring, automated written corrective feedback, and plagiarism detection as relevant comparators/context for ChatGPT in education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that ChatGPT can rapidly generate prose and draft a roughly 500-word essay, but the output lacked breadth, depth, and reliable citations; it also sometimes produced bogus references. In a Chinese composition task, the output was grammatically poor and logically weak, suggesting uneven writing quality across language contexts.
finding.measure: Quality of AI-generated written output on essay and composition prompts; presence/accuracy of citations and coherence

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that ChatGPT is less competent for higher-order thinking tasks requiring critical and analytical reasoning, even though it performs better on conceptual explanation. This is framed as a concern for assessment because students may over-rely on it for tasks that should demonstrate independent reasoning.
finding.measure: Author evaluation of performance on critical/analytical essay prompting and higher-order reasoning tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT can reduce workload and save time by generating answers, explanations, drafts, and feedback-like outputs within seconds to about 60-120 seconds. It is presented as potentially useful for teacher-facing tasks such as drafting materials, supporting feedback, and automating parts of assessment and administration, though no formal productivity study is reported.
finding.measure: Observed response speed and qualitative discussion of teacher workload/productivity implications

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that ChatGPT threatens traditional assessment practices, especially essays, because it can generate plausible student work that plagiarism detectors may miss. At the same time, the authors frame it as an institutional opportunity to redesign assessment, teaching policies, and AI governance, but these are conceptual claims rather than measured effects.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of implications for assessment integrity, institutional policy, and educational practice

paper_profiles.title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews empirical research on how teachers use artificial intelligence (AI) in educational settings, with a particular focus on what data are collected from teachers, what roles teachers play in AI-based research, what benefits AI offers, and what challenges teachers face. The authors searched Web of Science for English-language journal articles published over the previous 20 years and identified 44 studies that met their inclusion criteria. The review was motivated by the observation that AI in education has advanced faster than teachers’ pedagogical integration of it, and that teachers’ perspectives have been underrepresented in prior literature.

Across the reviewed studies, the most common teacher-related data were self-reports and grading data, with additional use of observation, video, interviews, feedback/discourse, log data, eye tracking, and audiovisual/accelerometry. Teachers were found to serve several roles in AI development and use: as models for training AI systems, as sources of data on professional development and student behavior, as validators of automated assessment, and as providers of pedagogical guidance. The review also found that AI can support teachers in planning, implementation, and assessment, especially by improving monitoring, feedback, intervention, and automated scoring.

At the same time, the authors identify important challenges, including limited reliability and technical capacity of AI systems, context dependence, limited infrastructure, and limited teacher knowledge. They conclude that AI currently tends to reduce workload and support instructional decision-making, but that broader teacher involvement, more multimodal data, and more attention to pre-service teacher education are needed to make AI systems more pedagogically useful and robust across settings.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review, but it is not a meta-analysis and does not provide pooled effect estimates. The evidence base summarized is largely qualitative/correlational and heterogeneous across settings and AI methods.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests practical benefits for teacher workflow and classroom monitoring, but it reports no pooled impact sizes and highlights important implementation failures and reliability limits. Overall impact appears promising but unclear rather than clearly moderate or large.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic review does not estimate a single effect size, but it synthesizes 44 empirical studies on teachers' AI use and finds consistent operational benefits alongside clear constraints. The main benefits were planning support, timely monitoring, immediate feedback, reduced teacher workload, and automated assessment/scoring; however, the review also highlights reliability, technical capacity, infrastructure, and usability problems that limit real-world efficiency gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative synthesis of reported teacher workload, monitoring, feedback, planning, and assessment functions across 44 studies

finding.finding_summary: The review covers AI-supported instruction and assessment across multiple subjects, with the strongest emphasis on supporting teaching practice rather than direct student achievement. It reports that AI can help teachers adapt content, monitor learning, and automate scoring, but also notes that many systems are context-dependent and sometimes fail to assess complex or multimodal student work accurately.
finding.measure: Reported instructional/assessment uses across subject domains (e.g., English readability, ICT literacy, mathematics, science/STEM)

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, AI was sometimes used to track engagement, concentration, and teacher/student interaction, suggesting potential benefits for monitoring participation and affective states. At the same time, the review notes that some systems were slow, uninteresting, or insufficiently adaptive, which can reduce teacher enthusiasm and limit sustained use.
finding.measure: Engagement, concentration, interaction, and teacher-reported interest/usability across reviewed studies

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in intelligent tutoring systems toward sustainable education: a systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how artificial intelligence (AI) and information technology are being used in intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) to support sustainable education, and what challenges, outcomes, and future directions emerge from that literature. The authors frame sustainable education as requiring more personalized, student-centered, equitable, and scalable approaches, while also acknowledging barriers such as access, teacher workload, privacy, bias, and explainability.

The paper is a systematic review rather than an intervention study. Using a PRISMA-based search and screening process, the authors reviewed 29 papers on AI/ITS applications in educational contexts (plus additional papers on broader sustainable education challenges). The reviewed studies included contexts such as K-12, high school, and especially university settings, across multiple regions including Asia, Europe, the Americas, and Oceania. The AI approaches discussed included supervised and unsupervised machine learning, natural language processing, emotion recognition, and explainable AI.

The main conclusion is that AI-enabled ITSs can improve performance prediction, identify learning behaviors, support early intervention, and enable personalization or adaptation, while also reducing some teacher workload. However, the literature still shows major gaps: limited explainability, fairness concerns, data and feature limitations, portability issues, and insufficient educational theory grounding. The authors argue that future work should emphasize human-centered, trustworthy, and explainable AI, along with better data, broader validation, and stronger alignment with educational practice.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review with PRISMA-style methods, but it synthesizes heterogeneous observational and design papers rather than running a new controlled evaluation. The evidence base is useful for mapping challenges and trends, yet the review itself does not provide high-credibility causal estimates.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful but mostly qualitative benefits for teacher support, engagement, and equity, without reporting pooled effect sizes or strong causal evidence. Its impact is therefore plausible and relevant, but the magnitude is unclear and cannot be classified as modest-to-large from the reported data.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of AI-enabled tutoring systems that use student log data, behavioral signals, and machine learning to predict performance, detect dropout risk, monitor engagement, and support instructor intervention in educational settings.

Review of AI-embedded intelligent tutoring systems for personalized/adaptive instruction, intervention recommendation, learning behavior analysis, and explainable decision support in sustainable education.
Review includes chatbot/NLP-based tutoring examples that answer student inquiries and provide feedback/interactions, but these are peripheral rather than the core focus.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, AI/ITS applications were associated with improved engagement, participation, and dropout prevention, especially through early-warning models and timely instructor notification. The review summarizes 5 studies reporting improved participation via early dropout notification and 2 studies reporting enhanced engagement; however, the paper does not report pooled effect sizes or standardized impacts.
finding.measure: Engagement, participation rate, dropout risk/early warning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI/ITS systems reduce teacher workload by automating performance prediction, monitoring, feedback, and some intervention triggers, allowing instructors to focus more on teaching and individualized support. It also notes that AI can offload routine grading/feedback/remediation tasks, but no quantitative workload effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, monitoring/feedback efficiency, instructor support

finding.finding_summary: The reviewed literature suggests AI-supported systems can help identify learning behaviors and support self-regulation and personalized learning, but the evidence is largely descriptive and based on individual studies summarized in the review. The paper notes 2 studies on self-regulated learning improvement and several studies on behavior analysis, yet it does not provide pooled estimates or consistent causal evidence.
finding.measure: Learning behaviors, self-regulated learning, personalization-related processes

finding.finding_summary: The review positions AI-enabled tutoring as supporting broader access, equity, and sustainable education goals by improving personalization and making remote learning more feasible. At the same time, it emphasizes institutional constraints such as infrastructure, privacy, bias, and interpretability, and argues that explainable and human-centered design is needed for trustworthy adoption.
finding.measure: Access/equity, policy and implementation considerations, trustworthiness, fairness

paper_profiles.title: The cognitive paradox of AI in education: between enhancement and erosion
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This opinion paper examines a central question in AI in education: whether AI tools enhance learning by reducing unnecessary effort or erode learning by encouraging cognitive dependency, overreliance, and shallow processing. The authors frame the discussion through Cognitive Load Theory, Bloom’s Taxonomy, Self-Determination Theory, and cognitive offloading, arguing that AI can simultaneously improve efficiency and undermine memory, critical thinking, motivation, and higher-order thinking if used uncritically.

The paper does not report a new empirical intervention. Instead, it synthesizes prior studies on AI-assisted learning, including work on ChatGPT, adaptive learning, pretesting, retention, critical thinking, creativity, and motivation. The cited evidence spans undergraduate students in the United States, vocational education students in Nigeria, and high school students in Turkey, alongside broader conceptual discussion of AI tutoring and language learning.

The main conclusion is that AI should complement rather than replace human instruction. The authors argue that AI systems must be designed and implemented to encourage active engagement, reflection, source verification, and teacher-guided discussion, while avoiding excessive dependence. They also emphasize fairness, transparency, and explainability to reduce bias and inequity in educational AI systems. The paper is especially relevant to concerns about failure modes such as overreliance and loss of critical thinking, but it does not present direct evidence about Khanmigo-like science tutoring in K-12 classrooms.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed opinion/theoretical article rather than an empirical study, and it reports no original methods, sample, or causal design. The paper synthesizes prior work but does not provide primary evidence meeting RCT/QED criteria.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear relevance to K-12 AI tutoring risks such as overreliance, hallucination-like passive acceptance, and equity, but it provides no original effect sizes or direct outcome data. Its impact is therefore conceptually important yet empirically unclear.

interventions.use_case: Uses generative AI tools such as ChatGPT-like conversational tutors as examples of AI integrated into learning, especially for personalized support, question answering, and study assistance in education.
Discusses adaptive AI learning systems that personalize pacing and content to learners’ needs as a broader category of AI-driven education tools.
References intelligent tutoring systems as classical AI tutoring tools that individualize instruction and provide guided support to learners.

finding.finding_summary: This is an opinion/theoretical paper, so it does not report new primary effects, but it synthesizes evidence that AI can both support and erode durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, and creativity. Across cited studies, AI-supported students sometimes improved on fluency/flexibility tasks, yet overreliance was associated with cognitive fixation, lower creative confidence, reduced conceptual understanding, and weaker critical scrutiny.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, divergent thinking/creativity, conceptual understanding, retention

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI may enhance motivation and competence through personalized support, but excessive dependence can undermine autonomy and relatedness. It cites prior studies and examples suggesting that AI overuse may reduce engagement and intrinsic motivation, while well-designed AI can support self-directed learning.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, autonomy, relatedness

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights equity and governance concerns, arguing that biased AI models may perpetuate educational inequalities unless transparency, explainability, multilingual data, and fairness-aware design are used. This is a conceptual argument rather than a tested institutional intervention, with no new effect estimates reported.
finding.measure: Algorithmic bias, fairness, inclusiveness, educational inequality

paper_profiles.title: Learning design to support student-AI collaboration: perspectives of leading teachers for AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the question of how K-12 learning should be designed when AI is introduced as a collaborative partner rather than only as a tool. The authors argue that existing AIED work has emphasized learning with AI or learning about AI, but less attention has been given to the quality of student-AI collaboration and the surrounding learning environment needed to support it.

The study is based on semi-structured, in-depth interviews with 10 Korean leading teachers in AI in education, drawn from primary and secondary schools participating in software leading schools, AI pilot schools, and AI convergence high schools. Using a thematic analysis informed by a student-AI collaboration framework, the authors examine views on curriculum, student-AI interaction, environment, and how collaboration evolves over time.

Teachers emphasized that SAC should build students' capacity, subject knowledge, and cross-disciplinary problem solving through authentic and creative tasks. They also argued for process-oriented assessment, explicit instruction in AI principles, data literacy, error analysis, AI ethics, and AI experiences in daily life, plus AI systems that provide scaffolding, intuitive interfaces, and varied digital tools. At the system level, the paper concludes that effective student-AI collaboration requires flexible classrooms, strong digital infrastructure, teacher professional learning, systematic policy support, collaborative school culture, and a safe-to-fail environment that treats errors as part of learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative interview study with 10 teachers using thematic analysis. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically coherent for eliciting practitioner perspectives, but it does not provide experimental or quasi-experimental evidence on intervention effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no measured student outcomes or effect sizes, so there is no demonstrated impact to score. Its value is in design guidance and identifying likely implementation needs, but actual educational impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: teacher perspectives on student-AI collaboration for K-12 learning design, including AI as a collaborative learning partner, scaffolding agent, and learning mate

finding.finding_summary: In interviews with 10 Korean leading teachers in AIED, participants emphasized that successful student-AI collaboration requires coordinated systemic supports: a nationwide AIED policy, cross-sector governance, flexible school structures, teacher professional development, and collaborative school culture. This is a qualitative perception study with no effect size reported; findings point to strong perceived institutional importance rather than measured impact.
finding.measure: teacher interview themes on policy, governance, school structure, and professional capacity building

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified capacity building, subject-matter knowledge building, interdisciplinary learning, authentic problem solving, creative tasks, and collaboration performance as core goals of student-AI collaboration. The paper reports qualitative consensus across 10 teachers rather than quantitative outcomes; no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: teacher interview themes on higher-order thinking, collaboration, creativity, and problem solving goals

finding.finding_summary: Teachers argued that student-AI collaboration should support motivation, persistence, confidence, and a 'safe to fail' mindset, and that AI should be designed to encourage students when they struggle. These are qualitative perceptions from 10 teachers; no quantitative effect size or confidence interval was reported.
finding.measure: teacher interview themes on motivation, persistence, engagement, and affective support

finding.finding_summary: Teachers viewed AI systems as potentially reducing repetitive work by automating parts of data collection, personalized support, and workflow integration with existing school platforms. However, the paper does not measure workload reduction empirically; it reports anticipated efficiency benefits and cautions that poor integration could add work for teachers.
finding.measure: teacher perceptions of workload, automation, and platform integration

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review and position-style overview of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular focus on chatbots and ChatGPT. It asks what AI technologies can do for teaching and learning, what challenges they introduce, and how they might be integrated responsibly into educational practice. Rather than reporting a primary intervention study, the article synthesizes prior literature on AI-enabled tools such as intelligent tutoring systems, automated grading, adaptive learning platforms, and conversational agents.

The paper emphasizes potential benefits for students and teachers, including personalized learning, immediate feedback, improved engagement, adaptive support, and reduced administrative workload. It also discusses ethical and practical concerns such as bias, privacy, academic integrity, transparency, dependency/overreliance, and the need for teacher preparation. The discussion is broad and not limited to a specific grade band or subject area, though it notes K-12-relevant examples and cites work on special education and inclusive AI education.

Overall, the authors conclude that AI and ChatGPT-like tools may contribute to more individualized and efficient education if used responsibly, but that successful adoption requires attention to ethics, equity, reliability, and human oversight. They argue that educators, researchers, and policymakers should work together to guide responsible implementation and to ensure AI supports rather than replaces meaningful teaching and learning relationships.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review/opinion-style article with no primary empirical design, no comparison groups, and no original quantitative analysis. It is useful for scoping issues and hypotheses, but it does not meet the criteria for rigorous causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits and risks for education systems, teachers, and students, but it reports no measured effect sizes or direct outcomes. The impact is therefore plausible but unclear rather than demonstrated.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual review of ChatGPT and related chatbots as educational assistants for answering student questions, providing personalized feedback, supporting tutoring, and assisting teachers with administrative tasks in education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI chatbots such as ChatGPT can reduce teachers’ and administrators’ repetitive workload by automating grading, scoring, answering routine questions, and providing feedback. No original effect estimate is reported because this is a narrative review, but the article specifically frames workload reduction as a major anticipated benefit in education.
finding.measure: Teacher/administrator workload and time savings from automated grading, feedback, and Q&A support

finding.finding_summary: The review claims chatbots and AI-enabled learning environments can increase student motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduce anxiety by offering personalized, comfortable, and low-stigma support. These claims are synthesized from prior literature rather than newly estimated in this paper, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student motivation, engagement, confidence, and anxiety

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights broad institutional opportunities for AI in education, but also emphasizes risks around privacy, bias, equity, academic integrity, and the need for teacher training and policy guidance. It does not provide original quantitative evidence; instead it synthesizes ethical and governance challenges and argues that successful adoption depends on responsible implementation.
finding.measure: Ethical, privacy, equity, and governance considerations in educational AI adoption

paper_profiles.title: Crowdsourcing a Word–Emotion Association Lexicon
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of building a large, high-quality lexicon of word–emotion and word–polarity associations, which was seen as a bottleneck for emotion analysis in natural language processing. The authors argue that existing emotion lexicons were small, costly to create, and limited in coverage, so they propose a crowdsourcing-based annotation approach using Amazon Mechanical Turk.

The intervention studied is not an educational intervention, but a crowdsourced annotation workflow. The authors designed mechanisms to improve annotation quality, including a preliminary word-choice question to guide annotators to the intended word sense and to filter out people unfamiliar with the term, plus careful question phrasing and automatic post-processing to remove low-quality assignments. They compared asking whether a word is "associated with" an emotion versus whether it "evokes" an emotion, and found the associated phrasing produced better inter-annotator agreement.

The study used English word and phrase targets drawn from the Macquarie Thesaurus, General Inquirer, and WordNet Affect Lexicon. Annotators on Mechanical Turk, who were required to be native or fluent English speakers, provided emotion ratings for eight basic emotions from Plutchik’s model. After filtering, the authors produced EmoLex, a lexicon of 8,883 terms with validated emotion associations. The main conclusion is that crowdsourcing can efficiently generate a large emotion lexicon with acceptable agreement when quality-control mechanisms are built into the task design.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a crowdsourced lexicon-creation and annotation methodology study, not an educational intervention study. It does not evaluate an AI tutoring, learning, or school-based system in K-12 settings.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured impact on learner outcomes, teacher workload, or K-12 institutional outcomes. The paper’s contributions are methodological for sentiment/emotion lexicon construction, with only a brief mention of tutoring as a potential downstream application.

paper_profiles.title: AI literacy in K‑12: a systematic literature review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is currently being integrated into K-12 education worldwide. The authors conduct a systematic literature review using Scopus and screen 750 records down to 179 papers that fit their inclusion criteria, focusing on school-level AI education rather than AI used only as a tutoring or computer-based learning support tool.

The review organizes the literature into two broad categories: learning experiences and theoretical perspectives. Learning experiences include efforts to help students recognize AI in artifacts, understand how AI works, use AI-related tools, and think critically about AI’s role in society. Theoretical perspectives include curriculum design, AI as a school subject, student perspectives, teacher training, support resources, and gender diversity. The paper argues that much of the field is still exploratory, with few studies assessing student learning outcomes rigorously.

The paper concludes that AI literacy in K-12 should be competency-based, interdisciplinary, and integrated into existing subjects rather than treated only as a standalone course. It emphasizes co-design with teachers, the need for clearer curricular frameworks, and more attention to ethical, social, and equity issues. The review also notes that undesirable consequences of poorly planned AI adoption have received little attention in the literature, and that teacher preparation remains a major gap.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review, so it has a clear methodology and synthesizes published K-12 AI literacy studies, but it does not present original causal evidence or effect estimates. Its conclusions are qualitative and descriptive rather than experimental.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has broad relevance for K-12 AI literacy design and highlights teacher co-design, curriculum gaps, and the lack of learning-outcome assessment, but it reports no measurable intervention impact. Its value is primarily as a field-mapping and agenda-setting review rather than evidence of direct student or teacher effects.

paper_profiles.title: Adaptive Hypermedia
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a broad state-of-the-art review of adaptive hypermedia research as it stood around the year 2000. It addresses the problem that traditional hypermedia systems present the same content and links to all users, which is inadequate for diverse audiences with different goals, knowledge, interests, abilities, and contexts of use. The paper’s purpose is not to report a single empirical study, but to organize the field, summarize major systems and techniques, and identify future research directions.

The paper reviews adaptive hypermedia across several application areas, especially educational hypermedia, online information systems, information retrieval, and personalized information spaces. It describes how systems model user goals, knowledge, interests, preferences, individual traits, and environment factors such as location and platform. It also classifies adaptation techniques into content adaptation and navigation support, including link hiding, sorting, annotation, direct guidance, and adaptive link generation. The review discusses developments such as Web-based adaptive courseware, adaptive encyclopedias, virtual museum guides, e-commerce personalization, and performance support systems.

The paper does not study a K-12 population or a specific intervention in schools. Instead, it argues that adaptive hypermedia had matured by 2000 and was expanding toward new application areas, new AI methods, mobile devices, and component-based architectures. Its main conclusion is that adaptive hypermedia is moving beyond static one-size-fits-all systems toward more context-sensitive, user-modeled, and dynamically generated support, with especially promising future directions in natural language generation, non-symbolic AI, open-corpus systems, and reusable development frameworks.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative state-of-the-art review and forecast paper, not an empirical study with a clearly identifiable evaluation design. It does not report original outcomes, effect sizes, or a systematic evidence synthesis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not demonstrate measured impact on learner outcomes, teacher workload, or equity; it mainly surveys the field and proposes future directions. No actionable effect size or intervention result is reported.

interventions.use_case: Review of adaptive hypermedia systems that personalize educational content, navigation, and presentation based on learner models (e.g., knowledge, goals, preferences, learning style) in Web-based education.

paper_profiles.title: Flipped classroom improves student learning in health professions education: a meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether the flipped classroom approach improves student learning compared with traditional classroom instruction in health professions education. The authors note that flipped classrooms had become increasingly popular, but evidence on learning outcomes had not yet been synthesized in a meta-analysis focused specifically on objective achievement measures.

The intervention studied was a flipped classroom model in which students reviewed pre-recorded instructional videos before face-to-face class meetings, and in-class time was used for active learning activities such as quizzes, discussion, and problem solving. The review excluded studies that relied only on reading materials, online-only courses without face-to-face meetings, or designs without a comparable traditional classroom condition. The included studies covered medical students, pharmacy students, nursing students, public health students, dental students, chiropractic students, and other health professions learners across multiple countries, with most studies using historical control designs and a smaller number using quasi-experimental or randomized designs.

Across 28 comparative studies involving 4,715 students, the meta-analysis found a significant overall benefit for flipped classrooms over traditional instruction on student learning outcomes. The effect was modest but reliable, and results did not meaningfully differ by research design, student type, or whether pre-class readings or exercises were provided. The strongest moderator finding was that flipped classrooms were more effective when instructors began in-class sessions with quizzes on the pre-class materials. The authors also found that most surveyed students preferred the flipped format, though they noted limitations such as inconsistent reporting of instructional details and a lack of long-term retention data.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis with a clearly described search strategy, inclusion criteria, effect-size synthesis, moderator analyses, and publication-bias checks. Although the primary studies vary in design quality and are mostly historical controls, the review itself is a high-level evidence synthesis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled learning effect is medium in size (SMD=0.33), exceeding the threshold for blue impact. The findings are positive and fairly robust across subgroups, indicating a meaningful effect on student learning in the studied population.

interventions.use_case: flipped classroom instruction using pre-recorded video lectures before face-to-face sessions, with in-class active learning and quizzes in health professions education

finding.finding_summary: Across 28 comparative studies (n=2295 flipped; n=2420 traditional), the flipped classroom produced a statistically significant improvement in student learning performance versus traditional instruction. The pooled standardized mean difference was SMD=0.33 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.46, p<0.001), based on objective post-tests/exams in health professions education.
finding.measure: Objective student learning performance on post-tests, exams, and similar objective assessments

finding.finding_summary: Learner perception and preference favored the flipped classroom: in five survey-based studies, 228 of 320 respondents (71%) preferred flipped over traditional classrooms. The meta-analysis also reports that more respondents preferred flipped classes, suggesting higher satisfaction/engagement even though this was not the primary outcome.
finding.measure: Student preference/satisfaction survey responses

paper_profiles.title: A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a tertiary review that maps the scope, methods, quality, and findings of secondary research on artificial intelligence in higher education. The authors ask what kinds of evidence syntheses are being conducted, where they are published, who is conducting them, what tools and methods are used, how well they are reported, and what AI applications and findings dominate the literature.

The study does not evaluate a single AI intervention in classrooms; instead, it synthesises 66 reviews published between 2018 and July 2023 that focused solely on AI applications in formal higher or continuing education. The corpus includes systematic reviews, scoping reviews, meta-analyses, mapping reviews, bibliometric analyses, and other review types. The authors coded publication characteristics, geography, collaboration patterns, software/tool use, quality indicators, and thematic focus using Zawacki-Richter et al.'s AI-in-education typology.

Findings show that most reviews were systematic reviews, published in education and computing-related journals, and often conducted collaboratively within the same country. Many reviews did not report use of dedicated review software, inter-rater reliability, or a formal quality appraisal. In terms of AI applications, reviews most often addressed adaptive systems and personalisation, followed by profiling and prediction, while intelligent tutoring systems were less commonly the primary focus. The authors conclude that AIHEd secondary research needs stronger ethical, methodological, and contextual rigour, plus more interdisciplinary collaboration and better reporting.

Because this paper is a review-of-reviews, it does not have a participant sample, intervention duration, or implementation setting in the usual empirical sense; its contribution is a descriptive and critical synthesis of the field.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed tertiary review with a defined search strategy, inclusion criteria, and structured quality appraisal, but it synthesizes mostly secondary literature rather than primary causal evidence. Its methodology is clear and systematic, yet it does not provide experimental estimates of intervention effects in K-12 settings.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear relevance for AI-in-education policy and research synthesis, but it does not estimate student-level impacts or demonstrate direct effects on K-12 outcomes. Its practical influence is mainly indirect, through identifying gaps, quality issues, and institutional use cases.

interventions.use_case: Tertiary review / review-of-reviews of AI in higher education, mapping AI applications such as chatbots, adaptive systems, recommender systems, and ITS across secondary studies rather than evaluating a single deployed tutoring product.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not test student learning directly; it synthesizes 66 AI-in-higher-education reviews and highlights systemic research and governance issues. The review finds widespread gaps in ethics, methodology, and contextual reporting, alongside uneven coverage of institutional uses such as admissions, scheduling, retention, and quality assurance.
finding.measure: Quality of evidence syntheses; thematic coverage of AI applications; reporting of ethics/methods/context gaps

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, AI applications were often discussed as improving efficiency in reviewable institutional processes such as admissions, scheduling, retention support, quality assurance, and automated assistance. However, this is a synthesis of reported claims rather than a direct estimate of workload reduction, so no pooled effect size is available.
finding.measure: Reported administrative efficiency, institutional process support, and workload-related claims within included reviews

paper_profiles.title: Evidence-Decision-Feedback: Theory-Driven Adaptive Scaffolding for LLM Agents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a core problem in LLM-based educational agents: how to make tutoring and scaffolding adaptive, pedagogically grounded, interpretable, and less likely to encourage overreliance. The authors argue that many LLM agents are still one-size-fits-all and may not support durable learning if they provide answers without attending to learner evidence or learning theory. To address this, they propose Evidence-Decision-Feedback (EDF), a theory-driven framework that structures agent behavior into three linked stages: extracting evidence from student actions and dialogue, making pedagogical decisions based on that evidence, and generating feedback aligned to the decision and to learning theory.

The paper instantiates EDF in Copa, a collaborative peer LLM agent for STEM+ problem solving in the C2STEM environment. Copa uses a multi-agent architecture to process student log data and chat turns, infer student state, select dialogue policies such as probing understanding or suggesting actions, and then generate feedback. The framework is designed to support adaptive scaffolding in open-ended, inquiry-based tasks while remaining traceable to student inputs and theoretical principles such as Evidence-Centered Design, Stealth Assessment, Social Cognitive Theory, and Social Constructivism.

The empirical evaluation took place in a high school science classroom in Nashville, USA, with 33 sophomore dyads working on kinematics tasks over six weeks. The authors analyzed environment logs, conversation turns, screen recordings, and exit survey responses, and also solicited feedback from participating educators. Results suggest that Copa’s scaffolding became more directive as mastery increased, students’ verbalized understanding aligned with their task mastery, and students relied less on the agent as they became more proficient. Interpretability analyses showed that Copa’s decisions and feedback were meaningfully grounded in student evidence. The authors conclude that EDF can support personalized, interpretable scaffolding without fostering overreliance, while noting that students sometimes preferred immediate answers and found the agent less useful than intended when it withheld them.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed classroom study, but the core analyses are correlational/observational rather than randomized, and the paper explicitly notes the absence of an RCT. Credibility is moderate because the evaluation uses real classroom data and multiple triangulated measures, but causal inference remains limited.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported associations are positive and sometimes moderate in size (e.g., ρ=0.42, ρ=0.40), but they come from a small single-site dyad sample and measure within-system behaviors rather than direct learning gains on standardized outcomes. Impact on the broader K-12 population is therefore promising but still unclear.

interventions.use_case: A multi-agent LLM pedagogical agent (Copa) providing adaptive scaffolding, probing questions, suggestions, and challenge-pushing feedback during open-ended high school STEM+C problem solving in C2STEM.

finding.finding_summary: In an authentic high school science classroom study with n=33 dyads, Copa’s support became more pedagogically advanced as task mastery increased: PROBE_UNDERSTANDING decreased (Spearman’s ρ=-0.34, p=0.034) while SUGGEST_ACTION (ρ=0.33, p=0.039) and PUSH_LIMIT (ρ=0.42, p=0.007) increased. The authors interpret this as scaffold fading and ZPD-aligned adaptation, indicating support for students’ metacognitive/problem-solving development rather than fixed-response tutoring.
finding.measure: Dialogue policy shift across mastery quintiles; Spearman correlation between policy frequency and task mastery

finding.finding_summary: Students’ verbalized understanding aligned with task mastery: response success rate after a probe increased with mastery deciles (Spearman’s ρ=0.40). This suggests students were better able to explain their code as they improved, consistent with active knowledge construction rather than merely gaming task completion.
finding.measure: Success rate of correctly explaining code after PROBE_UNDERSTANDING prompts

finding.finding_summary: Student reliance on Copa declined as mastery increased: requests for agent support were highest early, with about 59% of support occurring when mastery was low (<40%), and then decreased significantly with mastery (Spearman’s ρ=-0.26). The authors interpret this as growing autonomy, self-regulation, and self-efficacy rather than overreliance on the agent.
finding.measure: Percentage of agent support/interactions across mastery deciles

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the EDF framework produced interpretable feedback traces with non-random structure across three links: Grounding keyword recall was 0.43 vs 0.21 random, Alignment SBERT similarity was 0.64 vs 0.39, and Faithfulness similarity was 0.48 vs 0.24, all p<0.001. While not a direct teacher-workload measure, this indicates the system can expose decision rationales and learner evidence in a way that may reduce burden for stakeholder review and debugging.
finding.measure: Interpretability of internal reasoning chain (Grounding, Alignment, Faithfulness)
finding.effect_size: Grounding 0.43 vs 0.21; Alignment 0.64 vs 0.39; Faithfulness 0.48 vs 0.24

paper_profiles.title: Learning Assistant Supported Student Outcomes (LASSO) study initial findings
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports initial findings from the LASSO study, which examines how characteristics of Learning Assistant (LA)-supported STEM courses are associated with student learning outcomes. The central question is whether student, course, and instructor features predict gains on concept inventories in LA-supported classes, and whether patterns differ by gender, race, interaction time with LAs, and instructor experience using LAs.

The study analyzed pre/post concept inventory data from over 4,500 students and 17 instructors across 13 LA Alliance member institutions. Faculty completed questionnaires about course structure and LA use, while students reported demographics and time spent interacting with LAs. Outcomes were measured using concept inventories in physics, biology, and chemistry, with hierarchical linear models used to account for nesting of students within courses. The analysis also compared outcomes across disciplines and among student subgroups.

The main findings were that higher student interaction time with LAs was associated with larger learning gains up to a point, and that more instructor experience teaching a course with LAs was associated with better student outcomes. At the same time, the paper reports gender and racial differences in learning gains, suggesting inequities remain in LA-supported classrooms. Because the work is correlational and based on the first semester of a multi-year dataset, the authors emphasize that causal claims cannot be made and that further research is needed to isolate which LA practices are most effective.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed correlational multi-institution observational study using hierarchical linear models, but it is not experimental and cannot establish causality. The paper provides useful subgroup and contextual evidence, but credibility is limited by self-selection, missing demographics for a large subset, and reliance on pre/post concept inventories.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The study reports medium-sized learning gains overall (grand mean d=0.845) and a notable positive association between student-LA interaction and outcomes, which suggests meaningful impact in science courses. Because the evidence is correlational and not directly about K-12 Khanmigo-like tutoring, the impact is promising but not definitive.

finding.finding_summary: In this correlational multi-institution study of LA-supported science courses, students showed average pre-post gains on concept inventories, with a grand mean effect size of d=0.845 across 3,315 usable paired responses. However, gains varied substantially by discipline/instrument (e.g., FMCE d=1.230, BEMA d=1.130, CCI d=0.052), and the paper does not attribute these gains to a specific technology intervention beyond the LA-supported instructional context.
finding.measure: Pre/post science concept inventory scores (FMCE, BEMA, CINS, GCA, IMCA, CCI, GCIICS)
finding.effect_size: d=0.845 (grand mean); instrument-level d ranged 0.052 to 1.248

finding.finding_summary: Student interaction time with LAs was positively associated with larger learning gains up to 16–30 minutes/week, where that group had average effect sizes of 0.873 versus 0.369 for students reporting 0 minutes/week. The paper interprets the 30+ minute group as possibly reflecting selection effects among struggling students, so the pattern is positive but not uniformly increasing.
finding.measure: Self-reported weekly interaction time with Learning Assistants and associated pre/post concept inventory effect sizes
finding.study_size: n=3315 overall; interaction-time model used subgroup counts ranging from n=184 to n=318
finding.effect_size: d=0.873 for 16–30 min/week vs d=0.369 for 0 min/week; continuous slope not reported as standardized effect size

finding.finding_summary: The study found that more time spent interacting with LAs and more faculty experience teaching with LAs were associated with higher student learning gains, suggesting improved collaboration and sustained instructional support over time. For faculty experience, each additional term teaching the course with LAs was associated with a 0.154 increase in student effect size (p<0.05) across n=17 courses.
finding.measure: Student concept inventory gain effect sizes modeled against student-LA interaction time, student/LA ratio, faculty co-planning time, and faculty experience with LAs
finding.study_size: n=17 courses for course-level models; n=3315 for student-level analyses
finding.effect_size: 0.154 per additional term teaching the course with LAs; -0.005 per additional student/LA ratio; +0.004 per additional faculty minute/week meeting with LAs

finding.finding_summary: Across 13 institutions and 17 LA-supported courses, the study found inequitable outcomes by gender and race: male students had substantially higher average effect sizes than female students (0.749 vs 0.485), while white students outperformed Asian and 'other' students, with black students somewhat higher than white students. The authors frame these as correlational inequities in LA-supported classrooms and note that the findings motivate further work on equity and institutional practice.
finding.measure: Pre/post concept inventory effect sizes disaggregated by gender and race across LA-supported courses
finding.study_size: n=3315 usable pre-post pairs; n=17 courses; 13 institutions
finding.effect_size: Gender: 0.749 male vs 0.485 female; Race: 0.619 white vs 0.557 Asian, 0.669 black, 0.509 other
