paper_profiles.title: Do intelligent tutoring systems benefit K-12 students? A meta-analysis and evaluation of heterogeneity of treatment effects in the U.S.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) benefit K-12 students in the United States, and under what conditions their effects are strongest. The authors frame the work as both an effectiveness review and a heterogeneity analysis, focusing on internal validity and external validity across study characteristics.

The intervention studied is ITS software that provides personalized instructional support such as hints, feedback, worked-out examples, reading materials, and motivation support. Rather than evaluating one product, the paper synthesizes evidence across 11 different ITS used in school-based studies. The review includes 18 experimental studies and 77 effect sizes from U.S. elementary, middle, and high school contexts.

The main finding is that ITS have a small but statistically significant positive effect on student learning outcomes overall. Effects were similar across elementary and middle school grades, and across several student subgroups, including low achievers and general populations. The meta-analysis also found that treatment effects varied most by treatment-related features: worked-out examples, intervention duration, intervention condition, and immediate measurement were among the most important moderators. The authors conclude that ITS can be effective in K-12 education, but outcomes depend on how the systems are designed and implemented, with stronger evidence for some support types and shorter-to-moderate intervention durations.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-analysis of 18 experimental studies with multilevel meta-regression, heterogeneity analysis, and publication-bias checks, which meets the strongest evidence tier for the framework. The review also applies WWC standards and reports internal/external validity considerations.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The pooled effect is above the medium-impact threshold (g=0.271), indicating a meaningful positive effect on K-12 learning outcomes. Effects are observed across elementary and middle school populations and several ITS design variants, supporting practical relevance.

interventions.use_case: Meta-analysis of classical K-12 intelligent tutoring systems that deliver adaptive, turn-by-turn tutoring with hints, feedback/explanations, worked-out examples, and personalized practice across math and reading/writing domains.

finding.finding_summary: Across 18 experimental studies (77 effect sizes) of U.S. K-12 ITS, the overall effect on learning outcomes was positive and statistically significant (g=0.271, SE=0.011, p=0.001). The paper’s primary outcome is student academic achievement, with moderator analyses showing effects across settings, grades, and support types.
finding.measure: Student learning outcomes / academic achievement (standardized mean differences across outcome tests)

paper_profiles.title: Tareas matemáticas abiertas como respuesta didáctica a la inteligencia artificial generativa en contextos post-IA
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge that generative artificial intelligence poses for school mathematics, especially the risk that students can bypass interpretation, decision-making, and validation when tasks are easily solvable by AI. The author argues that in post-AI contexts, the central didactic issue is not the technology itself, but the kind of mathematical activity that classroom tasks elicit and how that activity is regulated.

To respond to this problem, the paper analyzes a classroom experience in secondary education where open mathematical tasks were implemented together with a didactic regulation device called COMPAS. COMPAS structures task work into phases such as understanding the situation, organizing assumptions and data, modeling, exploring results, validating, and socializing conclusions. The study uses a qualitative, descriptive-interpretive approach and examines student written work, classroom interactions, and teacher-observer notes.

The paper focuses on a secondary school classroom in Peru and on students working on open-ended mathematics tasks designed so that no direct computational shortcut would be possible. The tasks intentionally lacked explicit numerical data and closed instructions, forcing students to interpret the situation, make assumptions, build models, and justify their choices, while using AI only as a subordinate support tool when appropriate.

The main conclusion is that, when task design and classroom regulation are explicit, students can retain epistemic control over mathematical activity even in the presence of generative AI. The study suggests that open tasks, combined with structured didactic mediation, preserve student agency, support meaningful modeling and validation, and prevent AI from replacing the formative core of mathematics learning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative descriptive-interpretive classroom study with no control group, randomization, or quantitative effect estimation. It provides useful practice-based evidence but only meets limited credibility criteria for causal inference.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a modest positive instructional impact on mathematical participation and agency, but there are no measurable effect sizes or comparative outcomes. The impact is therefore promising but unclear in magnitude for general K-12 use.

interventions.use_case: Generative AI is used as an available support tool during secondary-school mathematics task solving, mainly to explore or contrast results rather than to deliver tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: In a qualitative secondary-school classroom experience, open mathematical tasks mediated by the COMPAS regulation device appeared to sustain students' mathematical activity and preserve epistemic control even with generative AI available. The study does not report quantitative effect sizes; it reports that students remained engaged in interpretation, modeling, and validation of solutions under explicit didactic regulation (n not reported).
finding.measure: Classroom observations, student written work, and interaction records focused on mathematical modeling, validation, and epistemic control

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that open tasks supported students' mathematical agency, decision-making, justification, and critical validation of AI-generated outputs. These are described qualitatively rather than measured with a statistic, and no sample size or effect size is reported (n not reported).
finding.measure: Observed agency, justification, negotiation of assumptions, and critical evaluation of AI outputs during classroom task resolution

paper_profiles.title: MDK12-Bench: A Multi-Discipline Benchmark for Evaluating Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents MDK12-Bench, a large multimodal benchmark designed to evaluate reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on real-world K-12 examination content. The authors argue that existing multimodal reasoning benchmarks are too narrow in scope, too small, and too weakly structured to assess high-order reasoning across school subjects and grade levels.

The benchmark spans six K-12 disciplines: mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, geography, and information science. It includes 141,320 questions, both text-only and multimodal, drawn from exams covering grades 1 through 12 and exam years from 2016 to 2025. The dataset is annotated with difficulty levels, detailed answer explanations, and fine-grained knowledge-point labels organized in a six-level knowledge tree. The paper also introduces a dynamic evaluation framework that bootstraps text and images through paraphrasing, word substitution, question-type permutation, spatial and visual transformations, and style transfer to reduce contamination from training data overlap.

The work is not a study of human learners or classroom implementation; rather, it is a benchmark and evaluation framework for model assessment. Experiments on several state-of-the-art MLLMs show that performance varies substantially by subject and difficulty, and that models are generally more vulnerable under dynamically perturbed test items. The main conclusion is that MDK12-Bench provides a more systematic and contamination-resistant platform for measuring multimodal reasoning in K-12 academic domains, while also exposing current models’ weaknesses in robust contextual reasoning.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark/assessment paper rather than a causal education intervention study. It is peer-reviewed-style technical work with a clear methodology, but it does not use an experimental or quasi-experimental design to estimate educational impacts on students.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper has clear relevance for evaluating AI systems used in K-12 science and math, but it reports model benchmark accuracies rather than student learning gains. Any educational impact is indirect and currently unclear.

interventions.use_case: A multi-discipline K-12 benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models' reasoning on exam-style questions, including dynamic bootstrapped evaluation to test robustness against text and image perturbations.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates multimodal reasoning performance on 141,320 K-12 exam questions across science-related disciplines (physics, chemistry, biology) and finds substantial variability by model, subject, and difficulty. For example, Gemini2-thinking achieved 59.4% overall on MDK12-mini, while open-source models such as InternVL2.5-8B scored 37.7%, indicating strong but uneven scientific reasoning performance rather than a clear intervention effect.
finding.measure: Accuracy on K-12 multimodal reasoning questions across physics, chemistry, and biology; also breakdown by knowledge points and difficulty levels

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark is explicitly designed to test higher-order multimodal reasoning, and dynamic evaluation shows model robustness is highly sensitive to textual and visual perturbations. Under bootstrapped questions, accuracy dropped substantially for several models (e.g., Gemini2-thinking from 58.1% to 41.6%, Δ=-16.5), suggesting limited generalization and context robustness rather than stable reasoning skill.
finding.measure: Accuracy under original versus dynamically bootstrapped questions; robustness to paraphrase, synonym substitution, and image transformations
finding.study_size: n=695 easy + 818 medium + 1,124 hard multimodal instances for dynamic evaluation; 141,320 total benchmark items

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics is one of the six benchmark disciplines, and models showed large variation by difficulty and knowledge point. Gemini2-thinking reached 60.9% on math in MDK12-mini, while InternVL2.5-8B scored 33.2%, indicating that current MLLMs can solve some K-12 math reasoning problems but remain inconsistent overall.
finding.measure: Accuracy on K-12 mathematics exam questions, including open-ended and multimodal items

paper_profiles.title: Evaluation Report on Large Language Models Solving High School Mathematics Questions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report evaluates how large language models (LLMs) perform on high school mathematics exam questions and considers their potential use in education. The paper is framed around a performance evaluation problem: whether LLMs can solve representative secondary-school mathematics items accurately, quickly, and with sound reasoning, and whether they can generate multiple valid solution paths.

The approach uses mathematics questions from college entrance examinations spanning 2019–2023 as the evaluation set. The authors test at least eight LLM APIs/models, including domestic and international systems such as GLM-4-Flash, ERNIE-Speed-128K, Spark Lite, Hunyuan-lite, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, gemma-2-9b-it, Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Yi-34B. They assess single-solution and multi-solution outputs using measures of accuracy, response time, logical reasoning, guidance responsiveness, richness, and solution complexity. The paper also varies prompts to examine whether role-based guidance (e.g., mathematician, student, teacher) changes performance.

The context is high school science/mathematics education in China, using exam-style problems from national college entrance examinations as the benchmark tasks. The population is therefore high school learners, although no student participants are directly involved because the study is a model-benchmark evaluation rather than a classroom intervention. The results suggest meaningful variation across models: some models are faster, some more accurate, and others stronger in logical reasoning or creative multi-solution generation.

Overall, the report concludes that LLMs already show promise for educational use, especially in automated problem solving and guided assistance, but they still need improvement in logical reasoning and creative problem solving. The authors argue that prompt design, model training, and algorithmic optimization could improve educational usefulness, and they suggest future work on other science subjects such as biology and physics.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a grey-literature style evaluation report rather than a peer-reviewed experimental study, and it does not report a clearly controlled design, random assignment, or inferential statistics. The methods are primarily benchmark-style comparisons of model outputs on exam questions.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful performance differences among LLMs for math problem solving, but the evidence is descriptive and the absolute performance levels are mixed and often modest. It implies possible educational utility, yet the impact on K-12 learning outcomes is indirect and unproven.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking general-purpose large language models on high school mathematics exam questions, including single-answer and multi-solution prompting to assess their tutoring/problem-solving potential in education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports heterogeneous math-performance results across eight LLMs on high school mathematics exam questions (2019-2023). Accuracy was modest overall, with the best single-solution comprehensive-question accuracies reaching 0.95 for ERNIE-Speed-128K and 0.85 for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, while multiple-choice accuracy ranged from 0.10 to 0.20 and fill-in-the-blank accuracy from 0.10 to 0.25. In the multi-solution setting, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct achieved the highest correctness rate (0.64), followed closely by ERNIE-Speed-128K (0.63).
finding.measure: Accuracy on multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, comprehensive questions; multi-solution correctness rate on high school mathematics exam problems

finding.finding_summary: The report explicitly evaluated logical reasoning and creativity as core performance dimensions of the LLMs. Logic scores were low-to-moderate overall (e.g., 0.28-0.42 in the weighted table), with Hunyuan-lite scoring highest on logic (0.42) and Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct lowest among the listed models (0.28), while creativity-related complexity scores ranged from 33 to 68, favoring GLM-4-Flash and gemma-2-9b-it. These results suggest that some models can produce multiple solutions and structured reasoning, but reasoning quality remains inconsistent.
finding.measure: Logical reasoning score, guidance attempts/success, and creativity metrics (complexity, richness) in multi-solution math problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds substantial differences in response time across models and problem formats. In single-solution tasks, the fastest models were typically Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and gemma-2-9b-it on easier items (e.g., 0.32-0.57 s for some formats), while Yi-34B and especially GLM-4-Flash were much slower on some tasks (e.g., 10.31 s and 16.01 s on question-and-answer tasks; 18.56 s on hard items for GLM-4-Flash). In multi-solution tasks, Spark-lite was fastest (688 s total) and GLM-4-Flash slowest (7400 s), indicating a clear efficiency tradeoff across models.
finding.measure: Response time for single-solution and multi-solution math question answering

paper_profiles.title: CMATH: Can Your Language Model Pass Chinese Elementary School Math Test?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces CMATH, a benchmark dataset of 1.7k Chinese elementary school math word problems drawn from real workbooks and exams. The motivating question is how the mathematical abilities of popular large language models correspond to elementary grade levels, and whether those models can handle arithmetic and reasoning tasks in a human-like, grade-specific way.

The study does not test an educational intervention; instead, it evaluates several general-purpose LLMs, including GPT-4, ChatGPT, and multiple open-source Chinese models, on the CMATH problems in a zero-shot setting. The dataset is annotated with grade level, answer, number of reasoning steps, and number of digits, allowing the authors to examine performance by grade and by problem complexity. They also create a small distractor dataset by adding irrelevant information to some problems to probe robustness.

The population context is Chinese elementary school math content, spanning grades 1 through 6. The main findings are that GPT-4 is the only model achieving at least 60% accuracy across all grades and the only one that remains robust under distractors. ChatGPT performs reasonably on lower grades but degrades on higher grades and is more easily misled by irrelevant information. The authors conclude that most current general-purpose LLMs still struggle with elementary math reasoning, especially as complexity increases.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed-style benchmark study with a clear methodology and systematic evaluation, but it is not an experimental K-12 intervention study and does not use causal identification or human learners. Evidence is therefore descriptive/correlational rather than rigorous causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear performance differences among LLMs on a math benchmark, but it does not test instructional impact on students or report educational effect sizes. Its educational relevance is substantial for model evaluation, yet the direct K-12 impact is unclear.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking general-purpose large language models on Chinese elementary-school math word problems, including zero-shot problem solving and robustness to distracting information.

finding.finding_summary: Across 1.7k CMATH problems, GPT-4 was the only model that achieved accuracy ≥60% in all six elementary grades; ChatGPT reached that threshold in grades 1-4, while other models generally failed. Accuracy declined with higher grade level, greater reasoning-step complexity, and greater arithmetic complexity; the paper does not report effect sizes, confidence intervals, or standard deviations.
finding.measure: Accuracy on elementary-school math word problems by grade, number of reasoning steps, and number of digits

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats correct solving as a proxy for general reasoning and notes that performance drops as reasoning steps increase, suggesting weaker multi-step problem-solving in most models. GPT-4 remained robust to distractors, whereas other models were easily misled by irrelevant information; no formal effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Accuracy as a function of number of reasoning steps and robustness to distractor-augmented problems
finding.study_size: n=1700 overall; distractor robustness subset n=60

paper_profiles.title: AMO-Bench: Large Language Models Still Struggle in High School Math Competitions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces AMO-Bench, a new benchmark for evaluating advanced mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs). The authors argue that existing high school math competition benchmarks such as AIME and HMMT are increasingly saturated, making them less useful for distinguishing top-tier models, and that some may also be vulnerable to memorization or leakage. AMO-Bench is designed to address these issues by providing 50 entirely original, human-crafted problems that are cross-validated to meet at least IMO-level difficulty standards.

The benchmark is not an educational intervention in the classroom sense, but an evaluation resource for K-12 mathematics competition-style reasoning. The included problems span algebraic equations and inequalities, functions and sequences, geometry, number theory, and combinatorics. Each item requires only a final answer rather than a full proof, allowing automatic grading; the paper also includes human-annotated solution paths and a grading pipeline using parser-based or LLM-based scoring depending on answer type.

Experiments on 26 LLMs show that even the strongest model achieves only 52.4% accuracy on AMO-Bench, with most models below 40%. The authors conclude that current LLMs still struggle with these harder olympiad-level problems, though performance improves with more test-time compute and higher output-token budgets. The paper’s main contribution is therefore a benchmark and evaluation methodology rather than a study of student learning or educational implementation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark construction and model evaluation paper, not a K-12 intervention study. It reports no student-level causal design, comparator, or educational outcome evidence relevant to classroom effectiveness.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not test impact on learners or instruction; it only measures LLM performance on advanced math benchmark items. Any educational impact is indirect and not established as a K-12 effect.

interventions.use_case: A mathematical reasoning benchmark for evaluating large language models on original Olympiad-level and higher math competition problems with final-answer grading

finding.finding_summary: Across 26 LLMs evaluated on AMO-Bench (n=26 models; 50 problems), the best-performing model (GPT-5-Thinking High) reached only 52.4% accuracy, and most models scored below 40%, indicating substantial difficulty on advanced mathematical reasoning tasks. At the same time, performance improved with greater test-time compute: top models showed a near-linear increase in AVG@32 as output length increased, and pass@32 exceeded 70% for top-tier reasoning models, suggesting meaningful headroom for further gains.
finding.measure: Accuracy on AMO-Bench; AVG@32; pass@k under varying test-time compute/output length

paper_profiles.title: Scaling Physical Reasoning with the PHYSICS Dataset
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of high-quality physics data and physics-specific evaluation methods for large language models (LLMs). The authors argue that physics reasoning is important, but existing benchmarks are limited in scale, difficulty coverage, language coverage, and evaluation robustness, especially for issues such as unit conversion and numerical simplification.

To address this, they introduce PHYSICS, a bilingual English-Chinese dataset of 16,568 physics questions derived from over 100 textbooks and exercise books. The dataset spans five domains: Mechanics, Electromagnetism, Thermodynamics, Optics, and Modern Physics, and covers difficulty levels from high school to graduate-level physics. The dataset is split into training and test sets, and the training portion includes reasoning paths generated by strong reasoning models. The paper also proposes a Rule+Model hybrid evaluation framework, combining rule-based verification with a fine-tuned model verifier specialized for physics answers.

The paper evaluates many open-source and proprietary LLMs on the PHYSICS test set and finds that even strong models struggle with physics reasoning relative to their math performance. Reasoning models outperform chat models, open-source models are closing the gap but still lag behind closed-source models overall, and performance varies across physics domains, difficulty levels, and languages. Fine-tuning on the PHYSICS training data improves performance on physics benchmarks and also yields some gains on math and general reasoning benchmarks.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark/dataset construction and model evaluation paper, not a K-12 intervention study or controlled educational trial. It provides useful empirical evidence on physics reasoning benchmarks, but the methodology is primarily benchmark-based rather than experimental with learners.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows clear performance gains for LLMs on physics reasoning tasks, but these are model-benchmark improvements rather than demonstrated learner outcomes. Its educational impact on K-12 is indirect and currently unclear.

interventions.use_case: Construction of a large physics problem dataset for LLM training and evaluation, plus a physics-specific hybrid Rule+Model answer verification framework (rule-based unit/simplification checks followed by a fine-tuned judge model).

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that fine-tuning on the PHYSICS training set improves physics reasoning performance across multiple benchmarks. For example, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct improved from 22.30% to 32.85% on PHYSICS (+10.55 points), and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct improved from 27.65% to 40.20% (+12.55 points). Similar gains were seen on GPQA (Physics), OlympiadBench (Physics), and UGPhysics, indicating stronger scientific/physics reasoning after training.
finding.measure: Accuracy on PHYSICS test set, GPQA (Physics), OlympiadBench (Physics), and UGPhysics

paper_profiles.title: Confucius3-Math: A Lightweight High-Performance Reasoning LLM for Chinese K-12 Mathematics Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents Confucius3-Math, an open-source 14B parameter large language model designed specifically for Chinese K-12 mathematics learning and educator support. The paper addresses the problem that many strong general-purpose reasoning models, while good on competition math, do not perform reliably on K-12 educational tasks and may generate incorrect answers that can harm learning. The authors position the work as an effort to build a practical, low-cost reasoning model that is accurate enough for real educational use.

The approach is a post-training reinforcement learning pipeline applied to a selected open-source base model (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B), with three technical innovations: Targeted Entropy Regularization, Recent Sample Recovery, and Policy-Specific Hardness Weighting. The system is trained on a mixture of open-source math/reasoning datasets and proprietary Chinese K-12 math questions and solutions, with emphasis on step-by-step explanations and answer correctness. The model is evaluated on internal and public math benchmarks relevant to Chinese K-12 learning, including CK12-MATH, GAOKAO-Bench (Math), MathBench K12, and CMATH, plus competition-level benchmarks such as MATH500 and AIME24/25.

The paper reports that Confucius3-Math outperforms several strong baselines, including DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-14B, and QwQ-32B, on nearly all reported benchmarks, with especially strong gains on the internal Chinese K-12 benchmark. The authors also emphasize practical deployment advantages: the model is lightweight enough to run on consumer-grade hardware, and the training cost is reported as only $26K. Overall, the paper concludes that strong domain-specific reasoning models for K-12 mathematics can be built efficiently with reinforcement learning and carefully curated data.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a technical arXiv model report, not a peer-reviewed educational evaluation, and it does not use a classroom RCT, QED, or student-level causal design. The evidence is benchmark-based model evaluation plus engineering measurements, so it does not meet the credibility criteria for stronger K-12 intervention evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports large gains on math benchmarks and strong efficiency improvements, but these are offline model performance results rather than demonstrated student learning effects. Educational impact is therefore promising but still unclear at the learner-outcome level.

interventions.use_case: A lightweight reasoning LLM trained for Chinese K-12 mathematics learning, intended to answer student math questions and provide problem-solving steps as learning support.

finding.finding_summary: Confucius3-Math achieved the strongest reported accuracy on the paper’s K-12 math benchmarks, including CK12-MATH (96.24%), GAOKAO-Bench Math (98.46%), MathBench K12 (95.10%), and CMATH (96.13%). Against its base model, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, gains were +13.38, +11.71, +6.70, and +18.72 points respectively; on AIME25 it improved by +26.98 points (to 69.95%).
finding.measure: Benchmark accuracy / pass@1 on Chinese K-12 and competition math benchmarks (CK12-MATH, GAOKAO-Bench Math, MathBench K12, CMATH, MATH500, AIME24, AIME25)

finding.finding_summary: The model was designed and evaluated as a low-cost deployment system, with reported inference throughput up to 31,994 tokens/s on H800 hardware and 4,956 output tokens/s on a single RTX 4090D in scaled comparisons. The paper reports a 15.8× throughput advantage over DeepSeek-R1 and a training cost of $26K for 13,109 GPU hours, emphasizing deployment efficiency rather than learner outcomes.
finding.measure: Inference throughput (tokens/s), deployment feasibility, and training cost

paper_profiles.title: VisScience: An Extensive Benchmark for Evaluating K12 Educational Multi-modal Scientific Reasoning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a gap in multimodal benchmark coverage for scientific reasoning in education. The authors note that existing evaluation sets for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) focus heavily on mathematics or general visual understanding and often underrepresent physics and chemistry. To address this, they introduce VisScience, a bilingual benchmark designed to evaluate K-12 multimodal scientific reasoning across mathematics, physics, and chemistry.

VisScience contains 3,000 questions drawn from K-12 educational materials, with 1,000 questions each in mathematics, physics, and chemistry. The benchmark includes both text and images, spans 21 subjects, and assigns questions to five difficulty levels from basic to expert. The paper also describes a two-stage collection and annotation pipeline involving large-scale question gathering, manual screening, and LLM-assisted categorization to ensure coverage, clarity, and balanced difficulty.

The paper evaluates 25 representative MLLMs, including closed-source and open-source models, on Chinese and English versions of the benchmark. The main conclusion is that closed-source models generally outperform open-source models, with performance varying by discipline and subject. The authors also provide error analysis showing that reasoning errors are the most common failure mode, especially in physics and chemistry, suggesting that stronger conceptual reasoning and visual interpretation remain key challenges for current models.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark construction and model evaluation paper, not a student-outcome study. It is peer-reviewed in the sense of an academic preprint, but it does not provide intervention evidence, experimental control, or causal estimates relevant to K-12 educational impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention is implemented or evaluated with learners, so there is no demonstrated student impact. The reported accuracies are system benchmarking results, not evidence of effects on achievement, reasoning, or engagement.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not test an instructional intervention; it introduces VisScience, a benchmark for evaluating multimodal scientific reasoning in K-12 contexts. The reported results are descriptive benchmark accuracies for 25 models rather than causal effects. For example, the best closed-source model achieved 53.4% accuracy in mathematics, 38.2% in physics, and 47.0% in chemistry on the benchmark.
finding.measure: Benchmark accuracy on K-12 multimodal science questions (mathematics, physics, chemistry)

paper_profiles.title: LLM Chatbots in High School Programming: Exploring Behaviors and Interventions
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 41st ACM/SIGAPP Symposium on Applied Computing (SAC ’26)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how high school students use an LLM-based chatbot for introductory programming, with particular attention to help-seeking behavior and whether students ask for conceptual help or direct solutions. The authors frame the problem through help-seeking theory, arguing that generative AI can either support learning or encourage unproductive, executive-style reliance if students use it mainly to get answers.

The study was conducted as a Design-Based Research cycle in elective Informatica classes at two Dutch high schools. Students in an Intervention Group used the JELAI environment, which embeds a Socratic LLM tutor directly in Jupyter Notebook, while a contemporaneous Comparison Group used the same tool without guidance. In the intervention phase, the researchers introduced a short instructional treatment: a class discussion contrasting instrumental and executive help-seeking, followed by brief individual reflection sessions based on students’ own query logs.

Quantitatively, the study found that higher overall LLM use and especially executive queries were negatively associated with exam performance in the unguided phase, while instrumental queries were not clearly related to grades. The intervention reduced the proportion of executive questions and shifted students toward more productive interaction patterns, but this behavioral change did not produce a statistically significant improvement in exam scores. The authors conclude that LLMs can support learning only when pedagogy explicitly scaffolds productive help-seeking; access alone is not enough, and underlying knowledge gaps may still limit achievement.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory design-based research study with small non-equivalent groups and correlational/pre-post analyses rather than a randomized controlled trial. It provides useful contextual evidence and process data, but internal validity is limited by selection effects and lack of random assignment.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The intervention produced a medium-to-large behavioral shift in help-seeking (r=0.560), but did not yield a statistically significant improvement in exam grades. Overall impact on achievement is therefore modest/unclear, though the behavioral change is educationally meaningful.

interventions.use_case: An embedded LLM chatbot tutor (Juno) inside a Jupyter Notebook environment for high school programming, used for in-class help-seeking, code explanation, and problem solving with Socratic guardrails rather than direct solutions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that unguided LLM use was negatively associated with programming exam performance at baseline, with total query frequency correlating with midterm scores at ρ=-0.502 (p=0.034) in the Intervention Group (n=18). However, after a targeted help-seeking intervention, students shifted toward more instrumental queries and reduced executive queries (Wilcoxon signed-rank W=15.0, p=0.036, r=0.560), while exam improvement from midterm to final was not statistically significant (W=34.0, p=0.083, r=0.409).
finding.measure: Programming exam scores (midterm and final), plus correlation with LLM query frequency and query-type proportions
finding.study_size: n=18 intervention group; n=19 comparison group
finding.std_deviation: SD midterm=2.00; SD final=1.97; prior programming experience SD=1.02; prior chatbot use SD=1.11

finding.finding_summary: The pedagogical intervention improved help-seeking behavior by significantly reducing executive queries and increasing instrumental, learning-oriented interaction patterns with the LLM. Sequential log analysis showed a shift from reactive 'error → ask for fix → paste code' workflows toward more proactive 'successful action → interaction → successful action' workflows, indicating better metacognitive use of the tool.
finding.measure: Query-type proportions, sequence analysis of interaction logs, and help-seeking behavior patterns
finding.study_size: n=14 paired pre/post for intervention analysis; full IG n=18; CG n=19

finding.finding_summary: In the baseline unguided setting, heavier LLM use was associated with lower performance and appeared to reflect struggling students rather than effective engagement, with the comparison group showing fluctuating use and eventual decline without self-correction. The intervention reduced executive help-seeking, suggesting improved self-regulation, but overall engagement change was not directly tested with a formal engagement scale.
finding.measure: Interaction frequency, engagement over time in logs, and help-seeking behavior patterns
finding.study_size: n=18 intervention group; n=19 comparison group

paper_profiles.title: A Chain-of-Thought Prompting Approach with LLMs for Evaluating Students’ Formative Assessment Responses in Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can automatically score and explain middle school students’ short-answer responses on formative science assessments. The authors focus on a challenge that is especially important in K-12 science: open-ended student responses are hard and time-consuming for teachers to grade, and they often require explanations tied to scientific reasoning rather than simple right/wrong matching.

The study develops a human-in-the-loop prompting approach using GPT-4, combining few-shot examples, chain-of-thought prompting, and a small active-learning loop. The method is applied to assessment responses from an NGSS-aligned middle school Earth Science curriculum (SPICE) on water runoff, where students interpreted and critiqued a diagram of a conceptual model. The assessments targeted both scientific concepts and scientific reasoning, and the prompt included rubric-based examples and explanations to help the model produce both scores and feedback.

Using manually graded data from two SPICE studies at one public middle school in the southeastern United States, the authors compare zero-shot, few-shot, few-shot with chain-of-thought, and chain-of-thought plus active learning settings. Results show that GPT-4 often aligned well with human scorers, sometimes reaching strong or near-perfect agreement, especially when few-shot examples and active learning were added. The paper concludes that LLMs can support science formative assessment scoring and feedback, but also warns that chain-of-thought and active learning can overfit, especially on simpler or ambiguous items, and that rubric and question wording may need refinement for open-ended science tasks.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical study, but it is not an RCT or QED on student learning; it is primarily a model-evaluation study using held-out test data and human scoring agreement. The methodology is clear and systematic, but credibility for causal educational impact is limited because the paper does not test instructional outcomes in a controlled design.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising practical alignment for automated scoring, with several subscores achieving strong agreement with humans, but it does not report student achievement gains or classroom outcome effects. The educational impact is therefore indirect and mainly pertains to assessment efficiency rather than demonstrated learning improvement.

interventions.use_case: LLM-based automated scoring and explanation generation for middle school Earth science formative assessment short-answer responses using few-shot prompting, chain-of-thought reasoning, and active learning
GPT-4 used as a teacher-like evaluator via prompt persona to generate rubric-aligned explanations and feedback for student science responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that GPT-4 with chain-of-thought prompting plus active learning can automate scoring and explanation generation for K-12 science formative assessments, reducing teacher workload associated with grading open-ended responses. On the held-out test set, the best configurations achieved strong agreement with human scoring across most subscores (e.g., QWK up to 1.00 on some subscores; 9 of 11 subscores/total scores reached QWK >= 0.8 at some point), indicating practical usefulness for efficient assessment workflows.
finding.measure: Automated scoring agreement with human raters on formative assessment responses; Macro F1, Cohen's Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK)

finding.finding_summary: The system’s performance on science-reasoning subscores was mixed: in some cases CoT + active learning improved alignment with human scorers, while in others performance declined and overfitting emerged. For example, Q3 Runoff Direction Reasoning improved to QWK=0.94 with CoT + AL, but Q2 Arrow Direction Reasoning fell to QWK=0.30 under CoT + AL, showing that the approach was not uniformly robust for reasoning-heavy responses.
finding.measure: Reasoning subscores on middle school Earth science formative assessment items; Macro F1 and QWK

finding.finding_summary: For science conceptual knowledge items embedded in Earth science formative assessments, GPT-4-based scoring generally aligned well with human ratings, especially after few-shot prompting and active learning. Several subscores reached strong or almost perfect agreement (e.g., Q1 Arrow Size QWK=0.95 with CoT + AL; Q3 Arrow Size QWK=0.83 with CoT + AL), suggesting effective automated scoring of content knowledge in this domain.
finding.measure: Conceptual knowledge subscores on Earth science formative assessment short-answer responses; Macro F1 and QWK

paper_profiles.title: FineMath: A Fine-Grained Mathematical Evaluation Benchmark for Chinese Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for a fine-grained benchmark to evaluate the mathematical reasoning abilities of Chinese large language models (LLMs), especially on elementary-school-level math word problems. The authors argue that prior datasets mainly reported overall accuracy or coarse grade-level results, which makes it difficult to identify which mathematical concepts and reasoning skills models have or have not mastered.

To address this, the paper introduces FineMath, a benchmark of 1,584 Chinese math word problems drawn from textbooks, workbooks, and the internet. The dataset is organized into 17 categories spanning elementary-school math concepts such as number and operations, measurement, data analysis and probability, algebra, geometry, and two special problem types. Each problem is also annotated by reasoning difficulty according to the number of steps required to solve it, and the original problems were transformed into multiple-choice format for easier automatic evaluation.

The benchmark is used to evaluate GPT-4, GPT-3.5-Turbo, and several Chinese LLMs, including ChatGLM2-6B, Qwen-7B-Chat, InternLM-Chat-7B, Baichuan models, and MathGLM variants. Results show that GPT-4 performs best overall, but performance drops as reasoning steps increase. The authors also show that prompt wording, answer format, and contamination from training data can substantially affect measured performance, and they recommend careful filtering and evaluation design when using the benchmark.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a benchmark/evaluation study with systematic experiments across multiple LLMs, but it is not a causal K-12 intervention study and does not use an RCT or QED for student outcomes. The paper is methodologically clear yet primarily assesses model performance rather than educational impact.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports substantial accuracy differences on math reasoning tasks, but these are model-evaluation results rather than learner outcome effects. Any educational impact is indirect and unclear for K-12 settings.

interventions.use_case: Benchmark evaluation of Chinese large language models on elementary-school math word problems, including direct generation and multiple-choice answer selection to probe mathematical reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates mathematical reasoning/accuracy of multiple LLMs on FineMath (n=1,584). GPT-4 achieved 0.73 overall accuracy under direct generation, while GPT-3.5-Turbo reached 0.62; Chinese models ranged from 0.08 (Baichuan-7B) to 0.49 (MathGLM-10B) under Prompt 0. Performance declined as reasoning steps increased, with GPT-4 still above 0.60 even on 3+ step items, but lower-performing models dropping sharply.
finding.measure: Accuracy on fine-grained elementary-school math word problems; performance by concept category and number of reasoning steps

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark analysis shows that evaluation protocol materially changes measured performance. GPT-4's overall accuracy varied from 0.73 with direct generation to 0.59 and 0.58 under alternative prompts, and from 0.73 generation to 0.62 under multiple-choice option prediction; similar prompt/task-form sensitivity appeared across models.
finding.measure: Accuracy under different prompts and evaluation formats (generation vs multiple-choice option prediction)

paper_profiles.title: Benchmarking quantized LLaMa-based models on the Brazilian Secondary School Exam
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates how well quantized open-source large language models based on LLaMA can answer questions from the Brazilian National Secondary School Exam (ENEM). The motivation is twofold: to test the practical usefulness of these models for question answering and to examine whether quantization makes them usable on home hardware without dedicated GPUs.

The authors build a dataset of 1,006 ENEM questions from 2010 to 2022, retaining only text-based items that could be processed by language models. They benchmark several model families and sizes, including LLaMA 1, Alpaca, Koala, Vicuna, and LLaMA 2, each quantized to Q4 and run locally on modest machines. Performance is measured by multiple-choice accuracy on Portuguese originals and English translations, and by inference time on two CPUs.

The results show that the strongest models reached about 46% accuracy on Portuguese questions and 49% on English translations, with LLaMA 2 13B performing best overall. Larger models generally performed better than smaller ones but took longer to run, though the authors conclude that the execution times were still manageable on consumer hardware. The paper frames the dataset and benchmark as a resource for future NLP and LLM research, including possible model training and broader exam evaluation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed benchmarking study with a clear experimental protocol and defined dataset, but it is not an educational intervention study and lacks a causal design for student outcomes. It primarily reports model accuracy and runtime rather than learning effects.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows some utility for local, efficient exam-question answering, but the educational impact is unclear because no learners were involved and the observed accuracies are modest. Its main contribution is technical benchmarking rather than demonstrated K-12 learning gains.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking quantized open-source LLaMA-family language models (LLaMA 1/2, Alpaca, Koala, Vicuna) on multiple-choice ENEM exam question answering on home hardware

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates exam-question answering performance on the Brazilian ENEM, a high-stakes secondary-school admissions exam, using 1,006 text-only questions. Best models reached about 46% accuracy on Portuguese items and 49% on English translations overall, with the strongest model (LLaMA 2 13b) reaching 0.615 accuracy in Humanities (Portuguese) and 0.636 in Humanities (English), but much lower results in Mathematics and Sciences.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on ENEM questions across subject areas and languages

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper does not directly measure student skills, it benchmarks reasoning-oriented question answering on exam items that require comprehension and inference. Performance varied substantially by subject and model, suggesting uneven support for reasoning-heavy tasks; no direct human learning gain was measured.
finding.measure: Accuracy on reasoning-heavy exam questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly measured inference time on modest home hardware and found quantized 7B models averaged about 17.5-21.7 seconds per question and 13B models about 34.3-64.2 seconds, depending on model and machine. This indicates the quantized LLaMA-family models can run locally without dedicated GPUs, with 7B models consistently faster than 13B models.
finding.measure: Mean inference time per question (seconds) on AMD Ryzen 5 3600x and Intel i9 9900k

paper_profiles.title: SMRC: Aligning Large Language Models with Student Reasoning for Mathematical Error Correction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a student-centered mathematical error-correction problem: how to adapt large language models (LLMs) so they do not merely produce a correct answer, but also preserve a student's original reasoning path when giving feedback. The authors argue that existing self-correction approaches are optimized for model-centric reasoning repair and are not well aligned with educational use cases, where teacher-like correction should support cognitive continuity and retain correct intermediate steps.

To solve this, they propose SMRC (Student Mathematical Reasoning Correction), a framework that combines a reward model with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS). The reward model is trained using process-level supervision inferred from outcome labels via breadth-first search and reward backpropagation, and its scores guide MCTS to explore correction paths that balance correctness with retention of valid student steps. The paper also introduces MSEB (Multi-Solution Error Benchmark), a benchmark built from 158 authentic high-school student mathematics solution records, covering algebra, geometry, matrices, and trigonometry.

The empirical evaluation compares SMRC against direct correction, thought-preserving correction, self-refinement, and self-check baselines on ProcessBench, MR-GSM8K, and MSEB. Results show that SMRC generally achieves the best balance between answer accuracy and correct-step retention, with especially strong performance on MR-GSM8K and MSEB. The paper concludes that structured search plus process-supervised reward modeling can improve educationally aligned mathematical feedback, though the authors note that their reward allocation is still relatively uniform and could be refined in future work.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed technical/engineering paper with a benchmark and comparative experiments, but it is not a causal K-12 evaluation and does not use a randomized or quasi-experimental design with learner outcomes. Evidence is therefore useful but indirect for educational effectiveness claims.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains on mathematical correction metrics are meaningful, especially on MSEB (HM 51.8), but they are algorithmic benchmark improvements rather than demonstrated student learning gains. Impact on K-12 education is therefore promising but still unclear.

interventions.use_case: teacher-style mathematical error correction with large language models that preserve a student's original reasoning path while generating minimally corrected solutions via Monte Carlo Tree Search and process reward modeling
automated step-level feedback and correction on high school mathematics solutions, including preservation of correct steps, error localization, and corrective reasoning generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that SMRC improves mathematical error correction performance on three benchmarks, including the K-12-relevant MSEB dataset. On MSEB, SMRC achieved ACC=40.1, CSRR=73.7, and HM=51.8, outperforming comparison methods such as Self-Check (ACC=27.2, CSRR=91.2, HM=41.9) and Self-Refine (ACC=35.2, CSRR=76.6, HM=48.1) on harmonic mean, indicating better balance of answer correctness and preservation of correct reasoning steps.
finding.measure: Reasoning accuracy (ACC), correct step retention rate (CSRR), harmonic mean (HM) on mathematical error-correction tasks
finding.study_size: n=158 for MSEB; additional evaluations on ProcessBench and MR-GSM8K not K-12

finding.finding_summary: A central contribution is preserving student reasoning processes, which is operationalized as CSRR rather than a direct learning gain measure. SMRC improves CSRR on MSEB to 73.7 while maintaining substantially higher accuracy than competing methods, suggesting stronger alignment with students' problem-solving strategies and more educationally coherent feedback.
finding.measure: Correct Step Retention Rate (CSRR), evaluated by comparing corrected solutions to students' originally correct reasoning steps

finding.finding_summary: The method is presented as a structured search-and-feedback framework that reduces reliance on manual process annotation by generating reward signals from BFS and back-propagation. The paper does not report time-on-task for teachers or students, but it does show that the fine-tuned 14B reward model and MCTS framework outperform prompt-only reward models, implying improved automated correction efficiency.
finding.measure: Performance of reward-model construction and search-based correction pipeline; benchmark correction metrics (ACC/CSRR/HM) as proxies for automation quality

paper_profiles.title: AI in the Classroom: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Intelligent Tutoring Systems for Multilingual Learners in Secondary Education
paper_profiles.venue: ASRC Procedia: Global Perspectives in Science and Scholarship
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) can support multilingual learners in secondary education, with particular attention to which system components and design features are associated with better learning outcomes. The review focuses on the challenge that multilingual students must learn academic content while also developing proficiency in the language of instruction, and it frames ITS as a possible tool for delivering personalized, language-sensitive support.

The paper synthesizes 110 peer-reviewed studies on ITS design, implementation, and effectiveness. It examines core components such as learner modeling, domain knowledge, pedagogical strategy engines, and user interface design, along with features including Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, Performance Factor Analysis, natural language processing, speech recognition, automated writing feedback, multimodal instruction, affect detection, and culturally responsive content. The population is multilingual learners in secondary education, with examples and discussion oriented toward classroom use in linguistically diverse secondary settings.

The review concludes that ITS can improve comprehension, retention, confidence, and engagement when they provide adaptive personalization, multimodal support, and linguistically sensitive feedback. It also argues that culturally relevant content, inclusive interface design, teacher training, infrastructure readiness, and ethical data governance are important for successful implementation. The paper notes that generative AI may expand personalization and interaction, but it also raises concerns about bias, privacy, and cultural preservation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review, but it does not present a new controlled study or meta-analytic synthesis with pooled estimates in the text provided. The evidence is therefore informative but primarily narrative and secondary, making it closer to a qualitative/correlational review than high-credibility causal evidence.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for multilingual secondary learners, especially for literacy, science comprehension, and engagement, but it does not quantify effects. Because the reported impact is promising yet unmeasured and heterogeneous across studies, the overall impact tier is modest/unclear rather than strong.

interventions.use_case: systematic review of ITS for multilingual learners in secondary education, emphasizing learner modeling, adaptive feedback, multimodal delivery, and culturally responsive scaffolding

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that ITS with linguistically sensitive feedback, multimodal support, and bilingual scaffolding were associated with improved reading comprehension, vocabulary acquisition, and confidence in academic writing for multilingual secondary learners. It cites a European pilot of FeedBook and other studies as showing measurable gains, but no pooled effect size or exact n is reported in the paper text.
finding.measure: reading comprehension, vocabulary acquisition, academic writing confidence
finding.study_size: 110 peer-reviewed studies reviewed; specific primary-study sample sizes not reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that in mathematics and science, multilingual students performed better when ITS provided bilingual glossaries, visual scaffolding, and step-by-step explanations. This is presented as convergent evidence from the reviewed literature rather than a single controlled estimate, so no effect size or exact sample size is available in the text.
finding.measure: subject-matter assessment performance in mathematics and science
finding.study_size: 110 peer-reviewed studies reviewed; specific primary-study sample sizes not reported

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly reports positive effects on learner confidence and engagement when ITS used adaptive personalization, supportive feedback, and multimodal interaction. These outcomes are described as improved through reduced frustration and more inclusive interaction design, but the article does not provide pooled effect sizes or confidence intervals.
finding.measure: learner confidence, engagement, frustration/persistence indicators
finding.study_size: 110 peer-reviewed studies reviewed; specific primary-study sample sizes not reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that ITS supported comprehension, retention, and learner self-reflection through techniques such as Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, performance factor analysis, spaced repetition, and metacognitive prompts. This is a narrative synthesis of the reviewed literature, so the text does not report a pooled effect size, confidence interval, or standard deviation.
finding.measure: retention, metacognitive reflection, self-monitoring of learning
finding.study_size: 110 peer-reviewed studies reviewed; specific primary-study sample sizes not reported

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that implementation success depends on teacher training, infrastructure readiness, ethical data governance, and careful bias/ privacy protections. These are framed as enabling conditions and risks rather than measured outcomes, so there is no quantitative effect size; the overall message is that institutional impact can be positive if implementation supports are in place, but harmful if bias and privacy issues are ignored.
finding.measure: implementation readiness, teacher training, infrastructure, ethical governance

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence-based personalised learning in education: a systematic literature review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) for personalised learning in education and asks what role it plays, what techniques have been proposed, what applications have been identified, and what impact these systems have had on teaching, learning, and assessment. The review is motivated by the rapid expansion of AI, including machine learning, recommendation systems, intelligent tutoring systems, and generative AI, and by the need to synthesise evidence across the education sector.

The authors conducted a systematic literature review of English-language, peer-reviewed journal and conference papers published from January 2015 to June 2025. Using multiple databases, they screened 371 records and included 125 studies. The reviewed work spans K–12, higher education, and institutionally supported online learning, with the paper explicitly discussing AI-based personalised learning across these settings rather than focusing on one specific intervention trial or one learner group.

The review organises the literature into major application areas such as content recommendation, tutoring and support, and feedback and assessment. It also summarises algorithmic approaches, including machine learning, non-machine-learning, and hybrid methods, and highlights the growing influence of generative AI such as ChatGPT. The main conclusion is that AI-based personalised learning has substantial potential to improve adaptability, feedback, engagement, and support for learners, while also creating opportunities and challenges related to data availability, evaluation, and implementation.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review with explicit search, screening, and thematic synthesis methods, but it is not a primary causal study and does not provide a meta-analytic effect estimate. The evidence quality is therefore moderate at best for inference about impact, with substantial heterogeneity and limited quantitative synthesis.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests potentially meaningful benefits, especially for engagement, SRL, and teacher efficiency, but it does not report pooled effect sizes or consistent causal estimates. Overall impact is promising yet unclear because the evidence base is broad, descriptive, and mixed across interventions and contexts.

interventions.use_case: Systematic literature review of AI-based personalised learning approaches across K-12, higher education, and online learning, including intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning, recommendation systems, automated feedback, and generative AI tools such as ChatGPT.

finding.finding_summary: This review synthesised 125 studies published from January 2015 to June 2025 and did not report a single pooled effect size. Across the literature, AI-based personalised learning was associated with improved learning outcomes, better curriculum sequencing, and more accurate assessment in some studies, but the evidence was heterogeneous and largely descriptive rather than experimentally quantified.
finding.measure: Reported learning outcomes, curriculum recommendation quality, and assessment/performance improvement across included studies

finding.finding_summary: The review identified multiple studies suggesting that AI-based personalised learning can increase engagement, motivation, and self-regulated learning. Examples included personalised chatbots for active learning/SRAL, clustering analyses of hint use and persistence, and AI-supported feedback intended to boost learner involvement, but the review does not report pooled effects or standardised estimates.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, persistence, and self-regulated learning as reported in included studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly highlights potential benefits for critical thinking, problem solving, metacognition, and time management through adaptive tutoring, feedback, and reinforcement-learning-based SRL support. However, these are synthesized claims from diverse studies rather than a single controlled estimate, so the strength of evidence is conceptual and qualitative overall.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem solving, metacognition, and time-management-related outcomes discussed in included studies

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that AI-based personalised learning may reduce teacher workload by automating marking, feedback, recommendation, and student modeling tasks. These efficiency gains are presented as recurring findings across the literature, but the review provides no pooled effect sizes or direct causal estimates.
finding.measure: Teacher workload reduction, automated feedback delivery, and system efficiency as described in included studies

paper_profiles.title: Agentic artificial intelligence-driven tutoring: a multi-agent cognitive architecture for personalized adaptive learning in Education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Applied Resilience and Sustainability
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the emerging literature on agentic AI-driven tutoring systems, focusing on multi-agent cognitive architectures for personalized adaptive learning. The central problem is that one-size-fits-all instruction does not adequately address diverse learner needs, especially in settings where learners differ in pace, cognition, motivation, and affect. The authors position multi-agent AI as a more flexible alternative to traditional intelligent tutoring systems because specialized agents can handle content delivery, assessment, feedback, motivation, learner modeling, and coordination in a more modular way.

The paper is a systematic review using PRISMA methodology rather than an empirical intervention study. It synthesizes research on agentic AI, intelligent tutoring systems, cognitive architectures, adaptive learning, affective computing, metacognitive scaffolding, collaborative learning, learning analytics, and related algorithms such as Bayesian knowledge tracing, reinforcement learning, natural language processing, and graph neural networks. The review also discusses development platforms and architectural patterns such as hierarchical systems, blackboard systems, and cognitive tutoring frameworks.

The paper emphasizes applications across mathematics, science, programming, and language learning, with particular mention of K-12 science and mathematics education. It concludes that multi-agent AI systems can improve behavior modeling, individualized learning processes, real-time feedback, metacognitive support, engagement, and achievement, but also identifies major concerns including privacy, transparency, scalability, fairness, and the need for stronger evaluation methods. The paper is primarily conceptual and maps current opportunities, challenges, and future research directions for educational AI.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative/systematic review with PRISMA framing, but it does not present primary controlled evaluation, meta-analytic synthesis, or extractable study-level causal evidence. The paper is largely conceptual and descriptive, with figures and tables summarizing claims rather than reporting a rigorously appraised empirical dataset.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests broad potential for AI tutoring across engagement, metacognition, and science/math learning, but most claims are non-causal and lack direct effect sizes. Reported quantitative values are limited to correlational/illustrative figures, so real-world impact remains unclear and modestly supported.

interventions.use_case: Agentic AI-driven multi-agent tutoring architecture for personalized adaptive learning, including pedagogical agents, learner modeling, feedback generation, metacognitive scaffolding, and domain expert coordination.
Personalized adaptive learning system that dynamically adjusts content difficulty, pacing, scaffolding, and instructional strategy based on learner performance, behavior, and affect.
Learning analytics and predictive modeling to forecast learner outcomes such as dropout risk, course completion, and mastery trajectories using performance sequences and engagement data.
Automated formative feedback generation for learner responses, including hints, corrective feedback, worked examples, and natural-language explanations.
Conversational tutoring interfaces and dialogue management using natural language processing and transformer-based language models to support learning interactions.
Stealth assessment and simulation-based learning environments used to embed evaluation in gameplay and science laboratory-style virtual experimentation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that agentic AI tutoring supports mathematics learning through step-by-step instruction, error-specific feedback, worked examples, and adaptive scaffolding in algebra, geometry, and calculus. However, this is a narrative synthesis rather than a direct causal evaluation, so no study-level effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Mathematics problem-solving, conceptual understanding, procedural fluency

finding.finding_summary: The review describes positive support for science inquiry learning via scaffolding of hypothesis generation, experimental design, data analysis, inference, and virtual laboratories. It also states that agentic AI can support guided simulation-based learning for hazardous or costly experiments, but it does not report primary-study effect sizes.
finding.measure: Science inquiry learning, hypothesis scaffolding, experimental design, data analysis, inference

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes applications in writing and language learning, including essay feedback, pronunciation support, vocabulary practice, and grammar/culture tutoring. It frames these as beneficial uses of AI tutoring but provides no controlled-study effect estimates.
finding.measure: Writing quality, essay organization, grammar, vocabulary practice, pronunciation support

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes that agentic AI can increase engagement, motivation, persistence, and emotional support through affective computing, motivational agents, and emotion-aware tutoring strategies. One figure reports a strong positive correlation between engagement time and achievement (r=0.78, p<0.001), with diminishing returns after about 15 hours and an estimated ~3.5-point score increase per additional hour, but this is correlational rather than experimental.
finding.measure: Engagement time, motivation, affective state support, persistence
finding.effect_size: r=0.78 (correlation); ~3.5 points per additional hour (descriptive slope)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that multi-agent tutoring systems can strengthen metacognition, self-regulated learning, and collaborative skills through metacognitive prompts, process visualization, dashboards, self-explanation support, peer matching, and collaboration facilitation. Figure 2 describes mastery gains over 12 weeks from roughly 20-30% to 75-85% across competencies including problem solving, conceptual understanding, procedural skills, metacognition, and transfer ability, but no formal effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-regulated learning, collaboration, transfer ability, problem solving mastery over time

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that modular multi-agent architectures improve scalability, maintenance, feedback generation, and learning analytics automation compared with monolithic tutoring systems. This is presented as a design and systems claim rather than a measured productivity outcome, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: System scalability, maintenance, automation of feedback and analytics

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies major implementation concerns including privacy, transparency, fairness, scalability, and the need for stronger evaluation frameworks. It presents these as unresolved governance and institutional barriers alongside the promise of AI tutoring, but offers no quantitative policy-impact evaluation.
finding.measure: Ethical/governance concerns, privacy, transparency, scalability, evaluation needs

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing graduate students’ evaluative skills through AI-supported collaborative marking
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how AI-supported collaborative marking can improve graduate students’ evaluative judgment when assessing research papers. The authors argue that prior AI-assisted assessment research has focused too heavily on score accuracy and agreement with human raters, while paying less attention to how interaction with AI may shape students’ reasoning, monitoring, and reflection during evaluation.

The study tests a collaborative marking framework in which students evaluate their own research papers with support from an AI agent grounded in an expert-informed knowledge base and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The AI system provides rubric-based feedback on four dimensions: rigor, originality, significance, and conventions. The population consisted of 121 first-year master’s students at Hubei University in China, who produced and self-evaluated approximately 8,000-word research papers as part of an AI in Education course. The study compared four conditions: student-only marking, AI-only marking, AI with RAG, and AI-supported collaborative marking. A smaller subset of students was also used for behavioral coding and lag sequential analysis of interaction logs.

Findings showed that AI-supported collaborative marking reduced deviations from expert ratings and improved consistency relative to student-only and AI-only conditions. The authors also found that students’ interaction patterns reflected differences in metacognitive monitoring and reflective reasoning, with senior students showing more structured and self-regulated evaluative behavior than junior students. Overall, the paper concludes that AI-supported collaborative marking can improve assessment accuracy while also supporting the development of academic assessment literacy and evaluative judgment in graduate education.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-method, single-study comparison with within-subject and benchmark comparisons, not an RCT or meta-analysis. It provides empirical evidence with reasonable structure and reliability reporting, but the design has important limitations for causal inference and general K-12 relevance.
paper_profiles.impact_tier_rationale: The observed improvement in marking accuracy is meaningful for the studied graduate population, but the context is higher education rather than K-12 and the evidence is specific to writing evaluation. The main effect reported is moderate in practical terms, but generalizable impact for the requested K-12 science-focused evidence base is unclear.

interventions.use_case: AI-supported collaborative marking of graduate research papers using rubric-based scoring and feedback, including expert-knowledge retrieval augmentation and discrepancy checking against expert benchmarks
A conversational AI agent (DeepSeek-V3.1-Terminus) that interacts with students during marking, prompts justification and reflection, and supports iterative calibration of scores

finding.finding_summary: AI-supported collaborative marking improved evaluative judgment and metacognitive regulation compared with student-only and AI-only conditions. The paper reports a reduction in mean absolute error from 3.260 to 1.221 versus expert ratings in the collaborative condition, alongside improved inter-rater consistency and more structured planning-monitoring-reflection cycles.
finding.measure: Deviation from expert ratings on rubric-based paper evaluation; inter-rater consistency; behavioral interaction patterns
finding.study_size: n=121 papers; n=121 student evaluators; interaction subset n=12 students / 269 coded events

finding.finding_summary: The intervention targeted assessment of academic writing quality across rigor, originality, significance, and conventions, and collaborative marking produced scores closer to expert benchmarks. Student ratings were especially improved relative to expert judgments on paper conventions and overall scoring accuracy, with MAE decreasing from 3.260 to 1.221 in the collaborative condition.
finding.measure: Rubric-based scores for research paper quality (rigor, originality, significance, conventions) and overall mark

finding.finding_summary: The AI-supported condition was associated with increased reflective engagement and self-regulated evaluation rather than mere score generation. Behavioral coding showed senior students more often engaged in metacognitive monitoring, reflective reasoning, and structured regulation, indicating that the collaborative process supported more adaptive engagement with the task.
finding.measure: Behavioral coding of interaction logs; qualitative/lag sequential analysis of AI-supported marking dialogue

paper_profiles.title: ПОКАЗНИКИ КРОВІ ДІЙНИХ ВІВЦЕМАТОК ПРИ ВИКОРИСТАННІ ПРОБІОТИЧНОГО ЗАСОБУ
paper_profiles.venue: Innovative Scientific Research: Latest Theories, Modern Methods and Practices (Proceedings of the XX International Scientific and Practical Conference)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether adding a probiotic preparation (“Bioferm”) to the diet of lactating ewes improves milk productivity and affects blood indicators associated with health and metabolism. The authors frame the problem as a practical need to raise milk yield in the Askanian Karakul sheep breed while maintaining animal health, and they use blood biochemistry and hematology as supporting indicators of physiological status.

The intervention was an oral probiotic supplement containing multiple microbial strains, including Bacillus subtilis, Lactococcus lactis, Lactobacillus casei, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Bacillus natto, Plantlactobacillus, Bacillus licheniformis, and Candida utilis. The study was conducted on lactating ewes at the Askania-Nova livestock research institute in Kherson region, Ukraine. Twenty-five ewes were screened, then 20 similar animals were assigned to control and experimental groups (10 each). The experimental group received the probiotic for 30 days; the control group received only the basal ration.

The main findings were that the probiotic group showed higher average daily milk yield and slightly better blood values than the control group. Reported effects included increases in red blood cells, hemoglobin, total protein, globulins, gamma-globulins, calcium, and live weight, with the authors interpreting these changes as evidence of improved protein metabolism and resistance. They conclude that 1.5 ml of Bioferm per 10 kg of sheep body mass can be recommended as a feed supplement for lactating Askanian Karakul ewes to improve quantitative and qualitative milk productivity.
paper_profiles.quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a narrative comparative essay about team management practices across countries and companies, not an empirical K-12 intervention study.
